Many schools ban cellphones, but I believe that permitting them in class can be helpful. When used for schoolwork, phones can make students feel more comfortable and motivated to complete assignments.

One benefit is that students can finish their homework or class tasks more efficiently. Today many learners receive a large amount of work, and some also have personal problems that make concentrating at home difficult. For instance, a student might struggle with a stressful family issue, which distracts them from studying. After‑school jobs add another layer of fatigue; I know friends who get home exhausted and barely have the energy to work on projects. Having a phone on hand lets them quickly look up answers, submit digital forms, and even start a task during a free minute in class. This flexibility can turn a pile of unfinished work into something manageable, allowing more time later for other responsibilities.

A second advantage is the ability to keep track of grades and pending assignments. Missing a lesson or forgetting an assignment is a common problem, especially when students juggle several subjects. If they can check the online grade book or view the day’s list of tasks on their device, they no longer need to rely on memory alone. They can also send a message to the teacher for clarification or to request an extension. My friend, who finds mathematics challenging, often uses his phone during class to view his worksheet, ask a question, and receive immediate help. This on‑the‑spot support helps prevent small misunderstandings from turning into major setbacks, ultimately leading to higher scores.

Some critics argue that phones are a source of distraction because students might text, browse social media, or play games. While that can happen if the device is left unsupervised, it does not have to be the case. Teachers can design activities that use the phones for learning, such as quick quizzes, polls, or educational games. These methods engage students in a way that feels familiar and enjoyable, so they stay focused on the subject matter rather than wandering off. Moreover, the claim that constant screen time slows the brain is not supported by recent studies; in fact, technology often reinforces memory when used purposefully.

In summary, allowing cellphones for educational purposes can improve students’ ability to complete work, monitor their progress, and interact with the material in a dynamic fashion. By embracing this tool, schools give learners more control over their study routines, which can boost both confidence and achievement. As part of the new generation, we should take advantage of the digital resources that help us succeed, rather than ignore them.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s idea that people can move beyond what they think they are capable of and thereby find a place in life. In his view, mastering something beyond ordinary limits opens doors that were once closed, and I believe this is exactly what personal growth requires.

First, it is important to pursue the goals we set for ourselves, not the expectations of others. Society often pushes individuals toward a particular career or way of living, but that does not guarantee satisfaction. Choosing a path based on personal desire rather than external pressure allows us to take ownership of our future. If we try to imitate everyone else’s decisions, we risk losing sight of what truly motivates us.

Second, mastering a key skill or milestone can start a chain of positive changes. For example, successfully completing a school program leads to a better job opportunity, where we can develop further and earn more independence. Along the way, building a family can provide emotional support and expand our network, both of which help us reach higher levels of achievement. Yet the core of this process is self‑belief and perseverance; believing that we are good enough to keep trying prevents us from quitting when others doubt us.

Third, when we set ambitious goals, we may face people who tell us we are not talented enough. These voices can be discouraging, but they should not dictate our actions. Staying focused on our own vision helps us stay resilient. Whether the aim is to become a famous singer, a political leader, or a professional athlete, thinking creatively and refusing to give up can turn a dream into reality. Even in fields that are not flashy, like soccer, confidence in one’s abilities can lead to success without the need for excessive show.

Finally, surrounding ourselves with negativity is a risk we should avoid. Instead, we should filter out unwanted advice and concentrate on the opinions of those who truly want us to succeed. When we do this, we leave our own mark, achieve what we intended, and make the people who believed in us proud.

In conclusion, agreeing with Emerson’s statement means trusting our own capacity to learn and improve, staying true to our chosen dreams, and not letting external judgments control our journey. By mastering what matters to us, we gain opportunities, grow as individuals, and ultimately fulfill the potential that lies within.

Another instance happened during a school field trip to a beach. I grew sad about having to leave early, but after changing into swimwear, picking up a camera, and walking along the sand, I let the steady waves and distant birds’ songs wash over me. The moment I entered the sea, the water’s embrace erased my worries and gave me a quiet joy.

Swimming also creates opportunities to bond with others. Whether I’m swimming solo or surrounded by friends, the activity becomes more pleasant when it’s shared. At a recent pool session, my friends joined me and we instantly started laughing while trying various tricks and short races. One time we tried to glide underwater and accidentally bumped heads, surfacing together and bursting into giggles. Even basic skills like floating become easier with a buddy who can guide you or pull you up when you’re struggling. I’ve noticed that learning dog‑paddle on my own feels boring, but doing it together makes the whole thing feel like play.

Lastly, exercising in water is simply more exciting. I signed up for weekly swimming lessons after school, which I didn’t like at first, but by my third session I was hooked. Within a few months my weight dropped from 145 lb to about 111 lb, and I noticed steady improvements in my technique. My early mindset focused only on losing pounds, and I saw little progress. As I grew more enthusiastic about the lessons, I started gaining speed and stamina, and the weight loss followed. The key was that enjoyment turned a chore into a rewarding workout.

In short, the swimming club delivers three main benefits: it helps me unwind when I’m upset, it encourages friendships, and it makes physical activity feel lively. My own experiences prove these points, and I hope sharing them shows why swimming can be a true source of happiness.

I agree with the statement because it can be very difficult to stay true to yourself in today’s world. Society constantly judges people’s choices and tries to dictate how they should act or look. Families often impose strict expectations, telling you what career to pursue, who to befriend, or even what clothing to wear. When a decision goes against their wishes, they criticize you harshly, which makes it hard to follow your own desires. The pressure to meet these external standards can feel overwhelming and leaves little room for personal expression.

Outside the family, the same pattern continues. Strangers may form quick opinions based on appearances—believing someone with tattoos is trouble, assuming a larger woman is unattractive, or dismissing a skinny girl for being too thin. Even harmless fashion choices, such as wearing a short skirt, can be labeled as “crazy.” Such snap judgments suggest that no matter what we do, we rarely satisfy everyone’s expectations. The constant scrutiny creates a sense that we must hide parts of ourselves just to fit in.

Nevertheless, it is essential to remain resilient and proud of who we are. We must work to show the world our true selves, even when it feels risky. Sometimes the stress of not fitting in can lead to negative self-talk, like “I’m never good enough” or “I’m not worthy.” These thoughts can erode confidence and make us doubt our abilities. To counter this, self‑love must become a priority because only we can decide if we are happy with our choices. If we do not value ourselves, others will rarely do it either. Accepting our decisions and embracing our identity is crucial for mental well‑being.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” His words resonate with my own experience. When I stopped seeking approval and began trusting my own instincts, I felt a sense of freedom and joy. I realized that pretending to be someone I am not only drains energy but also prevents me from enjoying life fully. By staying authentic, I have built a happier, more relaxed existence. In short, being true to yourself is challenging, but it is the most rewarding path, and I firmly support Emerson’s view.

When it comes to trying to be someone, is it better to improvise or follow the script all the time?

Everyone needs to have their own individuality and be original instead of trying to be something else because that way you learn more about yourself. Also, you are acknowledging different methods about how to be better than yourself. And one of the most important things, you could make a good influence in someone else's life and teach him/her how to find their path in their own way. No matter what happens, you always have to follow yourself.

When you learn more about yourself it means that you do not just learn things that you already know about yourself, you also learn new things that you did not know about yourself. For example, one day you are going to the basement of your house which is really big and put some good music. While you are listening to your favorite songs from your playlist, you are dancing according to the tempo and doing the dancing moves that you usually do. After dancing for a long while, suddenly you let the music take control over you and you make a back flip without practicing it before. You are very surprised because you did something that you did not know you could do and after that, you keep practicing that move and perfectioning it and it comes out natural. That is how you learn more about yourself.

You are acknowledging different methods to be better than yourself. This means you will do whatever is right in order to become a better person. For example, Robert Downey Jr used to have a terrible life by consuming drugs and other things that got him in trouble with the law. He even went to court for all the messy things he did. After a long time taking bad decisions, he finally decided to make things better for the people who cares about him and specially for him. It took him over 5 years for him to get back on his feet; with his own effort and the support from his family and friends, he started to make a good difference for the world. Right now, Robert is one the best actors in Hollywood, he has an excellent life with his wife and kids on his side, and is a great influence for millions of people. That is how you acknowledge different methods to be better that yourself.

Some people say that you are copying someone else when you try to be yourself. However, they are wrong because you actually are listening to those tips that you have heard and following them under your own perspective. That way you are definitely writing your own script but at the same time, giving the deserved credit to the person who gave you those tips. For instance, when you are trying to get a girl that you met in a party but you have no idea of what to do in order to get her attention. You ask your friend for some advice to accomplish your goal so you do not go through a bad experience. He tells you what to do exactly and shows you with some women at the party and now you have some ideas of what you can do. So before you reach out to that girl, your friend tells you "be yourself all the time" and you get the courage to talk to her. After following those examples in your own way, the girl started to have deep feelings for you and everything worked out a lot well and make some influence to some of your friends who need that kind of help. That is how you follow your own script with your own terms.

In conclusion, it is very important that you have be yourself all the time because it shows that you do not need somebody in order to be somebody. You learn about yourself so you can get to know your own person more than you can know about an anime character. You acknowledge new ways to become better than yourself like if you were in a videogame, you are going to the next level slowly. You make a good influence by doing things as right as possible and you give people some benefits out of it. To be yourself you have to do what your gut tells you to do if you think it is going to give some benefits in some way.

When faced with the question of whether we should improvise or stick to a pre‑written plan in order to become the person we aspire to be, my position is clear: staying authentic and improvising more often leads to a richer, more meaningful life. Trying to fit a mold that someone else has set for us may look easy at first, but it ultimately blocks the chance to learn what we are truly capable of and to impact others in a genuine way.

Being original lets us uncover parts of ourselves that we have not yet discovered. We often think we know all the traits that make up our identity, but when we step out of the comfort zone and act without a strict script, we can stumble upon hidden talents. Imagine walking through a long hallway of your house that you rarely explore, and putting on music that moves you. As the rhythm guides you, you start moving more freely than usual. Suddenly, you surprise yourself with a new motion that never appeared in any rehearsal—perhaps a swift turn or a balanced jump. The initial wonder turns into practice, and over time that movement becomes a natural part of your repertoire. This experience teaches you that you can develop abilities you did not know you possessed simply by allowing yourself to experiment rather than follow a rigid set of instructions.

In the same vein, embracing improvisation also opens the door to adopting methods that help us improve as people. When we accept useful advice, we are not surrendering our agency; we are simply gathering tools that fit our own circumstances. Robert Downey Jr’s comeback is a perfect illustration. After years of poor choices, legal troubles and addiction, he decided to change his course. With steady effort, the support of family and friends, and a willingness to try new ways of living, he transformed his life. Today he enjoys a successful career, a stable family, and serves as a role model for countless fans. By taking pieces of guidance and reshaping them to suit his reality, he reached a higher level of personal growth, just as a video‑game character advances after trying different strategies.

Critics sometimes argue that looking to others for inspiration means copying them, which undermines authenticity. Yet this viewpoint misses the nuance of how we interpret and personalize suggestions. For instance, suppose you want to make a good impression on someone at a party but feel unsure how to approach them. You turn to a close friend who gives practical tips. Instead of blindly mimicking the friend’s exact lines, you consider the underlying principle—being sincere and relaxed. When you follow that principle, you speak in your own voice and act naturally. The conversation flows, the connection deepens, and the friend’s advice is credited for the positive outcome, while you retain the authorship of the interaction. This balance between borrowing ideas and exercising your own judgment illustrates how improvisation can be rooted in helpful external input without losing personal integrity.

In short, constantly improvising, or “following your own script,” is essential because it shows that we do not need someone else’s approval to define who we are. It gives us the space to explore our strengths, to embrace growth strategies that resonate with our values, and to create positive ripple effects in the lives of those around us. By listening to our gut feelings and adapting useful advice to our own context, we stay true to ourselves while still benefiting from the wisdom of others. This approach, more than rigidly sticking to a predetermined plan, equips us to become the best version of ourselves and to inspire others to do the same.

Students ought to be given the chance to explore different occupations because they are eager to gain practical knowledge. Many teenagers imagine themselves in a future job and view work‑related experiences as a way to test whether those ideas fit their interests. Allowing schools to organize internships, job‑shadowing days or career‑talk sessions can help students clarify their goals and discover which paths truly appeal to them. When students have a clearer picture of what they want to study, they are more likely to choose the right college programmes and set realistic career targets. At the same time, giving youngsters access to professionals lets them ask questions about everyday duties and how those skills connect to academic subjects, which often improves their confidence and motivation.

Moreover, such opportunities create a dialogue between students, parents and teachers about what learning means for a future career. When parents see their child taking part in a workplace environment, they understand how lessons at school translate into real‑world tasks and can better support the decision‑making process. Even if a student is unsure about his or her long‑term goals, exposure to several fields can spark curiosity and help narrow down choices. The emotional satisfaction that comes from finding work that feels right also strengthens a student’s commitment to higher education and to staying in the chosen profession after graduation.

From a financial point of view, letting students earn money through part‑time work or summer jobs benefits both the young person and the family. By contributing to household expenses, students reduce the burden on parents and can start saving for college tuition. This early income also teaches budgeting, responsibility and the value of hard work, which are qualities that will serve them well in any future career. Parents can encourage this approach, especially for children who are also active in sports or other extracurricular activities, while still keeping academic requirements in view. The key is to balance school assignments, projects and other duties with the extra work, ensuring that grades are maintained and graduation is still on track.

Finally, schools have a role in guiding this balance. Integrating career‑related activities into the curriculum respects the importance of both academic learning and practical experience. It helps students develop time‑management skills, stay organized and understand the link between classroom content and job performance. By fostering a supportive environment that acknowledges each student’s dreams—whether they aim for a professional career, a college degree, or a particular sport—educational institutions can empower young people to pursue their aspirations responsibly and successfully.

Having a homework club at school is a practical and beneficial idea that every school should adopt. If a school runs the club at least three times a week, students will regularly have access to extra help with assignments and deeper explanations of the material. A homework club is a scheduled period where teachers are present to assist students who are struggling with specific questions, to clarify concepts, or to work together on larger projects. By providing this support, the club enables learners to gain a clearer understanding of the subject matter, to stay more engaged with classmates, and to feel more confident about their schoolwork.

One of the main advantages of the club is that students can collaborate with peers on group tasks. When a project feels too demanding to tackle alone, the club offers a space to finish it together with the guidance of teachers. If a learner has a question about a project’s requirements, he or she can raise it during the session and receive direct feedback. The more pupils attend, the more the atmosphere resembles a supportive community, where everyone shares ideas and helps each other solve problems. This teamwork is especially valuable because complex projects often benefit from multiple perspectives, and the club makes it possible to finish them on time without feeling overwhelmed.

In addition to project work, the club is an excellent venue for test and quiz preparation. Teachers can show how to create flashcards, review study guides, and even use interactive games such as Kahoot to reinforce the material. Students who find it hard to concentrate at home often benefit from a structured, group setting where they can focus on studying. Kahoot, for example, turns a typical review session into a lively competition, making the content more memorable and enjoyable. By attending the club regularly, learners can practice these study techniques in a distraction‑free environment, which usually leads to better performance on upcoming assessments.

Finally, the homework club helps students complete their assignments sooner. Teachers take the time to explain each task step‑by‑step, sometimes going beyond what is covered in regular lessons. This extra detail enables pupils to grasp not only how to answer the questions but also why the concepts matter. As a result, students can turn in their work ahead of the deadline and enjoy the feeling of relief that comes with having fewer tasks waiting at home. Math, science, history, and English teachers can each contribute to this process, sharing expertise that deepens students’ knowledge and prepares them for future classes.

Overall, a homework club creates a friendly, collaborative space where teachers and students work together to improve learning outcomes. It builds confidence, encourages active interaction with classmates, and offers focused support for both projects and examinations. To make it successful, schools need dedicated teachers who volunteer their time, and students should be encouraged to attend at least three sessions per week. With these efforts, homework clubs can become an essential part of school life, benefiting the whole community.

Many public figures—from Hilary Clinton and soccer athletes to government workers—have each encountered setbacks in their lives. No one is flawless; everyone makes mistakes and faces disappointment at some point. As human beings, we inevitably fail, but those failures need not define us.

When we retain our enthusiasm after a failure, the setback becomes a valuable source of growth. Failure supplies practical experience, letting us discover what does not work and adjust our approach accordingly. By examining our mistakes, we acquire knowledge that makes the next attempt smoother. For example, a student who performs poorly on an exam can review the questions that were missed, understand where knowledge gaps exist, and apply those insights the second time, improving the score. This process demonstrates that repeated effort with clearer understanding usually leads to better outcomes.

A third advantage is that failure teaches perseverance. After an initial disappointment many people want to quit, yet surrender halts progress entirely. Instead, a failure can inspire a fresh plan, a different strategy, or a revised timeline. I remember a personal incident when, at thirteen, I needed to pass a demanding entrance test for the high school I desired. My first try fell short because I had not prepared enough. My sister reminded me that walking away would not solve the problem; she urged me to try again. I studied harder, practiced repeatedly, and finally succeeded on my second attempt. This experience proved that renewed effort, guided by what went wrong, often leads to eventual achievement.

Patience also arises from failure. When a goal does not arrive immediately, frustration can set in. Yet learning to wait and to manage the small steps required to rebuild can foster resilience. My parents often said, “Good things will come if you stay patient,” a piece of advice that proved useful when I learned to tolerate setbacks before seeing improvement. Over time, each failure teaches us to cope with obstacles, handle stress, and maintain a steady pace, which eventually paves the way for success.

On the other hand, some individuals lose hope after an initial defeat and abandon their aspirations. Restarting can feel repetitive and demotivating, and working on the same challenge repeatedly may seem boring. Nevertheless, those who persist discover that the effort is worthwhile.

In short, failure functions as a key ingredient in the path to success. Without at least one setback, we rarely develop the insight, resolve, and patience needed to move forward. It is not something to be ashamed of; rather, it should be embraced as a learning opportunity.

Therefore, experiencing failure is a gift. It supplies experience, fuels determination, cultivates patience, and helps us chase our dreams with renewed vigor. The healthiest response is to stay positive, keep trying, and remember that every worthwhile goal has its own timetable.

The claim that “to be yourself in a world that constantly urges you to become something else is the greatest achievement” rings true for me. Embracing one’s genuine self fosters personal independence, strengthens self‑belief, and equips you with the inner power to support others.  

First, authenticity creates independence. When you accept who you are, you learn to act without waiting for external validation. You set your own goals, take responsibility for your actions, and make decisions based on your own values rather than on what others expect. Since relationships can change and people may disappear, relying on yourself guarantees that you have a solid foundation for any challenge. Demonstrating to friends or colleagues that you can reach milestones on your own reinforces both your confidence and theirs. Moreover, independence allows you to shape your own future without being constrained by others’ expectations.  

Second, staying true to yourself builds confidence and motivation. Recognizing your own strengths leads to positive self‑talk such as “I can handle this.” This inner encouragement fuels a growth mindset, which pushes you to aim higher in school, at work, or in personal projects. Confidence translates into better time management, higher grades, punctual attendance, and a willingness to take calculated risks—like starting a new hobby or pursuing a daring goal. When confidence grows, you become more willing to learn from mistakes and accept new challenges. Without self‑confidence, the drive to improve can fade quickly, making success harder to attain.  

The same self‑assurance that helps you succeed can be shared with those around you. A person who knows his own worth is better able to empathize with a friend who feels overwhelmed or a family member who is battling depression. You can offer steady encouragement, remind them that temporary setbacks are part of the journey, and inspire perseverance. I experienced a prolonged period of difficulty that lasted half a year; it tested my resolve but never broke my spirit. By focusing on what I can control and maintaining a hopeful outlook, I was able to support others while still moving forward in my own life. Because you understand your own struggles, you can offer practical advice and a listening ear.  

In sum, Waldo Emerson’s insight remains accurate: being yourself generates independence, solid belief in one’s abilities, and the capacity to uplift both yourself and others. Keeping a positive attitude, staying motivated, and never losing confidence are key ingredients for personal fulfillment and for creating a supportive community. Though the path may be rough at times, genuine self‑expression brings rewards naturally. Ultimately, staying true to yourself is a lifelong journey that continually pays off.

Some people claim that first impressions can never be altered. They argue that the way you behave, the language you use, and the way you look reveal who you really are, and once someone forms an initial view of you, it tends to stay. Most of us agree that these three elements—your conduct, your speech, and your appearance—are the main reasons why people judge you right after meeting.

First of all, the way you act when you meet someone for the first time is crucial. What you do is often more noticeable than what you say, so a friendly, polite attitude can set a positive tone. If you come across as unkind or rude at that early stage, the other person is likely to label you as unpleasant and avoid getting close later. Because the encounter is short, it matters that you do not make any mistakes or show a negative side; you need to keep your behavior smooth and respectful from the start.

When you begin talking to a new person, the words you choose also play a big role. Using offensive language can give the impression that you lack basic social skills, while choosing clear, respectful phrasing helps you build trust over time. You may try to sound impressive by using some more advanced vocabulary, but even simple, straightforward speech can be effective as long as it is delivered politely. Of course, nervousness can cause hesitation or stumbling, but most people will give you a second chance if they see you make an effort to speak clearly. It is also wise to avoid gesturing too much with your hands during the conversation, as too many movements can distract from your message and look unprofessional.

In addition, your look can be the most powerful signal of who you are. Whether you are wearing tidy clothes, keeping your hair neat, or maintaining good posture, these visual cues give others a first hint of your attitude. People usually pay attention to appearance first, even though they also notice behavior and spoken words, but the visual element often leaves the deepest mark. If you appear sloppy or unkempt, the listener may think you are careless or uninterested in making a good connection. A neat and pleasant appearance can help you attract potential friends, though the final decision also depends on the other person’s earlier impression of you.

Because of all these factors, the first impression you give tends to stick in people’s minds. It is difficult to erase the image they have formed, especially if it was negative, but it is not impossible to shift it a little. If you happen to have a rough day and behave unusually, some observers may understand that you are not always like that and give you another opportunity. This shows that while the initial view is strong, there is often room for a fresh look if you act consistently well later on.

To sum up, many believe that first impressions are essentially unchangeable, and the evidence they point to is the power of actions, speech, and appearance in shaping those early judgments. These three aspects are what we learn from, and they remind us to be careful about every move, word, and look we show to strangers. In everyday life we constantly meet new people, so keeping a mindful approach to each first encounter is worthwhile.

Students should not feel obligated to choose a career as soon as they start high school, especially if that means taking on a job before they have finished their education. Beginning a particular occupation can pull attention away from classroom responsibilities, prevent students from gaining a full educational experience, and reduce the time they have for hobbies and relaxation. High school brings increasing academic challenges, with more homework, projects, and exams each year, so learners need to devote energy to studying if they hope to graduate and attend a reputable college. Adding work duties early on can leave little room for review and preparation, which often leads to lower grades and weaker self‑confidence. For example, a teen who works at a salon after school still has to study for a history test; the extra shift hours can cause rushed studying, missed deadlines, and eventually a poor score.

At this stage of life, adolescents are still developing both personally and intellectually, so a long‑term job may disrupt that growth. While some high‑schoolers have a vague notion of what they might pursue later, they still need exposure to a wide range of subjects, skills, and ideas that a standard curriculum offers. This broad learning helps them uncover new possibilities, build a solid academic base, and ultimately qualify for higher‑paying positions. Diving into a specific occupation too soon can narrow their focus, leaving gaps in the knowledge and credentials they will need for the very field they think they are entering. Consider a student who is interested in computer science but takes a cashier job; the short‑term income may be helpful now, but the missing advanced math and science classes could hurt later attempts to enter a tech career.

Early employment can also rob students of activities they truly enjoy, which are important for mental health and motivation. Sports, music, art, or simply spending time with friends provide positive energy and help balance stress. When a job occupies most of a teen’s schedule, there is little chance to keep up these hobbies, and the pressure to meet both work and school obligations can lead to burnout. Picture a young athlete who loves playing on the school football team; the training and camaraderie lift morale and keep stress low. If the same student then works weekends at a fast‑food restaurant, practices are missed, study time shrinks, and the overall load feels heavier. Over time, the student may feel exhausted and find few opportunities to feel happy beyond the workplace.

In conclusion, high‑school students should focus mainly on their studies, using those years to explore different subjects and interests rather than rushing into a permanent job. Prioritizing school improves the likelihood of entering a respected university and, later, of finding a satisfying career. Balancing academic work with personal passions now creates a healthier foundation for future financial success and overall well‑being.

It is often argued that doing something all the time is the best way to achieve success, but I think that periods of inactivity are always valuable. Thomas Jefferson once observed that a great deal can be accomplished when people are ready to act, yet even he would have recognized that work must be balanced with rest. From my point of view, the moments when we stop and do nothing are not wasteful; they help us finish what we start, keep our bodies safe, and allow our minds to recover.

First, completing any task usually requires a series of steps separated by short breaks. Modern societies schedule weekends as days off, showing that the body cannot function without a pause. Imagine trying to run a marathon without taking any water stops; you would collapse before reaching the finish line. In the same way, if we never pause our work, we risk reaching a point where our stamina runs out and we are unable to move forward.

Second, continuous effort builds pressure inside us. If we stay busy without interruption, the mental and physical strain keeps growing, making it harder to fall asleep at night. Sleep is essential for processing information and repairing tissues, and a lack of rest can lead to illness or burnout. Even animals know this instinctively; after a long day of hunting or foraging they lie down, even for a brief moment, before starting again. The same logic applies to humans: a brief period of inactivity allows us to release that pressure and stay healthy.

Third, staying on the go without stopping can have dangerous consequences. Working while your eyes are heavy or your mind is foggy may cause accidents. A tired driver is more likely to miss a turn or fail to brake in time, endangering both themselves and others on the road. On the job, fatigue can lead to slips, falls, or equipment misuse, which might result in serious injury. In short, the risk of harming ourselves or people around us rises when we ignore the need for a break.

Some people counter that constant activity produces more results because it eliminates downtime and speeds up learning. They claim that if you study nonstop, you will grasp material faster, or that a construction crew that works without pause can finish a building ahead of schedule. They also compare it to a journey that never stops, suggesting that never halting means you will reach your destination sooner.

While those points have merit, they overlook the hidden cost of ignoring rest. Faster learning does not guarantee better retention, and pushing a building project without pauses can compromise quality and safety. Moreover, a journey that never stops may still need refueling, repairs, or rest for the driver. In the end, the decision to be idle or to keep moving rests with each individual. Recognizing that inactivity serves a purpose lets us design a routine that balances effort with recovery, ensuring that we stay productive, healthy, and safe.

Dear Manager,

I would like to arrange a visit to your workplace. Seeing your office first‑hand would give me a clearer picture of the daily activities, the technologies you employ, and the direction you plan to take in the coming years. Such a tour would also let me, and any other guests, observe how staff interact with one another and get a sense of the atmosphere in which they work.

Opening the doors of your company to visitors lets outsiders grasp exactly what your organization does in practice. It is one thing to read a description, but quite another to watch the work as it happens. Prospective employees as well as students weighing their study options can judge whether the environment matches their interests and expectations.

Tours can act as a practical guide when people are choosing schools or universities. Instead of spending countless hours scanning many institutions, a quick look at your workplace points them toward specific courses that prepare them for similar roles. This targeted approach saves time and makes decision‑making more efficient.

Overall, inviting people into your space promotes transparency and strengthens the public image of your firm. It builds goodwill, encourages future talent, and keeps the company present in the community’s mind. I think such visits are worthwhile and would appreciate the chance to discuss them further.

I agree with Emerson’s idea that each person should stay true to his or her own identity. To me, the world constantly tries to fit everyone into a certain mold, but when I follow my own sense of self I am able to explore life on my terms. For example, I can travel to places that reveal the natural world—deep forests, rolling hills, and flowering groves—without feeling pressured to become someone else.

Being myself while the world nudges me toward conformity makes it easier to appreciate nature. When I step into a forest, I do not see just a collection of trees; I notice the changing seasons, the new shoots that appear each spring, and the fresh fruit hanging from branches. Those details remind me that the landscape is alive and that my own perspective can bring new meaning to what I observe. Likewise, hills offer a gentler, more inviting backdrop compared with towering mountains. Standing on a hilltop, I enjoy a clear view of the land, a sense of openness, and a reminder that even simple landscapes—grass, a few scattered trees—carry stories from long ago. This view contrasts sharply with the harsh wind and cold of higher peaks, so hills fit my desire for comfort while still letting me feel the vastness of the environment.

Flowers and blossom trees are another source of personal joy. Walking through fields of varied blossoms, I can notice the subtle differences in colour and scent that reflect my own taste and interests. Experiencing such scenes reinforces the idea that authenticity allows me to connect with the world in ways that matter to me. Moreover, when the world pushes me toward a single path, stepping into nature provides a quiet space where I can reconsider and realign my goals, finding inspiration that is uniquely my own.

Some people argue that Emerson’s claim sounds vague or even unimportant, suggesting it lacks substance. However, I find the statement rich with meaning. It captures the reality that external forces—social expectations, cultural norms, even the very land we occupy—attempt to reshape us. Yet when we stay grounded in our own identity, we can still achieve remarkable things, because our personal vision guides us to recognise and value what the world offers. In other words, individuality does not isolate us; it equips us with the ability to interpret the world and draw out the greatest experiences from it.

In conclusion, staying true to myself allows me to enjoy nature’s wonders—forests, hills, flowers—while still navigating a society that tries to dictate my role. This personal authenticity explains many of my choices and successes, which is why I endorse Emerson’s view: being oneself in a world that constantly reshapes us is both possible and profoundly rewarding.

Staying active is the most reliable route to realising our ambitions. When we keep moving, we not only make progress toward the aims we set for ourselves, we also keep our bodies and minds healthy. The lessons we pick up through daily actions accumulate over time and become the foundation of our knowledge. From my point of view, three factors explain why an active life leads to better results.

First, an active lifestyle gives us more chances to achieve what we want. Persistence is essential: people who train regularly or practice a skill every day are more likely to win competitions or reach career milestones. Moreover, being active lets us explore the world around us, notice new places, and become curious about different ideas. This openness often translates into fresh ideas and better strategies. For instance, a student who participates in sports clubs learns how to plan schedules, cooperate with teammates, and handle setbacks—skills that are valuable in any future job. By staying engaged, we keep our eyes on the horizon and never miss the chance to seize opportunities.

Second, activity is a powerful source of learning and experience. Every time we try something new—whether it is learning a language, mastering a musical instrument, or taking part in community projects—our brain adapts and strengthens. Regular participation encourages us to ask questions, experiment, and reflect on outcomes, which fuels an inquisitive mind. As these actions become habits, they shape our character, making us more mature and intelligent. We also notice that our objectives become clearer and more attainable because we have tested them in real situations. Over time, the habit of doing builds momentum, so we are more willing to push forward and reach higher standards.

Third, staying active boosts our self‑esteem and confidence. As we accomplish tasks and see ourselves improve, a positive sense of self emerges. Our personality grows stronger; we learn to trust our abilities, which raises the rate at which we achieve personal goals. This confidence also keeps us resilient, so we can endure setbacks and keep trying. Interaction with other people—through team sports, group projects, or volunteer work—adds support and encouragement, reinforcing the belief that we can succeed when we work together. In short, the more we engage, the more we discover what we are capable of, and the higher we climb.

In conclusion, the evidence shows that a lively, active approach helps us do more, stay healthier, and grow intellectually. Physical activities, mental challenges, and social involvement each play a part in shaping a well‑rounded individual who can tackle complex tasks. Whether we win a game, finish a project, or simply walk a longer distance than before, those moments feed back into our determination, making it stronger and more nuanced. Being part of a team and cooperating with others gives extra motivation and a sense of belonging. Therefore, keeping active is not only good for the body—it is a proven strategy for reaching our dreams and maintaining a positive outlook on life.

The school board’s proposal to lengthen the school day does not make sense, in my view. I oppose this idea not just because I am a student, but because the consequences would reach all members of the school community. Adding extra hours would place a heavy strain on pupils, teachers, and the school itself, leading to outcomes that are mostly negative.

First, longer school periods tend to wear students out. When lessons stretch for many hours, concentration drops and tiredness sets in. This can cause restless or disruptive behavior in class and also weaken the ability to retain new material. As a result, grades often suffer, because students are less effective when they are exhausted. Moreover, there would be even less time left after school for completing homework, studying for quizzes, or preparing for exams. The balance between in‑school instruction and independent study would be upset, and many learners would find themselves lagging behind.

The extra time would also harm teachers. Educators already have personal lives outside the classroom, and many of them need to spend evenings with their families or attend to their own children. A longer school day would make it harder for them to get home early enough to enjoy these moments. The continuous demand for more teaching hours could increase stress and burnout, which might cause teachers to become irritable or less patient with pupils. In turn, classroom atmosphere could deteriorate, raising the chance of conflicts between staff and students.

Health‑related appointments are another practical issue. For instance, I must attend the orthodontist each month, and the visits always fall in the morning. With a longer school day, I would miss two or three classes, and catching up on missed work would be difficult. If the school day were not extended, I could schedule my appointments in the afternoon and avoid falling behind. Similarly, when a student falls ill and misses a day, the added hours would make the backlog of assignments even larger. The school would then have to provide extra support, which adds to the workload for both learners and staff.

A longer schedule also increases costs for the school. More instructional time means more meals, more paper and bathroom supplies, and a need for additional agendas with more bathroom passes. Administrators would have to deal with a higher number of student disputes and physical fights, as well as arrange more transportation to avoid bus overcrowding. If the day is extended by ninety minutes, a larger crowd of teenagers would leave the building at the same time as elementary school children, raising the risk of traffic accidents and making the roads around the campus busier.

Waking up early is already a challenge for many pupils. Adding several extra hours would push fatigue even further, so that students cannot absorb lessons properly and teachers cannot deliver them effectively. The overall quality of education would suffer, and the environment would become more chaotic.

In short, extending school hours would bring a variety of problems for students, teachers, and the institution. It would not only exhaust learners but also lower academic performance, disrupt family life for educators, complicate health‑related absences, raise operational expenses, and increase safety risks on the streets. Because many students share these concerns, the board should reconsider the proposal and take student opinions into account before moving forward.

Businesses and schools might think about adopting a four‑day work week because it could lower energy consumption. If the same amount of work is spread over four days instead of five, each day would be longer—roughly ten hours of instruction or office duties. Buildings would then be heated, lit and powered for fewer days, which cuts electricity costs and reduces the use of water and other resources.

For students this change would mean more time to complete assignments each day. Those who struggle academically could receive extra help during the longer lesson periods, and teachers would not need to stay after school to finish classes. A longer day also allows students to concentrate better, making the learning experience more effective.

An extra non‑school day would give pupils a break to rest, spend time with family, or take part in extracurricular activities. Students who have part‑time jobs could work on that day to earn money they need, while those with heavy homework loads could finish it all and still have time for sports or hobbies.

Because schools operate for fewer days, overall electricity use drops. Natural resources such as water and power are limited, so reducing the number of days buildings are fully operational helps preserve them for the future. The cost of keeping large school facilities running is considerable; cutting one day of operation would ease that financial burden.

Overall, a four‑day schedule would let schools and workplaces conserve energy and save money while also giving students more flexibility and support. That combination of environmental, economic and personal benefits makes the four‑day work week worth considering.

Nowadays many everyday activities can be done with little need for face‑to‑face interaction, thanks to advances in digital tools. Some people wonder why they still have to go to work when computers can handle most of the tasks. This line of thinking often makes employees feel upset, because they worry that automated systems will cut down the amount of work they do and possibly shorten the number of hours they need to spend on the job. In addition, when technology replaces jobs that normally involve minimal effort, it can shrink the overall number of positions available, which makes the job market less favourable for everyone.

First, relying heavily on machines can feel disrespectful to the people who are actually performing the work. Imagine you are trying to improve your skills at a certain task, but the colleague you would normally learn from has been replaced by a computer that already knows the best way to do it. In such a scenario the human element is lost, and many workers feel that they are being ignored or undervalued.

Second, reduced contact with other people often has a negative impact on people’s well‑being. While technology can be helpful in some cases, many individuals react badly when they realize it might be taking over their responsibilities. The decrease in interpersonal interaction can make people feel isolated, and the fear of job loss makes the help feel unwelcome rather than appreciated.

In short, I think that the spread of automation brings more harm than good. It pushes people out of jobs they could do well, creates a sense of resentment, and weakens the social connections that workplaces normally rely on. Although technology does make some tasks easier, its tendency to replace human roles ultimately hurts the workforce and undermines the very happiness that people seek at work.

When choosing how to finish a school assignment, people can either work by themselves or join a group. In my opinion, working in a team is usually more helpful for several reasons. Firstly, teammates can give you assistance when you are stuck. Secondly, the work can be split so each member handles a part they are comfortable with. Finally, interacting with others helps you discover new facts and ideas, which improves your overall understanding. Below I will discuss each point in more detail.

One of the biggest advantages of a group is the support it offers. If I am unsure about a problem, a classmate can point out where I am going wrong and explain it in a different way. I have experienced this in math class. My teacher formed a pair for a practice set, and I could not grasp a particular formula. I asked my partner to walk me through it, and she showed me two alternative methods. Thanks to her, I managed to complete the task and avoided staying stuck. This illustrates how a peer’s perspective can make a difficult concept clearer and give me tools I might not have thought of on my own.

Another strength of teamwork is the way tasks are shared. Instead of bearing the whole workload alone, each student can take a part that suits their strengths. This speeds up the process and lowers the chance of feeling overwhelmed. I recall a history project where the teacher assigned us into four‑person teams. My role was to locate the bibliography entries, another student collected data, a third gathered images, and the fourth selected video clips that illustrated our findings. By focusing on one specific area, we finished the whole presentation well before the deadline and earned an A. The division of labour also allowed us to give each other feedback, which helped the final product be more polished.

Finally, collaboration expands our knowledge base. While researching together, members bring up resources or viewpoints that may not appear in a solo search. This exchange often introduces fresh ideas and unexpected connections, which deepen comprehension. The same history assignment showed me sources I had never considered, and the video material provided a visual angle that clarified abstract points. As a result, I felt more prepared for the subsequent quiz. Moreover, the habit of discussing topics with peers helps me retain information longer and think critically about the subject.

In short, group work offers help when a problem is difficult, makes the workload manageable by splitting it into parts, and increases the amount of information and insights you receive. These benefits outweigh the occasional inconvenience of coordinating schedules, and they lead to better grades and a stronger grasp of the material. For that reason, I think teamwork is generally the better choice for most school tasks. Of course, arranging meetings and agreeing on roles requires some extra effort, but the overall advantages make the extra time worthwhile.

today’s world many people rely on their own judgment when faced with important choices, whereas others look for advice before deciding. Decisions driven by others often feel like obligations rather than authentic choices, which can diminish personal fulfillment. Therefore, allowing oneself to decide is crucial for developing confidence, responsibility, and a happier future.  

Ultimately, encouraging individuals to make their own decisions equips them with the self‑esteem and accountability needed to become better persons, and it paves the way for a more rewarding life. Self‑esteem is built on real achievement, not on empty praise for work that barely meets expectations. If a student is praised for a mediocre piece of writing, they receive a false sense of value and no reason to stretch themselves further. Praise for low‑quality work can give the impression that effort isn’t required, causing the learner to stop striving and settle at a level far below their potential.

My first point focuses on why genuine accomplishment is essential for confidence. When a paper is completed with thought and care, and the student can say with certainty that it was their best effort, receiving honest commendation reinforces the idea that the work itself is worthy of recognition. Such feedback tells the learner, “Your hard work paid off,” which strengthens a positive self‑image. The assignment might have been challenging, but the student didn’t allow laziness to creep in; instead, they aimed higher, showing a willingness to grow and refine their abilities rather than staying stuck in the same place.

The second reason links the teacher’s responsibilities to this process. Teachers are meant to guide improvement, and if they applaud sub‑par submissions while ignoring the chance for better work, students may conclude that mediocrity is acceptable. In that case, the teacher’s silence about the missed opportunities tells the learner they don’t have to try harder, which can erode self‑esteem. Instead of blanket compliments, educators should meet with the student and say something like, “This is good, but it wasn’t your best effort. I know you can push further.” This approach makes clear that praise is earned, not handed out arbitrarily.

Some might argue that letting students slide on a poorly done task keeps them motivated later, but this overlooks a crucial reality: when a teacher seems to ignore weak work, students may feel invisible or unimportant. If a pupil raises a concern and receives no follow‑up, they could assume the teacher doesn’t care about their progress. A teacher who acknowledges the issue and offers support shows that they are watching and invested, which in turn encourages the student to raise the quality of future work.

In the end, true self‑esteem does not arise from praise for an easy or half‑finished assignment. Recognizing effort that falls short only cements a low ceiling of performance. It signals to the student that staying at that level is enough, leaving little room for development and limiting their writing growth. By reserving commendation for genuine achievement and providing constructive feedback on weaker efforts, educators help learners build lasting confidence that comes from real, earned success.

Teen curfews have become a hot topic in many communities, and it’s worth looking at why they matter so much. When night falls, the streets can be more dangerous, and many parents worry that their teenagers might be at risk of harm. At the same time, the rules of daily life are changing, so it’s no surprise that a city council would bring up the idea of a curfew. The question is whether such a rule would protect young people or simply add another restriction to their already busy lives.

The council’s discussion is motivated by several concerns. First, there is the safety angle: officials want to keep teenagers from getting hurt in places where crime or traffic accidents are more common after dark. Second, they are concerned about exposure to negative influences that can affect a young person’s development, such as drinking or risky behavior that often happen late at night. Finally, the council wants to prevent possible legal trouble that might arise from teens being out after hours without supervision. All of these reasons feed into the argument that a curfew could be useful.

If a curfew were enacted, would any teen caught outside after the set time automatically be breaking the law? The answer is not straightforward. There are circumstances where being out late could be lawful. For example, if a teenager is on a job shift, is returning home after school for a part‑time job, or is responding to an emergency, the curfew might not apply. Traveling with an adult, such as a parent or guardian, also changes the situation, because the teen is not alone. However, hanging out with friends, going to parties, or simply staying out for leisure purposes would likely be considered a violation. In this sense, the law’s impact depends on the reason behind the teen’s presence on the street.

The next issue is whether curfews actually keep teenagers out of trouble or if they unfairly limit their freedom. Most teens feel that a fixed bedtime interferes with their desire to socialize, have fun, or explore their independence. From their point of view, curfew is another rule that tells them how to live, which can feel restrictive. On the other hand, many parents argue that the rule is a protective measure. They point out that the risks of being alone at night are real, and that a curfew can reduce the chance of accidents or harmful experiences. Teens must therefore weigh the benefits against the drawbacks: staying out late might bring excitement, but it also carries unknown dangers. Parents must consider whether the safety gains outweigh the loss of personal freedom.

In the end, the council’s debate shows that curfews are not a simple solution. They can help reduce certain risks, yet they also cut into the autonomy that teenagers are starting to develop. Whether the law keeps teens safe or infringes on their lives depends largely on how it is applied, the exceptions allowed, and the community’s willingness to enforce it fairly. A balanced approach—one that protects young people while still giving them reasonable leeway for work, emergencies, or adult supervision—might be the most sensible way forward.

Avid is a rewarding educational program that can turn a student’s dream into something tangible. I think it is enjoyable because it goes beyond ordinary classroom work and helps learners grow both personally and academically while guiding them toward higher education. From the start, Avid encourages students to organize their materials, attend weekly binder checks, and set clear goals. These small but consistent habits teach responsibility and perseverance, showing that success comes from steady effort rather than occasional bursts. The programme reminds us that if we want to reach college, we must stay focused and keep improving, even when distractions around us feel overwhelming.

A second major benefit of Avid is the tutorial sessions that let students share what they have learned with peers. After each tutorial, teachers can see where a student stands and spot areas that need extra work. At the same time, the student gets a chance to explain concepts to classmates, which boosts confidence and clarifies misunderstandings. Listening to other people’s questions and answers creates a collaborative learning atmosphere where knowledge is exchanged freely. It also helps shy students practice speaking in front of a group, turning nervousness into a useful skill that will serve them well in college and later in life.

In addition, Avid provides field trips that most regular schools do not offer. For example, students visit local colleges, talk with admissions counselors, and explore campus facilities. These experiences make the idea of higher education concrete and exciting. The trips are not only informative; they are also fun. They give pupils the chance to meet new people, practice teamwork on guided tours, and, after raising funds through class projects, enjoy a culminating outing like a day at a theme park. Such a reward feels earned and motivates everyone to keep pushing forward.

One of the strongest points of Avid is the sense of community it creates. The program feels like an extended family where everyone supports each other and encourages progress with the motto “Dream, believe, achieve.” If someone starts to feel discouraged, the group steps in, reminding them that they are not alone and that giving up would waste all the effort they have invested. This environment prevents negativity and builds trust, no matter where students come from. It also offers a safe space for those whose families may not provide strong encouragement, allowing them to be themselves and pursue their ambitions without fear.

In conclusion, Avid is enjoyable because it combines personal development, academic help, memorable trips, and a supportive family‑like network. It lets students meet new friends, take part in exciting activities, and stay motivated through collective effort. By stepping out of their comfort zone, participants discover that taking a risk can lead to a positive future. Avid not only prepares them for college but also equips them with the confidence and drive to become whoever they want to be in life.

Many people claim that an upbeat mindset is the most powerful factor in achieving one’s dreams, but I think this view overlooks the indispensable role of sustained effort. A hopeful outlook can keep you motivated, yet it does not automatically convert desire into results. Consider the steps needed to obtain an advanced high‑school diploma or to secure a job after several years of university study. Even if you select a degree program merely because it promises a better future, you still have to attend lectures, finish assignments, and pass examinations. Moreover, a strong work ethic builds competence, resilience, and a reputation that open doors when opportunities appear. In every arena—from sports to entrepreneurship—diligent practice outweighs merely feeling positive. Without such discipline, optimism alone cannot bridge the gap between where you are now and where you want to be.

If you set a concrete target—such as buying a car within the next twelve months—an optimistic outlook is not enough. You need to create a realistic budget, open a savings account, and perhaps increase your earnings through extra shifts. Purchasing a vehicle also requires paying for insurance, registration fees, fuel, and regular maintenance, which can quickly strain your finances. On top of that, parking fees, occasional repair bills, and the cost of accessories add up over time. Believing that everything will fall into place does not guarantee you will have the necessary funds when the moment arrives. A disciplined habit lets you calculate expenses, cut unnecessary spending, and ultimately allocate enough money to purchase the car you desire. Overcoming such financial hurdles illustrates why hard work is indispensable for turning a wish into a reality.

The belief that a sunny disposition can ensure high‑school graduation is unrealistic. Graduating after twelve years of schooling is a long‑term project that requires regular attendance, studying, and overcoming occasional setbacks. Think about the days when you fell ill and could not go home because no one was available to pick you up. On those occasions you probably felt anything but happy, yet you still had to stay in class and keep up with the material. Moreover, students often need to complete extracurricular projects, participate in tutoring sessions, and meet deadlines set by teachers. Success in school, and later in life, relies on perseverance rather than on a constant feeling of cheerfulness. Even when you feel tempted to quit, it is the commitment to keep working that keeps you moving forward.

University students frequently endure four years of coursework in a field they do not enjoy, hoping that a suitable job will follow graduation. This experience brings a heavy workload: late‑night study sessions, dozens of essays, group projects, and the pressure to stay current with readings. Many supplement their studies with part‑time jobs to cover living costs and tuition fees, frequently sacrificing sleep and personal time. On top of that, they often manage student loans, seek scholarships, and attend networking events to improve their chances after university. After leaving campus they face a competitive job market and must prove they can outperform other candidates. In interviews they must demonstrate practical skills, initiative, and the dedication required by employers. All of these achievements stem from diligent effort, not from hopeful thoughts alone.

Even after entering the workforce, the same principle applies. Advancing to a higher position, launching your own business, or mastering a new skill each demand continuous work. An optimistic mindset can inspire you to take on a challenge, but without regular practice, learning, and sacrifice you will not see measurable progress. For example, becoming fluent in a foreign language requires daily study, listening exercises, and often paying for classes or online resources. Likewise, building a startup means conducting market research, drafting business plans, and repeatedly testing ideas, all of which consume time and energy. Climbing the corporate ladder often entails taking on extra responsibilities, attending training sessions, and working longer hours than before. These processes underline that positive thinking alone does not produce results; it must be paired with a disciplined work ethic.

In summary, a truly successful life is built on meeting concrete milestones—completing high school, finishing university, and landing a suitable job—through steady effort and persistence. Not everyone has the chance to attend formal education, and for those who do, success still requires more than hopeful ideas. Relying on miracles such as a lottery win or hoping that circumstances will change overnight is not a reliable strategy. The only dependable route to progress is to commit to the tasks at hand, stay diligent, and transform aspirations into tangible achievements. By consistently applying hard work, individuals can overcome obstacles, develop valuable skills, and ultimately turn their dreams into reality.

I have a personal goal that I hope to achieve one day: to own a spacious mansion somewhere in California. Growing up, I have always lived in modest homes—townhouses or apartments—and I have never experienced the kind of living space that a large property offers. Owning such a house would represent the result of years of effort and determination, a tangible proof that my ambitions have paid off. At the same time, it would give me the chance to set foot on California soil for the very first time, a place that has always seemed distant and exciting in my imagination. Living in a cramped space surrounded by many similar houses has made me think about what a spacious, open environment could feel like.

The second reason I am drawn to a mansion is that it would serve as a clear display of my financial success. Modern mansions are expensive; they require a large amount of cash, both because of their size and because they often sit on exclusive, private land. You can find such houses in places like Florida, Texas, Nevada and California, but the latter is especially appealing because it is a wealthy state known for its iconic cities and rich history. I picture myself living in either a city like Calabasas, close to Hollywood, or perhaps Hollywood itself, where the surroundings combine glamour with natural beauty. Of course, the price varies a lot depending on location, square footage, and interior design, but the very act of buying a house at that level would be a significant milestone in my life. Choosing California also means being close to a variety of recreational options, from mountain retreats to world‑class theaters, which adds to the overall appeal of the location.

The third reason is my desire to finally experience California directly. My mother spent part of her youth in a small town near Downtown Los Angeles called Generic City. She told me stories about school, jobs, and the many sights she saw, such as Disneyland, the Hollywood sign, sporting events, and the bustling streets of the city. Since her move to Virginia when I was born, she has kept the memories of California alive and has encouraged me to visit. I would love to walk across the Golden Gate Bridge, stroll along Venice Beach, and soak up the hot summer weather while watching the ocean sparkle. Those moments would make the experience even more rewarding. Beyond the tourist spots, I would enjoy the everyday Californian lifestyle—sunny evenings on the beach, fresh produce markets, and a multicultural community that feels alive.

To sum up, I want a mansion in California for three main reasons. First, it would be the first big house I have ever lived in, symbolising the hard work and perseverance that have shaped my path. Second, the financial effort required to purchase such a property would demonstrate my economic achievement and let me show off my success. Third, it would give me the chance to explore California, following the stories my mother shared and seeing famous attractions like Disneyland, the Hollywood sign, the Golden Gate Bridge, and Venice Beach. Beyond that, everyday life in the state—such as beach evenings and fresh food markets—would allow me to live the California vibe I have always admired. Achieving this dream would be the perfect blend of personal accomplishment, financial security, and new experiences, and I am confident that with dedication it can become a reality.

Online Learning

Who doesn't want to be left in the house all day using an electronic device with online access? Although students save money and time by taking classes from home. It is not beneficial to learn online because students lose focus of what they are learning and tend to easily get distracted when they're in their house, students can't have a one on one conversation with a teacher nor discuss with classmates, and students could also face technical difficulties when attending online classes from home.

Losing focus has a big impact in learning. For example, my friend Generic_Name sent me a text message last month, right when I started studying for my history mid-term exam. I responded back to Generic_Name's text, and without realizing we kept on messaging past midnight. This shows how easily students get distracted at home with a cellular device and how easy it is to lose focus. The next morning I decided to get to school an hour early and review one on one with my teacher.

Secondly, taking classes online doesn't just mean you don't have a physical teacher or instructor that you can question lively, but also means that it will be challenging to find answers to your questions. I remember in my sophomore year a kid in our econ class named Generic_Name was really sick for a while so he had ended up taking classes online. Generic_Name was a straight A student, always was first to answer the teachers questions and he also used to ask questions. Thankfully Generic_Name healed towards the end of the year and I asked him if he benefited and if he recommends attending classes from home. The straight A student Generic_Name said it was a real challenge to take the class online and he finished the class a month after he should have with a B- average. Generic_Name had also said that one of the most difficult parts about attending a class online was his laptop not functioning at all times, and not having a teacher you can talk and converse with one on one.

Finally, using your personal computer and internet connection can always be an issue. You can't always depend on your computer, not just the computers but even people aren't perfect. Another main problem Generic_Name had when attending classes online was his laptop and network connection. Generic_Name explained that he always faced technical difficulties. When his laptop wasn't functioning right, the only thing he could do was to stop the lesson and wait for his dad to get the laptop repaired, which took time. Each month, either his laptop or internet connection would not cooperate, so he finished the class a month later than everyone.

In conclusion, Everyone would like to save money and time by taking classes from home. But getting distracted, not asking your teacher questions when you need to, and wasting money on laptop repair is not worth it at all. Learning from a far distance could also be an option but when asking if it is beneficial, we can say that it is not by looking at the listed reasoning.

Similarly, his home Wi‑Fi would drop at random times each month, extending his study timeline by weeks. The constant temptation to switch between social media, the lack of direct interaction with teachers and peers, and the frequent technical failures all make remote learning less effective. Life inevitably brings both pleasant and difficult moments. While joyful events bring smiles, success is something almost everyone welcomes, and its positive feeling can persist even after tough times have passed. In my view, keeping a hopeful outlook is essential for reaching success because it shapes how we handle obstacles and influences our long‑term growth.

First, a positive mindset expands the way we think. When we expect good things, we tend to explore ideas more freely, combining critical analysis with creativity. This openness lets us look for opportunities rather than dwell on setbacks. During a hard phase, optimism fuels the desire to keep moving forward instead of quitting. By believing that we can improve, we also gain confidence that will support us later, turning each struggle into a stepping stone for future achievements.

Second, I saw this principle in action when a classmate was preparing for a key exam. He was anxious, repeating that he might fail and that his parents would be upset if he did. I reminded him to focus on doing his best and to trust his abilities. After a short break, he returned visibly more relaxed, even jumping with excitement. When the results came out, he shouted that he had passed. This experience convinced me that encouragement and a cheerful attitude can turn a stressful situation into a triumph.

Third, the power of positivity does not depend on location or circumstance. Whether you are traveling on a plane or sitting in a classroom in Mexico, a good attitude can lift your mood and change your life’s direction. Whenever I feel stuck or sad, I tell myself, “I’ve got this” or “I can handle it.” Such self‑talk not only lifts my spirits but also pushes me toward bigger goals and prevents surrender.

In summary, life includes both good and bad experiences, but the pursuit of success is a common goal that brings happiness even amid hardships. Maintaining a positive attitude helps us think more openly, strengthens our resilience, and creates the mental confidence needed to overcome obstacles. When we adopt optimism in everyday challenges, we set the stage for better outcomes and a more rewarding path forward.
