a classroom where students are permitted to bring their smartphones for learning. At first glance it might seem convenient—information is just a tap away, and tools like online dictionaries or quiz apps could make lessons more interactive. Yet, I believe schools should keep phones out of the classroom because allowing them opens the door to cheating, creates constant distractions, and encourages habits of laziness and superficial study.

Some supporters argue that phones can be useful. They say a quick break after a test lets students relax with games or music, which they claim can actually improve concentration. Others claim that using a phone to look up unfamiliar terms or data makes research faster, while still others point out that certain apps help language learners or keep students engaged through review games. While these points have merit, they do not outweigh the problems that arise when phones are allowed during formal lessons.

First, phones give students a straightforward way to cheat on exams. If a device is visible, it is tempting to capture questions, send images to friends, or look up answers in real time. Because the information is already stored on the phone, learners may feel less pressure to memorize material, reducing the value of studying altogether. The logic of “Why spend time learning when I can copy answers on a screen?” becomes easy to justify, and this undermines the fairness of the assessment process.

Second, even a silent phone can become a major source of distraction. A sudden buzz or a faint sound can pull attention away from the teacher, and a student who is watching videos or listening to loud music can easily disturb the whole class. It is common to see peers glancing at screens, exchanging messages, or playing games, which forces others to lose focus. When a student’s device draws others into side conversations, it not only interrupts the lesson but also models inappropriate behavior for the entire room.

Finally, constant access to phones can foster laziness and a shallow approach to learning. When facts are just a swipe away, students often rely on quick searches instead of processing the information critically. This habit can lead to procrastination—students delay studying because they think they can look it up later. Even if grades appear high, the lack of deeper understanding means the knowledge does not stay with them, and the classroom becomes a place where effort is replaced by reliance on digital shortcuts.

Allowing phones in school does not guarantee better performance; it often replaces real effort with convenient distractions. The danger of cheating, the ripple effect of interruptions, and the temptation to skimp on real study are too serious to ignore. Schools should therefore ban cell phone use during class time, encouraging students to develop the discipline and critical thinking skills that cannot be downloaded from an app. Only by keeping phones out of the learning environment can educators protect the quality of education and the integrity of assessments.

A common question is whether showing an example is the most powerful way to influence someone, or just one of many. I think that an example is the decisive factor and actually the only factor that works.

Firstly, when we talk to others we usually mention other people’s experiences. Picture someone who was once careless but later changed his behaviour through effort and self‑reflection. This story offers a clear picture of how attitudes and ties can improve, letting the listener see a possible path. When it is paired with logical reasons and concrete steps, the other person can decide whether change is realistic and, if ready, start acting differently.

Secondly, influencing someone always means giving reasons—positive or negative—yet those reasons become effective only when they are linked to a fitting example. Preparing a well‑matched example makes the advice personal and credible, because people are more likely to act on something they can relate to.

In conclusion, the only reliable way to sway another person is by presenting an appropriate example, supporting it with clear reasons and actionable suggestions, and then offering personal guidance.

No matter where we go, most people are thinking about where they want to be or what they hope to achieve. Some manage to set aside the time needed to work on those plans, while others struggle to make progress. There are those who take initiative, and there are those who stay passive. Jefferson warned against idleness, saying that much can be accomplished when we keep ourselves occupied. I agree with his view that a busy, purposeful life leads to greater results.

First, taking action speeds up the path to our goals. When a task is assigned, we can either wait for luck or someone else to finish it for us, or we can start working right away. By tackling assignments promptly, we cut the time needed to finish them and create room for other priorities. For a student who wishes to obtain a scholarship, regular study and a well‑structured résumé raise the chances of college admission. Likewise, anyone aiming for a stable, long‑term career must acquire relevant skills and experience early. These steps make the later stages of the journey smoother, because each completed task builds momentum toward the next one.

Second, staying active builds confidence and resilience. After an exam turns out poorly, we can ignore the result and move on, or we can examine what went wrong, adjust our study habits, and prepare better for the next test. In my own experience, when a quiz was disappointing I look ahead at the upcoming material, take notes in advance, and study the next unit before the class even covers it. This habit of forward‑looking preparation keeps my mind engaged and less likely to drift into idle waiting. When we organize our study and note‑taking, we naturally spend less time sitting around and more time pursuing the goals that matter to us.

Critics sometimes argue that idleness can lower stress, especially among high‑school students who feel overwhelmed by heavy workloads. They point out that some learners rely on stimulants or energy drinks to stay awake while studying, which can cause health problems and burnout. While it is true that constant pressure can be exhausting, the alternative of doing nothing does not automatically guarantee a stress‑free life. Instead, being productive gives us the skills and experience that most employers look for. Almost every job description asks for prior experience or demonstrable competence, and having a track record of action makes it easier to answer those requirements. Moreover, the future is unpredictable, so we are better served by anticipating challenges and preparing for them rather than waiting for them to appear.

In short, I prefer to set clear objectives and work ahead of the schedule. Persistent effort keeps us involved, uncovers new opportunities, improves academic performance, and shapes us into valuable workers. Teachers and classmates often respect those who are diligent, and such people may become role models for others. Over time, these habits open the doors to the colleges we dream about and allow us to fulfil our personal ambitions. Keeping busy, as Jefferson suggested, is the most reliable way to reach the future we imagine.

I remember a situation from my high school days that taught me how quick first impressions can be. I was assigned a math teacher who looked serious, hardly smiled, and gave no explanation for the topics we covered. He seemed distant, and it felt uncomfortable asking him questions. After a few weeks I went to the school counselor hoping to switch classes, but she said the schedule was already set and there was no room for change. As the term went on, I found out that the teacher was actually very helpful. Whenever I struggled, he stayed after class, broke down the concepts step by step, and checked my quizzes to make sure I understood. This experience showed me that a cold exterior does not always mean a cold heart.

Many people claim that a person’s character can be judged from the first glimpse, but I believe this view is incomplete. The phrase “first impressions are almost impossible to change” sounds persuasive, yet it overlooks the fact that our mood fluctuates. Life is a mixture of good and bad days, and a sudden bad mood can turn even the most pleasant person into someone who seems harsh. Imagine someone dealing with a family crisis, a missed deadline at work, or a personal loss; those pressures can spill over into their interactions with others. When you meet someone for the first time and they act uninterested, it does not automatically mean they are rude. They might simply be carrying a heavy load that day.

The same logic applies to positive initial impressions. Someone who looks friendly and courteous could be deceptive, hiding motives that do not align with their outward behavior. The common proverb “Don’t judge a book by its cover” captures this warning. It reminds us that outward appearance tells only part of a person’s story. A person who dresses neatly and speaks politely may still betray your trust, while someone who looks unkempt might become a reliable ally when you need help. Judging solely on looks or a single interaction risks missing out on valuable relationships and support.

To form a fair assessment, you need more than a brief snapshot. Observing someone’s actions over time, listening to their explanations, and giving them chances to show their true nature are essential steps. Knowing the context behind a particular behavior helps you separate temporary circumstances from lasting character traits. In my own experience, waiting to learn more about my teacher allowed me to appreciate his genuine effort to help students succeed. If I had written him off after the first class, I would have missed an important source of guidance.

In summary, first impressions are not fixed facts; they can shift when we realize a person is having a bad day or when we discover their real qualities. It is wise to pause before labeling someone as good or bad based on a single meeting or appearance. A little patience can prevent us from dismissing a potential friend, mentor, or source of help. Ultimately, understanding a person’s character fully will guide us to make better judgments and stronger connections.

Curfews often spark debate because people wonder whether they actually stop teenagers from getting into trouble. In our city, officials are still discussing when the shut‑down should happen: one suggestion sets it at ten o’clock on weekdays, while another pushes it to twelve on Saturdays and Sundays. Anyone who stays out after that time would be breaking the law. Even if we disagree with some regulations, we generally accept that we must follow the rules we have agreed upon. From my perspective, the council should put a curfew in place for under‑age youths. We owe it to the community to protect teenagers, who are particularly vulnerable, and a curfew can make the environment safer for them.

Ask yourself: what could happen when a teenager is out without supervision? The world today contains many threats, from crime to accidents, and while we hope nothing will occur, anything is possible. Without adult eyes watching, minor missteps can become serious problems. Too many youths have ended up hurt or killed, often for reasons that nobody fully understands. A well‑planned curfew can be one tool that reduces these dangers. Even if a midnight rule on weekends doesn’t eliminate all risk, it is up to parents to teach their children the difference between right and wrong. If teens grasp why a curfew matters, they are more likely to be careful about where they go and when they return.

I can relate to this, because I have been on the other side of the issue. A few times I chose to stay out past my bedtime with friends instead of returning home as my mother asked. I later realized how much my safety mattered to her; the sleepless nights when she worried about where I was still haunt me. That experience showed me that a simple rule can make a huge difference for both the child and the parent.

I recently heard about a boy from New York who seemed perfectly reliable. His mother said he liked staying close to family and helped his younger relatives, kept good grades, and rarely caused any trouble. Tragically, he was attacked a short distance from his house. In the early evening, a group of strangers dragged him out of a small store, stabbed him, and he later collapsed on the sidewalk before anyone could reach him. The attackers later said they confused him with someone else. This incident illustrates that even a trustworthy teen can become a victim if left unsupervised after dark.

Some parents argue that they want to give their children the same freedom they had when they were young, believing there is no need for a curfew. They assume that trusting their child is enough to keep them safe. While it’s natural to want children to experience liberty, we also need to think about the strangers they might encounter after dark. During daylight many people are around, so a call for help or a quick run to safety is easier. At night most residents are asleep, and the streets can feel empty. That makes it harder for someone in trouble to get assistance. Even if you trust your child completely, you cannot control the behaviour of other adults.

Overall, the council should evaluate the evidence and approve a curfew for teenagers. This does not mean taking away all liberty – young people can still spend evenings in part‑time work, sports, or family events, as long as they finish before the designated hour. A curfew lowers the likelihood of accidents, assaults, or other hazards, and most citizens agree that protecting minors is a priority. By supervising teens after dark, we can keep them safe while still encouraging responsible growth.

The topic I am going to discuss is kindness. Kindness can change people’s lives because it improves how they feel in many different ways. For example, picking up litter on a sidewalk makes the neighbourhood cleaner and shows that someone cares about the community. A quick gesture is to help when a passer‑by drops something; bending down to retrieve it saves the person effort and proves you are willing to be useful in real life. Small, thoughtful actions like these can make a big difference in someone’s day.

Even when you are annoyed with someone, choosing to be kind can still have a positive effect. If you speak politely to a neighbour or classmate, you show respect despite any frustration you may feel. Kindness also includes assisting others in various tasks. Helping a classmate understand an English‑Spanish translation, or lending a hand with homework, can lift their mood and give them confidence. Such help demonstrates that you care about their success, not just about getting the job done.

Kindness helps both the giver and the receiver. When you go out of your way to assist a person who is upset, you create a sense of relief and connection. Offering to translate a sentence, or to tidy the kitchen after dinner, shows you notice their needs and are ready to act. Even a simple favour, like bringing a friend a glass of water, counts as a kind act. Over time, these little favours add up and make you seem more reliable and caring.

Acts of kindness also extend to animals and personal wellbeing. Petting a neighbour’s dog or taking it for a short walk can make the animal happy and give its owner a break. Helping a friend clean the dishes after a shared meal relieves stress for both parties. Small things like these prove that you are paying attention and willing to support others, even in routine situations.

Showing kindness can affect how you feel about yourself as well. When you perform a considerate deed, such as picking up trash or talking to someone who seems lonely, you notice a lift in your own mood. You feel proud because you have contributed something positive, and you develop a reputation as a person who looks after others. In fact, studies suggest that giving help often makes people happier than receiving it.

I believe kindness is valuable because it fosters goodwill and strengthens relationships. If you notice a classmate struggling with an assignment, offering a brief explanation or checking the work together can boost their confidence. If you encounter a person sitting alone in a café, striking up a friendly conversation can ease their loneliness. These examples illustrate that kindness is flexible: it can be verbal, physical, or digital, but its core remains the same—making another person feel seen and supported.

In short, kindness, even in its smallest form, has a lasting impact. Whether you pick up rubbish, assist with homework, translate a message, or simply listen to someone, you are creating a ripple effect of positivity. By choosing to be considerate every day, you not only improve others’ lives but also enrich your own, building a habit that makes you a better, more compassionate person.

Many people claim that remote education is an ideal solution for today’s learners. Indeed, a number of advantages make it attractive: students can often attend more regularly, face fewer disruptions, and gain access to learning even when they have disabilities or chronic health conditions. However, skeptics warn that staying away from the classroom may lead to disengagement and a lack of responsibility.

One of the strongest arguments for online schooling is the improvement in attendance. By removing the need to travel to a physical building and the early‑morning rush that many find stressful, learners have fewer excuses to skip lessons. When a course can be accessed from home, the temptation to stay in bed on a cold morning or after a long night is reduced. This flexibility not only keeps more students logged in each day but also eases the fatigue that comes from commuting and sitting for long periods.

Another crucial benefit concerns students who cannot easily move around a school. Children born with physical impairments, those living with serious illnesses, or pupils who rely on a stable home environment all deserve an education. Remote platforms allow these young people to participate without risking exposure to crowded corridors, limited wheelchair access, or the strain of long bus rides. Their right to learn is therefore protected, and distance learning serves as a practical tool for inclusive schooling.

The online setting can also cut down on common school‑related problems such as bullying and excessive drama. In traditional classrooms, a significant number of pupils experience harassment, while some create unnecessary conflict. When students study from home, they avoid daily encounters with peers who might trigger such issues, giving them more mental space to focus on the curriculum and less opportunity to become involved in petty disputes.

Critics argue that staying at home may breed laziness and irresponsibility. Yet, evidence suggests that the quality of education, not the location, determines a student’s work ethic. If a learner becomes idle, the fault lies with personal habits or motivation rather than the mode of delivery. Allowing students to choose their preferred learning environment encourages them to take ownership of their progress; those who succeed online will likely develop the same discipline they would need in a brick‑and‑mortar school.

In sum, remote learning offers several concrete gains for attendance, inclusivity, and a safer social climate, while the fear of increased laziness is overstated. The system’s effectiveness depends on students’ commitment, not on forcing everyone into a single classroom setting.

Many people claim that teamwork is the best way to get things done, while others argue that working alone has its own advantages. Below are some reasons that support each viewpoint.

I think working in a group is generally more helpful because it opens up a range of viewpoints. When several minds come together, fresh ideas appear that you might never think of alone. Also, the workload can be divided so that everyone can concentrate on a specific part, which often speeds up the whole process. For example, last year in my driving‑education class we were asked to create a campaign on road safety. First, we brainstormed individually, then shared our notes. After discussing and selecting the strongest points, each of us took responsibility for a section—research, design, writing—and we handed in the final project before the class ended.

Some argue that working solo lets you stay focused and follow your own creative path. Without the distraction of others, you can dive deeply into the subject and develop something truly personal. I recall a classmate in my biology course who decided to handle her final‑project alone. She stayed concentrated on the topic, gathered all the needed information, and then produced an imaginative poster that matched the theme perfectly. The teacher praised the work and gave her an A.

In summary, group work brings me the greatest benefit. It reduces the amount of effort each person must invest, combines multiple perspectives, and lets you discuss ideas freely. These advantages are harder to obtain when you work alone.

Would you be happy with a longer school day, adding two extra hours so that the week consists of only four days of ten hours each? My answer is a clear no. Making the school timetable longer would squeeze out the little space we have for family, other duties, and a proper rest period. It would also increase fatigue and make it harder to stay motivated. Below I explain why I think keeping the current schedule is the better choice.

First, many students need time to be with their relatives. Some families live far away, and the only moments they can spend together are short visits after classes end. If the school day stretches by two hours, those visits would disappear, making it tougher to keep close bonds with grandparents, aunts, or cousins. Others want to see their cousins more often, especially when weeks have gone by without a chance to meet. A quick get‑together after school can be a bright spot in the week, and adding extra school hours would force students to skip those gatherings.

Second, a number of pupils have responsibilities that start right after the final bell. A good number play sports and must head to a practice field or gym the moment school finishes. Adding two hours would leave them no time to reach the training ground or to rest before the session begins. Some have younger siblings to look after, because their parents work late or have other commitments. Those students must be home early, prepare meals, or keep the kids entertained; a longer school day would clash with these duties and could cause problems at home. A few teenagers also hold part‑time jobs, and they need to start work on schedule. For them, any delay would mean missing a shift, which could affect their earnings or their chances to keep the job.

Third, free time is valuable for everyone, not just for relaxation but also for simple enjoyment. Many students like to meet friends after school, go shopping, or spend a quiet evening with their parents. When the day already feels long, these activities are often the only moments when they feel free. If school were two hours longer, those leisure moments would disappear, leaving students stuck both at school and at home. The pressure would build, and enthusiasm for studying could drop.

Fourth, extending the school day would almost certainly increase exhaustion. Ten hours of instruction already leaves many feeling drained, and another two would make the fatigue worse. After such a long period, focusing on homework or personal tasks becomes difficult. I know this from experience: after classes I usually need to take care of my little sister while my mother is away. If my day were longer, I would arrive home too tired to help, and I might simply fall asleep instead of completing any work.

Lastly, we are still relatively young, and the years we have before adulthood fill up quickly. If we surrender more time to school now, the period for family trips, hobbies, and simply unwinding will shrink further. This could lead to burnout, especially for those who already feel the workload is heavy. Therefore, I believe the current schedule should be kept, and adding extra hours would not benefit students.

In short, lengthening the school day would take away family moments, clash with after‑school activities, eliminate leisure time, increase tiredness, and shorten the free years we have left. For these reasons, I oppose extending the timetable by two more hours.

Some researchers argue that teenagers who decide on a career path before entering high school are more likely to achieve success later on. While it is true that early focus can speed up progress in a particular field, I believe that encouraging such commitment at a young age creates more problems than benefits. The main difficulty lies in the mental strain that students experience during these years, the pressure they feel from external expectations, and the reality that high school itself changes many minds as students discover new interests.

First, high school can be a stressful environment if a student clings to a single career choice from the start. Although it may appear to be a straightforward time to pursue a dream, the school years are actually filled with many competing demands. By locking onto one professional goal, a student may feel constantly anxious about whether every action will bring them closer to that target. The fear of failure becomes stronger when the deadline feels early, and the young person ends up worrying that any misstep could jeopardise the entire plan. Moreover, concentrating on one path often narrows the ability to think creatively in other subjects. As a result, the student’s overall academic performance can suffer, and the stress may become difficult to escape. High school is designed to broaden horizons, not to cement a fixed trajectory, and trying to stay in a rigid position can be counter‑productive.

Second, the kind of pressure that comes with early commitment is not a healthy motivator. Many people treat pressure as something exciting, but in truth it can be overwhelming. When a teenager feels they must succeed to impress parents, teachers, or school administrators, the motivation shifts from personal interest to external validation. The more pressure builds up, the greater the risk of mental exhaustion, mood swings, and a sense of being forced into a role that does not belong to them. Over time, this emotional strain can lead to burnout or even depression, turning what was meant to be a source of strength into a source of weakness. Rather than thriving, the student may lose sight of who they really are, spending energy on pleasing others instead of exploring genuine possibilities.

Third, high school itself offers many opportunities that can reshape a student’s thinking. The difference between middle school and high school is significant: classes become more challenging, and a wide range of elective subjects is available. Because of this variety, many students change their minds about future careers after trying new courses. It is impossible to know what one truly enjoys without exposure to different disciplines, and committing early can close the door on those discoveries. For instance, a student who thought they wanted to become a journalist might find a passion for computer science after taking a programming elective, or a budding engineer could develop an interest in graphic design. These unexpected turns are valuable learning experiences, and resisting them only limits personal growth.

From my own experience, I have learned that it is wiser to keep an open mind during high school. I tried several subjects that interested me, kept those that resonated, and shifted to other fields when a new one seemed more appealing. The reality portrayed in movies and TV shows does not reflect how schools actually work; career choices are seldom made in a single decisive moment. Everyone’s path is unique, and treating “career” as a fixed label can be misleading. Rather than pushing oneself into a rigid plan, it is better to experiment, reflect, and let natural interests guide the journey.

In conclusion, while early career dedication may seem advantageous, the added stress, unhealthy pressure, and the dynamic nature of high school make it a risky strategy. Students should use their teenage years to explore a range of subjects, develop a solid foundation of knowledge, and discover what truly motivates them. By allowing flexibility rather than forcing early commitment, they can protect their mental health, stay adaptable, and ultimately make more informed and satisfying choices about their future.

Have you ever been to a new city or countryside where everything feels unfamiliar? I often ask myself what I would do to stay busy when I arrive. The main pastimes I enjoy are exploring sights, jumping into water, and moving through hills or forests to reach my goal.

If I could travel anywhere, Jamaica would be my first choice. This island provides a wealth of places to visit: sunny beaches, towering mountains, and lush tropical forests. On a beach I would swim in the clear ocean, feel the cooling water, and maybe search for sea creatures beneath the surface. In the mountains I would hike up to lookouts, breathe fresh air, and take photographs of panoramic views. I also like the idea of simply lying on soft sand, listening to the sound of waves, and enjoying the warm sunshine.

Food is another reason I would pick Jamaica. Local eateries serve staples such as rice and beans, while the countryside provides ripe coconuts and bananas hanging from trees. In rivers and streams you can catch crayfish and other small fish, then prepare them by frying. This mix of market dishes and foraged ingredients would let me try new flavors and change my usual eating routine.

The island also boasts a wide array of animals. You can see chickens wandering around, and hear the calls of birds that fly or perch on branches. Stray dogs are common on the streets, adding a lively touch to the scenery. Near water you may encounter crabs with claws or fish with fins, both of which are interesting to watch. I would also look for frogs—some poisonous, others harmless—and goats grazing on grassy patches. Snakes, some equipped with fangs, might also be spotted, though from a safe distance.

All these elements—ample outdoor opportunities, tasty local fare, and a diverse fauna—make Jamaica stand out from many other destinations. The natural beauty combined with the cultural richness offers something for everyone. For these reasons, if I could travel anywhere, Jamaica would be my top choice.

Most schools now provide a distance‑learning option that lets pupils join lessons from their homes using the internet or video calls. I believe this is a valuable addition to the range of educational choices because it can help many students manage their studies more effectively. A few years ago I faced a series of family difficulties that made attending school almost impossible. Had I been able to study at home, I could have kept up with the coursework without falling behind. Some young people simply do not thrive in a traditional classroom environment, and they often find it easier to concentrate when they are alone with their materials. Others who constantly find themselves in trouble with classmates or the school rules might benefit from a setting where there are fewer distractions and no peer pressure.

Parents often argue that school attendance builds character and prepares us for adult life. While I do not deny that regular school can be helpful, I think students should be allowed to decide which setting works best for them, and parents should support that decision rather than insist on a one‑size‑fits‑all approach. The amount of work we are required to complete does not change whether we are learning in a classroom or at home; all assignments, tests, and quizzes have the same deadlines and grading criteria. The only real difference is the location. By staying at home, we avoid the social friction that some students find stressful, and we can finish tasks without unnecessary interruptions.

One common worry is that distance learners might cheat more easily because there is no direct supervision. It is true that we cannot see exactly what each student does during an exam, but the same concern exists for any test taken at school if we do not have robust monitoring tools. The potential for cheating does not outweigh the advantages of flexibility, especially for those who struggle with interpersonal dynamics or personal circumstances. From my perspective, online or video‑conference classes are far from a disaster; they provide a genuine chance to learn without the added stress of fitting into a crowded environment.

Overall, allowing students to attend classes remotely offers a practical solution for a variety of situations. It respects individual needs, reduces the pressure of navigating school relationships, and keeps the workload fair for everyone. For me, and for many peers who have faced similar challenges, having the choice to learn from home would make school a less intimidating experience while still maintaining academic standards.

Education plays a major role in shaping the lives of young people, giving them the tools they need to think critically and solve problems later on. My view is that school leaders should not lengthen the school day. The present timetable already offers about seven hours of academic and personal growth, and adding another hour and a half could create more stress, reduce free time, and clash with the schedules of teachers and families.

During a normal day, students often begin by rushing to catch a bus or waiting at the school gates. Once inside, they try to keep up with lessons, tackle homework that was given earlier, and organize their belongings for the next period. Between classes they may worry about finding an empty locker, and after school they frequently debate how to split their time with friends who have separate project deadlines. These moments show that the current schedule already demands a fair amount of attention and can be quite taxing for pupils.

If the school day were extended, many of these challenges would become more intense. Teachers might hand out additional worksheets, and students would have to finish more assignments during the school hours themselves. Some subjects could lose interest because pupils would be forced to stay longer on already familiar material, while others would be cut short in order to fit everything into the extra time. Consequently, the day would feel even busier and less predictable, leading to higher levels of anxiety for many learners.

A longer school day would also cause difficulties for families and staff. Students who participate in sports, music, or other clubs need a solid block of time after school to practice or rehearse. Parents who rely on regular working hours would find it harder to pick up their children on time, which could affect both professional responsibilities and family routines. Likewise, teachers would be required to stay later to clean up classrooms, grade extra work, or supervise after‑school activities, creating an imbalance between school duties and personal life.

Of course, supporters claim that a longer day could help students complete homework on campus, explore subjects more deeply, and enjoy a longer lunch or gym period. While those points are true, they do not outweigh the wider problems. The extra time would most likely lead to an accumulation of low‑productivity tasks and a greater sense of overload rather than a clear improvement in learning.

In conclusion, I oppose any plan to lengthen the school day. The existing seven‑hour schedule already allows for substantial intellectual and physical development. Extending it would add more pressure for students, strain family and teacher timetables, and generate conflicts without guaranteeing better educational outcomes. Maintaining the current length seems the most sensible choice.

Thinking about a possible career while still in high school can give students a useful advantage for the years that follow. In many countries, schools expect pupils to decide what kind of work they want to do before they even finish secondary education. Some people believe that making this decision early is a smart move.

One clear benefit is that students can meet their long‑term goals a little sooner. By taking classes that relate to a chosen field, they often earn college credits while still in high school. This means they might enter university with a few semesters already covered, allowing them to finish a bachelor’s degree in two or three years instead of the usual four. Such early progress also saves money, because fewer semesters mean lower tuition fees. It also reduces the pressure of completing a full four‑year programme after other commitments.

Another advantage is that students develop a more serious attitude toward their future. When they select a pathway early, they are motivated to take relevant electives, attend career‑focused workshops, and set personal targets. These experiences help them view education as a purposeful tool rather than a vague requirement. They also learn that they, not their parents or teachers, have to decide which direction they want to follow. This sense of ownership can lower the likelihood of disengagement and make the transition to university smoother. In addition, the clarity of purpose can improve time‑management skills, which are useful throughout college and beyond.

Opponents argue that early specialization can be counterproductive. They claim that high‑school students already face heavy homework loads and extracurricular duties, and adding career‑related requirements might push them toward burnout. Moreover, some think that the extra workload could make students less interested in learning because the focus shifts from broad knowledge to narrow job training. These critics believe that teenagers should be allowed to explore a variety of subjects before committing to a specific path.

However, postponing the decision until university can be risky. At that stage, students must immediately select a major without having any prior knowledge of the field. If they choose poorly, they may invest several years in a programme they find uninteresting, leading to higher dropout rates or prolonged studies that increase debt. The lack of a clear direction often results in indecision, which can delay graduation and limit access to entry‑level jobs. Because they have less time to test different subjects, they may miss the chance to discover a field that truly excites them.

Overall, deciding on a career path while still in high school can be beneficial. It lets students shorten the time needed for a degree, saves money, and builds a stronger sense of responsibility. Although some worry about added pressure, the advantages of early clarity outweigh the downsides. By encouraging thoughtful career planning, schools can help young people enter adulthood with a clearer roadmap and higher chances of long‑term success. Therefore, providing career‑orientation programmes in secondary education is a worthwhile investment.

One issue that comes up often is whether genuine self‑esteem comes from being praised or from actually accomplishing something. Some argue that praising work that is sloppy lowers standards and suggests that only results can truly matter. I, however, think that praise itself is the stronger foundation for real self‑confidence. When teachers acknowledge a student’s effort, it encourages that student to become more self‑reliant, more motivated, and ultimately a better learner.

First, recognizing effort boosts a pupil’s ability to work independently. A comment that points out what a student did well tells him or her that they have the skill to finish tasks without constant guidance. Knowing that a teacher noticed their contribution makes the learner feel capable of handling future assignments on their own. It is also important that praise be earned; rewarding minimal or no effort can create the impression that success is guaranteed regardless of input, which discourages genuine improvement. When genuine effort is acknowledged, the learner sees a clear link between trying hard and receiving positive feedback, reinforcing the habit of working efficiently.

Second, praise builds confidence, which in turn leads to more consistent and thoughtful study. A student who feels confident in his or her abilities is more willing to engage with new challenges, ask questions, and persevere when obstacles appear. This sense of self‑assurance often stems from knowing that the teacher values the work done, not just the final grade. With confidence, learners are motivated to explore deeper concepts, practice more, and ultimately achieve better outcomes. In this way, confidence acts as an internal driver that pushes the student toward higher performance.

Third, regular praise signals that teachers care about each learner’s progress, and this care encourages responsible behavior. Students who consistently turn in work on time, stay focused, and demonstrate maturity are more likely to keep up these habits if they receive recognition for them. Such acknowledgment shows that being organized and attentive is valued, which helps those pupils develop a realistic sense of what it takes to succeed beyond school. In contrast, classmates who are more interested in being popular may ignore schoolwork, disrupt lessons, or otherwise treat education as unimportant. By rewarding disciplined effort, teachers shift the classroom culture toward achievement and away from fleeting popularity.

In short, praising students’ work fosters independence, confidence, and responsible learning habits. When teachers show appreciation, students feel respected and are more inclined to attend classes, stay engaged, and make the most of their opportunities. That, I believe, is where true self‑esteem originates.

Imagine a child learning in a living room rather than a classroom. How would his or her parents react? Would they feel confident that the child is getting a full education? While homeschooling can work for some families, most students are better off in public schools because those settings encourage participation, supply reliable learning resources, and let learners exchange ideas with their peers.

First, public schools push students to take part in lessons. Teachers design lessons that require movement and interaction, not just listening. For instance, physical education periods give children a chance to run, stretch, and play games, turning exercise into fun. Even if a student hesitates to join, the teacher’s gentle encouragement and the structured nature of the activity often draw them in. Outside class, schools organize clubs, sports teams, and field trips, all of which keep young people engaged and active. This continual involvement helps develop concentration, health, and a sense of belonging.

Second, public schools make it easy for students to obtain the information they need. Schools provide textbooks, online databases, and libraries that many families could not afford on their own. Teachers remain available after class to answer questions, and study groups form when students feel uncertain about a subject. If a pupil wants extra practice for an upcoming test, they can stay behind, work on homework with peers, or ask for tutoring. This support network ensures that misconceptions are cleared up quickly, and learning gaps are filled before they become problems. The key is that children know help is always within reach.

Third, public schools create opportunities for sharing ideas. Assignments are often completed in pairs or small teams, so each student hears a range of viewpoints. During debates, students must argue their points and respectfully consider opposing opinions. This collaborative environment teaches them how to articulate thoughts, listen actively, and build on one another’s ideas. Group work also builds social skills that are difficult to develop when a child studies alone. The exchange of perspectives often deepens understanding and sparks creativity.

Homeschooling, on the other hand, can feel isolating. A learner working at home may have no classmates to discuss topics with, limited access to a well‑stocked library, and few chances to stay physically active. Parents who lack expertise in certain subjects might struggle to provide the necessary guidance, leaving the child to navigate complex material alone. Such a solitary setting can raise stress levels and diminish motivation. In contrast, a public school offers a balanced mix of support, movement, and teamwork that helps children grow academically and socially.

Because public schools promote participation, provide accessible information, and encourage idea exchange, they are the most effective environment for most young learners. If every child attended school, societies would likely see higher academic achievement, stronger social ties, and more confident citizens. Daily schooling steadily builds knowledge and equips students with the skills they need for future challenges. For those reasons, public schools remain the best choice for most children.

I agree with Author Emerson because you can be perfect in what you do and perfect in life, but you have to try to do something beyond what you have already mastered to keep growing.

You can be a talented musician or an excellent soccer player, but becoming even better at what you love requires more than simply doing what you already know. In fact, Emerson’s idea that we must go past what we have already mastered applies not only to sports but also to personal achievements and everyday life. I am Alex, a student‑athlete at Oakridge High, playing both soccer and football. From my training in the gym and on the field I see clearly why Emerson’s view is right.

My first reason is that growth comes from taking bigger steps, not staying at the same level. If I want to increase my strength and stamina, I cannot keep lifting the same weights or running the same distances every day. The only way to improve is to add more intensity, increase the load, or extend the time. In the weight room my goal is to become stronger, yet I notice that a routine of identical lifts never produces results. Likewise, when I add extra repetitions or increase the difficulty of my drills in soccer and football, I see measurable progress. Emerson’s principle, therefore, shows up in the most practical way: without challenging yourself beyond your current skill, you stop improving.

A second point is that surpassing familiar limits gives you a better chance to win in competition. Think of the rivalry between Uber and Lyft. Both ride‑hailing firms have solid platforms, but Uber secured a larger market share by constantly expanding its services, improving its technology, and testing new pricing models. In my own teams I am not the only striker in soccer or the only cornerback in football, so to earn a starting spot I must train harder, practice smarter, and explore tactics that are beyond my usual comfort zone. By pushing past what I already know I can outperform teammates who are content with their current level, and that same effort translates into success on the field.

Third, striving for bigger steps is essential for life success. Jeff Bezos started Amazon from a garage; he could not have become the world’s most powerful retailer without daring to scale up, take risks, and invest in new ideas. The same logic works for Apple: each new iPhone generation offers more features and a better user experience, which keeps customers buying. Even Donald Trump, who already possessed wealth, fame, and a lavish lifestyle, decided to run for the presidency because he wanted to achieve something greater than what he already had. Many entrepreneurs get a loan, rent a larger space, and hire staff because they see that modest, incremental changes are not enough to reach their ultimate goals. All of these examples demonstrate that real achievement often demands leaps beyond what we think we can do.

Some might argue that simply trying new activities is sufficient for growth, without the need to go beyond existing mastery. Yet adding one more drill to an unchanged routine does not make me stronger, and staying in a garage does not automatically attract customers. Growth happens when you raise the weight, enlarge the market, or secure financing—actions that are more ambitious than the previous steps. In other words, true development depends on stepping further into the unknown, not just strolling into a slightly different part of the same path.

I agree with Emerson because perfection, whether in art, sport, or career, does not remain static. To keep moving forward you must consistently reach for something beyond what you have already mastered. This habit of pushing boundaries is what turns good players into champions, decent athletes into starters, and ordinary people into leaders. Without it, progress stalls and the chance to become truly successful fades.

I am opposed to lengthening school hours, because it would place an unreasonable burden on both pupils and staff and would treat teachers unfairly. Extending the day by an extra hour and a half is not a sensible solution, especially when other schools are already starting their lessons earlier. Insufficient sleep can hurt academic performance and classroom participation, and the same problem would affect teachers, making it harder for them to stay focused during the day.

If the timetable were increased by one and a half hours, many students would feel uncomfortable, as they need time for both study and relaxation. The extra time would cut into after‑school clubs and activities, leaving students exhausted and unable to finish homework or prepare for the next day’s lessons. Starting the day earlier would also disrupt sleep patterns, so pupils would struggle to stay alert in class and would miss out on the rest they need.

In addition, longer school days would squeeze out personal responsibilities. Homework and extracurricular practice often dominate evenings, leaving little space for chores or family duties. With sports, swimming, and gymnastics sessions taking up time, students would find it increasingly difficult to balance school work, activity commitments, and the basic tasks their parents ask them to complete.

The proposal would also strain teachers’ schedules. They would have to stay at school later, reducing the time they can spend with their own families. Moreover, the extra hour would require more preparation and grading, so teachers would be working harder after the regular day ends, which could affect their well‑being and job satisfaction.

These reasons make me strongly against adding an extra hour and a half to the school day.

I believe that changing the school’s lunch menu to include healthier choices is a positive step. Many pupils regularly consume fast‑food and other highly processed items, often at home or on the way to school, because they have become accustomed to these flavours and because unhealthy products are displayed at eye level in shops and vending machines. This constant exposure makes it harder for young people to pick nutritious foods even when they are available.

School cafeterias should be required to serve at least one piece of fruit or a serving of vegetables with every meal. Some students refuse these options because they are not interested in them or simply discard them. Nevertheless, fruits and vegetables provide clear benefits—for instance, carrots support eye health. When a student does not want a fruit or veg, it could be offered to a classmate who enjoys them, reducing waste.

Choosing a balanced diet reduces the likelihood of serious health problems, while regular intake of junk food can increase risks of obesity and related illnesses. Parents have an important role in monitoring what their children eat for breakfast, lunch, and dinner. If a family prefers home‑cooked meals, packing a lunchbox is a practical alternative, and allowing occasional treats once or twice a week is reasonable rather than eating unhealthy items every day.

In conclusion, schools should update their menus to reflect the shifting priorities of today’s society: more fruits, vegetables, and overall healthier lifestyles. Although a small amount of less nutritious food can still be part of a student’s diet, the overall goal should be to lower the frequency of junk‑food consumption and promote well‑being for all students.

Most students enjoy summer vacation, but some educators think that summer break is too long and students do not retain information as easily as they would in the fall. Because of this a lot of educators think we should have year- round school years. This would be shorter breaks in the summer (3-4 weeks) and longer more spread-out breaks throughout the year. I disagree with this statement and believe that summer break should stay the way it is.

The first reason I disagree with this statement is that it would ruin certain summer activities or even business plans. Think about all the activities in the summer that kids usually take part in, this could be sports, some sort of trip, etc. All of these activities students would preferably do during summer break. They have this preference because they see the summer as a perfect time to do all these activities without having to balance their education as well. They can put most of their time on this activity. The same preference applies to things like summer jobs or internships. During the summer they can learn important values like how to save and earn money. Or if a certain student has a chosen career path they can explore this career path by going in a internship for that spesicifc job. For all of these activities students at the very least would be discouraged to participate in if there was a year-round school year.

The second and probably most important reason is pertaining to the students mental health. An article, by Complex News writing about kids mental health stated, that over 40% of kids by the end of their freshmen year in high school are depressed or overall feel exhausted and depleted mentally. The article continues to say that this number from the time of their freshmen year only increases after each school year. Students use the summer break as a way for their brain to refresh from the long almost ten month school year. Students need this time to relax their brain and get ready for the next year of education. As a student, I can say that during school my brain goes into this state where I am mostly just focused on school work. And I can admit that my brain at multiple points during the year is worn down and damaged by always be in this state. My brain does not get a chance to heal from this until the summer, when school is over. So if we were to hypothetically have a year-round school year, this would mean that the brain would also be in this damaged state year round. If this were the case than the brain of the student would eventually just break and shut down. No student should have to experience that because of a year- round school year.

Although the strongest reason for this year-round school year is that students cannot properly retain enough information for the next school year, I think I have a much stronger counter claim and solution to this problem. A very simple way to take care of the problem of retaining information, is to make mandatory (but simple) assignments from the previous year for the student to complete so that they don't forget this information. This way students can have their long summer break to refresh their brain and do their activities, without them having to forget any information. You get the best of both worlds with no need for a year-round school year.

In conclusion I think my assertions for the summer break to stay the way it is is much stronger than year-round school year argument. Having a year-round school year would be unnecessarily tedious and dangerous as it would negatively affect summer activities and mental health. As someone said once upon a time "Don't fix it if it ain't broke."

School is a stage where students receive assignments and must decide whether to complete them. The way we approach our work influences how teachers see us and shapes our future growth. I take issue with a common practice: teachers who congratulate students who only give a little effort. In my view, true confidence arises from real achievement, and it is misleading to reward half‑finished work.  

Firstly, praising minimal effort makes learners overly dependent on external approval. When praise is the primary form of encouragement, pupils start looking for constant validation. In a world where help is not guaranteed, they may feel insecure and unable to keep going without applause. If that supportive voice disappears, they might simply quit because they lack inner motivation. Moreover, children who expect praise for trivial tasks become attached to that validation, relying on teachers to push them forward.  

Secondly, too much praise can prevent students from attaining genuine success. When someone is applauded for trying alone, they may think the task is already finished, even if it is incomplete. This false feeling of completion discourages further effort, leading to lower‑quality work and missed learning. Over time, such students may think they are competent while still lacking the skills needed for tougher assignments. When real challenges arise, they may fail because they never built the discipline required for deeper work.  

Nevertheless, encouragement can have positive effects. A sincere compliment can boost self‑esteem and keep a pupil motivated, even after school ends. Motivated students might also inspire classmates to work harder. However, teachers should not applaud the simplest actions, such as writing a name, or give praise that feels empty. Sometimes a firm comment is necessary to show what really matters, and an early correction can later promote growth.  

My recommendation is that educators direct praise toward genuine effort and measurable progress, rather than toward superficial tasks. They should still be ready to help, but only when a student shows a sincere willingness to try. This balance allows students to become independent while knowing support is available when needed. I hope schools will adopt this approach, rewarding those who strive hard instead of merely those who show up.

When a young runner crossed the finish line at the county meet, the crowd erupted in cheers. It was a moment that showed how much effort she had put into training and how rewarding it felt to achieve a personal goal. Sports, in particular, give them a chance to unwind, meet new friends, and focus on personal improvement. Recent studies have shown that active students concentrate better in class than those who remain sedentary at home. One student who joined a running group soon made friends and felt more energetic each day, turning a previously exhausting routine into a source of pride.

Before she started training, she felt constantly tired, but after a few weeks of regular practice she noticed a boost in stamina and mood.

Providing extracurricular opportunities not only fills the afternoons but also helps shy students form friendships and acquire new skills. When students start high school, many already have strong ideas about their future profession. For example, a young man named Generic_Name decided in his freshman year that he wanted to become a surgeon. He carefully selected relevant courses, pursued internships at hospitals, and eventually achieved his goal, earning a good income and stability. In some educational systems, pupils are encouraged to choose a career path before entering secondary school. I fully support this practice because early clarity offers practical benefits and eases emotional pressure.

The first advantage is that knowing your desired job allows you to map out the necessary steps. To qualify for positions, you must understand workplace demands, required qualifications, and earning potential. This means researching industries, identifying key skills, and selecting appropriate subjects. If someone aims to be a historian, they might focus on literature and social studies; aspiring doctors would prioritize biology and chemistry. Planning ahead also helps manage financial expectations, as certain careers require specific training costs or provide different salary prospects. Without this groundwork, students may waste time on irrelevant classes or miss vital preparation stages.

A second benefit is reduced stress during adolescence. Having a defined goal lessens the fear of the unknown. When you know what career you want, you can design your academic schedule around essential subjects, avoiding extra, unhelpful courses. This focus also encourages timely help-seeking, such as from counselors or tutors, which further prevents anxiety. On the contrary, delaying decisions often leads to last-minute scrambling—students might pick random electives, struggle with college applications, or feel overwhelmed by pressure. Clear choices foster confidence and smoother transitions into post-secondary education.

Critics argue that high school should prioritize social development over career planning. They claim young people might discover their interests later, perhaps in senior years, and forcing early decisions harms enjoyment. However, waiting too long risks academic disorganization and emotional strain. Without a plan, students often lack direction for college majors, struggle to find relevant internships, and face higher stress levels during crucial application periods. Early commitment does not eliminate exploration; it simply grounds it in actionable steps.

In societies where early career awareness is valued, students gain a head start in achieving their ambitions. By setting goals before high school, they can organize their studies effectively and minimize anxiety. This approach ensures they enter adulthood with a realistic roadmap and a sense of control over their future.

Adding an extra ninety minutes to the school day might seem like a way to cover more material, but it would most likely harm the students it intends to help. Picture a typical afternoon: after a long period of lessons, tests and assignments, a student finally steps out of the classroom. The school day then stretches for another hour and a half before they can go home. Most teenagers would feel exhausted, overwhelmed, and ready for a break rather than eager to study further.

One reason this extension is problematic is that it would increase the amount of work students already have to manage. The longer school day means more classroom time, which naturally leads to more homework and projects. Many pupils already struggle to finish the required tasks on time; adding an extra half‑hour would push them over the edge. Without enough time for rest, concentration drops, and grades could suffer. In practice, this means that students would be less able to participate fully in lessons and would probably feel a constant pressure to meet deadlines.

Another issue concerns extracurricular activities and personal safety. Young people often take part in sports, clubs, or part‑time jobs after school. If the day ends later, they might arrive at practice or games already drained. For instance, a classmate of mine who plays soccer collapsed on the field because her body and mind were too tired after the extended school session. Moreover, when the school day runs until dark, students return home under poor lighting conditions, which raises safety concerns and puts them at a higher risk of accidents or injury.

The longer school hours would also squeeze out time for family, friends, and relaxation. Students would likely have to postpone social gatherings or family meals to finish assignments, while teachers would find it harder to balance their own personal lives because of the increased workload. Even after school, the dominant thought would be about upcoming exams or papers, leaving little mental space for enjoyable activities. As a result, motivation to engage in hobbies or simply unwind would decline, and many would feel burnt out.

Finally, prolonged fatigue can affect mental health. Over time, students may become irritable, lose interest in school, or even develop depressive feelings. When energy levels are consistently low, attendance can drop, and the overall school environment suffers. The risk of students disengaging from their education becomes far greater than the benefit of a few extra lessons.

In light of these points, the school board should reconsider any plan to lengthen the school day by ninety minutes. The extra time would create more classwork, cut into after‑school activities, increase safety worries, reduce family and social interaction, and potentially damage students’ emotional well‑being. A shorter, more balanced schedule is far more likely to support both academic progress and personal health.

High school is often imagined as a blank slate for every interest, but in reality students must navigate a schedule packed with mandatory subjects that aim to pave the way to college. While science, math, and language classes meet graduation requirements and prepare for future study, electives such as art, music, and drama supply something the core curriculum cannot: a moment of relief from endless essays and formulas. In those rooms, learners can paint, compose, or act alongside classmates, turning a focused, sometimes stressful day into a playful exchange. The social atmosphere of such courses encourages collaboration, listening, and informal conversation, skills that are less emphasized in lecture‑driven subjects.

Because most high‑schoolers juggle grades, standardized tests, and college applications, the mental load can become overwhelming. When the pressure mounts, a dedicated arts period acts like a light‑weight break, lowering anxiety and offering a chance to recharge. Moreover, the relaxed environment often leads to spontaneous learning: a student who never imagined herself singing may discover a love for vocal performance, while another who never considered drama might find confidence on stage. Those experiences can reshape career dreams and broaden personal horizons, proving that a purely academic focus does not cover all routes to success.

Consider a student who hides behind a textbook, never raising a hand in math class, even when the teacher asks for a question each unit. If he continues through school without practicing speaking in front of others, it is unlikely he will develop the courage needed to give presentations or negotiate in a corporate setting, regardless of his intellectual gifts. Being able to express thoughts clearly is a social skill that fuels advancement; without it, even brilliant ideas remain unheard. Life’s climb—whether climbing a career ladder or overcoming personal challenges—demands more than knowledge alone.

Some argue that these electives waste time, describing them as safe havens for gossip and procrastination. Yet for students who feel invisible, sitting alone in a corner, never invited to share an opinion, these courses can be a critical bridge to social participation. Schools have a responsibility to nurture every learner, not just those who already command attention. The advertising slogan “Your voice opens doors” captures this idea: we only receive answers when we dare to ask. Intelligence is valuable, but it loses impact if a person never makes themselves heard.

In today’s competitive world, success often demands that people master several skills, but many settle for tasks that already feel comfortable. The challenge then becomes: how can we continue to improve? Ralph Waldo Emerson’s observation that we will not advance if we keep doing the same thing offers a useful guide. Staying within the limits of what we already know may keep us safe, but it also curtails our potential.

To start, many professions now require workers to broaden their expertise if they hope to advance. Take photographers, for example. Most spend their days capturing still images, yet adding video production skills can open doors to careers in filmmaking or journalism. By learning how to operate a camera on a moving set, they can work as cinematographers, produce documentaries, or report news. Similarly, doctors who are accustomed to a particular specialty often discover new avenues by exploring emerging research fields. A cardiologist who studies regenerative medicine, or a surgeon who adopts robotic‑assisted techniques, finds fresh ways to help patients. Students who study abroad also illustrate the point; living in a different cultural setting forces them to use language, navigate unfamiliar systems, and adapt their thinking, all of which contribute to personal growth. In short, stepping into unfamiliar territory equips professionals and learners with fresh perspectives and tangible benefits.

Furthermore, sticking to one routine rarely yields lasting development. A carpenter who masters building furniture may decide to launch his own business, yet fear of failure can keep him from taking the leap. The same cautious mindset affects entrepreneurs in any field; they might hesitate to invest in new tools or technologies because they are accustomed to proven methods. However, companies that continually upgrade equipment, adopt novel processes, or explore new market segments tend to expand faster than those that repeat the same practices year after year. Even well‑trained athletes illustrate this principle. While repetition builds muscle memory, the best players are those who modify training regimens, experiment with new tactics, and seek feedback from coaches. A soccer player who only practices the same drills will eventually plateau, whereas one who adds agility workouts or mental‑skill exercises often improves faster. The underlying lesson applies across professions: growth is tied to deliberate change.

In conclusion, Emerson’s insight holds true—people rarely achieve their goals when they repeat the same actions without variation. Exploring new domains, whether through career shifts, academic experiences, entrepreneurial ventures, or athletic innovations, is a practical path to continuous improvement. Embracing discomfort, testing new ideas, and taking calculated risks generally bring rewards that staying comfortable cannot provide. Ultimately, success is not about being the sole expert in one narrow field; it is about being open to learning and evolving in many.

The widespread use of digital devices limits the amount of face‑to‑face contact people have, especially for young people. This restriction weakens the development of essential interpersonal abilities. It also makes online harassment and provocation easier, which has become common in many social platforms.

Firstly, technology hampers the formation of social skills among students. When learners walk into a classroom, they often keep their phones close, checking messages or playing games instead of talking to classmates. The constant presence of screens pulls them into isolated worlds, preventing meaningful conversation and reducing opportunities to understand themselves and others.

Secondly, individuals can post content that damages another person’s self‑esteem. A video that ridicules someone may push them toward self‑harm or even suicide. Likewise, a photo showing a person drunk can be shared on Facebook or Instagram and tagged, making the embarrassment public. I have seen such videos on YouTube that illustrate how quickly harmful images circulate.

Thirdly, cyber‑bullying often spills over into real‑world aggression. A case from Australia shows a girl who suffers online abuse and also faces bullying at school; her family has moved at least three times to escape the harassment. This illustrates that online attacks can force families to relocate repeatedly, showing the deep impact on their lives.

Lastly, the internet can be a platform for dangerous meetings and false information. Chat rooms have been used to arrange encounters with violent individuals, and Twitter spread the false rumor that Michelle Obama intended to run for president in 2020. These phenomena demonstrate how technology can bring hidden threats into everyday conversations.

In my view, we should protect real‑world interaction by occasionally putting phones away for a day or two, and by holding social meals without any devices. Schools could ask teachers to keep phones in lock‑boxes at the door so they stay out of sight during lessons. Stronger anti‑bullying rules should also be enforced, because harassment can continue beyond the screen and affect both online and offline life. Overall, limiting phone use and tightening regulations can help restore healthy communication and reduce the harms that technology currently creates.

In my view, offering distance learning as the main way for students to attend school is something I would usually oppose. I’m not basing this on my own experience of a public high school; rather, I have come to this conclusion for several reasons.

First, relying on online or video‑conferencing classes can damage students’ ability to communicate. When lessons are held at home, students are not in the usual school environment where they meet classmates, form friendships, and practice everyday social interaction. Without that regular contact, they mainly interact with the teacher, which limits the chance to develop broader conversation skills. In a physical classroom, peers can help each other understand difficult concepts, share viewpoints, and give immediate feedback. If students learn only from the teacher, they miss out on those collaborative exchanges that are essential for well‑rounded communication development.

Second, online schooling reduces active participation. At school, lessons often include hands‑on activities, group discussions, and quick questions that reinforce the material. Engaging directly with the teacher and classmates helps ideas stick in the mind and lets misunderstandings be cleared up instantly. In an online setting, students may have to wait for an email reply or a chat message, which can slow down learning and lower the quality of feedback. The immediacy of face‑to‑face questions and discussions is hard to replicate, so participation skills tend to decline.

Finally, staying at home makes it easier for students to become unmotivated or to miss classes. The comfort of one’s own room can lead to poor attendance habits, such as sleeping in, forgetting about assignments, or simply losing focus. When a student isn’t disciplined, online courses can quickly affect grades and overall academic progress. This risk is especially true for people who struggle with self‑management. While highly organized learners might thrive in a virtual setting, for the majority, the temptation to slack off outweighs any potential benefits, making online education unsuitable for many.

These points show why I’m generally against making distance learning the primary option for attending school. Although some students have valid reasons for not being on campus, the drawbacks to communication, participation, and personal discipline outweigh the convenience. Schools can keep online learning as a supplementary tool, but they should not replace the regular classroom experience for most students.

Have you ever observed how a person’s judgment about you seems to form in just a few seconds? Many believe that a later encounter can undo that snap assessment, but I hold that a first impression is essentially permanent. It reveals one’s true character, prevailing attitude, and overall sense of self, and these traits are difficult, if not impossible, to disguise.

A first impression acts as a window onto a person’s personality. I once knew a classmate who attended a job interview in casual clothes that were far from professional. The hiring manager politely turned her down on the spot, explaining that the outfit suggested a lack of seriousness and responsibility. She later tried to apply for other positions, yet recruiters kept mentioning the same reason: her attire made them doubt her reliability. This experience showed me that how we dress and how we speak convey respect, maturity and accountability. If a stranger senses that we are careless or disrespectful from the outset, they are likely to treat us accordingly in all future interactions.

The same phenomenon applies to the way we behave in the moment. During high school I used to snap back at classmates, calling names when they asked for assistance. One day an elderly woman in the hallway asked for help carrying a heavy bag, and I shrugged it off, even hurling an insult at her. She warned that my actions would bring trouble later, but I brushed her words aside. Years later I realized how many friends still brought up that incident, even when I tried to behave more kindly. I even thought about apologising, but she had passed away, leaving the warning as a lasting reminder of how our initial conduct can continue to haunt us. That experience reinforced my belief that outward attitude is hard to overturn once it has been seen.

Beyond clothing and speech, a first impression often uncovers the real nature of a person. A recent news story featured a woman who opened a freezer in a convenience store, took an ice‑cream scoop, licked it and slipped it back without paying. When people discover such a lapse, they tend to label the individual permanently, unable to accept a later explanation that might have seemed sincere.

Some argue that a second chance can rewrite the narrative, yet even then the original image tends to dominate. While a few may be willing to overlook past mistakes, the majority will still recall the first encounter when they hear you speak or see you act. The lingering label can color how they interpret any subsequent behaviour, making it difficult for the impression to change at all.

In summary, the way we first come across tells a lot about who we are inside: our dress sense, our manner of speaking, and our underlying attitude. Because these signals are so quickly interpreted, they seldom get erased. Most people will judge you on that initial snapshot for a long time, if not forever. So ask yourself: would you prefer to be seen as courteous or rude, proper or improper, responsible or dismissive the very first time you meet someone? The answer often sets the tone for the rest of your relationship.
