Technology has become powerful enough to allow students and teachers to give and receive classes online. This raises the question of the disadvantages versus the advantages of taking classes online, a dilemma faced today by students deciding whether to take online courses. Often students work part‑time or full‑time jobs while attending school or college, so their time is valuable. Those students want to make the right decisions when choosing classes, and knowing the disadvantages and advantages is important. I believe online classes are a good opportunity for students because they provide flexibility, often offer any type of class desired, and give access to faculty, including accelerated courses.

To begin with, one of the best advantages of online classes is flexibility. A student can usually take a course at any time during the day or week. While custom essay writing and research assignments must still be completed, the precise time to attend the class often depends on the student’s desire. Students who work can schedule the class according to their own timetable. Many work in the afternoon. The flexibility therefore makes it possible to finish the course, whereas attending school or college in person might be impossible due to conflicting work schedules.

Secondly, another great advantage of online courses is that almost any type of course can be found online. Distance‑learning courses are often available from many colleges, and a person can simply use Google to locate a class. While many believe a disadvantage of online courses is that students cannot access faculty members, in fact many online courses provide greater access to faculty. Shy students are able to ask questions and receive answers almost immediately.

Lastly, online courses are convenient for most undergraduate and graduate students, who can study whenever they want and finish writing or researching assignments according to their own personal schedules. The fact is online classes offer flexibility and convenience that are often vital to students who work and have families. Many students also seek advanced courses to finish faster. The best way to advance in a course is to take it online, because in regular schools it takes longer as some students fall behind and teachers wait for them while everyone proceeds at the same pace.

To conclude, with online classes students do all the work at their own pace, as long as they meet their deadlines and participate appropriately online. Also, studying online requires more self‑motivation and time‑management skills because students spend a lot of time on their own without someone physically close to keep them focused on deadlines. Online courses will not only teach students geology or poetry; they will also help them become more self‑motivated—a trait that will make them stand out in the workplace and beyond. It will teach educators to maturely choose the right decisions, encouraging them to explore more and to be students with an open mind.

Technology has become powerful enough to let students and teachers exchange lessons over the internet. Today many learners must decide whether to study in a traditional classroom or online. Many of them work part‑time or full‑time while they pursue their degree, so the way they manage time matters a lot. In order to pick the right course, it helps to know both the drawbacks and the benefits. I think online study offers a valuable chance because it brings flexibility, a wide choice of subjects, easier contact with instructors, and often lets students finish programs faster.

First, flexibility is one of the strongest points of online education. Learners can usually log on whenever it fits their routine. Unlike a fixed lecture schedule, online sessions are recorded or live at set times that the student chooses. A person working evenings can watch a video in the early morning, while a student with a weekend shift can complete reading and assignments after work. Because the clock is under the student’s control, it is easier to balance study with a job and other responsibilities. Trying to attend a campus class at the same time might simply be impossible for someone whose schedule does not match.

Second, the range of subjects available online is impressive. A quick web search can turn up courses in nearly any field, from computer science to literature. Many universities offer their own distance‑learning programs, and a large number of platforms host lessons from different schools. This means that a student who wants to learn about a specific topic does not have to move to another city or wait for a particular semester. Moreover, reaching an instructor is often simpler. Most courses have discussion boards, email, or live chat where teachers respond promptly. Even shy learners who are uncomfortable speaking up in a large room can post questions and get answers quickly, something that can be harder in a physical setting.

Third, online courses often let students set their own pace, which can speed up a program. Instead of moving forward only when the class average catches up, learners can move through units as soon as they feel ready. If a student wants to finish a degree or get a new certification sooner, they can often choose accelerated tracks that skip material they already know or repeat parts they need extra practice. In a traditional classroom, the whole group must wait for the slowest learner, slowing everyone down. The online format removes that bottleneck.

In conclusion, taking classes online means most of the work is done on the learner’s own terms. Success depends on meeting deadlines and taking part in discussions, which calls for discipline and good planning. Because there is little face‑to‑face supervision, students must develop strong motivation and time‑management abilities. Those skills are not only useful for completing assignments; they also become assets in a career and in personal projects, such as caring for a family while studying. By studying online, a person gains knowledge and learns how to stay focused, which helps them stand out in the workplace and beyond. Educators, meanwhile, learn to guide students who are becoming more independent and open‑minded, ultimately creating a more mature learning environment.

First impressions act as a common way we respond to someone we meet, and these initial judgments often depend on whether the encounter feels frightening, amusing, or simply neutral. They appear quickly and usually cannot be altered because they arise instinctively. In other words, we have little control over them; they surface without deliberate effort and tend to stay with us unless we encounter a strong, contradictory experience later.

One reason is that these judgments appear naturally, without any conscious decision. When two strangers meet, each person instantly starts to assess traits such as friendliness, confidence, or nervousness, regardless of who the other is. The same happens when someone moves to a new town or country—each new street, neighborhood, or public place triggers a fresh set of impressions. Even in school, students begin to form ideas about a subject or teacher before they have had much experience, simply because the mind automatically categorises what it sees and hears.

A second reason is the central role of our mental processes in creating these first impressions. For instance, shoppers compare prices on a sale rack and immediately feel whether an item is overpriced or a good deal; the brain supplies the evaluative judgment. Hospital workers, who frequently see patients with serious illnesses, also receive mental cues that shape how they respond, making it easier to give quick assessments. Likewise, immigrants arriving in a new culture experience a sudden surge of thoughts about customs, language, and social norms; their minds adjust and produce impressions almost as soon as they notice differences.

Finally, people rarely anticipate first impressions because they arise spontaneously. When someone sits down for the first time in a cinema and watches a new film, they cannot predict the plot twists or emotional tone, so judgments start to form only after the lights dim. Turning eighteen, individuals suddenly find themselves responsible for many adult tasks, yet they often have not thought about how hard independence will be; the surprise of new duties generates instant impressions. In a workplace, newcomers learn by observing, and without prior knowledge of the job’s routine, they instinctively develop ideas about the environment, workload, and expectations.

In short, first impressions are difficult to overturn because they emerge automatically and are largely driven by our minds. They appear as soon as we encounter something new and we seldom have time to prepare for them. This combination of spontaneous formation, mental processing, and lack of forewarning makes it unlikely that initial judgments will change quickly.

Adding two extra hours to the school day would be a terrible decision. Schools are already places where students feel a lot of pressure, and a heavier workload can bring on headaches, fatigue and sleepless nights. If lessons were prolonged, pupils would have little space to finish their assignments at home, which could push them to pull an all‑night study session. The mental strain of trying to absorb a larger amount of material in the same eight‑hour day may feel like a pressure cooker, and some students could even develop serious health problems. Their bodies would not be able to cope with such constant demand, making it a risky and undesirable plan.

My view is that we should keep the current five‑day schedule instead of trying to stretch the day or take an extra day off. The notion of adding hours simply does not make sense; it would merely shift the same amount of teaching into a longer period. Students would end up spending more time on schoolwork, leaving less room for sports, clubs, family duties or part‑time jobs. Moreover, a six‑hour or eight‑hour school day would feel longer and heavier, raising stress levels, increasing the amount of homework to complete and making many feel exhausted. In my own experience, a longer day makes it harder to stay focused and adds to mental fatigue, which can also trigger headaches. Overall, five days of seven hours each provide enough learning time without overwhelming students.

I believe there are far more effective approaches to protect natural resources than simply lengthening the school day. For instance, schools could encourage recycling programmes, organise clean‑up campaigns for rivers and lakes, and promote simple habits such as turning off lights when they are not needed. These actions teach students how to look after the environment, and caring for the planet is an essential lesson that every school should provide. While many people are careless about waste, they would rather adopt these habits than accept a proposal that adds more hours to class, which would not reduce energy consumption or improve waste management. Using our intelligence, we should aim to create solutions that benefit the whole world, not just our immediate schedule. Volunteer projects, restoring damaged habitats, or forming eco‑clubs are examples of meaningful contributions. When many participants work together, these initiatives become powerful tools for sustainability.

Extending school hours would also cause widespread disappointment. By reducing the free time that students already enjoy, we would be depriving them of essential moments for rest, hobbies, and part‑time work. Overworking leads to physical and mental fatigue, making students lazy and less motivated, and this can upset the entire school community. In addition, exhausted learners are more likely to make mistakes while driving, which could increase traffic accidents. Recent statistics show a rise in crashes, and a longer school day would add to this risk. Therefore, beyond personal health, the social fabric of the school would suffer as well.

Finally, no reasonable person would support a longer school day because it puts health at serious risk. Continually exceeding one’s capacity leads to chronic fatigue, weakened immunity and burnout, which can harm both body and mind. I would not choose to overwork myself, and I doubt many students would either. Such an overload is dangerous and could even endanger lives. Therefore, extending the schedule is not a wise option.

I agree that a positive outlook is the main factor behind success in life. Maintaining optimism is not just a nice habit; it actually creates opportunities that would otherwise stay closed. When we approach school, relationships, or unexpected challenges with confidence that everything will work out, we open ourselves to new possibilities. This mindset helps us face each day’s hurdles—whether they are tough homework, demanding teachers, or personal problems—without becoming overwhelmed.

In school, a positive attitude can turn daily pressures into manageable tasks. Teenagers often juggle early mornings, classmates, and a heavy workload, yet they usually push through because they focus on the belief that they can achieve their goals. It is easy to forget that adults sometimes miss how difficult those years were, especially when schools have changed the requirements for graduation. For instance, today many students must pass SOL tests, a burden that a negative mindset would amplify. In contrast, someone who stays hopeful sees these tests as steps toward a better future, building self‑trust and making it easier to stay on track.

Every person encounters physical and mental obstacles. I experienced this firsthand when I moved to the United States. The language barrier and cultural differences made me feel like my life had been upended. Instead of sinking into frustration, I chose to stay optimistic, which helped me learn English quickly and feel more at home. I also thought about my family back home, who had sacrificed so much for my education, and I did not want to let them down. Those thoughts reinforced my determination to keep going, reminding me that obstacles can be overcome when we believe in a brighter outcome.

Some might argue that optimism is unnecessary if a person lacks confidence or has no one to encourage them. They claim that repeated failures can make anyone quit, regardless of attitude. However, I think a positive mindset changes the way we view failure. When setbacks happen, an optimistic person sees them as temporary and uses them as a chance to rebuild. This outlook keeps us moving forward rather than staying stuck, and it fuels the drive to pursue dreams even when external support is scarce.

In conclusion, waking each morning and expressing gratitude for another day is a powerful habit that strengthens resilience. Life inevitably includes periods when we feel stuck, but refusing to stay in negativity allows us to keep making progress. By holding onto optimism, we open doors to new chapters and maintain the ability to overcome whatever comes our way.

Technology, the crowning achievement of the twenty‑first century, is loved by nearly everyone. When I was younger, some adults warned that it would erode our social lives, and I dismissed those warnings. Yet today I recognize the grain of truth they contained.  

At its core, technology was intended to simplify ordinary activities, not to isolate us or damage our health. I believe that it still holds vast promise, yet we rarely tap into that potential fully. Instead of using it to cut down on routine chores, many people let it dictate unhealthy habits. Rather than cooking meals from scratch, we now habitually order from restaurants that often serve meals far higher in calories. A second major problem is that we have begun to centre our lives around digital devices; if the device were taken away, some feel as if they would collapse. Almost everyone spends time on social applications, and this reliance explains why face‑to‑face dialogue is increasingly sidelined in favour of scrolling through feeds.

Nonetheless, technology does bring clear advantages alongside its drawbacks. One of the most evident benefits is the reduction of wasted time on everyday tasks. Before the era of instant messaging, people relied on letters that could take days or weeks to arrive. Now a message reaches its recipient within a minute or two. In addition, digital tools enable more environmentally‑friendly designs: houses, vehicles and aircraft can be powered by electricity instead of fossil fuels that pollute the planet. Renewable sources such as solar panels, wind turbines and hydroelectric generators provide a continuous supply of clean power. These systems can keep running indefinitely, barring an unforeseen catastrophe such as a sudden loss of sunlight or a global wind drought. As long as the natural cycles persist, we can safely depend on these near‑limitless energy supplies.

From another angle, technology is undeniably a landmark invention for humanity. It carries a variety of negative impacts, but those can be mitigated relatively easily. If we stop allowing gadgets to dominate our existence and instead treat them as secondary tools for communication, the harm can be curbed. The journey of technology has been remarkable: it began merely lighting a bulb and now powers cars, homes, smartphones and entire cities. Practically every human‑made structure contains some technological component.

Finally, all these dazzling innovations have diverted much of our attention, leading to a gradual withdrawal from one another. I see technology as a brilliant creation, yet also as a serious threat to our social wellbeing. By nature, we are communal beings; anything that blocks the opportunity to interact will eventually produce adverse consequences. For millennia we have evolved to thrive through personal contact, and now we are trying to override that instinct. In short, technology is a valuable part of modern life, but it should not replace the social dimensions that define us. Maintaining a healthy balance between digital convenience and real‑world interaction is the key to ensuring that we enjoy the benefits without losing the essence of humanity.

Being yourself helps you discover the best version of who you are. When you stay true to your own nature, you give your inner qualities space to grow and show up in the world. Trying to become someone you are not, just to satisfy others or to seem more impressive, usually hides the real you and makes life harder.

First, authenticity makes you stand out in your own way. You do not need to change yourself to prove a point or win approval. Even if you feel shy, insecure, or have a sharp edge, those traits are part of who you are already. Of course, major events such as the death of a loved one, abuse, or long periods of depression can shift your outlook, but those changes are reactions to external circumstances, not a rejection of your core self. The more you push yourself to become a different person simply because you think that will make you “better,” the more you distance yourself from the person you truly are. If you decide to evolve, it should be to become a version of yourself that you respect, not to hide the original you.

Second, constant attempts to become a new version of yourself can erode the inner person you know. It is easy to mimic a popular style, adopt a popular opinion, or chase a reputation you think will earn admiration. Yet, the most lasting change comes when you do it for yourself, not because friends expect it. Family members often remind us that genuine respect and love come from staying honest about who we are. Even when our habits are unpleasant or our speech is blunt, those same traits can still earn affection within a close circle. Choosing to change only because others point out a flaw usually leads to resentment, because no one else will stay with you when the mask falls away.

Third, our personality is the window to our character. Nobody enjoys being around someone who constantly tries to out‑shine everyone else, as that signals insecurity rather than strength. It is better to present the background you come from, whether that background is modest or modesty itself, than to pretend you belong to a different world just for image. Many people feel pressure to alter themselves to avoid being judged, but doing so creates a false front that eventually feels empty. If a friend or cousin stops talking to you, it is usually because they cannot accept the real you, not because you have become “too quiet” or “unpopular.” Being brave enough to keep your true nature does not mean you become a coward; it means you trust your own judgment when others try to steer you elsewhere.

Fourth, reversing a transformation you have already made can be difficult. By the time you notice the need to go back, you may have developed new habits, formed different relationships, and built a reputation around the new version of yourself. Those connections can become sturdy, making it hard to break away and return to who you used to be. If you decide to change for the sake of improvement, you should accept that change and work with it rather than cling to the old self. The point is not to stay stuck, but to move forward while honoring the reasons that led you to evolve.

Finally, staying true to yourself is the most reliable path to a fulfilling life. It offers a sense of consistency that helps you navigate challenges, build lasting relationships, and feel confident in your decisions. You may not be liked by everyone, but those who matter will respect the person they see. In the long run, the version of you that remains honest will be the one that supports you as you grow older, move out of the family home, and pursue your own goals. So, be the genuine version of yourself, let it guide your actions, and let it bring the best out of you.

Can a person who has truly mastered one skill still continue to grow if they never venture into anything else? Some people argue that once they have reached a high level of competence in a single area, there is no need to look elsewhere. They feel it is acceptable to devote all their time to that one profession, believing that mastery alone is enough. While focusing on one craft can bring confidence, it also creates a narrow mental box that restricts further development. If someone decides to stay within the boundaries of what they already know, the overall expansion of their knowledge and abilities is likely to stop.

Consider the case of Ms. Lee, who runs a small shop selling houseplants and offers classes on caring for them. At first, she was passionate about showing customers how to nurture seeds and watch them become full‑grown plants. After a few years, the shop was thriving and many of the plants she tended had reached a stable size. Ms. Lee began to think that her job was finished once the seedlings were strong enough; she stopped checking on them regularly and assumed they would continue to flourish on their own. In reality, the plants stopped developing because they were no longer given proper care and attention. This mirrors what happens with individuals who rely solely on their mastered skill. Once they believe their expertise is sufficient, they stop seeking new challenges and their potential stops growing.

Growth, however, is closely tied to the breadth of knowledge a person accumulates. Knowledge can be deepened when people explore beyond their comfort zones. In the example above, Ms. Lee eventually recognized the gap in her understanding. She enrolled in an online course that covered tropical plants from distant regions and attended workshops on sustainable horticulture. Her curiosity led her to study botany at a community college, where she learned about ecological relationships and breeding techniques. These extra experiences broadened her expertise far beyond the original seed‑starting business. As a result, she earned a reputation as a leading specialist in rare and exotic flora, and her shop expanded to include a research corner where visitors can experiment with new growing methods. The lesson is clear: when people are willing to pursue additional learning, their overall competence increases.

Some might claim that mastering a single subject is enough because passion provides the motivation to keep improving. For instance, a friend named Joon pursued architecture at university, dreaming of designing skyscrapers. After graduation, he found a job as a construction site manager because the market for architects was limited. He settled into that role, believing his earlier training would carry him forward. Yet even after becoming proficient in construction logistics, he realized that ignoring the design side of his education left a significant gap. By joining a local design group and studying modern building aesthetics on the side, Joon was able to bring innovative ideas to his projects, enhancing his performance and opening new career possibilities. This shows that while initial expertise can be a strong foundation, ongoing openness to new information and skills is essential for true growth.

In conclusion, people will rarely progress if they refuse to step outside the limits of what they already know. Expanding knowledge requires consistent effort and willingness to explore unfamiliar topics. A single area of mastery can be valuable, but the most effective growth comes from a habit of learning something new every day. By staying curious and embracing challenges beyond their comfort zone, individuals can keep building on their foundation and achieve deeper, more meaningful development.

Students work hard there is no arguing that. They have schoolwork, homework, extracurricular and maybe work, all these things make a students life stressful so it is important that they get a break every once in a while. I believe that students should get a long summer break, instead of a year-round school year, because, firstly, there are other activities that can be done during the summer that keep students minds active, secondly their health is at risk and lastly, summer break is beneficial to school staff as well.

From time to time, people need to get a break from their day-today life they need to take a moment to relax and enjoy their life and maybe discover an interest that they may have. Although school is important and necessary for success later on in life, so are outside experiences that can contribute to the development of a student's 'real life skills'. During summer break there are multiple activities that can be done in order to keep a student's mind active, whether it may be sports, summer camps, summer jobs etc. All these activities allow for their minds and bodies to stay active. Eventhough, they are not keeping their brains engaged in terms of school work and studying they are exposing themselves to new activities that might require them to think critically, open-mindedly and collaboratively; which I feel is essential for real life. For example, a student might be at summer camp and they are put in a group with four strangers and are given a challenging task that requires them to collaborate with the other member of the group, critically analyzing the situation and coming up with solutions and be open-minded to listening and trying to understand the perspectives of their peers. This also reflects their environment in school therefore, it can be said that they are keeping their minds active while outside of school.

Although, not all students might be involved in activities outside of school, some are taking a break from the stress of life itself. Due to all the demands in their life during the school year summer break is a good way to take a breather and take care of themselves mentally. Depression has been very common in teenagers in recent years, and although it may not be entirely due to the stress of school, school does contribute to the detirriation of their mental health. In addition, over-working ones self has negative impacts overall whether they are depressed or not. Too much stress in ones life can have negative effects on their health overall. High blood pressure, hypertension, severe weight loss are a few examples of the effects stress. Furthermore, when stressed our body releases a neurotransmitter called Cortisol, this neurotransmitter in excess can impair a persons thinking and reaction time; which is very important for students as they are required to think in order to complete school work and homework, therefore, if they dont take breaks their grades are probably going to drop due to their inability to think effectively, further contributing to their detirriating mental health.

Lastly, summer break is and essential time for everyone that is involved in schools, such as teachers, administrators, councilors etc. Although schools are intended to educate students, its the school staff that make this possible. This is why we need to give our school staff a break because all the points I stated above also applies to them. In addition, with a long summer break teachers are able to have more time to thoroughly think about their lesson plans for their students as well as have an extended amount of time to live their lives and enjoy time with their family and friends, after all, teachers are humans too and they need to be able to life their lives and forget that they are required to do so much for such little pay.

To emphasize further, I believe that schools should give students a long summer break instead of a year-round school year because a students mind will stay active during the summer through various activities that require students to think open-mindedly, critically and collaboratively. Also, students need a break in order to de-stress for the sake of their health mentally and physically. Lastly, a long summer break is needed for school staff as well because they also need to take a break, as well as the students.

It has been claimed that first impressions are almost impossible to change. I think this claim is mistaken. First impressions can evolve because of personal growth, the influence of the people around us, and the unexpected ways life treats us. These three factors show that a first look at someone is not a permanent label.

First, as we grow older we tend to change our attitudes and behaviour. My mother often reminds me that the boy I was when I was seven or eight is no longer the same person I am now. Back then I was very shy, hesitant to speak in public and overly careful to avoid trouble. Now I feel more comfortable interacting with others, and I no longer worry about getting into trouble the way I did as a child. The same pattern applies to many people: they stop smoking, stop snapping back at teachers, or stop being the class clown once they start to think more about consequences. As maturity sets in, the habits and responses that shaped early impressions fade, and new ones replace them. Because of this development, a first impression formed in childhood can be completely rewritten by adulthood.

Second, the attitudes and actions of people close to us can reshape how others see us. My little brother provides a clear example. When he was younger he barely spoke up, always staying quiet around friends and teachers. After a while, he began to copy the way I behaved in social situations. I usually talk with confidence, calmness, and a willingness to take risks, even when the conversation feels unfamiliar. He observed these qualities and gradually adopted a similar style. Now he feels comfortable approaching anyone he likes and even joins in group discussions without hesitation. This shows that an individual can become a role model for others, and the image people have of them can shift as a result of such influence, whether positive or negative.

Third, life itself can intervene in ways that alter the way people perceive us. A week before my fourteenth birthday my father was arrested. I was devastated and felt that the world had suddenly become unfair. I did not want to celebrate and told myself that nothing would feel right again. The following morning, however, my classmates seemed to think I was still cheerful and carefree. They kept wishing me an early happy birthday, while I was still carrying the heavy news. My inner turmoil made my external mood look flat, and classmates noticed the discrepancy. Instead of greeting me in the usual friendly way, they gave me space, assuming I was upset. As the weeks passed, my lack of jokes and my more serious demeanor earned me respect; they no longer viewed me as a light‑hearted teen but as someone who takes things seriously. The unexpected event forced my reputation to change, proving that life’s twists can reshape first impressions.

In conclusion, saying that first impressions are essentially fixed ignores the reality of how people develop, interact, and experience life’s surprises. My own experience shows that a first look can be softened by maturity, re‑drawn by the actions of others, and altered by life’s unpredictable events. These three reasons together demonstrate that first impressions are not set in stone; they can be revised as we grow, as we influence those around us, and as the world intervenes in our stories.

people argue that a positive attitude is the secret to achieving success. I agree with this view because optimism shapes how we handle setbacks, helps us grow as individuals, and makes us more appealing to employers.

First, a hopeful mindset lets us reinterpret difficult experiences. When something goes wrong, a positive outlook pushes us to search for hidden benefits or lessons instead of focusing solely on the failure. Rather than feeling defeated, we look for ways to improve or adjust our approach. For example, if a student receives a low mark on a science test, they might see the result as a cue to review the material more thoroughly for the next exam. This habit prevents discouragement and keeps motivation high.

Second, an upbeat attitude benefits those around us. Many individuals struggle with financial stress, family disputes, or health concerns. When we respond with kindness, encouragement, or a simple smile, we can lift their spirits and help them feel supported. By listening, offering assistance, or sharing a positive story, we add value to their lives and contribute to a healthier community. Recognizing that our behavior can affect others creates a sense of pride and fulfillment.

Third, positivity improves our professional performance. Modern companies value employees who show enthusiasm, teamwork, and a willingness to help customers. Someone who greets clients warmly, resolves complaints calmly, and participates actively is more likely to succeed in their role. Moreover, a good attitude can attract new job opportunities because recruiters seek candidates who seem eager to learn and improve the workplace atmosphere. In other words, optimism is an asset both inside and outside the office.

In modern life many people believe that it is wiser to set modest targets and reach them than to aim high and risk falling short. I do not share this view. Michelangelo, one of the most celebrated artists, warned that settling for easy victories can be dangerous, because he himself only achieved fame after a long series of setbacks and errors. He felt that it was more valuable to try something ambitious and fail than to succeed at something trivial. I agree with Michelangelo because striving for larger aims lets us learn from mistakes, forces us to take calculated risks, and ultimately helps us grow as individuals.

Michelangelo’s story shows how failures can become stepping stones. He did not become a master overnight; his early work was criticized and reworked countless times. By confronting these setbacks, he sharpened his technique and broadened his artistic vision. We can see a similar pattern in everyday experiences. In a television cooking competition such as *MasterChef*, contestants are judged every week and the weakest are eliminated. Those who are cut lose a momentary triumph, yet they still have the chance to examine what went wrong, adjust their methods, and try again. Likewise, when a teenager prepares for the driving‑permit test, a single wrong answer can feel like a disaster. By reviewing the incorrect questions and studying the missed material, the learner turns a setback into a future success.

Risk‑taking also plays a crucial role in reaching ambitious goals. Big decisions—like choosing a career path, enrolling in a demanding course, or starting a new business—require courage and often involve uncertainty. In the television program *Shark Tank*, inventors pitch their products to investors and most walk away empty‑handed. Those who are rejected do not quit; they revisit their ideas, adjust their strategies, and eventually find a way to secure funding. This perseverance builds self‑confidence and improves communication skills. A comparable example is a job interview. While an online meeting is convenient, meeting in person forces the candidate to present themselves, answer unpredictable questions, and demonstrate commitment. The added pressure makes the experience richer and helps the interviewee learn how to handle real‑world challenges.

Larger goals naturally push us beyond complacency. When a target is easy, we may feel satisfied but stop seeking further improvement. By contrast, a lofty aim demands effort, focus, and continual learning. The skills we develop while pursuing it—problem‑solving, time‑management, perseverance—are far more valuable than the temporary relief that comes from a small win. In this sense, modest objectives can become excuses for avoiding difficulty; ambitious ones force us to stretch our abilities and prepare for any obstacle that lies ahead.

In the end, I maintain that aiming high and occasionally falling short is preferable to achieving modest success with little effort. The experience of trying something challenging teaches us where we need to improve, encourages us to take risks, and upgrades our overall character. Michelangelo’s warning remains true: a small, easily‑reached goal may hide a hidden danger, while a bold goal that we sometimes miss brings far greater long‑term rewards. Embracing this mindset prepares us for the complexities of life and lets us turn failures into future successes.

Some people have heard this quotation before: “The greatest danger for most of us lies not in aiming too high and falling short, but in aiming too low and reaching that modest target.” It is often attributed to the renowned artist Michelangelo. Although not everyone may endorse this view, I believe that setting ambitious goals is generally the wiser choice. By pursuing higher aspirations, we open doors to larger achievements, cultivate distinctive ideas, and increase our chances of fulfilling more meaningful objectives.

First, ambitious targets broaden the range of opportunities available to us. When we think about career prospects, is it better to apply for a straightforward position, such as washing dishes, or to explore as many fields as possible, even those that appear challenging? The latter approach can uncover skills and connections that would otherwise remain hidden. The same principle applies in education. A student who is uncertain about a future career might consider enlisting in the armed forces—a clear but limited path—or enrolling in a university with a wide selection of programs. University studies can improve employment options and may lead to a more rewarding profession than a single, predetermined military route.

Second, aiming high encourages original and deeper thinking. Individuals who keep their goals modest often restrict themselves to familiar routines and rarely test the limits of their imagination. In contrast, those who pursue challenging objectives are compelled to explore new ideas, experiment, and reflect on alternatives. This process stimulates mental growth and can produce unique perspectives. Historical examples illustrate this point: many celebrated artists produced groundbreaking works precisely because they refused to limit themselves. Had they set low expectations for their abilities, they would likely have produced less innovative creations.

Third, high‑impact ambitions make it possible to accomplish larger achievements than modest ones. Consider a school assignment: a student who settles for meeting only the basic requirements will probably receive an average grade, whereas another who strives to exceed the brief will often earn a higher score. When the aim is low, there is a tendency to abandon effort before a worthwhile task is completed. A lofty aim, however, fosters persistence and the willingness to push through obstacles. Thus, aiming higher reduces the chance of giving up on valuable projects.

Critics sometimes argue that ambitious goals can be stressful or lead to burnout. While intense pressure can be harmful, it is not necessary to set unrealistically low targets to avoid stress. The key is to strike a balance that respects one’s own capacities while still encouraging growth. Stress is not always detrimental; in many cases it serves as a motivator that sharpens focus. For example, a student who felt overwhelmed in Japan chose to return to school after realizing that avoiding work only increased anxiety and lowered self‑esteem. By confronting challenges head‑on, she eventually found renewed confidence.

In conclusion, choosing the easy route and settling for modest achievements may seem safe, but it carries the hidden risk of limiting potential and fostering regret. The most satisfying path is one that encourages individuals to aim as high as realistically possible, even if the results are not perfect. Doing so allows us to explore many possibilities, develop unique ideas, and accomplish meaningful goals. By avoiding the temptation to take the low‑risk, low‑reward option, we can live a life with fewer regrets and a richer sense of accomplishment.

Have you ever imagined a school where students of different ages work together on projects, share ideas, and learn side by side? I think such a programme would be valuable for many reasons. First, talking to peers who are close in age often makes explanations clearer. Younger learners sometimes feel shy asking teachers for help because adults can seem intimidating. When they turn to a slightly older classmate, the conversation feels more relaxed, and the older student can present the same material in a way that matches the younger learner’s level of understanding.

In addition, a mixed‑age gathering gives students the chance to meet people they would not normally encounter during the day. While we usually talk to our close friends, there are classmates sitting next to us or in other classes who remain strangers. Organising regular activities where older and younger pupils come together breaks down those invisible barriers. It creates a sense of community where everyone feels welcome, and it encourages friendships that might not develop otherwise.

The programme would also provide a platform for peer tutoring. Older students can offer help on subjects they already mastered, and younger ones can bring fresh perspectives or different ways of thinking. This exchange of knowledge is not limited to the programme itself; it spills over into daily school life, so that every student might learn something new from a peer they pass in the hallway or sit beside in a lab.

Finally, if we want this idea to become reality, the first step is to talk to teachers or the principal. Sharing the thoughts and suggestions that have arisen in our heads shows initiative and gives adults a concrete plan to consider. With their support, we could design the activities, schedule meetings, and monitor progress, making sure the programme meets the school’s goals.

In short, a programme that brings older and younger students together would boost learning, reduce anxiety about asking for help, broaden social networks, and foster a culture of mutual support. By approaching the school staff with a clear proposal, we can start a positive change that benefits everyone in the building.

A positive attitude can be the most effective way to meet your goals, or at the very least a useful extra that makes many aspects of life smoother. When you carry a friendly outlook, you tend to encounter more opportunities and achieve success in your career, relationships, and social circles. For instance, regularly helping coworkers and delivering reliable work makes it far more likely that a supervisor will notice your dedication and consider you for a better role. Similarly, being warm, confident, and caring draws people toward you, and they often respond with similar affection, creating a mutually supportive dynamic in romance.

First of all, displaying a good attitude is often the clearest route to climbing the career ladder. Most managers appreciate employees who are well‑liked because such staff lift overall morale and contribute to a more productive workplace. I saw this in action last year at my uncle’s company, where three staff members were up for a promotion. The majority voted for the person who was approachable and dependable, not the one with the most technical expertise alone. In short, when your attitude aligns with that of your colleagues, they are more inclined to support you and follow your guidance, trusting your judgment as a result.

Second, a thriving romantic partnership depends heavily on a constructive attitude and open communication. Most long‑lasting relationships work because both partners respect each other and discuss issues calmly rather than resorting to conflict. My parents serve as a good illustration: they rarely argue and instead talk things through, finding solutions together. Their experience taught me that a steady, respectful demeanor helps keep love alive and can even prevent a marriage from breaking down.

Some people argue that attitude isn’t essential for success. They claim a tough or abrasive personality can be a marker of achievement and doesn’t block a promising career. A familiar example is the president of my country, whose behavior is often unsettling, yet he has a flawless record in office and remains in power. Nevertheless, everyday citizens remark that they need him as a leader more than they admire his style, saying, “We support him because we need him, not because we enjoy his approach.” This shows that one can attain power despite an unpleasant attitude, but genuine affection from the public will always be limited, and people will never fully embrace someone whose demeanor is off‑putting.

People who combine a pleasant personality with a constructive attitude find daily tasks easier because they communicate more clearly and are perceived as approachable. In contrast, those who keep an odd or hostile manner, regardless of how well they speak, seldom attract friendships. As a result, maintaining a likable, charismatic stance not only opens doors in the workplace but also enriches personal life, making success feel more natural and rewarding. In conclusion, adopting a positive attitude is what turns ordinary interactions into meaningful advantages and transforms life experiences for the better.

The first impressions can change depending on each person. Each person has a different reaction the first time they see something. After that, however, your thoughts can change when you learn more about the other person. The first impressions are important because they are the first reaction of each person. First reactions sometimes can change after one hour or one day.

When a person forms a bad impression of a class on the first day because the class is boring, their reaction can change if the class is fun on the second day. First impressions sometimes depend on your attitude; if you have a negative attitude, your first impressions are negative too. First impressions can be bad, and if a person reacts poorly it can reveal what kind of person they are.

Sometimes first impressions are impossible to change because many people won’t change their initial reaction, but a good impression can shift if the person does something bad.

First impressions can change when you have a good impression of a work because you think it’s easy and fun and you make friends. However, on the second day you meet your boss, who has a bad attitude toward you. That can alter your impression and your thoughts about the work, because you don’t like your boss’s attitude.

A first impression is an important moment because it reflects your first thought about a person or something. This is important because if you have a good impression of someone you can make a good friend.

In conclusion, the first impression can change depending on each person and on your attitude, but it does not always change. Sometimes many people do not change their thoughts about something. Do you imagine if the first impression did not change? That would be bad, because when your impressions remain fixed simply because you think the other person is not cool, you cannot have that connection; you need to know more about the life of the other person.

First impressions are not the same for everyone; each person reacts in a different way when meeting a new situation, and those reactions can shift once more details are learned. The initial feeling matters because it is the very first response we have, and sometimes it evolves after just a few hours or a day of further experience.

When a student steps into a class for the first time, a dull atmosphere can create a negative feeling about the subject. However, if the next lesson turns out to be lively and enjoyable, the original view may change quickly. This shows that early judgments often depend on our own mindset. If we enter a new place with a pessimistic outlook, we are likely to form a pessimistic first impression, and a poor reaction can reveal something about our own character.

In some cases the first impression seems to be fixed, especially if a person already expects the worst and refuses to adjust their opinion. Many individuals hold onto their early thought and do not allow it to be reshaped by later events.

A positive impression can also be altered if the other person later behaves badly. For example, a new job might appear easy and fun at the beginning, and you may make friendly connections with coworkers. If, on the second day, you meet a boss who treats you harshly, your feelings about the work can drop sharply. The impression you have formed influences the decisions you make, such as whether you would consider someone a potential friend.

Because the first impression marks the moment we form an opinion, it can be decisive. A favourable first impression may lead to a good friendship, while a wrong one can cut off future opportunities.

In short, first impressions can change depending on the individual and their attitude, but they are not always flexible. Some people keep their original judgment despite new evidence. If we want to judge fairly, we must keep an open mind and try to learn more about the other person’s life, rather than sticking to a single, initial feeling.

Most students at Generic School are against the idea of lengthening the school day by an additional hour and a half. Roughly nine out of ten pupils say they do not want the board to push the school schedule later each day. Their main concern is that a great many of them already have part‑time work after classes, and a sizable number also have to care for younger brothers or sisters before their parents return home. Giving them even more school time would only increase the strain on already busy routines.

First, a large portion of the student body needs to earn money after school. These jobs help them pay for food, clothing and bills, so they can support their families and avoid asking for an allowance. Because they are often tired after a long day, staying at school for extra hours would make it harder for them to attend their shifts, jeopardising their earnings. In addition, many students look after their siblings while their parents are away. This involves watching the younger children to make sure they do not get hurt, feeding them, changing their clothes and tidying up the house. When the siblings are asleep, the house is quieter and chores become easier, but the responsibility is still a heavy load. Trying to fit in that family duty together with homework, projects and studying leaves little room for rest or leisure.

The regular school workload also adds pressure. Homework is a constant, and while it can be managed, projects are often demanding and take a lot of time. When a project is tough, students sometimes turn to classmates for help, which can be useful but still eats up extra hours. Working together with friends on assignments can be enjoyable, but it also means that students are already spending time outside of class collaborating, leaving even less time for a longer school day. Moreover, the goal of passing high school is a big incentive for families, and students want to show their parents that they are succeeding without having to sacrifice the time they need to earn money or look after younger siblings.

Holding a job, however, has its advantages. It provides personal income, so teenagers can buy things they want without relying on parents. It also gives them a sense of independence and responsibility, and they appreciate being able to avoid a regular allowance. Working with friends at the same place makes the experience more pleasant, as they can travel together and chat during breaks. All of these benefits reinforce why an extra school period would be counterproductive for most students at Generic School.

In short, the majority of students argue that adding another hour and a half to the school day would create too much conflict with their part‑time jobs, sibling‑care duties, homework and project work, and the personal advantages they gain from employment. Because these factors already fill up their evenings, they believe the board should keep the current schedule.

Thomas Jefferson once remarked that taking action is preferable to standing idle. I agree with this view because real progress only comes from doing something, whether the result is a major breakthrough or a small everyday task. Even modest actions add up, turning vague intentions into tangible achievements.

Consider learning a musical instrument despite having no prior knowledge. By sitting down with a book and practicing regularly, the skill gradually improves. Imagine wanting to explore other realms or travel back in history—building a device that makes such journeys possible is possible only when someone starts designing, testing, and refining it. Likewise, everyday chores like tidying a room, preparing a meal, or finishing schoolwork can be completed when we stay focused and keep moving forward.

These accomplishments can be achieved alone or together. In sports teams, players collaborate to win a match, illustrating how joint effort creates results that no single athlete could attain. A video‑game studio brings together programmers, artists, and designers who work side by side to produce games that entertain millions. Even in online multiplayer games, strangers unite to complete quests or dominate opponents, showing that collective action produces outcomes worth celebrating.

Of course, rest also has its place. After a long stretch of work we need sleep, a brief nap, a meal, or time to unwind in front of a television screen. Such pauses help restore energy, keep motivation high, and prepare us for the next day’s challenges. Even a short stroll to the store or a quick cleaning session counts as progress when the alternative is to stay inactive all day.

However, when inactivity becomes a habit, it breeds laziness. We start looking for the easiest way out of every problem, and that mindset can become permanent. Constantly avoiding effort means we lose the drive needed to meet obligations at school or at work. For this reason, staying motivated and actively pursuing our duties is far more rewarding than drifting through life without doing anything at all.

I agree with the idea of individuality because I think it is important to decide for yourself what kind of life you want to live. In my opinion, people who take the initiative to follow their own wishes often feel more satisfied, and that freedom is appealing. I have a large circle of friends, but sometimes they simply imitate what the majority does, which makes it hard for me to stay true to my own preferences. I would rather act on my own thoughts and interests instead of reacting to the expectations of others.

My family does not always understand this point of view. When they speak, I often sense a dismissive tone, as if they do not want to hear my opinions. This creates a feeling of resistance on my part, because I want them to listen to me and support the choices I make. Because of that, I have come to see myself as a person who values personal autonomy; I want the right to be heard and to pursue what I feel is right.

It is clear that many people today depend heavily on other individuals for decisions and reassurance, and I think that dependence can be limiting. The history lessons reminded me that in earlier times, societies placed a stronger emphasis on conformity than on personal expression. Still, I notice that modern life creates a different kind of pressure: people seem to seek attention and validation from peers, which sometimes pushes them to follow popular trends instead of charting their own path.

I believe part of this attention‑seeking behavior comes from the way we judge ourselves by how others view us. In everyday settings, we constantly wonder how we look, what others think about us, and whether our actions align with what is socially acceptable. This can make us overly reliant on external approval rather than trusting our own judgment.

What I like most about my identity is that I try to be friendly and generally positive. I trust my own instincts and do not worry too much about criticism from people around me. If I feel like helping someone, I will do it; if I want to pursue a hobby or a goal, I go ahead without hesitation. My confidence comes from knowing who I am and being comfortable with my own values.

Writing this essay has not been easy for me, mainly because I still struggle with English. I am aware that my language skills are improving, but sometimes the thoughts I have cannot find the right words on the page. Nevertheless, I keep writing because I want to share something meaningful.

Let me tell you about my own life, even though I do not know exactly how to organise these ideas. Two years ago I moved from Puerto Rico to a new country, and my circumstances changed completely. Since then I have begun to appreciate each small thing I obtain, realising how much effort and sacrifice goes into earning them. Even with all the challenges I still feel a strong desire to grow and improve myself.

Adapting to a different language and culture is far from simple. The customs, the accents, even the ways people interact can feel unfamiliar and intimidating. Yet I stay here because I believe in myself, and I have noticed that whenever I set a goal, I usually achieve it—though slowly and sometimes with difficulty.

When you arrive in a new place and meet new people, the experience is mixed. Some individuals are welcoming and supportive, while others are indifferent or even hostile. I enjoy discovering new subjects, new places, and new ideas, but one issue still bothers me: although I am a U.S. citizen and not undocumented, I often feel treated as an outsider because Spanish is my first language. People sometimes assume I am undocumented, which adds an extra layer of misunderstanding and frustration.

The biggest challenge for me over the past two years has been school. It has been one of the hardest obstacles I have faced. Walking into a classroom can feel overwhelming when you feel completely alone. The inability to ask questions or to communicate with classmates makes it difficult to keep up. You watch everyone else engage, and you sit silently, hoping that the lesson will make sense without you speaking up.

In the first months after arriving, I started missing school and performed poorly, partly because I had no guidance at home or at school. The feeling of isolation was intense, and I did not know how to ask for help. Today I still wonder whether I belong in this environment. The only reason I continue to stay is my mother. I want to help her improve her situation and give her the chance she deserves, just as she has always tried to provide for us in Puerto Rico, despite the difficulties.

Looking back on life in Puerto Rico, I realise that despite the hardships, my family always tried to give the best for each other. That same spirit drives me now: to persevere, to learn, and to become the person I aim to be. While the path is not straightforward, I keep moving forward because I know that I am capable of reaching the goals I set for myself, and I hope that one day the world will see me as an individual rather than a stereotype.

Thomas Jefferson once asked, “Do we achieve more when we are always busy, or does inactivity also have a purpose?” People’s answers differ, and I tend to agree that a mostly active life is more productive, though occasional pauses can be useful if they lead to fresh thinking.  

First, some argue that constant activity is harmful and that rest is needed to avoid burnout. It is true that short periods of calm can help us recover and reflect, but those moments should not become long stretches of passive waiting. The value of “doing nothing” lies mainly in its ability to prepare us for the next step, rather than in delivering results by itself.  

Second, many think they cannot improve their situation because of existing limitations. For example, individuals facing financial hardship or limited education may feel they lack the resources to create new opportunities. However, history shows that hardship often sparks unexpected motivation. My grandfather experienced extreme poverty: his family ate only once a day, and his children struggled to survive. Yet he never gave up. He kept saying, “One day everything will change.” After a tragedy, he searched for new ways to earn a living, eventually moving his family out of poverty. His story demonstrates that even when circumstances seem discouraging, persistent effort can uncover new paths.  

This leads to the first core point: genuine progress usually requires struggle. To reach any meaningful goal, we must confront obstacles and push forward, even when it feels uncomfortable. Struggle builds skills, confidence, and the network needed for future success. When we ignore difficulties and stay idle, we miss the chance to develop these resources.  

A second key factor is how we use our time. Those who plan their days carefully and allocate moments for focused work often achieve their dreams faster. Imagine a person who works part‑time, saves money, and follows a realistic schedule to buy a car that costs one million won. Because they manage their hours wisely, they can afford the vehicle while still meeting other responsibilities. In contrast, someone who wastes time on idle activities often finds that the clock has run out before they have saved enough.  

Finally, being connected to other people broadens the range of possibilities. Helping friends, sharing knowledge, and maintaining relationships create a support system that can open doors we might not see alone. When we stay socially involved, we receive advice, job leads, or practical aid that accelerate our own growth. Moreover, cooperation itself generates new opportunities for both parties, turning a solitary effort into a collaborative venture.  

In short, achieving many chances and dreams depends on a balanced mix of activity, thoughtful pauses, effective time management, and social interaction. Those who stay passive or keep doing the same thing day after day usually miss out on transformative experiences. A person who embraces struggle, exploits each hour purposefully, seeks new relationships, and occasionally pauses to assess their direction stands a far better chance of owning the car, buying a house, or realizing other aspirations.  

If we combine these habits—working hard, using time wisely, reaching out to others, and allowing brief moments for reflection—we make the most of our lives. Conversely, if we remain lazy, refusing to move forward or to invest in our future, we may end up feeling regret and longing for the opportunities that passed us by. The choice, then, is clear: a life driven by purposeful action, complemented by strategic rest, is the route to a richer, more fulfilling experience.

Positive attitude is the key to success in life. I agree with this view because a hopeful mindset is what enables us to achieve real progress in work, study, and personal relationships. When we face daily challenges—whether at school, on the job, or while interacting with friends—seeing them as manageable rather than overwhelming makes a huge difference.

One way a positive attitude helps is by improving how we relate to others. Optimism fosters kindness and patience, which are essential for building strong connections. If a coworker becomes upset, a calm, upbeat response can change the tone of the conversation and turn tension into cooperation. Likewise, showing appreciation and empathy encourages people to return the same respect, creating a cycle of trust and mutual support. In my own experience, keeping a friendly outlook has often made it easier to resolve misunderstandings and to work together toward common goals.

A second benefit is the ability to stick with our ambitions. When we expect setbacks, a positive attitude treats them as temporary hurdles rather than final defeats. This mindset gives us the energy to try again, adapt our methods, and stay focused on the end result. I remember a time when a project seemed impossible because I felt stuck and discouraged. By reminding myself that progress, no matter how slow, still counts, I kept pushing forward until I finally completed it. That persistence, which I attribute to my optimistic outlook, is exactly the kind of drive that leads to achievement.

Finally, optimism boosts professional performance. Employers tend to notice and reward employees who show enthusiasm, take initiative, and learn quickly. A constructive attitude encourages us to seek feedback, explore new tasks, and contribute ideas that improve the workplace. Over time, this recognition can translate into promotions and higher pay. In my own career, staying upbeat helped me master new skills faster, take on additional responsibilities, and ultimately earn a better position than I might have otherwise.

In conclusion, maintaining a positive attitude matters because it shapes how we work, study, and connect with other people. Without it, doubts and negativity can prevent us from taking action; with it, we feel empowered to pursue whatever opportunities arise. By keeping optimism alive, we make it possible to turn effort into real success.

Some argue that allowing cell phones in the classroom can be helpful because they give quick access to the internet for research and collaboration. However, the disadvantages outweigh these supposed benefits.  

First, letting students keep phones in the classroom creates noise and visual distractions. When a phone rings or a student watches a video, the sound can interrupt the teacher’s explanation, and classmates nearby may be drawn away from the lesson. Some learners use earphones to play music or follow entertainment apps, which often means they stop paying attention to the material being taught. If a teacher asks a student to stop using the device, a disagreement can arise, leading to arguments or confrontations. Moreover, one student who constantly uses the phone tends to cause repeated interruptions; over time, the class may become disruptive, and the school may decide to ban that student from attending class or even expel them for repeated offenses.  

Second, phones become a source of informal communication during lessons. Even when the teacher is speaking, pupils often type messages or scroll through social media, which splits their focus and makes it difficult to absorb the content. This behavior also encourages students to exchange jokes, memes, or inappropriate images, sometimes sending rude or offensive material to classmates. Such actions can damage a student’s reputation, lower self‑esteem, and make them feel embarrassed or afraid to participate in class. The fear of being mocked may cause some learners to avoid answering questions or volunteering in front of peers, reducing overall confidence.  

Third, cell phones enable easy cheating on assessments. When an exam is handed out, a student with a phone can quickly search for answers, copy from online sources, or consult hidden notes. This gives an unfair advantage over classmates who rely on their own preparation, and it can inflate the grades of those who cheat. For honest students, seeing peers succeed through dishonest means undermines their belief in the value of studying, leading them to feel discouraged and to consider shortcuts themselves. Consequently, the integrity of the assessment process is weakened.  

Fourth, constant phone use reduces opportunities for active involvement and harms health. Teachers often pose questions or run interactive activities, but when students are glued to their screens they ignore these chances to speak up, collaborate, or demonstrate understanding. The time spent watching videos or listening to music replaces physical movement, eye‑focus exercises, and face‑to‑face interaction, which are all beneficial for mental and physical development. Extended screen exposure can strain the eyes and alter brain patterns, making it harder to shift attention to other tasks. Therefore, phones not only waste classroom minutes but also contribute to a less engaged and healthier learning environment.  

In conclusion, while some claim phones can aid research and collaboration, the drawbacks outweigh the benefits. Phones cause noise, distraction, and potential conflicts in the classroom. They encourage off‑task chatting and the spread of inappropriate content, which damages confidence. They make cheating simple, eroding fairness and motivation. Finally, they limit participation and expose students to health risks linked with excessive screen time. For these reasons, students should be prohibited from using cell phones during lessons.

From what I have observed, the idea that a first impression can never be changed is inaccurate. I think people often make this claim because the individual they are talking to appears uninterested in the conversation. Nevertheless, the initial encounter does not always reveal a person’s true nature. It would be unfair to define someone based solely on that brief snapshot, since people are capable of growth and shifting attitudes.

One reason the claim is not absolute is that the mood of the person you meet can influence how they behave. If they are having a bad day, they may seem distant or uncomfortable, which can create a misleading impression. That temporary state does not reflect their usual demeanor or willingness to form connections.

To illustrate, my closest friend was someone I first met in a math class. At that time he seemed reluctant to engage; when I asked about a problem, he ignored my request and did not answer. Over the following weeks, his attitude changed, and we began to share ideas and support each other. The relationship that developed proves an early negative vibe can be transformed.

In addition, among my broader circle of friends, two individuals initially gave me a poor impression. At first glance, they seemed aloof or dismissive, yet now we enjoy close friendships. Their later behavior shows that judgments based on first encounters can be premature.

In conclusion, I disagree with the notion that a first impression is essentially permanent. Because people can adjust their attitudes and because situational factors can temporarily distort how we appear, it is reasonable to give others another chance. The experiences with my friend and the two others I mentioned clearly demonstrate that initial judgments should not be taken as final truths.

Today there is a lot happening around us that we must address, and Thomas Jefferson’s words still ring true: “Resolve never to be idle… it is astonishing how much can be accomplished when we are constantly active.” If we all decide to act together, the results will not only help one individual but uplift everyone in society.

First, we need to condition ourselves to stop waiting for change to arrive. By preparing our own lives and taking purposeful steps, we can make things happen instead of letting them happen to us. Being useful and helping both ourselves and others creates a shared sense of progress; when each person contributes, the collective benefit multiplies. Picture a simple habit: instead of littering, we pick up waste whenever we walk past it. Such tiny actions can turn past neglect into present improvement, showing that we are capable of bettering our community each day without anyone having to force us.

I have witnessed groups worldwide taking meaningful steps for the planet—cleaning rivers, restoring parks, organizing volunteer drives. These examples prove that determination to act can spark lasting change. We should adopt a similar mindset, recognizing that our own small contributions matter. When we stay focused on a purpose and continue to act, we transform idle thoughts into productive deeds.

Being active in our surroundings is essential. By regularly engaging in community projects, we turn abstract ideas into concrete possibilities. Determination combined with consistent effort makes the difference between stagnation and growth. Ultimately, doing something—whether it’s organizing a cleanup or advocating for a cause—always beats simply waiting for others to lead. Let’s keep our actions purposeful, our energy directed, and our society moving forward.

When searching for guidance, it’s common to consult more than one source rather than rely on a single person. Doing so often leads to a more balanced decision because you reduce the risk of depending on just one perspective, which could limit the range of choices available to you. In most cases, people reach out to several friends, family members, or professionals to explore different viewpoints before finalizing a plan. This habit helps lower the chance of regretting a hasty decision and spreads the opportunity cost across multiple opinions rather than placing it entirely on one individual.

One advantage of seeking advice from many people is the variety of options they present. Each adviser can highlight aspects of the situation you might not have considered, expanding the pool of possibilities you can evaluate. By comparing these suggestions, you can decide which path aligns best with your goals, personal values, or circumstances. At the same time, every choice carries an opportunity cost—whether you opt for a promising solution or unintentionally select a less suitable one. The outcome may influence various parts of your life, such as your mood, future prospects, or overall satisfaction, so having several viewpoints gives you a clearer picture of what each alternative could bring.

Another benefit is that you gain insight into different people’s experiences and can identify patterns that have helped—or hurt—them in the past. Listening to these stories allows you to filter out options that have proven ineffective for others and adopt those that have worked well. Moreover, the knowledge you collect can be shared with others facing similar dilemmas, creating a ripple effect of support. You may also apply the lessons you learn to future decisions, avoiding the same mistakes or replicating successful strategies.

However, consulting multiple advisers can sometimes be a drawback. Conflicting recommendations might confuse you and shift your initial preferences, leading to indecision. Different people often interpret the same problem in distinct ways, and their advice could steer you toward a choice that feels riskier or more stressful than the one you initially envisioned. The mental effort required to weigh each opinion and decide which to follow can increase pressure, especially when you worry that a selected path might turn out poorly.

Overall, while gathering advice from several sources broadens your perspective and reduces the chance of overlooking valuable information, it also brings challenges like contradictory input and added stress. Managing these pros and cons wisely allows you to make more informed decisions while still keeping the opportunity cost manageable.
