Although some schools provide distance learning as an alternative, letting students join lessons from home through the internet or video calls, many institutions avoid offering this option because they consider it an unsatisfactory way to study. In my view, schools should not prioritize remote learning as a main educational method.

First, students who learn from home often lose quick access to help when they encounter a problem. In a traditional classroom, a teacher can answer a question right away or a classmate can explain a point on the spot. When lessons take place online, a learner may have to wait for a reply or struggle alone, which can slow down understanding and deepen confusion. This lack of immediate support makes it harder for many students to keep up with the material.

Second, a school environment provides the tools, schedules, and social interaction that most learners need. Libraries, labs, and quiet study areas give students the chance to work on assignments hands‑on, while classmates encourage discussion and teamwork. Many students, especially younger ones, also depend on regular routines and guidance from teachers to stay focused and organized. Removing these elements reduces the overall quality of education.

Third, while it is true that some pupils have duties outside school—such as working after classes, caring for younger children, or learning a new language in a foreign country—these circumstances do not automatically make remote learning advantageous. Those who must balance work and study often need extra tutoring or clarification that a physical school can supply more reliably. Moreover, a home setting can be filled with distractions like smartphones, TV, or family members, which can interrupt concentration and lower productivity.

Video conferencing can work for a few motivated learners, yet it limits spontaneous questioning. If a student hesitates to interrupt a lecture to ask for clarification, the gap in knowledge may grow. In contrast, attending school daily encourages active participation, enables teachers to gauge understanding in real time, and builds a habit of disciplined study that is essential for long‑term success.

Older adults often remind us that perseverance leads to achievement: “If you want to succeed, keep going.” The same spirit applies to education—if we aim for a brighter future, we should take full advantage of the resources and structure that a school provides. Relying solely on distance learning may eventually lead to missed opportunities and regret.

Overall, I believe the majority of students benefit more from face‑to‑face classes than from studying from home. Schools should keep distance learning as a supplemental option rather than a primary one, ensuring that learners receive the support, focus, and community they need to succeed.

Self‑esteem plays a crucial role in how students see themselves and how they perform in school. It can be shaped in two main ways: through personal achievements and through external praise. Both have their own strengths, and together they help learners develop a steady sense of confidence.

First, an achievement gives a student concrete proof that they are capable. When a child completes a difficult project, scores well on a test, or wins a small competition, the result is more than a letter grade; it is evidence of effort turned into success. That feeling of “I did it” stays inside the student and becomes part of their self‑image. Because the source of the pride is internal, it is less likely to fade when the surrounding circumstances change. In addition, high achievers often become role models for classmates. Seeing a peer succeed encourages others to try harder, and the overall classroom atmosphere becomes more positive. As a result, achievements act as a solid foundation for a healthy self‑esteem that can withstand occasional setbacks.

Second, praise from teachers, parents, or peers can also lift a student’s confidence. Even if a learner does not yet produce a perfect result, hearing words of appreciation for their hard work makes them feel valued. A short comment like “I can see you’re trying very hard” or “Your improvement this week is impressive” signals that someone notices effort. This external support motivates the student to keep going and to aim for higher quality in future tasks. Moreover, when praise is given consistently, it creates a supportive environment where students are more willing to take risks and experiment with new ideas. In this way, praise helps turn ordinary work into something that feels worthwhile, encouraging pupils to do their personal best.

The two approaches are not independent; they reinforce each other. When an achievement is recognized with praise, the student receives both internal satisfaction and external validation. The praise highlights what was done well, while the achievement shows that the effort paid off. This double feedback loop strengthens the learner’s belief that success is possible and that they are capable of reaching it. On the other hand, praising effort even when the result is modest prevents students from feeling discouraged. It tells them that the process matters, and that improvement will eventually be reflected in results. Both strategies together encourage perseverance, which is essential for continuous learning.

Of course, relying only on praise without any real achievement can be risky. Empty compliments may boost morale temporarily, but if they are not linked to genuine performance, the feeling of confidence can quickly disappear when challenges appear. Likewise, focusing solely on results while ignoring effort may make students feel that only perfect outcomes matter. To avoid these problems, teachers should balance the two: acknowledge the outcome when it is achieved, and also recognize the hard work that led there. This balanced approach ensures that students understand that self‑esteem comes from both what they accomplish and how they are treated along the way.

In everyday classroom life, many students work diligently on every assignment. Even though their work may not be the top‑most in class, regular praise for their persistence helps them push a little farther each time. The feeling of being appreciated encourages them to try new strategies and to stay motivated. Over time, this cycle of effort, recognition, and modest success builds a steady self‑esteem that is not dependent on a single high score or award.

Self‑esteem that is rooted in achievement is also important for long‑term development. Students who regularly succeed learn to trust their abilities, and that trust spills over into other areas of life, such as sports, friendships, or future work. Achievements give them a reliable sense that they can set goals and achieve them, which is a key ingredient for adult confidence.

In short, both praise and personal accomplishments are essential for healthy self‑esteem. Achievements provide the internal proof of competence, while praise offers the external encouragement that keeps students engaged and willing to keep improving. When educators combine the two—celebrating successes and acknowledging effort—they help students feel good about themselves, motivate peers, and create a classroom where each learner can steadily grow in confidence and ability. Ultimately, a balanced focus on both elements equips students with the emotional tools they need to succeed not only in school but throughout life.

Several companies have experimented with a four‑day week, working ten hours each day to reduce commuting and energy consumption. Some propose that schools copy this idea, keeping four teaching days but lengthening each one by two hours. I disagree with such a change and believe it would be unsuitable for our school.

One major issue is the clash between school and students’ after‑school commitments. Many pupils already hold part‑time jobs, volunteer positions, or care for family members. If school ended at four o’clock each day, a student who must start a job at the same time would lose that opportunity or be forced to rush homework when already exhausted. This problem would not be limited to a few individuals; anyone with similar responsibilities would face the same dilemma, making the timetable unfair to those who depend on after‑school income.

Another drawback is the added fatigue it would cause. Two extra hours in each class would push lessons longer than they are now, and teachers would have to deliver more material in a single block. Students are likely to become weary, leading to poorer concentration. When they finally get home, they are often too tired to complete assignments, so missed homework becomes common. Missing tasks frequently result in lower marks because teachers rely on regular practice to assess progress. Moreover, the strain from a longer day could spill over into other subjects, reducing overall performance.

Lastly, attendance could be harmed. Consistently finishing school late makes many students feel drained the following morning, and some may skip a day just to recover. Poor attendance is already a concern for schools, and lengthening the daily schedule would probably make it worse, hindering teachers’ ability to cover essential content.

In summary, although a four‑day week may appear attractive, extending the school day by two hours would create more problems than benefits. It would interfere with after‑school work, increase tiredness and lower focus, reduce homework completion, and jeopardize attendance and grades. For these reasons, I think our school should keep its present timetable.

Bullying and negative conversations often create difficulties in social settings. I’ve noticed that when people gain a better understanding of others, their attitudes can improve significantly. However, some individuals remain unkind and continue to bully or talk negatively about people without attempting to know them. This kind of prejudice leads to feelings of isolation, which explains why I frequently find myself alone. There is too much gossip in groups, and I dislike how people discuss others behind their backs. Those who threaten others might feel even bolder because they assume their targets won’t stand up to them.  

I make an effort not to worry about what others say; their words are their own concern. But when someone is hurt and needs assistance, they usually reach out to me. Whenever I feel angry or upset, playing soccer helps me clear my mind. If I could organize something, I would create soccer events so that anyone interested can participate and also forget their daily struggles. That’s why sports exist—to offer enjoyment without conflict. Beyond soccer, activities like watching movies with friends, viewing basketball or volleyball matches, and other group experiences can also help people connect. In my opinion, every issue has a resolution. The real obstacle is our failure to show proper respect to others. If we practiced mutual respect more consistently, situations would change for the better.  

Safety is a priority for everyone, particularly in neighborhoods without gangs. Gang members often exploit others financially or emotionally. We should unite families to confront those who harm others. Many individuals strive to study hard to build a better future and escape difficult family circumstances. With a high school diploma, one can typically secure a stable job, even if it isn’t ideal. This achievement allows people to move away from problematic situations.  

If belongings are stolen, reporting the incident to the police is advisable. People shouldn’t live in constant fear because displaying fear might encourage others to act aggressively. We are intelligent creatures and should use our minds wisely. Being skilled in one area doesn’t guarantee kindness from others. Showing calmness instead of anger can prevent provocation, as aggressive individuals are less likely to cause harm when their targets remain composed.  

To avoid conflicts, I suggest inviting the other party to play sports or spend time with friends. Visiting the beach for relaxation might transform an acquaintance into a lasting friend. However, it’s wise not to share your deepest vulnerabilities. If friends learn your most sensitive traits, they might use them against you during disputes. This is why I believe no one should be fully aware of another’s crucial weaknesses.

Failure plays an essential role in reaching success. When we fail, we receive a clear signal about which actions to avoid next time. In this way, each setback offers a lesson that helps us improve our approach.  

For instance, imagine someone who wants to join a professional soccer league. They have already played for top clubs and earned praise as the most valuable member of their team, never having been released from any squad. One day a coach announces a professional trial the following week and asks the player to prepare. He gives a schedule outlining diet, workouts, and recovery routines. Each day the player must eat properly and train intensively. Occasionally the player feels lazy and skips a session, slipping back into unhealthy habits, but they push themselves to stay on track. When the trial arrives, the player feels as prepared as possible, completing the warm‑up and all the drills. He performs exceptionally, looking like the best talent on the field. However, at the end of the day the selectors bring everyone together and announce which candidates were accepted. This individual does not make the cut. The disappointment marks a point where motivation becomes crucial. The player can either abandon soccer for another path, or choose to stay committed and try again. Facing failure reveals whether a person is patient enough to keep working toward a goal and whether they are ready to endure repeated setbacks.  

A similar story appears in a book titled *The Persuasion of Happiness*. The main character builds a small machine and attempts to sell it. Nobody buys it at first. He is a single father living in a modest house, and after several unpaid bills, he is evicted and spends a few weeks homeless. Despite the hardship, he continues to market his invention, never giving up. Eventually, after a series of ups and downs, a buyer takes interest, tells others about the device’s benefits, and sales begin to rise. His success stems from refusing to quit his dream, even though he was constantly rejected.  

Both examples illustrate that failure is not a dead‑end but a stepping stone toward eventual achievement. By learning from each disappointment, we discover what works and what does not, and we become more determined to persist. When we keep trying despite setbacks, we test our patience and prove our willingness to fail repeatedly in pursuit of success. Thus, embracing failure can be the most powerful tool for turning a dream into reality.

Self‑confidence plays a vital role in helping people feel satisfied with who they are. For many students, developing this confidence can be a struggle, often because of the way they were raised or how they are treated by friends, teachers, and family. Nevertheless, cultivating a healthy level of self‑esteem is essential for navigating life’s demands and finding personal fulfillment.

The environment in which a young person grows up can shape their belief in themselves. If encouragement is scarce or criticism is constant, it becomes harder to trust one’s abilities. Even when external support is limited, students should learn to motivate themselves based on internal reasons—personal goals, curiosity, or a desire to improve. While the first steps of learning may feel overwhelming, they are only part of a broader set of tasks that require steady effort. Over time, the difficulty of these tasks tends to lessen as students acquire the skills and habits that make progress smoother.

Some critics worry that praising work that falls short of expectations might weaken learning standards, arguing that students could become satisfied with mediocre results. However, the most effective way to build confidence is to complete assignments that meet one’s own standards. By taking on work that they understand well enough and can manage independently, students reinforce the belief that they are capable of handling challenges. This approach keeps the standards high while still allowing room for personal growth.

It is true that achieving genuine self‑esteem is not a quick or easy process. Not everyone agrees that confidence comes naturally from praise alone. In fact, the strongest sense of worth usually stems from concrete accomplishments rather than superficial compliments. Successes earned after weighing risks and putting in hard work—whether in class, sports, or artistic projects—provide the foundation for lasting confidence. These victories demonstrate that effort leads to tangible results.

There will inevitably be moments when a student feels tempted to quit, especially when a task seems too daunting. Moments of doubt and fatigue are part of the journey, but persisting through them reinforces the idea that they can overcome obstacles. Each time a student pushes through a setback, their belief in their own capabilities strengthens, turning potential failure into an opportunity for growth.

In summary, self‑confidence grows out of taking on challenges, seeing them through, and celebrating the achievements that follow. Rather than relying on endless praise, it is the real, earned results that build a durable sense of self‑esteem. As students navigate the ups and downs of academic life, the cumulative effect of these personal victories will ultimately shape the confidence they carry into adulthood.

The author Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote about individuality. I disagree with him because there are many occasions when you need help from someone in life. Being individual is not just about managing your life in your own time. In this essay I will talk about some ways we can work together. First I will explain job issues and results. Second I will explain society and how being less individual can be advantageous. Finally I will explain how to take decisions and make them work. This may prove that individuality does not prevent you from becoming what you want to be.

There are many ways we can experience individuality. In your job, you might encounter someone you do not like because of his or her behavior. Trying to work with that person does not mean giving up your individuality; you may need his help one day. If you work with him and break the barriers inside yourself, that can be an advantage in relating to others. Another occasion of individuality at work arises when you are not doing what you originally dreamed of becoming. That does not mean you cannot fight for your goals—if you dislike your job, try doing something you like, even while working in a job you do not enjoy. This is a typical way of expressing individuality. Many companies work as a team to achieve their goals, and you can collaborate with others in your job just as a company does.

Some people prefer to be alone most of the time; we can call them asocial. These people simply want to be alone because they feel comfortable that way. Others do not like being around other people because they prefer to do things by themselves. They enjoy being the focus of attention; we can call them individuals. Not all of them are the same, because there may be reasons that make them act that way—perhaps their background. Being part of society can sometimes be more complicated than it appears, especially if you know people like that. You can try to work with them or sometimes these people change. Some change because they seek help, while others change because someone close to them helps them for the better.

We all make decisions in life, but some of those decisions can lead us to act wrongly or become a different person. Trying to be someone else is not just wanting to be that person; it requires a decision. You can decide whether to let the world push you, or to make your own decision about what you want to do. Many people accept the world’s management of their lives because they think it is better, or because it is the easy way. A president may decide to work alone and do as he wishes, but he knows that, by himself, he cannot accomplish everything; he must cooperate with the people in Congress. Like the president, we can choose whether to work together or not. You can set your own goals to fight for what you want, or to be constantly pushed by the world to become something else.

In summary, we all have the choice to select which path to follow. I have discussed job issues and results, and I have written about how we can live within society and resolve conflicts. Finally, I explained how we can make our own decisions, to become what we want, and how a goal can guide us toward change or a fight for it. This shows that Ralph Waldo Emerson was wrong about being constantly pushed by the world, because we can change that and become what we want.

Ralph Waldo Emerson famously argued that staying true to oneself is the most important thing a person can do. I believe his view is overly narrow because, in reality, we often need the help of others to get through life’s challenges. It is not enough simply to be independent; we also must learn how to manage our lives within a shared social world. In this essay I will discuss three situations where cooperation is essential. First, I will examine workplace problems and how they can encourage collaboration. Second, I will consider the role of society and why being overly individualistic can be harmful. Finally, I will explore how decision‑making works and why we must balance personal goals with the influence of those around us. These points will show that individuality does not mean isolation, and that Emerson’s insistence on constant self‑reliance misses an important truth.

There are many moments in life when working with other people becomes more productive than trying to go it alone. At work, for instance, you may have to interact with a colleague whose habits or personality clash with yours. If you refuse to cooperate, you risk losing valuable support that could later be crucial for your own success. Trying to force your own ideas on others or ignore their contributions can create tension and waste energy. Instead, finding a way to work together even when you disagree can turn a potential conflict into a useful partnership. Another workplace situation involves feeling unfulfilled in a job that does not match your long‑term aspirations. It is tempting to stay in such a role because it feels familiar, but remaining in it does not automatically prove that you are living authentically. Many companies rely on team‑oriented effort to reach their targets, and individuals can contribute effectively by collaborating with their coworkers rather than insisting on a solitary approach.

Some people prefer to spend most of their time alone, often described as antisocial. These individuals claim that solitude makes them feel safe and comfortable, and they sometimes seek the spotlight by acting as the center of attention. In such cases, being seen as a lone star can give them a sense of power. However, not everyone who avoids group settings does so out of choice. Their background or past experiences may push them toward isolation, or they might worry that the social world is more complicated than it appears. While it is true that society can sometimes be messy, especially when you deal with people who are aloof or self‑absorbed, it is still possible to build bridges with them. Some of them eventually accept help, and others change their behavior when a close friend or family member encourages them to do so.

Every person makes choices that affect their future, but not all decisions lead to the same outcome. Trying to become someone else is not merely a matter of wanting a different identity; it requires making deliberate choices. You can let external forces push you toward a path that feels easier or safer, or you can take charge and decide what truly matters to you. A good example comes from politics: a president may appear to act alone, yet he knows that governing without the support of the legislature would be impossible. The president must work with members of Congress to pass laws and manage crises. Likewise, in our own lives we can decide whether to follow the crowd or to pursue our own goals. Those who choose to stay in a system that seems to dictate their behavior often do so because they think it is simpler or more beneficial in the short term. Yet people who set their own priorities, even when it means confronting resistance, usually find a clearer sense of purpose.

In summary, each of us faces choices about which direction to take. By looking at workplace dynamics, the broader social environment, and the way we make decisions, I have shown that individuality does not have to be a rejection of others. Instead, it can be a flexible balance between personal ambition and the help we receive from those around us. This means that Emerson’s claim that we should constantly push against the world’s influence is not entirely accurate. While self‑direction matters, recognizing when cooperation is useful allows us to shape the person we want to become, rather than being forced into a solitary mold. Therefore, I argue that a realistic view of individuality acknowledges both the need to be independent and the unavoidable presence of interdependence in life.

What talent or skill do I have, and how do I practice and use it? My skill is drawing. I pick up a pencil when I need a mental break, and I practice it in an art class.

First, everyone has some ability. Drawing is a refuge. It helps me clear my thoughts because putting lines on paper forces me to think visually. Many say sketching works as a mental filter, letting worries fade for a while. The focus required during drawing reduces distraction.

Second, I view drawing mainly as fun, not as a duty. This keeps the activity light and free of pressure. When I feel upset, I sketch the feeling onto the page, turning emotions into shapes and colors, which calms me. Famous painters see art as a way to express feelings, not as homework. I draw because it feels good, not because I must.

Finally, I enrolled in a local art course to develop my technique. The lessons covered proportions, shading, and step‑by‑step composition planning. Using these basics made the process smoother and my work improved. Some people learn on their own, but classroom feedback kept me on track while I experimented.

Overall, drawing serves as my hobby for relaxation and for handling thoughts, and taking formal lessons has helped me grow the skill. Combining self‑directed play with structured learning lets me enjoy and improve my talent at the same time.

I believe that a ten‑hour workday is more advantageous than the traditional eight‑hour schedule. By spending ten hours at the job each day, employees can accomplish the same amount of work in fewer days, which reduces daily consumption of electricity, heating and other utilities. For instance, four ten‑hour shifts already equal a standard forty‑hour week, and any extra hours can still be taken on Friday and Saturday if needed. This arrangement also leaves a larger block of time for personal activities, so workers are not forced to cram tasks into a short day.

Applying a similar principle to schools could also be beneficial. If the school day were lengthened to ten hours—from, say, ten in the morning until ten at night—students would finish the same curriculum in only four days instead of five. The extra two hours would allow children to return home earlier, get a decent night’s sleep, and still hold part‑time jobs after school. With a four‑day school week, teachers would also enjoy three days off each week, giving them more rest and the chance to pursue professional development.

More sleep and less early‑morning stress improve concentration and motivation. When pupils are well rested, they can focus better in class and have enough time to complete homework on weekends. Many high‑schoolers already work long hours; extending the school day would give them a predictable schedule that helps balance studies, employment and rest. Consequently, students would be more likely to meet their academic objectives and stay energetic throughout the term.

Finally, a condensed school week would lower overall energy use. Buildings would be heated, cooled and illuminated for fewer days, which reduces electricity consumption and water usage. The same logic applies to workplaces; longer daily periods can be more efficient in terms of resource management. In short, a ten‑hour day for both work and school seems to offer practical benefits while supporting health, productivity and sustainability.

In many societies the idea that doing nothing can be beneficial is widely accepted, yet in reality most individuals require some form of activity to give their lives direction. Everyone feels a need to have something to focus on each day. Observations show that a person who spends excessive time idle often influences others negatively, because they lack the motivation to contribute. Those who stay active can reach accomplishments that reshape both their personal circumstances and the prospects of younger family members. The more productive a person is, the higher the likelihood of attaining personal ambitions.

Today, a large number of people around the globe are without steady employment, but instead of searching for work they remain passive. They become comfortable with staying where they are and spend their hours doing little or nothing. By filling time with emptiness, they also ignore any planning for the future, which explains why many families remain trapped in poverty. If they stopped squandering hours, they would be able to build a more secure future. In several nations you see adults who refuse to work, so they go to public places asking strangers for money. These individuals overlook the opportunities that exist around them. A person who chooses to stay inactive disregards whether a job is available or not; they simply value having free time. Such a lazy approach leaves a life without a clear purpose. Consequently, many children endure hardship because their parents have no job. Young children often have to start working early simply to support families where the adults are idle.

The majority of the world’s population tends toward laziness, and this habit often appears at school as well. Many students avoid involvement in group assignments, preferring the simplest portion of the task. When they later become adults, this avoidance becomes a problem because they have not learned how to tackle difficult work. Most pupils want everything to stay easy, believing that life will continue as smoothly as school years. However, real life presents challenges that they are unwilling to meet, preferring to stay at home instead of looking for a job. This habit of shying away from effort makes it even harder for them to find employment when the opportunity arrives. Students ought to be encouraged to participate actively. If a young person remains inactive for a long period, the consequences can stretch far into the future. It is essential that they develop a sense of purpose rather than drift aimlessly.

Unemployment is a widespread issue, and some claim it gives them more time to spend with family. Nevertheless, they still need to perform useful tasks for their household or community. Economists argue that fewer inactive adults would lead to stronger economies. When a smaller portion of the population wastes time, resources can be allocated more efficiently, reducing poverty rates. Thus, a reduction in inactivity contributes directly to a healthier national economy and lower levels of deprivation.

In summary, being idle does not provide any genuine advantage. People should strive to engage in meaningful activities on a regular basis. Consistent effort alters the trajectory of one’s future and creates pathways to success. An active individual works with intention, making it easier to achieve goals. On the contrary, an inactive person lacks direction, which prevents any real progress. Consequently, we must avoid laziness at all costs and adopt a proactive mindset in order to become more successful in life.

I agree that attitude is a vital part of life. It shapes the way we act toward other people and determines how they respond to us. When you meet someone, your demeanor is what they notice first. If you are polite, courteous, and humble, the other person is more likely to think you are trustworthy and worth talking to again. A good attitude creates a positive impression, encouraging others to seek you out and to engage in further conversation.

Consider the first time you speak with a loved one, such as a parent. The parent looks past your words and focuses on your overall conduct. They check whether you show respect, maintain a calm tone, and treat them with kindness. If the parent perceives that you are respectful and humble, they will feel proud and believe you are a good person. This not only builds confidence in them but also strengthens the relationship, making future interactions smoother and more meaningful.

Later on, when you become a parent yourself, the importance of attitude becomes even clearer. You must teach your children to treat others kindly, to listen carefully, and to keep a respectful tone. By helping them develop a positive attitude early, you are equipping them with tools that will enable them to form healthy friendships, succeed in school, and contribute positively to society. Seeing their children grow into considerate individuals can give parents a deep sense of accomplishment.

In everyday life, attitude is often the foundation of success. People who consistently show respect, humility, and empathy are usually viewed as having valuable qualities. Those who lack such attitudes, on the other hand, find it hard to earn trust because they may come across as rude or dismissive. Without respect, communication can break down, and misunderstandings become frequent.

Therefore, cultivating a good attitude is essential for personal growth and for building a supportive community. It helps you convey your ideas clearly, earn the admiration of others, and live a life that is both fulfilling and socially rewarding. In short, attitude is the key to meaningful relationships, effective interaction, and a well‑balanced existence.

Ralph Waldo Emerson claimed that unless we try tasks that are beyond our present ability, we cannot make progress. I agree because staying inside what we already master leads to stagnation. Repeating the same activity only reinforces what we already know and does not generate new skills. Growth happens when we step outside our comfort zone, confront unfamiliar problems, and acquire fresh abilities.

Many people fall into a daily routine of doing the same work over and over. They feel safe sticking to familiar tasks, but this habit can become a trap. While they perfect one skill, time slips away that could be used to explore a new interest or learn a different craft. By varying our activities we use our limited time more wisely and keep our minds adaptable.

From my viewpoint, Emerson’s statement is correct: trying new things is essential for learning. Each new experience adds a layer of competence, enriching overall expertise and paving the way for future development. Relying solely on what we already excel at is not enough.

In short, focusing only on familiar tasks blocks personal improvement. To grow, we must leave our comfort zone, accept new challenges, and keep learning through diverse actions.

John Lubbock, a nineteenth‑century British naturalist and politician, once observed that ‘your character will be what you yourself choose to make.’ This view is shared by the writer, who believes that we have the power to shape who we become, even though earlier events sometimes appear to limit us.

It is true that childhood experiences, family circumstances and past hardships can leave a deep imprint. Growing up in a violent household, for instance, can feel like a heavy weight that drags a person down. Yet, the same person can decide to use those painful memories as a source of motivation rather than a curse.

The key lies in the choices we make after the fact. A child who witnesses cruel behavior may end up repeating it, but can also learn to break the cycle by deliberately practicing kindness, patience and self‑respect. In this way, the hardships become stepping stones that help us forge a tougher, more compassionate character.

It is worth distinguishing character from personality. Personality describes the immediate reactions we show to everyday situations – whether we are shy, outgoing, or quick to laugh. Character, on the other hand, reflects the deeper values and habits that guide those reactions over time. Our own assessment of character matters far more than anyone else’s label such as ‘she is mean’ or ‘he never shares.’

When others try to judge us before they truly understand our story, they are looking at a cover, not the pages inside. By working on our character, we create a legacy that will be admired long after we are gone. People often ask, ‘How did she stay so strong?’ or ‘How did he become independent?’ The answer lies in the consistent decisions we have made, which are invisible to onlookers but evident in our results.

Consider a moment when a close family member passes away due to illness. The grief and denial can seem overwhelming, but choosing to honor that person by living each day purposefully shows a remarkable inner strength. The effort we put into valuing every minute, despite occasional sadness, is a clear demonstration that our character can grow even in the face of loss.

Almost everyone faces moments of doubt, when the mind whispers that a goal is impossible. It is tempting to listen to those negative thoughts, but they only hold us back. Our character is meant to push us forward, to smash through the walls that life erects. Recognizing that the obstacles are temporary, we can redirect our focus toward constructive action instead of rumination.

The most important advice is to trust your inner sense and let it guide you. Do not wait for external approval before acting on what feels right. When you allow yourself to make the decisions that align with your deepest values, you stand out, and your character becomes a source of pride. In the end, Lubbock’s claim rings true: the person we become is the result of the choices we make, and we are the only ones who can decide how those choices will shape us.

After‑school homework clubs are a waste of time if you have other commitments after school. It’s difficult to do two things at once, so you shouldn’t join them. If you like sports, you should pursue them because you need to finish homework on your own time. Joining after‑school homework clubs adds extra hours to your school day, which you might not want.

Imagine being forced to stay at school longer than necessary when you could be playing a sport, hanging out with friends, or simply relaxing. In my view, after‑school homework clubs should not be compulsory for students. Beyond the obvious extra hours spent in the classroom, such programs create practical problems that affect family life, athletic commitments, and personal hobbies like gaming or streaming. The three points below explain why the policy is more harmful than helpful.

First, attending an after‑school club often means missing out on planned family activities. Parents try to keep a routine for their children, such as a weekly dinner at a favourite restaurant. However, a student who must stay after the bell cannot join that plan. For example, Maya tells her mother that she has a tutoring session on Tuesday. Maya’s mother had already reserved a table at Red Lobster for that evening. Maya’s call forces the family to cancel the reservation, leaving her mother disappointed and the child feeling guilty. This simple situation shows that after‑school clubs can break family routines, reduce quality time together, and cause emotional strain for both sides.

Second, extracurricular sports suffer when students are kept at school later in the day. A typical sport practice requires punctuality because even a few minutes of delay can affect the entire drill. Consider Leo, a high‑school basketball player who has to attend an English‑language workshop after school. On Wednesdays he must finish the workshop before heading to his team’s practice. This schedule makes him arrive five minutes late, earning his coach’s first warning. When Leo tries to explain his situation, the coach says, “You can’t be both in school and on the court.” After three warnings, Leo is removed from the squad. The loss of a beloved sport and a possible future career clearly illustrates how after‑school homework clubs can jeopardise athletic ambitions.

Third, modern hobbies such as video‑gaming or content creation are severely limited when after‑school sessions are imposed. Many young people now stream their gameplay on platforms like YouTube, and they rely on weekday evenings to maintain a steady audience. Suppose Alex, who runs a popular gaming channel, joins an after‑school study group. School ends at six‑thirty, but the drive home takes half an hour, so he doesn’t reach his house until seven. At that point Alex is still too tired to record a stream and also has to finish assignments from the club. Consequently, his weekly videos are postponed, his followers become impatient, and his subscriber count drops dramatically. Moreover, a newly released game that he bought can only be played on the weekends, making his free time even tighter. The decline in his streaming success and the frustration of missing out on gaming highlight another downside of compulsory after‑school clubs.

All three examples—family gatherings, sport participation, and online gaming—demonstrate that after‑school homework clubs can be detrimental rather than beneficial. They force students to split their limited time between essential school work and activities they value. Instead of extending school hours, schools should encourage learners to finish assignments at home or during regular class periods. If extra help is needed, optional tutoring sessions can be offered, but they should not become a default requirement. By protecting personal time, schools can foster healthier relationships, stronger athletic programs, and more vibrant digital communities among their pupils.

I believe technology is overall beneficial because it makes everyday tasks easier through the internet. Our smartphones are now essential for almost everything we do, from checking emails to managing appointments. The internet has become a central part of our lives, allowing us to stay connected, informed, and productive while we’re on the go.

One major advantage is the speed and convenience of online shopping. Items can be ordered from anywhere in the world and usually arrive within a few days. This saves a lot of time and effort compared to visiting stores in person. Likewise, people who feel unwell can quickly search for health advice, symptoms, and remedies using their phones. In the past, such information was hard to find, but today it is just a few taps away.

Communication has also transformed dramatically. Earlier generations could not video‑chat with relatives living abroad, but now platforms like FaceTime and Zoom let families see each other instantly, no matter the distance. This helps keep personal relationships strong even when travel is not possible.

When we need to learn new skills, such as cooking or baking, the internet provides step‑by‑step guides, pictures, and video tutorials. Searching for “how to make a cake” on Google often brings up several recipes and alternative methods, giving us more options than before.

Social media has become another useful tool. It works like a modern newspaper, delivering news updates, entertaining videos, and reports on recent inventions. Users can also share moments from their lives and discover new ideas from around the globe. Through messaging apps and video calls, people can talk, make friends, and collaborate on projects without ever meeting in person.

Overall, technology offers an easy way to complete many tasks without leaving the house, and most of us spend a large portion of our day browsing, watching videos, or interacting on our devices. I think technology has taken over much of our daily routine, and for many individuals, life feels impossible without their phone. Therefore, I maintain that technology is a positive force in modern society.

First, a partnership between schools and businesses means that educational institutions work together with companies to give students a taste of real‑world work before they enter university. These collaborations let learners visit workplaces, see what tasks are performed there, and discover which fields match their strengths and interests. I believe schools should pursue such partnerships because they help students make informed choices about their future careers. If selected for a program like this, I would benefit from the opportunity to interact with people, figure out which jobs appeal to me, and gain hands‑on experience.

Many people feel uncomfortable around strangers, but I actually enjoy being in social environments. I think working with colleagues creates a positive atmosphere, regardless of the industry. Even if you don’t like everyone on your team, you must cooperate. I remember a group project at school where I didn’t know any of my teammates. At first I was unsure how to start a conversation, but once we talked, we became friends. That experience showed me how quickly a brief interaction can turn into a lasting connection. Whenever I meet new people, I feel at ease after just a few minutes of dialogue.

While some students already know the path they want to follow, I still haven’t pinpointed my own strengths. I often ask myself, “What am I good at?” but haven’t reached a clear answer yet. If I join a company through a school partnership, I will be able to explore several positions and see which ones spark my interest. Understanding the direction I want to take will make my future decisions more satisfying. It’s common to see people stuck in jobs they dislike simply to support their families. I believe everyone should be able to choose a career that brings them joy.

For example, I once wanted to work in a restaurant but didn’t know what the role involved. I asked a friend who worked there and later did some online research. Some positions don’t require prior experience, yet many ask for at least a brief on‑the‑job test. My long‑term dream has been to become a nurse, so I’ve already tried to learn about the profession by volunteering and observing. If I am chosen for a partnership program, I would gain the chance to explore nursing more deeply and obtain genuine experience.

In summary, I think the committee should select me. My enthusiasm for working with people, my wish to discover the type of work that truly interests me, and my eagerness to try various jobs make me a good fit for these collaborations. Selecting me would give me the opportunity to experiment with several roles—especially in nursing—so I can decide which career I want to pursue. Starting a job with a clear sense of personal interest tends to lead to greater satisfaction and success.

Having good attitudes is the best way to successes. There are two types of attitudes: a good attitude and a bad attitude.

Good attitudes can help you in many ways. For example, if you disagree with your boss about your paycheck, you can talk with him using a good attitude and reach an agreement, or talk with a bad attitude and get fired. Good attitudes can also help during bad or boring times—for example, when you and your family are having a difficult trip, a great attitude can make everyone feel better.

You can have a good attitude when you sleep well, when it is sunny outside, when you receive a gift, when you go to your favorite restaurant or eat your favorite food, when your friends come to your house, when you visit your family, when you go on a trip and are having a good time, or in many other situations.

Bad attitudes can lead you down the wrong path. Many people have a bad attitude almost all the time, making it difficult to get along with them; such people often have few friends or none. One example of a bad attitude is when you come to school stressed, disagree with your teacher, and start yelling at him; the teacher then sends you to guidance, and you end up with a report card. Or someone else with a bad attitude wants to fight, and that can go badly.

You can develop a bad attitude when you are tired, have a lot of work, cannot go outside because it is raining, receive a bad attitude from someone else, are mad at someone, are hungry with bad food, or experience other similar situations.

When I have good attitudes, I always have the best time. Things that make me have a good attitude include receiving my favorite food, getting a present, or being with my family. For example, yesterday was my cousin's birthday at a fun place; I had a good attitude because we played together and then ate great food. I also have a good attitude when my family and I go on a trip because I love traveling and visiting new places. Another example is that my science teacher's good attitude gave us one more day to turn in a project.

There are many benefits of having good attitudes. One benefit is when you have an important exam, study, and feel secure about it; the next morning you wake up with a good attitude, feel secure about yourself, and are likely to get a good grade. I think the best benefit is having a good time, because happiness is the best feeling a person can have.

In conclusion, having good attitudes can help you in many ways, such as work, school, and family reunions. Now that you know this, the next time you feel bad or have a bad day, the best way to handle it is to have a good attitude.

A positive attitude is the most effective way to achieve success. People generally hold either a supportive mindset or a hostile one, and the former has far more influence on outcomes. When a disagreement appears, for example, a worker who approaches the boss calmly can negotiate a raise, while a confrontational response may end in dismissal. Likewise, a cheerful outlook can lift spirits during a dull or stressful day, turning a rough family trip into a pleasant memory for everyone.  

There are many everyday situations that encourage a good mood. Getting enough sleep, enjoying sunny weather, receiving a surprise gift, eating a favorite meal, spending time with friends or relatives, and taking an enjoyable vacation are all simple sources of optimism. Such moments make it easier to stay upbeat and ready to face challenges.  

On the opposite side, a negative attitude can lead people down the wrong path. Individuals who habitually complain or act angrily often find it hard to keep friends, because their behavior tends to drive others away. A concrete example is a stressed student who reacts with loud complaints when a teacher’s decision disappoints him; the reaction can result in a warning, a guidance meeting, and a damaging report card.  

Several conditions usually generate a bad mood. Tiredness, an overwhelming workload, rain that prevents outdoor activities, being provoked by someone else’s negativity, personal anger, or an unsatisfying meal can all feed into a sour disposition. When these factors pile up, it becomes easy to fall into pessimism.  

In my own experience, I notice that simple pleasures improve my mood. I feel happier when I eat my favorite food, receive a present, or simply be with family. A recent birthday party for my cousin took place at a lively venue; I stayed positive by playing games and then enjoying tasty dishes. Family trips also boost my spirits because exploring new places together creates shared excitement. Moreover, my science teacher once showed patience and gave us an extra day for a project, which motivated me to complete it without stress.  

The advantages of maintaining a positive outlook are numerous. After a well‑prepared exam, a calm, confident start usually translates into a solid performance. I have found that a good mood not only raises productivity but also brings the best feeling a person can have—happiness. It enhances confidence, improves relationships, and makes everyday tasks feel more manageable.  

In short, cultivating a good attitude supports success at work, in school, and during family gatherings. Whenever you encounter a low point, remember that shifting to an optimistic mindset can turn the situation around. By making small, positive choices daily, you can build a life that feels rewarding and resilient.

Summer is an ideal season for enjoying outdoor cycling. When you ride a bike you can easily discover neighborhoods and streets you might otherwise overlook. The journey can take you past shops, cafés, rivers, and you may even catch a glimpse of birds or passing cars. Because you can carry food with you, it’s simple to pause for a picnic whenever you feel like it. Along the way you often spot other cyclists—some stopping to buy a snack at a nearby store, others just riding for the pleasure. The scenery changes constantly, offering chances to visit well‑known landmarks such as museums, parks, or restaurants, and to snap photos of people and architecture. You can also ride to attractions like a zoo, where vibrant flowers bloom and visitors capture memorable shots. The feeling of excitement grows as you experience fresh air and varied landscapes, especially when you share the ride with family members, children, or friends. Bringing your own food enhances the fun, and it gives you an opportunity to uncover hidden spots that feature interesting design elements or art installations. In short, cycling in summer blends exercise with visual discovery, creates a sense of freedom, and leaves you feeling energized and connected to the world around you.

Dear Principal,

I want to let you know that I believe replacing the current cafeteria meals with healthier, more varied options would be a good move for our school. Introducing new dishes that are both nutritious and unfamiliar to many students would give everyone a chance to try something different and improve their diets.

One reason I support this change is that it can break the monotony that some students feel after eating the same meals almost every day. On the other hand, there are students who have grown accustomed to the existing menu and enjoy it regularly. The best approach would be to ask the cafeteria manager for a list of the foods most and least liked by students. By keeping the popular items and replacing the unpopular ones, we can satisfy both groups without removing what many enjoy.

When the menu changes, students are likely to be pleased because they will see their favorite foods still on the table while also discovering healthier alternatives. This could also set our school apart from others and inspire nearby schools to adopt similar menus. If several schools make the switch, more families would benefit from the trend. Parents often spend extra money when their children complain about the cafeteria food and buy meals elsewhere. A menu that meets more students’ preferences would reduce those extra purchases and help families save money.

Another advantage is that students may no longer feel the need to skip class to buy lunch outside. Walking off campus for food can be risky, and parents worry when they receive calls about a student’s absence. A better selection in the cafeteria could keep students on campus and lessen those concerns.

In addition, a healthier lunch brings tangible health benefits. Nutrient‑rich meals that contain less saturated fat and more protein can boost energy, support growth, and lower the risk of becoming overweight. Some classmates have allergic reactions to items that are currently served; offering fresh, varied foods might also give them more safe choices. A balanced diet would contribute to overall well‑being and reduce the number of sick days taken each year.

Overall, asking the cafeteria staff to identify the foods students enjoy most and those they rarely eat, then adjusting the menu accordingly, will make the change smoother for everyone. It will keep the dishes most loved, introduce healthier options, cut down on outside purchases, protect student safety, and improve health outcomes. I hope you will take these suggestions into account and consider updating the lunch program for the benefit of all students, parents, and staff. Thank you for your time and for supporting a healthier school environment.

People often believe they have full control over the choices they make in life, and this belief can be true to an extent. We all tend to avoid activities that do not match our interests or ambitions, and we naturally shape our decisions according to personal goals and preferences. However, the process of making those decisions is rarely straightforward. Some choices require a long, steady effort, while others seem to promise quick results but can bring unexpected difficulties.

The more demanding path usually involves hard work and dedication, such as studying to achieve good grades or gaining practical experience through a career. This route often takes years of planning and perseverance, but it can lead to stable jobs and higher earnings over time. The alternative, sometimes called the shortcut, relies on having enough money or resources at the start of one’s future plans. For example, a young adult who can pay tuition upfront may avoid a lengthy period of part‑time jobs. Yet this shortcut is not always easy; it demands quick financial decisions and can be risky for those who cannot secure the initial capital.

A person’s financial situation strongly influences which option feels feasible. Someone from a wealthy family may have the luxury of choosing a career that aligns with personal passion rather than immediate income, because the cost of education or equipment is less of a burden. In contrast, a student from a low‑income background must weigh many practical concerns—rent, transportation, or paying for a car—before deciding to continue schooling or start a job. For many of them, the decision to postpone education and take a temporary job appears logical, yet it often means they must work even harder later to catch up.

I have seen these trade‑offs in the lives of close friends. One classmate, just before finishing high school, told me he would rather earn money right away than attend college. He left school and began working as a nail technician. His earnings are irregular, and he now feels stuck without a clear career trajectory. If he had stayed in school, he would have been eligible for a diploma and could have entered a field with more predictable pay. His regret shows how a hasty decision can limit future possibilities.

My brother faced a similar dilemma. After two years of university studies, he decided to quit because he wanted a salary sooner. He started working at a local shop, but the jobs available there have low growth potential. If he had completed his degree, he might have qualified for positions with better prospects and higher wages. By cutting his education short, he missed out on opportunities that could have improved his long‑term stability.

Many individuals are uncertain about their future because they lack clear information about which career paths suit them. Some are unsure which subjects interest them or which professions would be rewarding. Without guidance, they can feel stuck and unable to choose effectively. Family members, teachers, or mentors can provide the direction needed to explore options and avoid regrets. External support often makes it easier to evaluate the pros and cons of each decision and to create a realistic plan.

Even when people do have the ability to decide for themselves, the quality of their choices can be enhanced by the assistance they receive. Communities, relatives, and professional advisors can share experiences, point out hidden obstacles, and suggest resources that the individual might not see alone. This collaborative approach tends to produce more balanced decisions and reduces the chance of costly mistakes later on.

Ultimately, personal agency is valuable, but it works best when paired with knowledgeable help. By shaping their own lives and putting in the necessary effort today, individuals can secure a more comfortable future for themselves and, indirectly, for their children. When young people receive encouragement and practical support, they are more likely to make informed choices that open doors rather than close them, creating a cycle of better opportunities for the next generation.

Most people do not run the greatest risk by missing a target that is too ambitious; instead the real danger comes from aiming too low and staying there. When a goal is set beneath our true capabilities we can end up satisfied with mediocrity, losing the chance to improve and grow. On the other hand, an overly lofty aim may be hard to reach at first, but it pushes us to work harder and learn new skills. Falling short of a high goal still teaches us something useful, whereas settling for a low one can keep us stuck in the same place forever.

I find Michelangelo’s remark that “it is not necessary to be the best, as long as you put effort into something you can achieve anything” partly accurate. Effort is indeed a powerful driver of success; with consistent work we can accomplish tasks that would seem impossible at first glance. However, I disagree with the implication that a low standard of ambition is acceptable. If we habitually lower our expectations, we risk never reaching our full potential. True achievement often requires both a strong commitment to effort and a willingness to aim higher than what feels comfortable.

A concrete illustration can be found in my own studies. I am currently working toward my secondary‑school diploma. If I set a modest goal—just passing each class—I would still meet the minimum requirement. Yet by striving to earn top marks I push myself to revise more, ask questions, and develop a deeper understanding. In the end, the extra effort pays off, even if the result is not perfection, because I have learned more and built confidence that will help later in life.

We encounter this pattern in everyday situations, whether at work, in sports, or during personal projects. History shows the same pattern among societies that failed to pursue ambitious reforms while others thrived because they dared to set higher aspirations. Moreover, the phrase often reflects a common tendency: many individuals impose modest standards on themselves, assuming they cannot do better. Recognizing this habit is the first step toward changing it.

Therefore, the safest approach is to aim high while valuing the effort we put in. Setting lofty goals creates the pressure needed to stretch our abilities, while the dedication we apply ensures we move forward regardless of how high the bar is placed. This balance captures the essence of both effort and ambition and keeps us from the complacency that comes with settling for too little.

In everyday school or workplace situations, a common question arises: does taking a break from one task help a person finish other work, or does being constantly busy make it harder to achieve everything? I believe that periods of inactivity can actually be useful. When someone is not working, they may use that time to catch up on assignments, and this prevents them from later claiming they never had enough time. Moreover, being occupied does not always guarantee success, because a heavy workload can limit the time available for other duties, and rushing to meet tight deadlines often leads to mistakes and poorer outcomes.

First, allowing idle moments can enable learners to complete unfinished work. If a student is not engaged in a particular activity, the spare minutes can be spent finishing reading, writing, or problem‑solving tasks. This strategy avoids the excuse of “I had no time” and helps the teacher or employer see the student’s effort. On the other side, those who are busy may argue that they have too many assignments to handle, which indeed can leave little room for additional tasks. However, once a person finishes a given assignment and still has some time left, they should be given extra work so that their period is fully utilized rather than spent doing nothing.

Second, staying occupied can sometimes hurt productivity. When a person is juggling several things at once, the pressure to finish quickly may force them to hurry. This rush raises the chance of errors, which in turn produces lower grades or weaker performance reviews. Consequently, busy students or workers may end up not accomplishing their goals because of the limited time and the mistakes they make.

In sum, both completing work while actively engaged and completing it during idle moments have their place. Some individuals manage to finish tasks while working, while others need a break to catch up. Nonetheless, when a person has finished the required work but still has time before the class ends or the shift ends, they should be assigned further duties rather than simply sitting idle. This approach respects the idea that inactivity can serve a purpose in making sure all work is done.

I believe the most valuable achievement a person can reach is when another individual urges you to stay true to yourself, without forcing you to play a role you are not. In a world that often values polished images, living authentically feels both rare and rewarding.

When someone pretends to be someone they are not, they are essentially lying about their real character. Choosing to adopt another persona is, in my view, the worst decision anyone can make. It is true that people have different opinions about this; some argue that acting differently helps society progress. Nevertheless, I strongly disagree with that idea. The burden of keeping up a false front creates stress and can lead to decisions that do not serve personal well‑being.

We should stop worrying about what others expect of us and concentrate on our own needs. The most supportive relationships are with those who accept us exactly as we are. When we meet people who listen without judging, we can express ourselves openly, and that acceptance becomes a genuine accomplishment. Recognizing each other's uniqueness and refusing to change for the sake of conformity is the highest gift anyone can give.

I do not agree with Emerson’s claim that the greatest success comes from constantly reshaping ourselves to fit the world. Trying to become someone else at all times is exhausting and unnecessary. The true victory lies in showing who we really are, because every person carries something special. When we are authentic, we contribute to a more diverse and richer community.

Being yourself with another person often brings the deepest satisfaction. In today’s culture many people struggle to be genuine around others; some mock those who appear exactly as they are, while others simply ignore them. I think that is the way it should be—people should not feel obliged to wear a mask. We now see a broader range of identities, including gay, transgender, bisexual and homosexual individuals, which many accept as normal. Yet some still choose to hide or disguise themselves, sometimes creating confusion. Authenticity, even in these cases, helps clarify who we are.

A situation from my teenage years illustrates why honesty matters. At sixteen I had a classmate who always claimed to be rich. In reality she came from a modest family and her parents’ income was average. Because of this falsehood she attracted a lot of new friends, and some of my own friends stopped spending time with me, urging me to party, drink and smoke. My answer was always “no,” so they stopped asking me. Eventually the truth came out—her wealth claim was a lie— and my former friends told me everything. Their reaction made it clear that pretending does not always work out well. It also showed that trust depends on being truthful about who we are.

That experience taught me a simple lesson: encourage others to be themselves, no matter how difficult it feels. The best thing anyone can do is stay true to their own nature. People need to learn to accept others as they are, rather than demanding two faces. Nowadays many are willing to say whatever they want without caring what others think. Most of us are more focused on our own lives than on judging strangers.

When we reveal our real selves to someone, the reason is often that we feel comfortable with that person. In my view, honesty and authenticity create the strongest bonds, because they allow us to be seen without fear. This is why I always tell my friends, classmates and anyone I meet: be yourself, and let others see the person you truly are. The world will be better off when we stop living double lives and start living one genuine life.

Dear Mr. [TEACHER_NAME],

I understand that students are ultimately accountable for their academic performance, yet the rule that a B average is required to join any extracurricular program feels unreasonable. Most of us are already struggling to reach a C level, and tightening the standard would only increase the number of upset parents and disappointed classmates. I doubt you would want to be seen as the antagonist in this debate.

In my view, the school should at least lower the cutoff to a D average. If a student truly wishes to play a sport or take part in an activity, keeping grades above an F is a sensible baseline, as it shows they are passing their courses while still pursuing interests outside the classroom. At the same time, we all know that school is not just a fun break from studying; academics must come first. Maintaining respectable grades opens doors later in life and demonstrates discipline that benefits both personal and community goals.

Parents often argue that sports help keep youngsters away from trouble, which is true to an extent. However, if we raise the GPA requirement, a student who previously stayed on track might fall into a pattern of seeking trouble and even involve law‑enforcement services. Please consider how such a change would ripple through our student body and the broader community. Adjusting the policy could protect those who need a gentle reminder to prioritize school while still allowing them room to enjoy sports and other activities.

Sincerely,  
A concerned student.

I agree with the idea that first impressions are almost impossible to alter. The reason is that believing in yourself is a prerequisite for creating a lasting image of who you are. When you enter college or begin your first job search, confidence in your abilities helps you take the necessary steps—saving money, choosing the right career path, and handling the practical challenges that arise. As you gain experience, you learn more about yourself, discover which tasks feel comfortable, and gradually build the skill set that supports the impression you want to project.

This self‑affirmation makes the impression you give off appear consistent and genuine. Because you act in line with the belief you have about yourself, others tend to treat it as your real personality. It is therefore hard for a person who never adjusts his or her self‑view to change the way they are perceived. While everyone’s initial impression varies—some people’s images remain static because they never make an effort to try new things or because they think they already have all the knowledge they need—their lack of initiative keeps the original view intact.

In contrast, individuals who manage to reshape their impression usually display greater self‑confidence. They are willing to invest time in purposeful activities rather than idle pastimes, and they understand that personal growth requires effort. However, if a person adopts a careless attitude, sees no value in planning for the future, or views himself or herself as useless, any possibility of transforming the initial impression disappears. The statement, therefore, holds true: without genuine self‑belief, the first impression tends to stay fixed, and only those who actively nurture confidence can alter it.

Why should anyone claim the authority to tell us what truly matters in life or dictate our choices? Life gives each person the chance to shape their own existence, especially when they can rely on themselves. With self‑reliance, a person does not need external instructions; they can decide freely based on personal values.

Even when we are unsure, we should still act on our own judgment. Selecting without complete confidence can teach us how to refine our approach. The process builds confidence, which is useful for later decisions. At the same time, making those choices ourselves lets us discover, step by step, what is most meaningful to us.

Mistakes are inevitable when we make decisions, but they are not failures. They serve as practical lessons, showing us what does not work and how to adjust it. Many people turn to specialists for major choices because they fear making the wrong move. While seeking expert advice is understandable, we should first examine our own intuition before paying someone else to decide for us.

When we choose our own options, we gain a sense of security about our actions, strengthening our capacity to make future decisions independently. If a chosen path turns out wrong, the experience provides a valuable reference, allowing us to improve without needing constant external help.

No one else can fully know what is meaningful for you, because each person’s priorities differ. It is essential to invest time in reflecting on personal values, rather than simply accepting a one‑size‑fits‑all answer. By taking responsibility for our own decisions, we respect our uniqueness and align actions with our own vision of a worthwhile life.

In summary, deciding for ourselves promotes confidence, offers opportunities to learn from errors, and lets us define what is truly important. Trusting our own judgment, even when uncertain, leads to a more autonomous and fulfilling life.

The prompt asks us to consider how failure fits into the process of becoming successful, and I largely agree with the view that setbacks can become a bridge toward achievement. It is easy for us to feel stuck when we keep failing, and at times the monotony of repeated attempts can even make us reconsider our goals. Nevertheless, some people believe that repeated failure guarantees the opposite outcome—that you will never succeed. In the workplace, for example, if a candidate constantly misunderstands what a manager asks, the employer may conclude that the person is unsuitable and reject the application.

I also find Churchill’s statement compelling: success does not come without effort because the journey is hard by nature. To obtain a job, a home, or enough food, individuals must persist despite obstacles. History shows that many people lack these basic necessities precisely because they stopped trying. Real success usually means moving from one failure to another, learning each lesson and using it to improve. No one is born with a ticket to success; we all start from scratch.

In short, while failure can be discouraging, it also provides valuable experience. It can teach us what does not work and push us to try new approaches. This cycle of trying, failing, and trying again is the engine that eventually leads to success.

Some students think the current summer vacation is too short. They argue that the break should be longer and that the spring holiday should be eliminated. The spring break could be used instead for the SOL (state‑level test), giving students extra time to study and prepare.

If we keep spring break, it only adds a week that could otherwise be used for test preparation. Instead, schools should start the summer period in June and finish it in August. Starting earlier, in May, is problematic because the weather is still cool in many parts of the country. June offers warmer temperatures, more daylight and a better chance to enjoy a proper vacation with family and friends.

By removing spring break, the week that was once a break becomes a focused study week for the SOL. Teachers can use that time to give extra instruction, conduct mock exams, and review material for the final tests. Students will have more time in class to ask questions and receive help, which improves overall learning.

Another benefit of a June‑to‑August summer is that it allows more organized school‑based activities. The schools could plan sports tournaments, cultural trips, museum visits, university tours, and other extracurricular events during the extra time. This gives both students and teachers a chance to relax, explore, and gain new experiences while still keeping the academic schedule balanced.

In addition, a longer summer break would give students three full months to recharge before the next academic year. With no spring break, there is no interruption that could delay curriculum progress. This means more instructional weeks and a smoother flow from one term to the next.

Overall, I agree with those who say that the school calendar should be adjusted. Extending summer to June and August and canceling spring break would give students additional weeks for the SOL, final‑exam preparation, and meaningful extracurricular activities. It would also improve the quality of classroom instruction and make the learning experience more productive for everyone.
