I believe that honesty is usually the right thing to do, even when the truth is uncomfortable. While it is true that speaking bluntly can cause short‑term pain, the long‑term benefits of being truthful outweigh those moments of discomfort. Honesty builds trust and helps people grow, which is why I support it in most situations.

First, when friends keep each other honest, their relationships become stronger. If one person points out a mistake, it may feel awkward at first, but it prevents repeated errors and shows respect. If everyone pretends everything is fine, trust eventually erodes and misunderstandings pile up. I have noticed that friends who tell me directly what I am doing wrong often express gratitude later because the correction helps me improve. In contrast, those who hide the truth may seem kind in the moment, but the truth usually surfaces later, leaving both parties disappointed. Although telling the hard facts can sting, I think it is better to face those short bursts of hurt now than to deal with the fallout of deception later.

Second, honesty with parents creates a safety net when problems arise. If I am in trouble at school or need guidance, my parents are more likely to step in quickly if I have been straightforward about my situation. They can help me find solutions, give useful advice, or intervene when necessary. If I keep silent or exaggerate, they may suspect something is wrong and become distant. Their trust in me depends on whether I have been truthful in the past. I have learned that when I own up to my mistakes, my parents respond with support rather than criticism, which strengthens our bond and makes future talks easier.

Third, lying damages one’s reputation quickly and permanently. Imagine someone makes a bad choice and then hides it. The longer they stay quiet, the more likely they will be caught, and the impact of the discovery will be harsher. In my view, it is far simpler to confess the error right away; then the outcome can be controlled, and the damage stays limited. Moreover, people who discover dishonesty often feel betrayed, which makes rebuilding trust a lengthy, painful process. On the other hand, an upfront admission, even if it hurts at the moment, usually earns respect and reduces the chance of future misunderstandings.

These points show that, despite occasional discomfort, honesty brings more advantages than disadvantages. Truth‑telling may cause a temporary sting, but it prevents deeper wounds that arise from secrets and lies. I value honest people because they deliver the real picture early, saving me from later disappointment. In adult life—at work, within a family, or while handling daily challenges—being truthful prepares you for the inevitable unfairness of the world. If you can face reality head‑on, you are better equipped to cope, solve problems, and keep relationships healthy.

Overall, while there are moments when truth feels painful, I still think honesty is a valuable quality to cultivate. I would rather have honest friends and family who tell me the facts now, than encounter betrayal later when a lie is finally uncovered. By practicing openness and taking responsibility for my words, I can build a life built on trust and mutual respect, even when the path is not always fair.

People often claim that we achieve more when we stay busy. In reality, it is those who work consistently who bring inventions like car radios, televisions, and computers into everyday life. Individuals who do not engage in productive activity miss out on the rapid pace of technological growth. Technology must be built, refined, and updated, and it not only creates jobs but also provides a way to earn a living. When a larger portion of the population remains active, daily life changes, quality of life improves, and societies around the world benefit. The most influential items that have evolved over the years are computers, televisions, and radios, and we use them almost every day.

If we aim to accomplish more, we need to keep doing something. The radio serves as a clear illustration of this idea. When radios first entered the market, engineers faced difficulty in getting the sound settings right, and their perseverance produced a popular breakthrough. Because people kept working on the radio, it grew and improved over time. This continual effort opened the door to the first television sets.

Television represented another major leap forward. Unlike silent movies, TVs offered both sound and moving pictures on a screen, which attracted a wide audience. The strong desire among developers to deliver clearer audio and video meant that societies could view events from home, including the first televised election. Those who devoted time and skill to TV products were driven to make the devices reliable and to win consumer trust, and their success laid the foundation for the rise of computers.

The earliest computers were quiet machines programmed to perform basic tasks. Engineers wanted to turn them into useful tools, so they added features and improved performance to increase sales. The work invested in early computers eventually enabled later innovations such as solar panel testing and many other advanced applications.

In short, constant activity fuels progress. Ongoing work leads to faster improvements in the tools that shape how we live.

I still remember the interview I had when I applied to a private secondary school. The headmaster asked me what I intended to do professionally after graduation, and his response was clear: the school expects students to have chosen a specific career path before they start high school. He explained that many of the courses offered are geared toward preparing learners for particular occupations, so it helps when applicants already know the direction they want to go.

I agree with the article’s view that teenagers should decide on a career by the time they enter high school. Knowing what you want to study and practise early gives you a clear target and prevents you from wasting years on subjects that do not support your future profession. When you pick a field you genuinely like, you are more likely to stay motivated and invest the extra effort required to become skilled.

For example, I have always been interested in cars. Working on automobiles feels satisfying, and I imagine that a career as a mechanic could provide both personal fulfilment and a stable income. If you love an activity, you naturally spend extra time honing the related abilities. I also spend much of my summer practising soccer because it is one of my favourite pastimes; the hope of becoming a professional player keeps me focused on daily drills and training.

Not everyone gets the exact job they imagined right away. My sister wanted to be a nurse from a young age. She began learning nursing tasks early, studied hard, and today, after six years of experience, she works as a certified nurse. Her dedication shows that with consistent practice and perseverance you can turn a long‑standing dream into reality.

In short, I think students should identify a career they feel passionate about, work on it regularly, and remain committed even when setbacks appear. This approach helps them acquire the expertise they need and raises the likelihood of achieving their professional goals.

If I could pick one destination to explore, I would choose Paris. This city offers three attractions that excite me the most: the Eiffel Tower, live performances by famous actors and singers, and a visit to the world‑class roller coaster at Cedar Point in Ohio.

The first reason is the Eiffel Tower. I have always wanted to stand beneath it and feel how massive it truly is. By climbing to the top, I could enjoy panoramic views of the city lights at night and imagine how the structure is illuminated for special events. A trip with my family would be perfect because the tower symbolizes unity and beauty, making it an unforgettable memory for everyone.

Next, I would spend time watching renowned artists in action. Paris hosts many large theaters, concert halls, and film festivals where top actors and singers perform live. I could watch a favorite movie star on stage, hear my beloved singer sing a hit song, and even ask them a few questions about their career paths. The chance to collect an autograph or receive a quick tip would feel like a personal connection to the people I admire.

Finally, I plan to travel to Ohio to ride Cedar Point’s famous roller coaster, which claims to be the fastest in the world. The excitement of hurtling forward at high speed, the wind rushing past, and the sharp turns would make me nervous yet thrilled. I would like to learn from the engineers who built the ride what materials and designs allow such speed, turning a simple curiosity into a deeper appreciation of roller‑coaster technology.

In summary, visiting Paris would let me experience the Eiffel Tower’s grandeur, encounter talented performers, and set the stage for a thrilling roller‑coaster adventure in Ohio. Each of these experiences promises something different, yet together they would create a trip full of awe, inspiration, and unforgettable moments.

Most of us have to choose what to do each day, and there is often a debate about who should make those choices – the person themselves or someone else. In my opinion, individuals are better off deciding for themselves. First, deciding on their own helps people develop confidence. When we take responsibility for a choice, we learn that we can handle different situations, and this experience builds trust in our own judgment. If we always let others decide, we may start to doubt our abilities and feel less sure about future actions.

Second, making personal decisions tends to lead to greater happiness. People who follow their own ideas and values are more likely to feel satisfied with the outcomes because the results match what they truly want. In contrast, when we merely follow someone else’s instructions, the sense of fulfillment can be weaker. Even when life presents victories and defeats, having a voice in the decisions that shape our experience makes those moments feel meaningful.

Finally, the process of deciding trains us to face difficult moments. Tough choices often require weighing risks, evaluating alternatives, and committing to a path. This practice strengthens resilience, so later challenges are met with a clearer mind and a stronger will. It is true that those who avoid making decisions may seem to have an easier life with fewer worries, but they miss out on the growth that comes from confronting and solving problems. 

Overall, allowing people to choose their own course encourages confidence, promotes happiness, and prepares them for life’s challenges. Even though it can feel more demanding, the benefits outweigh the comfort of letting others decide.

I do not support school districts implementing programs that enable students to earn their high school diploma in three years rather than four. While finishing sooner may seem efficient, this compressed timeline typically creates more problems than it solves.

First, spreading coursework over three years demands an unsustainable pace. Students would need to study heavily during summers and evenings, leaving little room for mental recovery. Such relentless effort often results in fatigue, diminishing their capacity to learn effectively. Moreover, with reduced hours available, elective subjects—essential for discovering interests and shaping career paths—are frequently sacrificed, limiting personal growth.

Although completing the diploma faster offers a slight time advantage, the drawbacks outweigh the benefit. The additional workload does not adequately compensate for the loss of a balanced school experience. In contrast, a four-year program allows a more manageable schedule, enabling students to retain electives without pressure and maintain regular breaks. This extra year also provides valuable preparation time before university, helping learners reflect on their future goals and deepen their knowledge.

Ultimately, the four-year diploma remains the preferable choice because it prioritizes student well-being and long-term success. The additional year fosters both academic stability and personal development, equipping graduates with stronger readiness for post-secondary education and the professional world. Investing time in thorough high school preparation yields better outcomes than rushing through a shortened curriculum.

In my view, moving lessons to a home‑based setting through online platforms or video calls does not help students. I believe the supposed advantage of being able to join class from anywhere is largely outweighed by the problems it creates.

First, studying at home usually brings many interruptions. A living room or bedroom often contains televisions, smartphones, games consoles, and other household activities that pull attention away from schoolwork. Even when a student tries to focus, siblings playing, pets moving around, or household chores make it hard to stay on task. Because of this, teachers have reported that students who attend remotely are less engaged, and schools must find other ways to keep lessons effective.

Second, face‑to‑face instruction offers benefits that a screen cannot replace. When students sit in a classroom, they can hear a teacher’s explanations immediately, ask follow‑up questions, and see the teacher’s body language. This personal contact makes the material clearer and helps students retain it better. Moreover, classmates can discuss ideas with each other, encouraging deeper thinking. In contrast, online sessions tend to be more passive; students watch videos or listen without much interaction, which reduces the overall learning impact.

Third, the home environment often clashes with the needs of academic work. Many pupils share a house with several family members, and noise from conversations, laughter, or background music can become a constant distraction. Personally, I have three brothers and a sister, and their presence makes it difficult for me to concentrate on school tasks. Such conditions are rarely available in a school setting where the atmosphere is designed for learning.

Lastly, timing also matters. Some students feel more alert in the morning, but staying in front of a computer all day can lead to fatigue, especially if they are required to log on in the evening. Although the technology makes lessons flexible, this flexibility does not automatically translate into better understanding or memory retention.

In conclusion, the evidence suggests that students learn more when they attend school rather than through distance learning. My parents share this view, because they see higher grades and more enthusiasm when I study in a classroom setting. For these reasons, I support keeping traditional classroom attendance.

Modern life means many routine activities can be finished without face-to-face interaction. For example, borrowing a book from the library, buying groceries, or playing video games often happen online without talking to a cashier, librarian, or fellow player. Although this saves time, it also cuts down on natural human contact that used to happen in daily life.

Humans have always depended on social bonds, and studies show regular contact is vital for mental well-being. Over history, communities created marketplaces, schools, and workplaces to bring people together. That’s why building new friendships matters—technology overuse can make us forget these links, so stepping away from screens occasionally is necessary.

Digital services make shopping and entertainment simple, yet they can’t satisfy our biological need for personal connection. We’ve grown accustomed to doing nearly everything remotely, but friendship requires shared experiences. Children illustrate this trend: many receive tablets before they walk, leading to kids who sit alone glued to phones at school or work. They miss chances to learn teamwork and conversation skills.

In short, while technology improves convenience, it also creates isolation. Heavy reliance on devices, especially during childhood, may prevent forming new bonds. Balancing virtual tools with real-world communication should be a priority for everyone’s social health.

Allowing pupils to bring smartphones to school can be beneficial. In many cases a student might face a sudden problem, such as an injury, a car crash involving a parent, or a personal safety concern while walking home. Having a phone means the child can quickly contact a guardian or the authorities. For instance, if a parent becomes ill, a child could call to be picked up or inform the school. Similarly, if a student feels threatened or someone nearby faints, a phone enables an immediate call to the nurse or emergency services.

The school should therefore permit phones but set clear limits. Phones may be used during lunch breaks for personal messages or socialising, and they can be kept on in corridors for genuine emergencies. In classrooms they must be switched off, stored in bags or lockers, to minimise distraction. The principal can enforce this policy by reminding teachers and posting signs that indicate when phones are allowed. In this way students retain a safety tool while maintaining a focused learning environment.

In sum, giving pupils access to phones under controlled conditions helps protect them in unexpected situations without compromising academic work.

I think it is a good idea to stay true to ourselves wherever we go. In my view, being who we really are is better than pretending to be someone else just to fit in. It means we trust our own judgement, ignore the noise of people who want us to change, and stay firm about what matters to us. When we act according to our inner values we become stronger, and that strength shows others what we are capable of. It also gives us a clear direction as we work toward our personal goals.

For example, if we keep our authentic self, others can see our determination. This can encourage them to believe they can also improve their own lives. In this way, being genuine can spread a positive influence, helping the people around us feel more confident.

Society is constantly trying to shape us into a standard version of success. It pushes us to accept new habits, wear new clothes, or adopt certain attitudes that it considers “best”. While some of these suggestions may seem helpful, many of them are simply attempts to make us fit a mould that does not fit our needs. When we notice that the path society proposes is not right for us, we can choose a different route. However, we should be careful, because changing our habits can affect other people in ways we may not see. Even if we have a good reason for our own change, we need to think about how it might impact those around us.

Being true to ourselves does not mean ignoring advice altogether. It means we keep our own principles while still listening to useful information. This balance lets us respect ourselves and also respect the people we live with. When we act with self‑respect, we tend to receive respect in return. It also makes us more honest in our relationships, which can reduce misunderstandings and conflicts.

Trusting ourselves is essential when the people around us try to hold us back. Some individuals, groups, or even social norms may want us to fail in order to keep us from achieving our dreams. Working hard to stay focused on our own goals can protect us from that negative influence. If we lose confidence, we might give up or let others decide our future, which would stop us from reaching the success we want.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once observed that society often urges us to change in order to improve, but he also reminded us that true progress comes from listening to our inner voice. When we believe in our own abilities and keep our eyes on the target, it becomes easier to move forward, even when external forces try to push us off course. As long as we keep a strong sense of purpose, we are less likely to be diverted.

Finally, staying authentic brings satisfaction. It means we do things that make us happy, follow our own interests, and keep our integrity. Even when others suggest a different approach, we can recognise that we know what is right for us. This confidence can inspire them, but it also protects us from being misled. In short, being yourself is the most reliable way to reach our goals and to live a life we respect.

Do you agree with the claim that success is found in moving from failure to failure without losing enthusiasm? In my view, Winston Churchill’s quotation rings true because life rarely offers a straight path to flawless results. It is natural to stumble, and the crucial factor is how we respond to those stumbles.

Take my experience with an English exam last year. I studied intensively, hoping to earn an A or at least a B. When the results arrived, I fell short of the grade I wanted, which left me disappointed. My teacher, however, told me I could retake the test. I seized the second chance and achieved an A‑minus, feeling a surge of excitement. This incident taught me that the number of times I slipped up matters less than the persistence I display. Whether the setback is a bad score on a test or a rejected proposal, what counts is my willingness to keep trying, learn from each mistake, and stay motivated.

A similar pattern appears in the life of my aunt, who dreams of visiting her mother in El Salvador. She first tried to book a ticket, but the price seemed too high for her budget, so she postponed the trip. Seven months later she returned to the airline’s website. The fares had risen even more, yet she decided to proceed. While purchasing, she discovered her passport had expired, making the booking impossible. She felt upset because she had forgotten to renew the document, but she quickly arranged the renewal. After that, the new passport arrived after several weeks, and during that waiting period she missed another scheduled departure. Although she still cannot travel, she continues to talk about the upcoming visit with enthusiasm. Her experience shows that setbacks, even when they feel discouraging, need not kill the dream.

Some critics argue that Churchill’s idea is overly optimistic, suggesting that repeated failures make a person look incompetent. They point out that after two unsuccessful attempts, one might be labelled a loser or a weak individual. Yet, I think this negative viewpoint stems from losing motivation. When enthusiasm fades, each failure becomes a sign of defeat rather than a lesson. Keeping a positive attitude allows us to view errors as stepping stones toward improvement.

In conclusion, the statement that success involves repeatedly encountering obstacles while maintaining enthusiasm is valid. My own academic experience and my aunt’s travel planning illustrate how setbacks can be overcome by staying driven and learning from them. For anyone aiming to achieve goals, the key is not to avoid mistakes but to keep the fire burning, turning each hurdle into an opportunity for growth. Only by persisting can we become stronger and ultimately succeed.

Some teachers suggest a four‑day school week in hopes of saving energy. They say fewer days would reduce lighting, heating, and equipment use.

I disagree, because if the total teaching hours stay the same, each day would become roughly two hours longer. Students would spend about ten hours in school each day, needing more lighting, air‑conditioning, and heating, which would increase electricity consumption.

A longer school day also raises the demand for everyday supplies. More class time means more printed worksheets, extra paper for notes, and greater water use in restrooms and cleaning. These natural resources would be exhausted faster, and the school would have to find ways to limit waste.

In addition, technology stays on longer. Computers, tablets, and projectors would remain powered for most of the day, adding to the power load in every classroom and possibly causing overheating.

Overall, the four‑day schedule would stretch the daily operation, leading to higher use of energy, water, paper, and electricity. Therefore, it is unlikely to help conserve resources and should not be adopted in schools.

Living in an environment where I am constantly called on to give my all feels like a cornerstone of real achievement. I agree with Emerson’s view that personal uniqueness is the engine that drives us toward any goal. Without a clear sense of self, the steps we take can easily lose direction, and we risk staying stuck in the same routine. Recognising that we must earn our ambitions through genuine effort keeps us focused on the work ahead. Knowing that our performance depends on our own commitment pushes us to stay diligent, to sharpen our skills, and to aim higher than the next person. Individuality gives us confidence that we can chart our own path, and it pushes us to look for alternatives that fit our own lives rather than blindly following a crowd.

Working alone is a powerful motivator. When a person tackles a task without external partners, the responsibility rests entirely on him or her. The drive to fix every detail, to make the final result shine, often leads to a higher standard of output. Think of a solo project you finish early—feeling a surge of excitement, you anticipate the praise or reward that follows. Everybody craves acknowledgment, yet the reward comes only after we have built the capacity to earn it. Many people, like me, find that taking on their own work sparks a stronger emotional response, helping them increase both quantity and quality of what they produce. In factories, workers who handle their own assignments usually show a noticeable rise in productivity, which in turn brings more resources to the organization.

Competition can sharpen individual output. It is easy to think that rivalry only divides teams, but when it becomes a personal challenge it can actually lift everyone. For example, when one employee begins to earn more money because of excellent performance, others notice and feel a spark of desire to match that success. Even though the distribution of pay may seem uneven, the presence of a competition pushes each worker to hunt for new ways to outperform their peers. In a busy plant, the simple act of seeing a colleague finish his task ahead of schedule can trigger a rush of emotion in the rest of the crew, prompting them to seek out faster methods or more efficient tools. Thus, competition turns solitary work into a source of both challenge and reward.

Pursuing recognition also fuels perseverance. In today’s world, we often face criticism, bullying, or other obstacles, yet the path to standing out requires staying patient and steadfast. The belief that our true worth lies within us, not in the opinions of others, allows us to keep moving forward. If we want to be different and truly reach our objectives, we must rely on our own decisions and support. History shows countless leaders who achieved greatness by forging ahead without waiting for others to pull them along. A soccer team, for instance, relies on the captain who constantly pushes the players to improve. Similarly, a company’s top executive must outpace rivals who also dream of leadership. In both realms, the ability to decide and act independently is what separates the ordinary from the exceptional.

Choosing to work on our own projects also forces us to manage risks and rewards. Each time we step away from a group setting, we take on a personal commitment to the outcome. The mental weight of that responsibility sharpens our focus and encourages us to seek creative solutions. In many organizations, owners look for ways to reward those who generate the most output, offering extra pay or free time. This structure encourages a division of labor where each employee strives to be the most productive. As a result, competition thrives, and overall performance rises. The same principle applies to governments, where officials compete to propose the best policies. The benefits of this competition—faster decision‑making, higher efficiency—show that individuality can drive progress across society.

Overall, I maintain that a life full of demands that push us to exceed our limits is the best training ground for success. When we set out on our own, we pour effort and dedication into the task, and that investment eventually pays off in achievement. Working in groups is valuable, but the additional pressure that comes from personal competition creates a unique boost of energy. Individuals who embrace this pressure often become the difference‑makers, influencing their fields positively. Emerson’s claim rings true: individuality, coupled with a healthy dose of competition, is what helps us unlock our full potential, whether in a factory, a corporation, a nation, or a football field.

In the 21st century, individuals are encouraged to form their own opinions and take charge of their choices. The rapid pace of technological and cultural change has given people more freedom than ever before, yet that liberty often goes hand‑in‑hand with impulsive risk‑taking. While many feel confident about the decisions they make on a daily basis, there are countless occasions when they ignore professional counsel, trusting their intuition alone.  

Expert advice can be a valuable safety net because professionals possess knowledge that most people do not. Whether it is a medical specialist, a financial planner, or an experienced industry mentor, these individuals have already navigated similar problems and can point out hidden pitfalls. Consulting them does not mean surrendering personal judgment; rather, it adds perspective that sharpens the final choice. Studies repeatedly show that people who incorporate expert input tend to achieve more balanced and successful outcomes.  

Take the entertainment industry as a concrete illustration. Many famous performers rely on managers who act as advisors and gatekeepers. These managers evaluate contracts, negotiate terms, and help artists maintain focus on long‑term goals. If a star decides to bypass this support and make decisions alone, the likelihood of missteps increases. History provides examples where a well‑known musician dropped his manager, only to see his popularity tumble because he lost a clear career direction.  

A more tragic illustration appears in Jon Krakauer’s book *Into the Wild*. Christopher McCandless abandoned all professional advice and set out solo into the Alaskan wilderness. He packed insufficient supplies, neglected basic survival training, and failed to check weather forecasts. His fatal isolation is a stark reminder that even the most determined self‑reliance can backfire when crucial information is ignored. A brief consultation with a seasoned outdoorsman might have saved his life.  

The broader point is that thoughtful decision‑making is rarely a solo endeavour. Successful entrepreneurs often surround themselves with mentors and board members, while athletes rely on coaches to keep performance on target. Seeking advice does not diminish personal responsibility; it simply spreads the burden of risk across more knowledgeable shoulders. By doing so, people become less vulnerable to blind spots, better prepared for setbacks, and more likely to keep their goals on track.  

In short, it is wise for anyone facing a significant life choice to ask for guidance before proceeding. Whether the decision involves a career move, a health issue, or a personal adventure, input from experts adds credibility and reduces the chance of costly mistakes. Ignoring that input, as Christopher McCandless did, can lead to disastrous results. Therefore, cultivating a habit of consulting knowledgeable advisors is a practical way to turn ambition into lasting achievement.

Living in today’s world, I believe I can go on without constantly depending on the people around me. I have learned that many of the things I achieve are the result of my own effort rather than the help of others. My education, career steps, and personal goals have all come from what I have done myself, and I have never felt that I need a crowd to lift me up. Relying on myself, I can keep moving forward, even when the people nearby are absent or unhelpful.

The people I meet are not always trustworthy. In the environment I know, I often see that others hope for my failure instead of my success. Some friends try to pull me into wrongdoing, suggesting shortcuts or bad choices, and the school system sometimes appears indifferent to my growth. It seems that many adults and peers would rather see me struggle than see me thrive. If I were completely alone, I think I could build a brighter future without those negative forces dragging me down.

A concrete example is a friend I once called Maya. At first she was friendly and supportive, and we spent time together studying and chatting. As time passed, however, she began urging me to skip school, arguing that learning would never help me become someone important. Her family situation was also shaky, and she kept getting into trouble with them. My parents stopped approving of her, and I realized that she was leading me toward harmful behavior. Because I felt uncomfortable with the direction she was taking me, I stopped speaking with her. I needed to protect myself from the influence she was offering.

I have also experienced the difficulty of working alone during a class test. In a math exam, a classmate asked me to give him the answers so he could cheat. I refused because the teacher could have punished both of us, and I did not want to risk my own grade for his short‑term gain. When the test finished, he complained that his score was low and blamed me for not helping. I reminded him that the only reliable way to improve is to study for himself; no one else will be there to write his answers when he faces the next exam. This moment reinforced my belief that relying on myself is the safest path to success.

Staying determined has been another key factor in my progress. My cousin once told me I would never graduate because I am not smart enough. Instead of letting her opinion stop me, I chose to ignore it and keep working hard. I devote evenings to review lessons, ask questions online, and practice problems until I understand them. Even on days when her words make me want to cry, I refocus on the effort I am putting in. Knowing that I am doing my best keeps me motivated, and I am confident that I will finish school this year, regardless of what others think.

In summary, I think I do not need a large circle of people around me to reach my goals. Some of them push me toward negative choices and can even cause real damage. If I stay on my own, I avoid the risk of being harmed by others’ bad intentions. The world can be dangerous when people are hostile, and keeping a distance reduces my exposure to that danger. By concentrating on my own actions, I keep my stress limited to what I can control. Independence lets me keep my mind clear and my focus sharp, making it easier to achieve the things I want without having to worry about someone else’s problems.

Therefore, my conclusion is that a solitary path is not only possible but also preferable for me. The support I get from my own determination outweighs the uncertainty and potential harm that come from relying on unreliable people. I will continue to pursue my ambitions on my own terms, because that is the way I can protect myself and still succeed.

Many people think that a first impression is not set in stone and can be revised later. A negative picture that someone leaves behind, for example because they appear rude or speak unkindly, does not have to stay the same if the person decides to act differently.

First of all, a person who has seemed disrespectful can learn to behave politely. With a little self‑reflection and effort, they may start showing courtesy in everyday situations. When you meet them again, you may notice that their attitude has improved, and the original judgment no longer matches the reality you see. This shows that someone’s outward behavior can change, and that change can influence how we perceive them.

Secondly, a bad first impression is often a product of the moment rather than a permanent trait. Someone might be short‑tempered because they are tired, stressed, or dealing with a personal problem. Meeting them later, after that temporary condition has passed, can lead to a much smoother conversation. In other words, a single negative encounter does not capture the whole personality, and subsequent interactions may reveal a more balanced side.

Thirdly, although the mind tends to retain the first image, it is not completely frozen. New experiences, extra information, or repeated contact can update that mental picture. While it is true that the initial impression stays in the background, it can be reshaped by what we learn about the person later on. Therefore, the idea that first impressions cannot change is too absolute.

In conclusion, it is unwise to decide on someone’s character before giving them a proper chance to show themselves. Everyone has the ability to evolve, and a fresh opportunity can overturn a previously negative view. By waiting to see more evidence of their behavior, we avoid premature judgments and allow for the possibility that a person can indeed change the way we think about them.

Whether the mistake is in a project or in a personal interaction, reflection and correction are essential for progress.

There are many everyday ways to stay informed and keep growing. Reading newspapers, watching news broadcasts, and simply asking questions of knowledgeable people open doors to new perspectives. These actions remind me that learning does not have to be formal; curiosity can be sparked anywhere.

By acknowledging this, we see that everyone—young or old—has something to contribute.

People often come to me for advice because they trust my willingness to listen. I try to offer the same support I have received, encouraging friends to express their ideas and helping them find practical solutions. In turn, I learn how to be more empathetic and attentive.

If you need guidance, would you rely on a single individual or gather input from several people to obtain a range of viewpoints? I believe the latter is the more sensible approach. Seeking counsel from more than one person provides a wider set of perspectives on the matter you are facing.  

Firstly, consulting multiple sources lets you see the issue from different angles. One friend might focus on practicality, another on emotional impact, and yet another on long‑term consequences. By comparing these angles, you can form a clearer picture of what the situation actually entails and avoid overlooking important details that a single advisor might miss.  

Secondly, a diverse group of advisors helps you judge whether a choice is truly dangerous or simply unfamiliar. For example, consider a risky decision such as pursuing a career change. A protective parent may warn you against it out of concern for safety, while a daring colleague might encourage you to seize the opportunity. Listening to both views equips you to weigh the risks more objectively and decide whether the action is genuinely harmful or worth the potential reward.  

Finally, depending on just one person can produce a biased judgment. By obtaining advice from several trusted people, you increase the chance of reaching a balanced decision that supports rather than hinders your progress.  

In short, gathering advice from multiple individuals enables you to spot both the pitfalls and the benefits of any option. This broader awareness greatly improves your ability to make choices that serve you well in the long run.

Do you follow the advice of professionals and authority figures, or do you prefer to decide things for yourself? In my view, most decisions should be made by the individuals who are directly affected by them. I will explain three reasons why relying on others can be risky and why taking personal responsibility leads to a healthier, more confident life.

First, no one has perfect knowledge. Even experts can be mistaken, biased, or simply unaware of the unique circumstances that surround a particular choice. When we accept another person's guidance without questioning it, we may be basing our actions on outdated information or personal preferences that do not match our own situation. For instance, a trusted friend might believe that a particular career path is the best for everyone, yet that advice ignores your interests, abilities, or the current job market in your region. Acting on such counsel can result in regret or avoidable trouble, whereas checking facts yourself reduces the chance of making a blind move.

Second, only you truly understand what you want in life. Your values, hopes, and long‑term goals are personal and cannot be accurately gauged by anyone else. Listening to other people’s opinions can provide useful input, but it cannot replace the internal reflection that reveals what truly matters to you. Whether it is selecting a university major, deciding to move abroad, or choosing a hobby, the decision must reflect your own motivations. If you let others dictate your path, you risk pursuing something that feels empty or forced, and that feeling can linger for years.

Third, copying others often leads to poor choices. The media constantly shows examples of people who follow a trend and end up in trouble, whether that means legal trouble, financial loss, or damage to their reputation. When you simply imitate what you see others doing, you ignore the fact that each individual faces different consequences. In school, students sometimes make mistakes because they go along with peer pressure rather than thinking through the risks. By standing apart from the crowd and evaluating each option on its own merits, you not only protect yourself but also set a positive example for classmates who might be uncertain.

Trusting others completely also creates a dilemma. Imagine a best friend trying to decide whether you should accept a scholarship abroad. You might hesitate because you cannot be certain if their judgment is correct, or if they have hidden motives. In life, people are not always honest or objective, and putting your fate in their hands means you are surrendering control over a crucial part of your future. Taking personal responsibility, on the other hand, lets you learn from your own successes and failures, and you can adapt your choices as you gain experience.

When it comes to decision‑making, it is wise to ask yourself a few simple questions before acting. “Does this choice align with my values?” “What could go wrong, and how would I handle it?” “Am I comfortable with the possible outcomes?” Answering these prompts helps you avoid impulsive actions and gives you confidence that you have thought things through. You should also be willing to say “no” to an option that feels uncomfortable, even if peers pressure you to go along. No one else has the right to decide for you, and insisting on that right encourages independence and self‑esteem.

My own experience of picking friends illustrates this point. When I started a new school, I deliberately evaluated each potential friend based on shared interests and mutual respect rather than jumping into a group simply because it seemed popular. By being selective, I avoided being drawn into negative behavior and kept my social circle positive.

In summary, allowing yourself to make decisions empowers you to shape your life according to your own ideas and experiences. While advice from experts can be helpful, it should never replace your own judgment. I believe it is always beneficial to be truthful, even when the truth could make someone feel upset. Honesty may be uncomfortable, but it shows respect for others and keeps relationships clear. For instance, if a classmate shows romantic interest and you are not interested, it is kinder to let them know directly rather than lead them on. Although it might sting, the person will appreciate your honesty and avoid confusion later.

Another experience taught me this lesson. One afternoon I accidentally kicked a soccer ball that struck my neighbour’s car. The next day my mother asked me to explain what happened to the neighbour. I was nervous because I thought he would become angry, but I went over and admitted that the ball had hit his vehicle. He was upset and I received some blame, yet I felt better for having spoken the truth.

When I was younger, I broke my mother’s favorite vase. She called out for the culprit, and I was scared to admit I had caused it. My cousin urged me to come clean, so I went to my mother and confessed that I had knocked the vase over. She was angry at first, but she respected the fact that I told her, which eventually eased her disappointment.

Similarly, during a playful sparring session with my cousin, I unintentionally punched his face, leaving a small bruise that later bled. The following morning my aunt discovered drops of blood in the bathroom and asked what had happened. I told her about the accidental punch, and because I was truthful, she did not feel the need to punish me harshly.

These examples illustrate that telling the truth, even when it leads to temporary frustration or responsibility, helps build trust and prevents misunderstandings. Therefore, being honest at all times is essential, and we should always share the truth whenever we have done something or feel something.

Many people argue that schools should introduce distance learning, allowing pupils to take lessons from home using the internet or video calls. I agree that such programmes can be a great help because they offer several clear advantages.

The most important advantage is the flexibility they provide. Traditional schools require a fixed timetable, which makes it difficult for students who also hold a part‑time job or have family duties. Online classes let learners choose when to join the lesson, so they can schedule study around work shifts, household chores or other commitments. This makes it possible to finish school while still earning money, paying bills or helping at home. In my own case I wanted to complete my degree but found the campus schedule impossible because I needed to work several evenings. Distance learning gave me the chance to attend lectures in the evening and complete assignments in the morning, allowing me to balance work and study without feeling overloaded.

A second benefit is that students often produce higher‑quality work when they study from home. With more uninterrupted time, they can research topics in depth and prepare projects with extra detail. The internet makes it easy to access a wide range of resources – videos, articles, forums – which pupils can use to improve their homework. Moreover, avoiding long daily commutes and early wake‑up times reduces fatigue, so students are more alert when they finally sit down to study. In contrast, a full‑day school schedule can leave learners exhausted, especially when several classes are followed by heavy homework. When the same pupils attend classes remotely, they tend to focus better and finish assignments with less stress.

A third point is that distance learning gives students more time for family and personal activities. They can join their family for meals, go for a short walk or simply relax after a lesson. In addition, weekends become freer, allowing pupils to pursue hobbies, exercise or even plan a quick outing to a cinema or park. Some critics fear that students will waste time on their phones at home, but parents can set clear rules, and many families already use the extra free time to spend together. Thus the time saved by not travelling to school can be turned into meaningful family moments rather than lost screen time.

Opponents claim that online learning may lead to procrastination, because students are left on their own and could spend hours on unrelated activities. While this risk exists in any environment, the key is self‑discipline and supportive guidance. Teachers can keep regular check‑ins through video conferences, and schools can provide a structured timetable with set deadlines and live Q&A sessions. When these mechanisms are in place, the chance of falling behind is comparable to, or even lower than, the chance of failing to keep up in a crowded classroom.

In conclusion, distance learning should be offered by some schools because it lets students learn more effectively, complete better work and enjoy extra time with their families. These advantages can help young people achieve their academic goals while still meeting personal and financial responsibilities. When schools give clear expectations and maintain regular contact, the potential pitfalls of remote study can be avoided, making this option a worthwhile addition to the education system.

In many countries high‑school students are urged to choose a future job before they finish school, and I believe this expectation is a good one. Deciding on a career early gives teenagers a clear sense of direction and helps them set realistic goals for the years ahead.

First, when young people are encouraged to think about their work life, they naturally begin to imagine what they will need in order to support themselves and their families. For instance, many students understand that picking a suitable profession can make a difference in the quality of life their parents enjoy, especially if older relatives still need help with daily expenses. Knowing what they want to study also lets them plan for the skills they will acquire and the responsibilities they will take on, which often means a more orderly and purposeful journey through school.

Second, a large number of people worldwide share the desire to improve their living conditions for themselves and for the people they love. This wish is strongest when they can identify a career that offers stability and opportunities. There are countless occupations available—ranging from technology and engineering to teaching, law enforcement and other technical jobs—that can provide steady income and a sense of accomplishment. The sooner students recognise which of these paths aligns with their interests and strengths, the easier it becomes for them to focus their studies, seek relevant internships and eventually enter the workforce with a concrete plan.

However, some adolescents resist thinking about a career while they are still in school. They may argue that they are still young and want to enjoy friendships, romantic relationships and everyday school life. Others worry that the pressure could distract them from having fun or lead them into risky behaviours such as drinking, drug use or fighting. While these concerns are understandable, ignoring future planning can make it harder to decide later on when career options may have already narrowed, and it can leave them feeling unprepared when the time for real‑world employment arrives.

In summary, agreeing with the idea that students should select a career before graduating makes sense. Having a clear idea of a future profession simplifies the preparation process, reduces uncertainty and helps families count on a reliable source of support. The earlier the choice is made, the more time there is to build relevant skills, earn a decent salary and contribute positively to loved ones’ lives. Therefore, encouraging high‑schoolers to think about their work path early is both practical and beneficial.

I support the idea of having an after‑school homework club because it would give many students the extra help they need to succeed. When homework becomes hard, some pupils give up and choose other activities, which can lower their grades. A club would let teachers be available outside regular class time, so pupils can work through problems with guidance and avoid feeling stuck. At home, some families already pay for private tutoring, but not every parent can afford that extra expense. If a school provides a free after‑school program, families would save money while still getting quality support for their children.

Having a club also means the session can last longer than the typical forty‑seven minute slot. More time would allow students to finish assignments and get feedback, which can improve test scores and overall confidence. During these extended periods teachers could either help directly or encourage students to work together, letting the instructor rest while peers assist one another. This collaborative environment makes difficult tasks feel manageable and builds a sense of community.

In short, an after‑school homework club would benefit students academically, reduce the burden on parents’ budgets, and give teachers a chance to recharge. I believe it would make a noticeable difference in how well students perform and how they view their schoolwork.

As far as I understand, music, drama, and art courses are not compulsory in most schools. Students may enroll in them only if they wish to explore those fields, and such subjects function as electives rather than mandatory requirements. For instance, a pupil who chooses art does so for personal interest and the chance to earn extra credit; it is not a class that counts toward the set of courses needed for graduation. If a student decides to replace one of the four required courses with an art class, he or she will be mistaken. Since art classes are not part of the graduation list, the student would fall short of the credit total needed for graduation, regardless of how many electives are taken.

Some teachers eliminate art or music for seniors because they expect seniors to have fewer slots in their schedule. In those cases the seniors simply opt for other electives, and juniors are free to take the same art or music classes to boost their scores. This flexibility shows that these subjects are always optional, even if seniors happen to drop them.

The list of required classes typically includes English 11, geometry, mathematics, CIS, world history, and several other core subjects. These courses must be completed, and each of them is linked to a SOL assessment. When a student reaches the appropriate grade level for a required subject, he or she has to take the SOL test. The test is offered twice a year, and a passing score of at least 300 points is needed. If the first attempt falls short, the student may retake the exam to meet the threshold.

Because electives such as art, drama, and music cannot fulfill the role of required courses, they should remain optional choices that let students pursue personal interests without threatening graduation eligibility.

I agree with the idea that having a positive attitude makes a real difference. When we approach work, study, or any daily task with optimism, we are more likely to see useful results right away. A hopeful mindset not only changes what we do, but also changes how others see us. Because we treat colleagues, friends and family kindly, they often describe us as pleasant and reliable. In this way a good attitude helps us build strong relationships and creates a sense that people can count on us in many parts of life.

In life we sometimes encounter difficulties that leave us feeling sad or discouraged. It is natural to think about giving up when things go wrong, but I think it is important to keep trying. Instead of allowing problems to dominate our thoughts, we should stay focused on finding solutions and leave the past behind. By maintaining a cheerful outlook we can continue moving forward and eventually turn obstacles into learning experiences.

At school a positive attitude also brings practical benefits. Teachers notice students who remain calm and try their best, and they are more inclined to support those pupils. In contrast, classmates who are constantly negative may lose interest and even drop out. By staying motivated and respectful, we show that we are working toward passing exams and completing our education, which sets us apart from those who give up easily.

Looking ahead, being honest and well‑prepared increases our chances of reaching our goals. If we trust our abilities and plan carefully, we can choose the career we want and create a better life for ourselves and our families. This sense of purpose makes it easier to face challenges, because we believe they are steps on the way to a brighter future.

Overall, a good attitude makes everyday events smoother. When we stay upbeat, people tend to treat us kindly, and they are more willing to help us. As a result, wishes become more attainable, relationships improve, and we feel more confident in handling whatever comes our way. In my view, cultivating such an outlook is a practical way to lead a more successful and satisfying life.

Success, as Winston Churchill once observed, is not the absence of setbacks but the ability to move from one failure to the next without losing hope. Although failure is often defined as the opposite of success, it also signals a loss of the motivation that helps us get back on track. As people we sometimes feel our capacity to start over diminish after we slip, yet Churchill’s words remind us that keeping enthusiasm alive is what separates those who quit from those who keep growing.

In reality, failure is a regular part of the human experience. We all encounter obstacles that interrupt our progress, whether at school, in work, or in personal projects. These moments make us wonder why things go wrong precisely when we are striving for something important. Often we assume that failure means we did something wrong or didn’t try hard enough to land a job, ace a test, or manage our problems. Yet failure occupies a central place in everyday life, shaping how we respond to challenges.

The true value of a failure lies not in the disappointment itself but in the insight it provides. By reflecting on what went wrong we can identify the weaknesses that need fixing. Accepting that mistakes are a necessary part of learning helps us avoid repeating the same errors. Each misstep becomes a fresh lesson that prepares us for a better outcome later. In this way, failure is not an end point but a stepping‑stone toward future success.

Science offers a clear illustration of this principle. Researchers perform countless experiments, many of which do not produce the expected results. While these trials may appear wasteful, they often uncover new facts that were not originally the goal. The unexpected findings become the basis for further inquiry, leading to breakthroughs that would have been impossible without the earlier failures. Thus, regardless of how often we stumble, there is always something to learn, something to discover, and a path forward.

Staying optimistic can be challenging, especially after a setback. The popular belief that we must always look on the bright side creates pressure, and that pressure can turn into extra stress. It is normal to feel tension, self‑doubt, or insecurity after a failure; these feelings can actually strengthen our resolve if we acknowledge them rather than ignore them. Unfortunately, many people respond to repeated setbacks by slipping into sadness, losing hope, and abandoning their goals. When enthusiasm fades, motivation follows, and progress slows down.

Literature shows how perseverance looks in ordinary people. One book, which the students of Generic School read last year, tells the story of a young boy living in a reservation in India. Life gave him little encouragement, but a teacher introduced him to a different perspective outside the community. Though he faced many disappointments, the boy chose to keep trying, turning each defeat into a lesson about his own potential. His experience demonstrates that even when optimism feels hard, it is still possible to push forward and find a way out of hopelessness.

In sum, the most effective way to achieve success is to treat mistakes as opportunities. Every failure brings a new experience and a new lesson that can guide future actions. By staying enthusiastic, by learning from what went wrong, and by recognizing that setbacks are part of a larger journey, we become more capable of reaching our goals. I agree with Churchill: feeling excitement for what lies ahead is far more powerful than we imagine. When we believe in ourselves, maintain a positive outlook, and understand that failure is simply another part of life, we increase our chances of success and learn that life, while demanding, is not an insurmountable obstacle.

Online classes have become an attractive option for many schools, allowing students to study from home through video‑conference platforms. In my view, this approach is a positive development because it offers flexibility that traditional on‑site attendance cannot provide.  

First, distance learning suits learners who have to balance school with part‑time jobs. Many workplaces set rigid schedules, which often clash with class times. After finishing a shift, a student can log in from their bedroom, eat a quick meal and continue studying without having to rush to a campus. This extra time reduces stress and helps the learner stay focused, as the environment is quieter and less distracting than a busy hallway. Moreover, online study frees up slots in the day for other pursuits, such as joining a sports club, meeting friends or completing personal projects.  

Second, health and transportation problems are less of a barrier when classes are held virtually. If a student catches a cold or a more serious illness, attending school in person would risk spreading germs to classmates and also demand time away from recovery. Remote learning lets the student stay isolated while still keeping up with lessons. Likewise, bad weather, heavy traffic or the lack of a car can make the commute impossible, especially for students who live far from the campus. By logging in from home, they avoid the need for parking fees, public transport delays or winter road hazards.  

Third, family responsibilities make online schooling especially valuable. Some students are parents themselves and need to watch over children while studying. Others have caregiving duties for relatives or themselves require special accommodations because of a disability. In both cases, a physical classroom can be hard to reach, but a virtual classroom fits easily into their daily routine. Parents can check on their kids, adjust study times, and still attend important lectures. Disabled learners, who may have difficulty traveling, can participate without worrying about inaccessible facilities or long walks. This inclusion helps students stay in school despite personal challenges, ensuring they do not miss lessons.  

Finally, the technology that supports distance learning improves overall quality of life. It lets people organize their schedules, reduce commuting time and recover lost hours that would otherwise be spent waiting for buses or searching for parking spots. For busy families, the ability to study from home means they can allocate moments to family activities while still meeting academic requirements. In short, online education uses modern tools to reclaim time and energy, which can be redirected toward health, relationships and personal growth.  

Taking everything into account, I think offering online classes is a wise decision. It respects students’ work, health, family duties and personal circumstances, making learning more accessible and less stressful for those who need the flexibility. By embracing this option, schools can create a learning environment that works better for the diverse needs of today’s learners.

The most hotly debated issue these days is whether schools should copy the recent trend among some companies of moving to a four‑day week with ten‑hour shifts. My school could try a similar change by adding two extra hours to each regular day. Some people claim that longer hours simply mean more electricity for lights, computers and other devices, but I think the advantages outweigh the extra cost.

First, the extra time can be used to teach students how to use energy wisely. Lessons could focus on turning off lights when rooms are empty, unplugging chargers, and choosing efficient appliances at home. Encouraging such habits early helps students spend less on their own bills, and over time the school’s overall power consumption may drop.

Second, a longer schedule gives us room to tackle other waste, especially water and paper. Students could create posters reminding everyone to close taps, report leaks quickly, and recycle correctly. These campaigns raise awareness and cut water use and paper waste, saving money that could be spent on better equipment.

Finally, the two extra hours provide a realistic window for school‑wide environmental projects. Teachers and pupils could organise a sustainability campaign, build an online guide with tips, or start a recycling club. Having dedicated time for planning and action makes these initiatives possible and reinforces the idea that everyone can help protect the planet.

In my opinion, extending the school day by two hours would turn the campus into a place where careful use of resources is taught and practised, and it would give students and staff the time needed to work together on lasting environmental improvements.

I disagree with the claim that using smartphones and computers has only positive consequences, because I think it actually weakens the way we interact with people. Below I list five reasons that illustrate how constant digital contact can lead to a loss of real‑life communication.

First, when we spend most of our time online we no longer need to go out to shop for everyday items. In my home country I used to ride my bike or walk to the nearest store, which gave me a chance to see neighbours and chat with them while waiting in line. After moving to the United States, my mother simply calls a delivery service and the products arrive at the door, so I rarely step outside. This routine removes a simple social moment and replaces it with a quick, faceless transaction.

Second, playing sports or games with friends becomes less common when everyone prefers virtual entertainment. A friend back home told me that kids used to meet at a park and play soccer or hopscotch, but now they spend hours on mobile games and hardly ever gather in a public space. The shared excitement of physical activity is fading, and the social bond that comes from playing together is being replaced by solo screen time.

Third, younger children are developing a strong attachment to screens, which limits their willingness to explore other interests. My little brother, who is only two years old, cries if we take his phone away and refuses to join in any drawing or building games. He wants only videos and games, which shows how early immersion in digital devices can narrow a child’s curiosity and reduce interaction with siblings or the world around them.

Fourth, when we travel or visit relatives we often feel tempted to stay glued to our devices instead of engaging with the people or places we encounter. While visiting my family, I found that leaving the phone in my pocket made the trip more enjoyable because I could listen to stories, try new foods, and take photos of the scenery without constantly checking notifications. Without that distraction, I was able to communicate more naturally and remember the moments.

Finally, there is a clear risk of addiction to phones or computers that interferes with daily responsibilities. A classmate in school often plays games or watches videos during lessons, even when the teacher looks at him. He hides the device in his backpack or sits at the back of the room to avoid being caught, which shows how hard it can be to resist the urge to stay connected. Over time, this habit can erode attention, reduce productivity, and replace genuine conversation with fleeting online chats.

Overall, while technology offers convenience, it also cuts us off from the personal, face‑to‑face contact that is essential for strong social ties. I believe that unless we limit our screen time, the quality of our relationships will continue to deteriorate.

I believe that completing one training programme before beginning another is a worthwhile strategy. When a person finishes a course, they immediately gain extra time to explore a second career path. That spare time also makes it possible to start a small business while still young. If the venture does not succeed, they still have a chance to try a different idea because they have not yet committed all their years to a single profession.

First, if someone discovers that the field they have studied is no longer satisfying, they are not stuck. They can enroll in another programme or find a new job. For instance, a close friend of mine will be 23 when she finishes university next year. She has already thought about taking a different degree that would better match her interests. This flexibility helps young adults avoid ending up in a career they dislike.

Second, the early years of adulthood are full of creative ideas. Young minds often generate many concepts for projects, and they can test them quickly. Suppose a person wants to start a business hiring workers. They might begin with something simple, such as a cleaning service. Imagine being required to take part in a school activity that the principal has decided for everyone. For many students this situation would feel unfair because some need a break, while others simply do not enjoy the type of sport or exercise being offered. Moreover, children already have limited time for relaxation and should be allowed to pursue the things they like.

First, pupils already have a heavy academic workload and often feel exhausted. After a full day of lessons they need a chance to recharge. If the school forces them to stay active, they may not have enough energy for the next classes or for other projects they enjoy. Resting also lets them spend time with friends. When a scheduled activity fills the whole break, kids cannot chat, share jokes, or just unwind together. This informal hanging out is an important form of rest because it provides mental relief and helps keep them motivated for later tasks.

In addition, many students prefer indoor pastimes. They enjoy playing video games, reading, or exploring hobbies with classmates, and some feel uncomfortable outdoors or have no interest in organized sports. If the school insists on a single activity for all, these students will be forced to do something they do not like, which can reduce their enjoyment and willingness to participate.

In my opinion, making students join a compulsory activity is not a good idea. If I were the principal, I would let each child choose what they want to do. Those who are tired could stay inside, those who want to keep playing video games could continue, and others could join a club that matches their interests. Giving pupils more freedom respects their need for rest and their personal preferences, and it makes the school environment more positive overall.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” While some critics dismiss this idea, I wholeheartedly agree. Modern society pushes individuals to adjust their views, adopt new cultural habits, or abandon the beliefs they once cherished. In such an environment, the act of holding onto one’s true self is indeed a notable achievement. Here are three reasons supporting Emerson’s claim.

First, persistence matters most. The external pressure to conform can be strong, and many people give in to avoid criticism. Yet, staying true to yourself requires a steady resolve. Whether others approve or not, the only person who needs to feel at ease with your choices is you. By refusing to surrender, you demonstrate that personal integrity outweighs momentary popularity.

Second, learning to love and celebrate your own identity builds inner confidence. Mistakes are inevitable, but they should be treated as lessons rather than reasons to abandon who you are. Each trait, habit, and quirk contributes to a unique combination that sets you apart. When you accept your strengths and flaws alike, you create a solid sense of self that resists the urge to be molded into someone else’s expectations.

Third, remembering your roots anchors you in reality. Immigrants, for example, often face expectations to abandon their heritage in favor of local customs. Choosing instead to honor where you come from—your language, traditions, and values—shows that you can thrive while still preserving what makes you distinct. In a world eager to reshape you, this balance proves you are capable of both adaptation and authenticity.

So, what are you waiting for? Don’t let external forces dictate your identity. Keep striving, nurture self‑appreciation, and stay connected to your origins. When you do, you turn the simple act of being yourself into a true accomplishment.

British Prime Minister Winston Churchill once observed that “success is about moving from setback to setback while keeping enthusiasm alive.” I find this view persuasive because real achievement seldom comes without a series of hurdles, and each one can teach us something valuable if we stay determined.

Life is full of challenges that can knock us off course. It is easy to feel discouraged when things do not go as planned, yet the key is to keep going and treat every obstacle as a chance to learn. Churchill stressed that experiencing failure does not mean losing drive; rather, it is the persistence through those moments that eventually leads to success. When a goal looks unattainable—say, the cost of university—the temptation to give up can be strong. Still, a thoughtful person will search for alternatives, perhaps working part‑time while studying, so that the financial barrier can be overcome and the degree pursued.

To reach success you need a solid work ethic, a refusal to surrender, optimism, and the ability to solve problems creatively. Learning new skills along the way also matters, because they expand your options and make future obstacles easier to handle. All of these steps reinforce Churchill’s idea: true progress is not a straight line but a series of attempts, each one marked by renewed enthusiasm.

In short, staying positive and resilient after every failure makes the path to accomplishment possible. It is this continuous forward motion, even when the road is rough, that turns perseverance into achievement.

From the moment a child leaves the womb, the first act is a loud, instinctive sound. If a newborn stays quiet, a nurse may gently tap the back to trigger a cry. This early cry begins a unique vocal pattern that each infant will later refine, with its own rhythm and pitch. Even twins, who share many features, possess completely different fingerprints, demonstrating that bodily markers of individuality appear right from birth.

Soon after, the infant’s brain starts to respond to basic needs. Babies learn to signal hunger, discomfort, a need for a diaper change, or a desire for attention. As they move into the toddler stage, they imitate the adults and peers around them. By watching others walk, speak, and handle utensils, they pick up practical habits—holding a bottle, using a fork, arranging their toys. All of these early behaviours arise from observation and imitation rather than from an innate blueprint.

When children reach the ages of six to twelve, they begin to seek a place within their peer group. Television, music, and popular figures expose them to a wide range of professions: athletes, actors, doctors, police officers, chefs, and many more. These role models provide a range of possibilities, and children often adopt preferences based on what they see, shaping their nascent sense of identity.

During adolescence, from thirteen to nineteen, the pressure to belong becomes stronger, but individuals also start to develop their own voice. Parents continue to offer advice drawn from their own experiences, hoping to spare their children from pain, yet they also recognize that occasional failures are valuable lessons. This period marks the transition from following adult guidance to making personal decisions, a step toward independence.

Entering adulthood brings a further shift. The safety net once provided by family no longer shields us; we must shoulder responsibilities such as jobs, bills, and social obligations. These duties reveal whether we are dependable, sociable, tolerant, patient, or forgiving. Our reactions to everyday challenges define aspects of our character, and we learn whether we can meet the expectations placed upon us.

I believe that people are not born with fixed labels. Our mindset shapes the way we experience life. Someone who grows up in difficult circumstances can still maintain a hopeful outlook, while another who complains about missing material comforts may feel dissatisfied. A strong, resilient mentality leads to a constructive, respected self; a weak, defeatist attitude produces a negative, fragile character. Hence, our personalities are built through the choices we make and the experiences we undergo, not handed down by some higher authority. Ultimately, we create and refine our own identity as we navigate the complexities of society.
