I think one of the most pleasant ways to spend free time outdoors is to gather family and friends for a casual cookout. We can grill burgers, hot dogs, slices of carne asada, taco fillings and slowly‑cooked barbacoa, then share the dishes while we chat and laugh. After the food is ready, we can head to a nearby field and play soccer, football or organise bike races and sprint challenges, or even set up a quick baseball game. If someone feels like it, a portable speaker can play some music, but the volume should stay low enough that neighbours won’t complain. We might also invite a child, a boyfriend, a girlfriend, or the partner’s parents and bring extra snacks for the afternoon.

Spending the day in the park feels a lot like a mini‑camping adventure. If the area has a river we can try fishing, catch a few fish and later grill them together. The main point, however, is to have fun, to enjoy each other’s company and to let the natural scenery lift our spirits. It is easy to forget daily worries when we hear birds singing and feel the wind on our faces. Being outdoors gives us a chance to reconnect with our relatives and to remember how valuable that love really is. Many people have no family or friends and spend their time alone, which makes us appreciate the support we receive and feel thankful for those around us.

When the sun goes down, we can light a small fire, roast marshmallows and serve cookies on a plate while sharing spooky stories or funny jokes. The crackle of the fire and the cool night air provide an extra sense of adventure. Breathing fresh air from the trees helps us feel refreshed and energised.

Parks that belong to the city, state or nation play a vital role for the community. They offer a space where friends, couples, and families can gather for a party, run, walk a dog, or simply sit and think. A short visit can be enough to break the monotony of everyday life and let us enjoy the moment. Because parks are home to many birds, animals and plants, we should look after them so they can continue to thrive.

In my view, outdoor activities with loved ones are not only enjoyable but also essential for mental wellbeing and the health of our environment.

Has the reduction of face‑to‑face contact because of modern technology been more helpful or harmful to people’s everyday life?  

I think it works both ways. Some people benefit, while others experience problems. It really depends on how each person chooses to use the tools that are now available.  

On the positive side, digital devices help those who feel isolated stay engaged. Instead of being completely alone, you can read e‑books, shop online, play video games, listen to music on streaming apps, or watch favourite shows on YouTube, Netflix, or similar services. I have known many people who would rather stay at home and enjoy a film rather than attend a family gathering, and for them, a wide range of online content can be a safer, more enjoyable alternative. Those options keep the mind occupied and can prevent the serious damage that extreme loneliness—such as imprisonment, unemployment, or death—might cause. My grandfather often said, “There must be bad things so the good can exist,” which reminds us that every advantage comes with a drawback.  

At the same time, technology also brings negative effects. A growing number of people lose interest in ordinary activities, including family reunions. While I personally have never cared much about such gatherings, I always preferred spending time with cousins and old friends rather than sitting at home talking about mundane matters. Today, however, many conversations are interrupted because participants are glued to their phones, scrolling through messages, social media, or videos. This can be seen as a sign that someone does not value what you are saying, which may lead to annoyance and even dislike.  

Additionally, the convenience of technology promotes laziness. Why walk to a shop when you can order groceries from a phone? Why meet someone in person when video calls are instant? Over time, people may start asking themselves, “If my small device can do everything, why should I do it myself?” That line of thinking can weaken basic social skills and leave individuals feeling isolated when they finally understand how limited human interaction becomes.  

Nevertheless, technology remains one of humanity’s greatest inventions. It makes communication faster and easier, offers endless entertainment, and keeps us informed about events happening anywhere—from local news to space missions—without the need to read lengthy books or reports. The overall message is balance: use technology only when it is needed and do not let it dominate our thoughts.  

In conclusion, modern technology has both advantages and disadvantages for personal contact. Its effect depends largely on individual habits and priorities. When used wisely, it improves life; when misused, it can erode the very human relationships it was designed to support.

Summer, in my view, is a season meant for taking in the pleasant climate, spending time with family, friends, and if one has a pet, with that companion as well. It is hard to imagine anyone eager to focus on school assignments or sit down with a stack of homework. During a semester, students work hard for months, and I believe they deserve a genuine rest period afterward.

This need for a pause is not limited to youngsters. Adults also feel exhausted after a year of professional duties; many jobs ask for only a short vacation, and workers often return feeling stressed. I am not trying to say that adults have the same responsibilities as children, but both groups need the same amount of recovery time. When workers are allowed a week or two off, they can recharge and return with better concentration, just as students benefit from a longer break.

From a student’s perspective, the main draw of summer is the freedom it offers. The warm wind, the scent of the sea, and the lack of grades or deadlines create a sense of liberty that a short holiday cannot match. Teachers, meanwhile, also appreciate the chance to step away; they may worry about students forgetting material, but the break nevertheless provides them with a moment to relax and prepare for the new term.

Many students use the summer months to set personal objectives. Some look for a part‑time job to earn extra money, while others save for tuition or other college expenses. This planning shows how the break serves both leisure and practical purposes. Educators share the same view: they see vacation as an opportunity to help students build toward future goals.

Most schools already provide a three‑ to four‑week summer break, a longer winter recess, and brief pauses in spring and autumn. For many, the timing is ideal. The weather is pleasant, beaches are open, and there is enough time to travel or stay home with family. Those who wish to work can still earn extra cash, and those who prefer to relax can enjoy the season fully. In my opinion, the current schedule already offers what students and teachers need.

Self‑reliance is the habit of making decisions for yourself and, when needed, for others, without waiting for someone else to tell you what to do. It is a skill that students and adults alike should develop, especially in today’s climate of rapid change and frequent crises. One immediate issue that illustrates the need for this trait is the repeated threat of a government shutdown. When the federal budget is halted, paychecks stop, contracts pause, and ordinary people lose income, the uncertainty spreads to stores, farms, and small businesses. In such moments, being able to gather reliable information, ask questions, and discuss possible solutions becomes essential. It does not mean that only one person should speak; rather, a community of voices should be heard, each adding new perspectives and concrete ideas. By encouraging open dialogue we avoid a single‑person monopoly over the truth and improve our chances of finding workable answers.

Teaching self‑reliance to children does not turn them into obedient followers; it plants the seeds of leadership. Leaders often start by seeking advice from mentors, colleagues, or experts, recognizing that knowledge expands when it is shared. As time passes, they accumulate experience and confidence, yet they continue to ask questions because no amount of information can replace fresh insight. This blend of independence and curiosity helps people in all walks of life. Employees who can assess problems on their own and then consult supervisors, parents who can manage household finances while asking for help when needed, and students who can propose their own solutions after researching the topic all benefit from this balanced approach. The skill is not limited to any age group; it is equally useful for teenagers navigating school, for adults planning careers, and for retirees handling finances.

The importance of self‑reliance becomes even clearer when we look at the military. Soldiers must decide quickly under pressure, knowing that lives are at stake. They undergo rigorous training that sharpens both physical readiness and mental flexibility. Officers may issue orders, but the troops must interpret those orders, evaluate risks, and adapt if circumstances change. The habit of asking questions, requesting clarification, and seeking feedback is built into boot‑camp routines because it saves lives. This same mindset helps civilians when we face large‑scale decisions, such as voting on foreign policy or reacting to economic downturns. Whether it concerns the family budget, a child’s education, or a national crisis, we need to keep a clear head, ask the right questions, and stay alert to new information.

A government shutdown also reminds us why staying informed matters. When the federal budget is delayed, many private companies lose revenue, families miss essential services, and confidence in the stock market can dip dramatically. If we rely solely on past successes or ignore warning signs, we risk repeating past mistakes. Instead, we should use our voices, our professional skills, and our personal networks to push for a resolution. By sharing ideas, gathering data, and encouraging leaders to listen, we help the system recover faster. The same principle applies to everyday decisions: before buying a new car, consider the broader economic impact; before choosing a vacation spot, check whether local businesses will be affected. In short, asking “why” and “how” improves not just personal outcomes but the collective well‑being.

Ultimately, self‑reliance does not mean we work in isolation. It means we are prepared to act, ask for help when needed, and contribute ideas that improve our families, jobs, and communities. No matter our race, gender, age, or background, these habits empower us to face both immediate problems and long‑term challenges with confidence. Let us remember that every small question we raise today may prevent a larger crisis tomorrow, and that sharing knowledge now creates a foundation for future generations to thrive. Seek guidance, stay curious, and keep the conversation alive.

Technology makes it possible for people to do many everyday activities without meeting anyone face‑to‑face. Borrowing books, shopping online, or playing games can all be done from home. While some worry that this reduces personal contact, I think the overall impact of technology is positive. It lets us stay connected with loved ones, work from any location, and meet new people from around the world. Below I will explain why I believe these three areas show the main benefits of modern technology.

First, technology greatly improves communication with family members who live far away. Video chats let us see each other’s faces, hear their voices, and share updates instantly, even when we cannot travel. Imagine if we had no video calls; we would miss birthdays, holidays, and daily news, and over time we might even drift apart. In emergencies, such as an accident or sudden illness, being able to call or locate relatives through their smartphones can be life‑saving. At work, the same tools help us inform a boss or a colleague that we cannot come in, without waiting for a physical letter or a long commute. This flexibility means we stay productive and keep important relationships alive, something that would be difficult without digital devices.

Second, working online eliminates the need for long commutes and gives people more control over their schedules. When jobs can be done from a home office, employees save money on fuel, parking, and public transport. They also gain extra time that can be used for family, hobbies, or rest. Parents can balance childcare duties while still meeting work deadlines, because they can supervise their children without being physically present at an office. Moreover, technology opens doors for people who cannot drive; they can simply log in to their computer or tablet and perform their tasks. For those who enjoy traveling, the same setup lets them move abroad while continuing their employment, adding extra income to their adventure. In short, remote work makes life more efficient and gives people the freedom to manage both work and personal life.

Third, technology expands our social circles and helps us learn about other cultures and languages. Social media platforms bring together people from different countries, so we can chat, share photos, and discover new traditions. This exposure encourages curiosity and builds friendships that would otherwise be impossible. When traveling abroad, translation apps let us ask questions, navigate streets, and find local information even if we do not speak the language. For example, a traveler can quickly ask a local for directions or read a menu by using a phone’s translation feature, avoiding the frustration of being lost and unable to communicate. These tools also help students practice new languages by speaking with native speakers online, turning everyday devices into powerful learning resources.

In conclusion, although technology can reduce face‑to‑face interaction, its advantages clearly outweigh any drawbacks. It lets us stay in touch with distant family, work flexibly from anywhere, and meet new friends while exploring other cultures. By making communication, productivity, and social learning easier, technology enhances modern life and should be seen as a valuable aid rather than a threat.

Thanks to modern education, schools now provide a wide range of programmes designed to match each pupil’s unique talents. Students who enjoy artistic subjects can easily join special classes and discover where they excel. After a couple of intense learning periods, learners need a way to unwind; the arts give them a chance to relax, restore energy and prepare for the next set of tasks. While this approach works well for those who take part actively, it can become a waste of time for pupils who do not use the session.

High‑school life today can feel dull for many teenagers because they struggle to find what truly interests them. One effective antidote is to include enjoyable, low‑stakes activities that break the monotony. Joining a music ensemble, performing in a play, or experimenting with visual arts can lift spirits, cut down anxiety and help students return to their studies refreshed. These options also serve as a form of motivation, reminding learners that they have autonomy over their timetable.

Participating in an arts session does more than provide a pause; it clears mental clutter. When the brain is overloaded after a long lesson, a short burst of singing, acting or drawing can relax the mind, making it easier to absorb new concepts in the following block. The effectiveness of this reset depends partly on the kind of creative outlet each student prefers—people tend to relax best when they engage in the type of entertainment they already like.

Nevertheless, making art subjects compulsory can generate problems. If a large group of students enroll only because the class is mandatory, many will not be genuinely interested. Some may fall asleep, chat loudly or distract classmates, turning a supportive environment into a source of annoyance. This situation undermines the purpose of the sessions and harms the learning atmosphere for those who are trying to concentrate.

Overall, art‑based lessons help students feel revitalised after a demanding day, boost their motivation and improve their ability to take in information. The benefits are clear, but the classes should stay optional so that each pupil can decide based on personal interest and time constraints. Offering them as electives respects diverse abilities and prevents pupils from spending valuable periods on activities they find irrelevant. In this way, schools can keep the advantages of the arts while ensuring that all learners stay engaged and undisturbed.

Technology is a powerful aid in contemporary life, offering support to individuals in a wide range of activities—from everyday tasks to social interaction and leisure. In recent years it has advanced at an astonishing pace, and most people now rely on smartphones, tablets, or computers to stay informed, keep in touch with parents, friends, and classmates, and manage many daily routines.

One of the main reasons technology benefits society is its ability to simplify shopping and entertainment. Devices let us enjoy music, play video games, or read e‑books without needing to travel to physical stores. A large number of applications are available, often free or low‑cost, providing tools such as GPS navigation, language translation, and digital libraries that anyone can access online.

Several specific points illustrate why technology is indispensable in daily life. First, it offers practical help at any moment. For example, if a person gets lost, a mobile phone can locate their current position and guide them to the destination or the nearest shop. Similarly, finding a supermarket or completing a quick errand becomes much easier when the device displays maps and directions. When used responsibly, such tools solve a variety of everyday problems.

Second, technology supplies a rich source of entertainment. When bored, people can stream songs from any artist or genre, download games, or look up e‑books with just a few taps. A smartphone lets users search for a title and instantly receive several alternatives, something that would be far less convenient in a traditional bookstore. Moreover, the internet hosts thousands of games catering to sports fans, adventure lovers, puzzle enthusiasts, and many more, broadening the options for leisure.

Third, modern communication tools bridge long distances. Platforms such as Facebook, WhatsApp, Instagram, and Messenger are easy to operate, allowing anyone to stay in touch regardless of location. These apps let families and old friends share photos and short videos, keeping relationships alive. While they are valuable, it is important to use them wisely to avoid unnecessary distractions or conflicts.

Another advantage is the ability to solve practical problems. Short video clips on YouTube or step‑by‑step guides on Google show how to prepare a dish, fix a car, or address household issues. By watching a tutorial, a person can learn a new skill or locate a professional who can provide further assistance, turning a frustrating situation into a manageable one.

Technology also expands job prospects. Companies now accept applications through online forms, which is much simpler than handing a paper résumé in person. Anyone with a phone, computer, or tablet can submit a profile, increasing the pool of candidates. Businesses promote their products via the internet, reaching customers worldwide and boosting profits. Consequently, a firm can become international within a short time, making technology a key driver of economic growth.

In conclusion, modern technology serves as a versatile resource that improves communication, offers entertainment, assists with navigation, provides educational content, and opens up employment opportunities. The endless applications available on devices—from social media to GPS and instructional videos—help people stay informed, enjoy themselves, solve problems, and connect with others across the globe. If used thoughtfully, technology strengthens daily life and fulfills its original purpose of supporting and bringing people together.

I believe individuals should be the ones who decide for themselves, and I have several reasons why. First, when we act on our own ideas we develop personal skills that we might otherwise miss. For instance, we can learn how to design a house from scratch or practice leading a community as a mayor. Relying on our instincts also helps us find quick solutions to difficult situations, such as finding an escape route out of a dangerous pit or catching a ball with precise timing. By choosing our own direction, we discover the genuine aspects of who we are. I am not against asking others for advice; guidance can be useful when we feel stuck. Yet I still favor making decisions independently because it makes the task more demanding and leads to real growth. If I simply followed what others told me, I might accomplish the task, but I would not have learned anything new. Therefore, I prefer to tackle challenges on my own. Accepting help when needed is fine, but the ultimate aim should be self‑driven learning.

I think it is useful to get several opinions before making a decision. Listening to more than one person often points out things you may have missed and can prevent you from spending too quickly.  

My uncle kept a hundred‑dollar bill in his wallet and gave me ten dollars while keeping the rest. I told him to save the money for fuel the next day, but he bought shirts, pants and a hat right away. The following morning he asked for cash to fill his tank. He was happy with his purchases, but by ignoring the warning he ran out of money for an essential need.  

A friend once wanted to pay for a cinema ticket. All his friends urged him to stay home and watch the movie on a DVD, which would be much cheaper. He bought the DVD, saved a lot, and still enjoyed the film.  

My father gave me a small amount, saying I needed a white shirt for a job interview. I used the cash for a video game instead. Later I asked for money to buy the shirt, and he reminded me of his original suggestion. The extra expense could have been avoided if I had listened.  

These examples show that hearing more than one viewpoint changes the situation. One opinion may be limited, but another brings in price, future use, and opportunity costs. Even if one person is right, the additional advice makes the decision clearer.  

Therefore, I agree that it is okay to talk to several people before deciding. Seeking multiple opinions does not eliminate mistakes, but it greatly reduces the chance of making a hasty choice that harms your budget. In daily life, a quick discussion with friends or family can keep you from wasting money and can guide you toward a better result.

I agree with the view that a successful life is built on three key habits: treating everyone with kindness, keeping inner peace, and surrounding yourself with supportive people. These habits shape the way we handle challenges, earn respect, and stay focused on long‑term goals.

First, being a genuinely good person helps us stand out in a world where negative behaviour is common. It shows that we value ourselves enough to act calmly, even when others are rude or dismissive. If problems arise, approaching them with a steady, positive attitude leads to better solutions than reacting with anger. Kindness also creates a ripple effect—people feel respected when we treat them well, and they are more likely to treat us the same way. By staying friendly with family, classmates and acquaintances, we avoid unnecessary conflicts and build a reputation that others admire. For example, I try to stay polite with everyone I meet. My friends often say they enjoy spending time with me because they know I listen without judgment, and my family appreciates my willingness to help with small chores. Over time, this attitude has earned me the trust of people who see me as reliable and caring.

Inner peace is another essential component of personal success. A calm mind lets us enjoy life’s moments and remain resilient when unexpected difficulties arise. Although it can be hard to stay peaceful, making time for activities we love—sports, music, reading, or simply quiet walks—helps reduce stress and prevents us from overreacting to minor setbacks. I learned this the hard way when, at twelve, I fought with my younger brother over a petty misunderstanding. The resentment lingered for years, weighing on my thoughts even now that I’m twenty. Eventually, I chose to focus on gratitude for his support rather than the old hurt, and that shift has restored a sense of tranquillity in my soul.

Finally, the quality of our relationships influences our future. Positive friendships and mentors guide us toward growth, while negative influences can distract us from our ambitions. I once had a classmate in seventh grade who always completed his work on time, earned top marks, and seemed destined for university. By ninth grade, however, he began hanging out with a group of peers who skipped school and avoided homework. Soon his grades dropped, and his attitude toward studies changed dramatically. The contrast taught me that choosing friends who encourage healthy habits and share constructive values is crucial for keeping one’s trajectory on the right path. It does not mean we must avoid anyone who is fun, but we should be selective about who we allow to shape our daily decisions.

Together, these three elements—being kind, maintaining inner peace, and nurturing good connections—create a solid foundation for a fulfilling and prosperous life. They remind us that the attitude we display to others and the attitude we carry inside are both decisive factors. When we combine them, we are more likely to earn respect, stay focused on our goals, and enjoy the journey toward success.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once remarked, “Unless you attempt something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” I agree with his insight for the reasons outlined below.  

First, neglecting to broaden one’s skill set often results in a life lacking direction and limited prospects. When people limit themselves to only what they already know, they miss out on the opportunities that arise from acquiring new competencies. For instance, a job seeker whose résumé contains only a single set of qualifications may find it difficult to secure a better position, because most employers now look for candidates who can adapt to changing demands. Without the additional knowledge that a new field requires, such individuals cannot contribute meaningfully to their community or the nation, and their chances of advancement remain low.  

Second, possessing a variety of knowledge gives a clear advantage in the job market and everyday life. Knowledge, unlike material goods, cannot be purchased, and the more of it a person accumulates, the more powerful they become. Those who devote time to learning different subjects tend to solve problems more efficiently, because they can draw on multiple perspectives. When faced with a challenge, a well‑rounded individual is often able to choose the quickest or most effective route, whereas a narrow specialist may be forced to work harder or accept fewer options.  

Lastly, avoiding difficult tasks keeps one stuck in the same place. Growth inevitably involves stepping outside comfort zones and confronting challenges that push one’s abilities. Consider a teacher who remains in the classroom for years, never exploring leadership roles such as principal or curriculum developer; such a person may never experience the professional expansion that comes from taking on greater responsibility. Embracing demanding projects not only adds experience but also sharpens confidence, paving the way for future successes.  

In sum, Emerson’s statement captures a fundamental truth about personal development: continuous effort beyond what is already mastered is essential. By expanding our expertise, leveraging knowledge as a versatile tool, and daring to face tougher challenges, we move forward and become more capable contributors to society.

Many students believe that starting a career at a young age is a good idea because after completing courses they can go to college, after college they can get a job, and they don’t have to worry about making one in the future. Students will quit their courses—for example, after attending class and taking a course for three weeks they usually give up. This also leads people to lose interest in their career, and teens who quit their courses have a hard time because it is difficult for them to keep up. When making a career, kids often write “don’t know,” and they usually return to their hobby. Thus, it is essential to make a plan first before making a career at a young age.  

Making a career at age twelve or under is careless because it makes people overthink, causes them to go back to previous activities, and creates a negative attitude toward their courses. Whenever they take a class for two or three weeks they usually give up. Kids often write “don’t know” on their career paper, and making a career takes time for people to decide, but they shouldn’t give up easily if they can’t keep up.

In many cultures children are expected to decide on a future job before they even start high school. Those who begin working early can sometimes achieve their goals, and it is common for them to seek advice from school counselors. A large number of students think that taking a job at a young age is a smart move because they can go to college after finishing their training, find a job after graduation, and avoid the stress of making a decision later on. However, I believe that starting a career at a young age is actually harmful. It can lead students to drop out of school, cause them to spend a great deal of time trying to decide what to do, and waste valuable time that could be used for other activities.

First, many young people quit their courses when they try to earn money early. For example, after attending a few weeks of a vocational program they often lose motivation and stop attending. This is especially true for teenagers, who find it difficult to keep up with both schoolwork and a part‑time job. The effort required to manage two responsibilities at once makes it hard for them to stay focused, and they may start to dislike the subjects they are studying. In this way, a premature focus on employment can reduce school attendance and lower the chances of completing a diploma.

Second, trying to choose a career while still in school creates a lot of mental pressure. Adults often need months or even years to decide on a job, weighing many options and gathering information before making a final choice. Teenagers are not prepared for that same level of deliberation. They tend to think first about getting paid, and only later about which field interests them. This rush to earn money can lead to quick, poorly considered decisions, and many young people end up changing their plans frequently. As a result, they may spend a considerable amount of time in indecision, feeling uncertain about the path they are on and delaying any real progress.

Third, early career attempts can simply waste time that students would otherwise use more productively. Many adolescents spend hours playing video games or engaging in hobbies, and they often see a career as a school‑related task rather than a personal goal. When asked to write a career plan they frequently write “don’t know” or return to their favorite activities, showing little commitment. These habits indicate that they are not ready to commit to a serious job search, and that the time spent trying to define a career could be better spent on education, personal development, or exploring different interests.

In conclusion, encouraging children to start a career before age twelve is careless because it makes them over‑think, draws them back to unproductive activities, and creates a negative attitude toward school. Whether they stay in a class for only a few weeks or fill out career worksheets with “I don’t know,” the overall effect is the same: a loss of direction and wasted potential. To avoid these problems, it is better to allow young people to finish their schooling first and then make a thoughtful decision about their future work. This approach respects their developmental stage and gives them the time needed to build a solid foundation for whatever career they ultimately choose.

When students accomplish goals early, parents feel proud and are more inclined to back their child’s chosen route. The confidence and recognition gained from these early successes can boost self‑esteem and keep motivation high.  

In conclusion, shortening the high‑school period to three years can make life easier for many learners. They can absorb more knowledge, collect practical experience, and become productive members of society sooner. By offering the chance to study longer subjects, work, and achieve success quickly, early entry to college or work can raise overall competence and make future opportunities more visible in a shorter time.

Taking courses online or through video conferencing can be a powerful solution for students who lack the financial means to attend a traditional university, as well as for older learners who missed earlier educational opportunities. In today’s world, many families struggle with tuition, housing, and daily expenses, which makes paying for on‑campus accommodation or commuting costs an added burden. Because of that, a large number of people have to work part‑time jobs while studying, and balancing work and school often becomes stressful.

Transport and parking are also major concerns on most campuses. Large colleges may not have enough parking spaces for all students, and not everyone owns a car or can afford a regular bus fare. By studying from home, students avoid the risk of being late, especially after a long, demanding workday. They can start a lesson whenever it suits them, which makes the learning process smoother and less exhausting.

When lessons are delivered remotely, students usually manage to finish assignments more quickly and understand the material better. The home environment can be quieter, so distractions are reduced and concentration improves. Learners can pause the video, ask questions in a chat window, and review the content several times until they feel confident. At the same time, instructors often give online groups a lighter workload, providing fewer projects and more room for the students to absorb the information.

In short, online or video‑based courses give learners the freedom to handle other responsibilities, arrive on time, and help those who cannot travel to a campus because of money or transport issues. By saving on transport, housing, and time‑lost commuting, they become more organized and efficient, and they gain the chance to reach their educational goals that might otherwise stay out of reach.

Technology surrounds us, shaping the way we work, study, and even feel safe. While it opens many doors, it also creates limits on face‑to‑face interaction. In my view, technology generally offers more advantages than disadvantages, but the way we use it determines the outcome.

First, technology has become essential in everyday work life. Employees can instantly look up information, solve problems, and complete tasks without having to ask a colleague in person. This saves time and makes it possible to earn a living even when physical help is unavailable. In offices and factories the same devices also make production smoother: computers track inventory, robots assemble parts, and machines perform repetitive jobs far more quickly than a human workforce could. Even if the machines reduce the amount of manual labor, the overall result is higher productivity and more opportunities for people to learn new skills.

Second, education has been transformed by digital tools. Students now write assignments on laptops, submit them through online platforms, and research topics on the Internet rather than relying solely on textbooks. In many U.S. schools, about half of classroom activities involve screens—students watch videos, take quizzes, and collaborate on shared documents. This shift makes learning more interactive and up‑to‑date, especially for subjects that change rapidly. Teachers also benefit because they can instantly show examples, grade work remotely, and keep class records digitally. In the medical field, doctors use a wide range of high‑tech instruments—from imaging scanners to robotic surgery systems—that allow them to diagnose illnesses more accurately and perform procedures that were impossible just a few decades ago. As a result, patient survival rates have risen and trust in technology now often outweighs reliance on older reference books.

However, the same advances can have drawbacks. In many homes, gadgets have turned into “digital babysitters,” with children spending hours on tablets or phones while parents attend to other chores. This reduces the amount of direct supervision children receive, which can affect social development and learning habits. Moreover, the power of the Internet can be misused for deception and crime. Some individuals use social media, messaging apps, or gaming platforms to trick older adults or minors, stealing personal data, committing fraud, or breaking into bank accounts. A small but vocal group treat technology as a weapon for illegal activities, exploiting loopholes in security systems to launch scams or hack private information. These cases show that technology can amplify negative intentions when users lack awareness or ethical restraint.

Beyond the safety and efficiency it provides, technology reshapes how people think and behave. Smart locks, video doorbells, and home security cameras give families a feeling of protection against intruders, something that would have required a physical guard in the past. People who want to share their talents can now become content creators, posting videos on platforms such as YouTube, Instagram, or TikTok and reaching audiences worldwide without a traditional studio. Communication itself has evolved; instead of writing letters, most people exchange messages, video calls, or voice notes. This makes it possible to stay in touch with friends and family on different continents while still maintaining a connection, even if the interaction is mediated through a screen. Online gaming illustrates another point: players must coordinate with teammates in other time zones, often using voice chat to build strategies and friendships that would otherwise be impossible.

In spite of these benefits, face‑to‑face contact still matters in several key situations. At work, a simple misunderstanding can be cleared up more quickly in a real meeting than through a series of email exchanges. In personal relationships, only hearing a voice or seeing someone in person can convey tone, body language, and genuine emotion, which a text message alone cannot fully capture. In classrooms, while online resources are valuable, teachers still need to guide discussions, check comprehension, and give feedback that goes beyond what a search engine can provide. Therefore, it is wise to balance digital tools with human interaction rather than letting one completely replace the other.

In conclusion, technology brings convenience, speed, and new ways to learn and earn, but it also creates gaps in the personal connections that are vital for trust, clarity, and emotional support. When we recognize both the positive effects—such as better work efficiency, richer educational experiences, and improved medical care—and the negative consequences—like reduced supervision for children, fraud, and a sense of isolation—we can make informed choices about how to use it. Maintaining regular, meaningful human communication should be a priority alongside the many advantages technology offers. Only by respecting the limits of both realms can we build a society that is both innovative and socially cohesive.

Many people argue that aiming high is the fastest route to success, but I believe that beginning with modest goals is often the smarter strategy. When we set a low initial target, we create space to notice and correct the tiny errors that otherwise slip past us. These small adjustments may seem insignificant, yet they lay the groundwork for stronger abilities and a broader range of skills. By taking time to review what still needs improvement, we avoid overlooking fundamental flaws and gradually build confidence that lasts longer than a hasty leap.

Those who start at a modest level tend to be the ones who actually reach their dreams. They do not simply pretend that they are already competent; they learn from each mistake, allowing those experiences to shape character and increase resilience. In this way, a series of small steps makes them capable of tackling more demanding tasks later on. Their success is not a matter of luck but of persistent effort combined with careful self‑assessment.

Conversely, individuals who launch straight for ambitious goals often assume that problems will disappear without any real work. They may believe they can solve all issues in one go and miss the reality that big challenges usually require systematic effort. By beginning a bit lower, we can develop the disciplined mindset needed to earn our objectives, rather than risking a spectacular failure that erases all progress.

For instance, imagine someone who decides to take on every opportunity at once, risking everything they have earned. Without pausing to think, they may act impulsively, make careless errors and lose the very foundation they aimed to expand. A more measured approach—starting with a single, manageable task, learning from each step, and then adding complexity—helps avoid such costly setbacks. It lets the learner improve gradually while still moving forward.

Setting goals at a low level of risk also protects what we have already built. It encourages us to pause, reflect, and refine our plans before committing fully. This habit of thoughtful planning means we do not throw away valuable resources in a single reckless decision. Instead, we keep what is hard‑earned and steadily enhance it, step by step.

Some may say that occasional challenges are necessary for growth, but those challenges should not threaten our existing stability. A balanced method includes a gentle start, careful thought about the next move, and a gradual increase in difficulty. By testing ourselves within safe parameters first, we develop the strength to eventually handle higher stakes without losing everything.

In my view, the key to reaching the top is to think before we act. Beginning with modest aims, reviewing our performance, and making small improvements creates a reliable path to success. It prevents the disappointment that follows impulsive, over‑ambitious attempts and ensures that progress is sustainable. Ultimately, a mindful approach—setting low‑risk goals, reflecting on them, and then building upward—offers a realistic and effective way to achieve our aspirations.

Many people think a first impression lasts forever, but it can actually shift as we gain more knowledge. The brief meeting we have with someone usually reveals only a small part of their personality, and we often label them as negative simply because that label pops into our head right away. Further interaction can bring hidden qualities to light, showing that the first impression is not the final one.

Relying only on a first impression is dangerous because it can hide real strengths or create unnecessary distance. We may ignore valuable traits or turn away from potential friendships based on a fleeting glance. Different people form completely different initial views of the same person, often without knowing their background or motives. For instance, I judged a classmate as rude because he seemed quiet and didn’t show respect to teachers, and therefore decided to avoid him.

In tenth grade, I kept my distance from him, never trying to talk, because I thought his apparent lack of courtesy would turn into hostility. My impression was that he was distant and indifferent. As a result, I never discovered who he truly was. When our class teamed up for a project, I realized his quiet behavior was actually confidence, not disrespect. He listened carefully, offered helpful ideas, and treated everyone—including teachers—with respect. Over time we became close friends, shared meals, and I recognized him as one of the most trustworthy people I’ve ever known.

Overall, the experience shows that first impressions can change. If we assume they are fixed, we might miss chances to form genuine connections. It is sensible to wait for more information before deciding. A first glance can be a helpful cue, but it should not be the sole basis for judgment. Remaining open to revising our view helps us build real friendships and avoid unfair conclusions.

Thomas Jefferson, a former president, once wrote something that encourages people to keep working on their tasks consistently. In my view, this is a valuable piece of advice because regular effort makes a big difference in how well we perform and learn.

When we stick to a routine, tasks become easier over time. The more often we practice a skill, the quicker it settles in our minds, so future repetitions feel smoother. Of course, doing the same thing every day can sometimes seem tedious, but the payoff is clear: repeated work builds confidence and competence, and those who never take the time to repeat will never reach the same level of mastery.

I try to apply this principle to my daily life—at my job, during sports practice, and while studying. By repeating actions, I improve my memory and eventually can share what I’ve learned with others. For instance, if I read a book every day, I pick up new ideas and information faster than someone who only reads occasionally. Meanwhile, classmates or coworkers who never keep up with their responsibilities tend to stay stuck and miss out on growth.

Looking at it from a broader perspective, there’s a clear contrast between people who are consistent and those who are not. Those who turn in homework on schedule, go to bed at a reasonable hour, attend training sessions, or show up for work each day usually achieve more than those who let laziness dominate. Consistency in these areas leads to better grades, healthier bodies, and stronger work habits.

When school first began I didn’t take my homework seriously and often skipped study sessions. My friends pointed out that neglecting these tasks made everything harder later on. Their reminders helped me see the importance of a steady routine, and now I feel grateful for the habit I’ve built. I hope that anyone who reads this will adopt the same habit and remember to keep their work up, never letting it slip away.

On top of that, eating nutritious meals regularly supports our health, so we’re less likely to need doctor visits. In short, staying on a consistent path—whether it’s study, sleep, sport, or job duties—provides clear advantages.

If we all commit to doing our responsibilities regularly, we’ll see progress both personally and collectively. So let’s keep up the practice, because the results are worth it.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once wrote, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have mastered, you will never grow.” I think he is absolutely right. Mastering a task means performing it consistently, without hesitation, and that alone does not guarantee personal development. Growth begins when we deliberately step outside our comfort zone and aim for the next level of competence.

The first step is to set clear, personal goals. These goals can be modest. For instance, if you can already ride a bicycle, challenge yourself to ride a motorcycle. If you can bake a simple cupcake, move on to a full cake recipe. If you can stay afloat in water, learn how to swim. Each new, slightly more difficult activity builds on what you already know, sharpening your abilities and expanding your confidence. It is true that not every skill comes instantly. Some require years of practice, but with steady effort and self‑confidence you can eventually reach a higher level of mastery.

A realistic approach also demands perseverance. You must be willing to try repeatedly until the new skill becomes second nature. Because if you give up after the first failure, you will never improve. With enough dedication, the obstacles you face become steps toward your larger aims. The crucial point is that your future achievements depend on how far you push yourself now. Unless you keep testing your limits, the goals you set will remain out of reach.

In the end, it is your choice whether you wish to evolve or stay where you are. Decide today to pursue the next challenge, and you will move beyond your present abilities. Choose to stop, and you risk staying stuck. Growth starts with a single step beyond what you already master.

A national park is an ideal destination for families, children, and adults who want to spend quality time outdoors with friends, pets, and relatives. The grounds are filled with lively attractions that suit every age group, from classic board games and sandbox toys for little ones to picnic spots, sports fields, and interactive games for older visitors. These activities create a relaxed atmosphere where people can unwind, have fun, and strengthen their bonds while enjoying fresh air and natural scenery.

In addition to recreation, the park organizes charitable projects that give visitors a chance to make a positive impact. One such initiative is a donation drive aimed at feeding homeless individuals in the surrounding area. Anyone who contributes to the fund receives a special T‑shirt as a thank‑you, which serves as both a souvenir and a visible sign of community support. This simple reward encourages more people to take part and shows that every act of kindness matters.

The park will host a series of scheduled events from March 21 to March 29, 2019, each offering something unique for visitors to enjoy. On March 21 a friendly soccer match pits two teams against each other, and the winning side is awarded a prize at the end of the day. A playful “toggle war” competition follows on March 22, where boys and girls compete in a series of quick challenges to discover who claims the victory. March 22 also features a chess tournament, and patrons can enjoy a promotional deal of buy‑two‑get‑one‑free ice cream.  

The week continues with a pie‑eating contest on March 21 that crowns a champion, and on March 23 a teamwork race involving twenty groups will run for roughly three hours. Participants pay a modest $10 fee each, which helps fund the prize pool and supports park improvements. On March 24 the park runs another donation collection focused on urgent relief, encouraging guests to assist people who need food and shelter. The following day, March 25, a dog‑adoption fair brings rescued animals to families who can give them a loving home; otherwise, many of these animals would wait months for adoption. I disagree with the idea that school principals should force every student to pick up litter or take part in community service. Many students have other responsibilities at home, and demanding extra work could conflict with those duties. Younger pupils, like those in elementary school, usually have more free time because their schedules are less packed, so they might be able to help with simple clean‑up tasks. However, middle‑school or high‑school students often have after‑school sports, clubs, jobs, or family commitments that leave little room for mandatory community service. Even students who do not play sports can be busy with homework, projects, or caring for younger siblings. Some schools have policies that require all pupils to volunteer, but such an approach may be unfair to those who already have heavy loads. It would be more reasonable to encourage participation and let volunteers sign up rather than imposing a uniform requirement. I would be willing to help on weekends when I have fewer classes, but during the week I am already occupied with assignments and extracurricular activities. Principals could instead ask students who behave poorly to do extra service, which might teach them responsibility, but making it compulsory for everyone seems unnecessary and could lead to resentment. In short, community service should remain a voluntary activity that fits around each student’s personal schedule.

Dear Council Members,

I believe the council should implement a curfew for teenagers because it would reduce the amount of misbehaviour that occurs after dark. Many youths stay out late, often playing video games, and this leads to conflicts with neighbours or minor offences. By requiring them to be home by ten o’clock, we provide a clear deadline and also support those who need to get up early for school and need a good night’s sleep.

If the curfew becomes law, the council can pass a simple regulation stating that anyone seen on the street after ten p.m. is breaking it. This gives police and families a straightforward rule to follow, making enforcement easier.

At the moment a large number of teenagers end up in detention centres for actions that are not allowed. Some carry gaming consoles they are not legally permitted to own, and these devices occasionally appear in public places, prompting officials to link the youths with each other and add extra penalties. A curfew would stop many of these situations before they start, keeping young people from getting involved in unnecessary legal trouble.

Opponents say a curfew limits teenagers’ freedom and development. It is true that the rule reduces some liberty, but many of the youths who stay out late are already involved in risky behaviour. The purpose of the curfew is not to punish but to protect them from dangers such as traffic accidents, violence or drug exposure.

In short, a ten‑p.m. curfew respects the need for early rest and school attendance while offering a clear legal boundary. It aims to keep teenagers off the streets after that hour, which should lower their chances of getting into trouble. For these reasons I ask the council to consider the proposal seriously.

Thank you for your attention.

My view is that the first impression we form about something or someone is not set in stone; it can be reshaped as we gather new information and experiences. Some people pay little attention to that impression and simply do not care, while others let it shift after hearing more detailed accounts of what happened. How a person reacts often depends on the background they already have. If someone starts with a strong dislike, they might never bother to reconsider, especially when they feel indifferent to the matter. However, when a situation or a person truly harms them, the negative impression can become a trigger for change. Many people keep repeating the same routine and ignore criticism, but once a fresh impression appears they tend to reflect on their earlier actions and examine what went wrong. Transformation normally takes time, and many individuals change slowly because they keep repeating old habits without stopping to think. Rapid change is rare unless the need to become a different person becomes urgent.

In romantic relationships, the first impression can be altered by experiences of betrayal. When a partner is unfaithful, the emotional impact can be so strong that it changes the other person’s view of trust and loyalty. Such relationships often involve jealousy, toxicity, and negative influence, and many teenagers have suffered tragic outcomes after being led to believe their boyfriend or girlfriend cheated with someone else. The purpose of a relationship should not be to impress others and make them jealous; instead, it should provide a safe space for personal growth. Adapting to this reality can be challenging, but it is a worthwhile path toward a healthier partnership.

From my own life, I once thought that changing my attitude was impossible. During a period when friends told me I let them down with my behavior, I felt a constant sense of negativity and believed I could not match the abilities of others. I was accustomed to ways that worked for me but not for those around me, which made it hard to shift. Eventually, I decided I would become the person I wanted to be, regardless of how difficult it would be, and that decision helped me change, even without outside assistance. Now I understand that change shows others we are evolving, and each new impression offers an opportunity to avoid repeating the same mistakes. It is true that we cannot erase what we did in the past, but by making a daily effort we can improve. No one is flawless, yet we can improve our attitudes toward trust, learning who to rely on and who not to.

Working with a group or working on your own

In some situations, teamwork can feel rewarding, especially when you are paired with people you enjoy and who are skilled at the task. The chance to share ideas and receive feedback can help you develop a project more quickly. However, I have found that working alone offers several practical advantages that are often overlooked.

Group projects sometimes turn into situations where individual effort is minimized. If everyone leans on the others, you may end up doing very little while the work still gets completed. This dynamic can leave you feeling insecure about your own abilities, as the success of the assignment depends more on the group’s collective input than on your personal contributions.

As a student, I do like to collaborate with friends because the social aspect makes the work feel lighter. Unfortunately, I have often noticed that some classmates copy parts of my work without acknowledging it. This behavior not only steals credit but also makes me doubt whether those friends can manage on their own later in life. It also creates an unfair situation when the person who actually did the research is not recognized as the main author.

Because of these experiences, I strongly prefer to work independently. When I share a task with others, I rarely gain anything beneficial; I may even encounter cheating or uncooperative attitudes, which undermines my motivation. By contrast, solitary work gives me a clear sense of ownership, encourages me to keep pushing forward, and allows me to measure my progress without worrying about others’ expectations or hidden agendas. It also lets me set my own pace and address problems in a way that suits my strengths.

Reflecting on what I have learned, I realize that placing myself first is essential for both academic and personal growth. I have come to understand that I must think about my own needs, protect my ideas, and support myself. In my view, group work should be limited to cases where it genuinely improves the outcome, because otherwise it can make people feel useless or dependent. Staying focused on my own goals has helped me develop confidence and a solid sense of responsibility.

Author Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, "Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow". It is a true fact and you should try to be a better human or person in life and become someone that people can look up too.

I agree that “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” In my seventeen years I have learned that staying in a place of comfort tends to freeze progress. When we choose the easy path, we waste time that could be spent building stronger skills and deeper knowledge. Instead of moving forward, we drift in the same familiar routines, and the chance to become a better version of ourselves slips away.  

Choosing comfort may feel rewarding at the moment, but it prevents us from reaching our full potential. We end up using our energy on tasks that do not challenge us, which means we stop learning new things. By stepping out of our comfort zones, even a little bit each day, we turn ordinary moments into opportunities for growth. This growth is not only personal; it also gives us the tools to share what we know with others. Knowledge that comes from hard work can help friends, family, or strangers who are struggling, creating a ripple effect of support.  

Some people argue that they have already mastered the skills they need and therefore see no reason to push further. They may think that focusing only on themselves is acceptable, or that they have reached a final stage where improvement is unnecessary. However, this view ignores the fact that human beings are always capable of learning more. Whether we are fathers, mothers, sons, or daughters, we can keep refining how we solve problems, communicate, and understand the world. Settling for “good enough” means missing out on the richer experiences and deeper connections that come from continued effort.  

Every day we should try to add a little something new to our repertoire. Small improvements—like learning a new phrase, trying a different approach, or asking for help when we need it—do not hurt us; they enrich us. When we open ourselves to learning from others, we also create stronger communities. As Ralph Waldo Emerson noted, “Unless you try to do something beyond what you have already mastered, you will never grow.” This statement captures the truth that growth requires risk, effort, and a willingness to face discomfort.  

In short, staying cosy is not the best route if we want to develop personally or assist others. By regularly stretching ourselves and sharing what we have learned, we become people others can look up to. Growth is a habit, not a one‑off event, and it starts the moment we decide to do a little more than we already know.

Many people argue that teenagers ought to choose a future profession before they start high school, and that the subjects they study should be selected to point them toward a particular career. I disagree with this view because students at that age are rarely prepared to make such a permanent decision.

First, most learners have not yet experienced real‑world work, so they cannot accurately judge which occupation fits them best. High‑school students generally lack practical exposure to any field, and choosing a career without that background often leads to a mismatch between their interests and the demands of the job.

Second, adolescents tend to be impulsive and may later realize that a particular path no longer appeals to them. For instance, one of my classmates enrolled in a technology course during freshman year, only to discover the earnings were lower than expected. He then switched to a program focused on construction and materials, having to repeat several subjects that he had already taken. This illustrates how premature decisions can waste time and resources.

Finally, waiting until later in school allows students to concentrate on achieving solid grades and building a broader academic foundation. By the time they reach senior year or college, they have a clearer understanding of their strengths, interests, and the requirements of various careers. At that stage, selecting courses with a specific vocational aim becomes far more rational and effective.

In conclusion, expecting teenagers to commit to a career early on is unwise. High‑school should first be about developing academic abilities and general knowledge, reserving career‑focused choices for a later, more informed stage.

My central idea is that personal success feels most complete when it is tied to the well‑being of other people. I agree with Emerson’s view that a life lived for the benefit of others creates lasting value. I will present three reasons that support this opinion: first, creating something that helps other people; second, having a concrete, purposeful job; and third, possessing a skill that enables you to aid others. My examples aim to show how each element can make a difference.

I concur with Emerson because it is deeply meaningful to produce something that benefits the people we wish to assist. When we design a program, a product, or a service that improves someone’s life, we develop a continuous motivation to keep helping many others reach their dreams, goals, and sense of purpose. Imagine, for instance, starting a local tutoring centre that offers free lessons to children from low‑income families. Their parents see their children’s grades rise and feel proud, while the children gain confidence and a clearer path toward their ambitions. Another illustration could be an online platform that provides emotional‑support resources for people struggling with personal challenges. By giving others a reason to move forward and to fulfill their aspirations, we turn our own drive into a powerful force that spreads outward.

A concrete job also plays a crucial role in lifting many people. When we focus on a particular profession, we are able to guide others in selecting that path and preparing for it. For example, as a career adviser I collect up‑to‑date information on engineering internships and university programmes. I share this data with students who are unsure about which field will give them the best chance to achieve their goals. In doing so, I help a large number of individuals discover an occupation that aligns with their talents and values, leading them to experience meaningful success. Moreover, by supplying reliable advice, I enable people to gain better employment opportunities and to feel satisfied in their work.

Finally, having a valuable skill that can be used to serve others is a true accomplishment. The skill may be communication, computer programming, or problem‑solving; whichever it is, the act of applying it to assist others can be incredibly rewarding. Suppose you are proficient in public speaking and decide to give workshops on time‑management for busy parents. You can see how participants improve their daily routines and feel more in control of their lives. This kind of assistance not only enriches the recipients but also brings personal satisfaction, knowing that your talent is making a positive impact.

In conclusion, by helping others find a clear purpose and reach their goals through a well‑defined career or a useful skill, we create lasting happiness for ourselves and for those we support. A fulfilling job, combined with a desire to contribute, makes life richer, and the constant pursuit of dreams never ends.

I think students would gain a lot if they were allowed to join lessons from their own homes. One of the main reasons is that they can start class more prepared and stay focused. At school some learners feel embarrassed about showing their abilities, especially when others say they are not good at something. If they could study online, they would not have to compare themselves with classmates and could concentrate on the material instead.

For instance, a student who is alone at home might have many questions about the online lesson. He can search for answers by himself, pause the video, or look up extra information without feeling rushed. When he needs a break, he can quickly cook something, refresh his mind, and then return to his screen. If a doubt remains, he can send a message to the teacher and get clarification right away.

This flexibility also helps students who are shy or need more personal attention. A friend of mine shared her experience while she was pregnant. She kept going to school until the delivery, but she was extremely tired and worried about her baby being at home with a teacher who could not always be present. Once she switched to online classes, she could stay in a comfortable setting, attend lessons whenever she felt able, and still give her child the care it needed. After giving birth she returned to school, but the idea of being able to study from home had already shown how supportive such a system can be.

Another advantage is the freedom from the early‑morning rush and the cold weather. Students do not have to worry about choosing the right clothes or waiting for a bus in winter, which often makes the school environment unpleasant. They can also avoid unwanted conversations or conflicts with peers that sometimes distract them during a lesson.

There are clear benefits to attending class at home. Learners can spend more time using computers, which improves technical skills and lets them access helpful tools whenever they need them. They tend to focus better on homework because there are fewer interruptions, and they can study at any hour of the day. They no longer need to chat with friends during the session, and tasks are usually completed faster without distractions. Having a phone nearby makes it easy to look up information quickly, and they can keep working even after the school day ends.

On the other hand, not every student has the same resources. Some families cannot afford reliable internet or devices, and others have to work to support themselves. For those who need to earn money, a hybrid schedule can be useful: they attend a few in‑person days and spend the rest studying online, which reduces the pressure of juggling work and school. Even if circumstances are difficult, persistence is key. By asking for help when they do not understand something, by researching extra material, and by putting effort into each assignment, students can still succeed.

Overall, allowing remote attendance gives many learners a healthier and more effective way to study. It helps those who feel shy, those with special personal situations, and those who need to manage time around other responsibilities. If schools offer reliable online options and support, students will be better able to keep learning without giving up.

Being true to yourself in every circumstance can help you reach the highest achievements in life. I believe that constant self‑respect and confidence open doors that otherwise seem closed, because no external barrier can stop someone who knows their own strengths and keeps moving forward. The sky truly is the limit when you combine inner power with unwavering faith; together they create a mindset that treats any goal as possible.

Faith is the engine behind this mindset. When you trust that your abilities are enough, doubts lose their grip and obstacles shrink in size. History shows how powerful this combination can be. Martin Luther King Jr. always stayed focused on his vision of equality, never wavering even when many doubted his path. He kept a positive outlook, surrounded himself with belief, and ultimately stood before a crowd in Washington D.C. where his dream took shape. His success proves that a clear, heartfelt purpose and self‑belief turn aspirations into reality.

Cristiano Ronaldo’s story follows a similar pattern. Growing up without his father and facing financial strain, he could have given up, but instead he nurtured a fierce love for soccer. Starting as a child‑laborer in the mornings and evenings, he trained relentlessly, turning personal hardship into fuel for his ambition. By the time he was fifteen he was already playing for the national youth team, and later became one of the world’s most celebrated athletes. His journey illustrates how dedication, personal passion, and belief in oneself can overcome any barrier.

Even if you doubt your abilities today, remember that confidence and consistent effort make the impossible possible. When you begin an endeavor, keep your faith alive, stay patient, and don’t surrender when challenges appear. All it takes is to stay authentic, keep the fire inside, and let it guide you forward. Anyone with a dream, a deep desire, or simply a spark of curiosity can achieve greatness by simply staying true to themselves.

Because schools do not always have accurate records of every student’s dietary restrictions, altering the menu could accidentally introduce ingredients that are harmful. That would put vulnerable students at risk and undermine the purpose of trying to improve meals.

Third, updating the menu requires a budget, and the money is wasted if the new dishes are not accepted. In some countries schools have plenty of funds for extra activities, but they do not always realize that most students will reject unfamiliar foods and simply throw them away. This not only harms the school’s finances, it also shows that the effort is futile when pupils are not satisfied.

For these reasons, the cafeteria should keep the existing menu. Keeping the current choices avoids extra costs, prevents food waste, and protects students who have allergies. It also respects the preferences of picky eaters, allowing them to feel comfortable with what is offered. By preserving the menu as it is, schools can save money, students will be less likely to discard uneaten meals, and nobody will face health risks.

Have you ever spotted a forgotten object on the sidewalk and thought about keeping it for yourself? That moment can feel like a harmless game, yet it actually involves dishonesty. When you pick up something that isn’t yours, you can’t be sure who it belongs to. If the item turns out to be cash, a small electronic device, or a child’s favorite toy, the owner may return looking for it only to discover it missing because someone else decided to walk away with it. Such a move is essentially theft, even if you never intended to cause harm.  

In my own school days, I regularly saw classmates drop pencils, notebooks, or even a few dollars on the ground. Instead of slipping them into my pocket, I usually handed the items back or alerted the person who had dropped them. I’ve also seen the opposite happen—some students would take a stray item and claim it as theirs. While that may feel exciting at first, it creates a pattern of mistrust that can hurt both the finder and the original owner.  

The reason many people give for taking a stray item is simple: it’s there, no one is watching, and it might be useful. But this logic fails when we consider that most objects we encounter have owners who rely on them. A favorite stuffed animal, for instance, could be a birthday gift that a child saved for weeks. If that child loses it because someone else claimed it, the disappointment can be lasting. The real test is whether the item is truly needed or simply wanted. If you genuinely need something, you can purchase it at the nearest store. If the desire is just to have a new toy to show off or to satisfy a fleeting curiosity, then keeping a found object is unnecessary and unfair.  

Schools often address this issue with clear messages posted around the hallways: “Leave it where you found it. Return it to the owner.” At my elementary school, colorful signs reminded us to act responsibly, and many of us followed the guidance. Still, peer pressure can sometimes override those rules. A classmate might persuade you to take an unattended item, insisting it’s no big deal, but resisting that pressure is crucial for personal integrity and social harmony.  

The consequences of ignoring these lessons become obvious when you consider how valuable everyday objects have become. A few years ago, I lost an iPad on a bus. A stranger spotted it, kept it, and never identified himself. I only learned later that someone else had taken it for convenience, not necessity. I felt upset because I relied on that device for schoolwork and entertainment, and the replacement cost was high. Smartphones present a similar scenario. Today, a phone can easily exceed a thousand dollars, and many people depend on it for communication, navigation, or even safety. If a lost phone is kept by someone, the owner will likely experience anxiety, anger, and perhaps even a sense of being stranded.  

That is why teaching this principle early is so important. Parents sometimes overlook the need to reinforce honesty, leaving schools to fill the gap. When a child drops a prized possession, the simple act of returning it can restore trust, relieve worry, and teach a valuable lesson about empathy. If you ever find something lying on the ground, the safest course is either to leave it untouched or to locate its owner and hand it back. By being vigilant, resisting peer pressure, and showing kindness, we help preserve a culture where lost items are reunited rather than kept, and we demonstrate that honesty matters more than the temporary thrill of “free” possession.
