Why do many people finish school at a very young age? Some think it is because they are smarter than their classmates, but the real reason is simply that they have graduated early. Although a few might claim that graduating after three years is a bad idea, I believe it is actually beneficial because it helps young people become more mature for the real world and teaches them to take full responsibility for their own actions.  

The first reason is that early graduation encourages maturity. In today’s society, many teenagers have little experience of how life really works. They often do not consider the consequences of risky behavior, such as drinking and driving, which can lead to accidents and harm to themselves and others. Parents sometimes step in to bail their children out of trouble, which means the teen never feels the full weight of their mistakes. If a student leaves school after three years, they would enter adult life sooner and begin to understand what is right and wrong. They would learn from real situations rather than being shielded by family support, which makes them more ready for the challenges they will face later on.  

A second advantage is that early graduation forces learners to handle their own finances. At home, most teenagers have their bills paid for them, whether it is a phone bill, electricity, or water. Because they never have to worry about where money comes from, they may waste resources without thinking about the cost. For example, if a teen uses too much light or water, the bill might increase dramatically, but a parent usually covers it. When a young adult must pay rent, utilities, and other daily expenses, they quickly realize that money is limited and that careful budgeting is necessary. This hands‑on experience teaches responsibility and helps avoid the surprise of a high bill that can only be handled if the individual knows the real value of what they consume.  

Some people argue that graduating early robs young people of fun and adds unnecessary pressure, suggesting that teens miss out on the carefree moments that define adolescence. They say that stress and a lack of relaxation can become overwhelming. While this point is understandable, the trade‑off is worth it. The life lessons gained from early independence, such as managing money and making sensible choices, far outweigh the temporary enjoyment of staying in school longer.  

In conclusion, graduating after three years is a good idea because it pushes students toward greater maturity and personal responsibility. By confronting real‑world problems earlier, they learn how to act wisely and avoid costly mistakes. Moreover, paying their own bills helps them understand the value of money and resources, which prepares them for future adult life. Although early graduation may reduce some moments of teenage fun, the benefits of becoming a more responsible and aware individual make it a worthwhile decision.

I think that students’ self‑esteem largely grows from what they accomplish. When a learner puts effort into school work, sports, or any extracurricular activity, each successful result reinforces a sense of pride. That pride then turns into genuine confidence, which in turn strengthens self‑esteem. It is difficult for anyone to feel good about themselves if they have never tasted success.

Many students work long hours, meet deadlines, and even hold part‑time jobs after class, yet they still struggle to see themselves in a positive light. In their eyes the problem is a lack of self‑confidence; without that inner belief they cannot appreciate the achievements they already have. At the same time there are students who seem confident from the outside, even without any recognisable awards. They may talk freely, appear cheerful, but have not yet built a solid self‑esteem because they have not linked that confidence to real accomplishments.

To move forward, students need to aim for tangible outcomes. Earning a certificate, finishing a project early, or mastering a new skill all provide concrete evidence of progress. When achievements accumulate, confidence naturally follows, and confidence fuels further effort. A practical way to start is by being diligent, keeping a schedule or checklist, and setting daily or weekly goals. These habits show that effort can be planned and measured, which makes it easier to see results.

Nowadays, I often wonder why many pupils appear reluctant to work hard. Some blame technology for making it too easy to avoid responsibilities, while others simply lack motivation to chase goals. I have seen that even a modest increase in study time at home can lead to noticeable success in school. If a student simply opens their backpack and spends two hours reviewing material each night, they are likely to start gaining recognitions that boost their self‑worth.

Confidence and achievement also depend on supportive figures around a student. Teachers spend a significant amount of time with learners, often more than parents do in a week. While teachers are not always expected to deliver confidence‑building talks, they can show the right steps to reach goals – whether it is improving a grade, learning a language, or taking part in a club. When students see a clear route to success, they begin to think about how they can move along it, and that mindset often leads to increased self‑confidence.

I remember moving to the United States in 2017 with no English and no friends. Entering a classroom where I could not speak to anyone made my face flush with embarrassment each time someone tried to talk to me. At that time I felt powerless and shy. Through daily practice, extra tutoring, and gradually joining group activities, my language skills grew, my interactions became smoother, and the blush faded. I now feel confident, more like the best version of myself, and I have a supportive group of friends who help me study and have fun.

In short, confidence and effort toward achievement are the key ingredients for building students’ self‑esteem. Parents, teachers, and the students themselves must all encourage this cycle. When learners recognize that their hard work brings results, they will naturally become more confident, and that confidence will sustain the self‑esteem that helps them thrive both in school and beyond.

I agree with Emerson’s claim that without mastering a skill you cannot expect to grow. When people acquire a deep understanding of their field, they usually perform better, open up new possibilities, and move up the career ladder faster than those who lack such expertise.

On the other hand, some critics argue that formal mastery is not always essential. In certain cases, individuals without a formal qualification manage to excel in a role, delivering results that surpass those of someone who has studied the subject intensively. This viewpoint acknowledges that talent and practical experience can sometimes compensate for a missing diploma.

Firstly, a solid mastery enables someone to carry out tasks more efficiently. Because the skill has been practiced for a long time, the required steps become second nature. For instance, a chef who has completed a culinary program needs only recall the basic recipes, while an untrained cook must also remember the specific ingredients, equipment, and preparation techniques. The trained chef therefore spends less mental energy on the basics and can focus on creativity and quality, leading to higher overall performance.

Secondly, mastery creates more chances for advancement. Employers often look for proof that a candidate is ready for a given position, and a recognized certification serves as that evidence. A restaurant that wants to fill a managerial post, for example, usually prefers someone with a culinary degree; the degree signals that the applicant has already mastered the standards required for leadership. Consequently, the certified person can command a higher salary and gain access to roles that are unavailable to non‑certified staff.

Thirdly, having a mastery boosts one’s chances of occupying the most rewarding roles. Experience and training are evident on a résumé, making it easier for hiring managers to place a qualified worker in positions of authority. In a kitchen, a person with a recognized certification is more likely to be appointed as a supervisor, whereas someone without formal training is often assigned to tasks such as dishwashing. Even if the untrained worker later wishes to become a manager, they must invest considerably more time and effort to catch up.

In conclusion, people who have mastered their craft enjoy better job performance, broader opportunities, and higher positions compared with those who have not. While it is true that some without formal mastery can succeed, the overall trend supports Emerson’s view: without mastery, true growth is limited.

Thomas Jefferson’s words, “it is wonderful how much may be done if we are doing,” highlight the power of constant action. This idea suggests that whether we work for others or ourselves, staying engaged helps us achieve more. The question remains: does constant activity lead to greater accomplishments, or does taking time off also have value? Some argue that periods of rest are essential because they give us strength and mental clarity. Yet, many believe that relentless effort is preferable, since hard work often results in reaching goals and contributing to the wider community.

Every day, millions of people rise early to start their jobs, striving to give their best. However, what about those who currently lack employment? Even without a paid position, they can still serve society through volunteering or personal growth. For example, they might assist neighbors, join community projects, or study new skills—all of which keep them active and meaningful. Of course, rest is necessary; we cannot function well without breaks. Still, excessive inactivity risks letting dreams slip away and goals become distant.

Doing something positive is always worthwhile, especially when it’s driven by passion and commitment. Most workers have a purpose: some aim for financial security, others chase personal passions or want to support their families. My mother often says, “If you want something, go after it.” This advice reminds us that a better future requires effort. That’s why many of us believe it’s healthier to stay active rather than do nothing at all.

From a societal standpoint, being busy is often expected because basic needs—food, shelter, bills, taxes—must be met. This usually means holding a job, but it also includes other forms of involvement, such as helping others or learning new abilities. If we care about our work, even unpaid activities can build character and benefit others. In other words, staying productive makes us more valuable members of society.

Ultimately, human progress depends on people taking initiative. Dreams and objectives push us forward, while inactivity might cause us to lose motivation. Jefferson’s quote encourages us to think about how we spend our time. Breaks are helpful, but they shouldn’t overshadow the goals we want to achieve.

When people set goals for their careers, help friends or family, or even learn new skills, they are being active. Physical inactivity is linked to problems such as obesity, heart disease, and weakened muscles. It also keeps a person away from social networks and opportunities for growth. For instance, individuals who stay indoors, avoid work, or drop out of school often end up feeling isolated and unhealthy.  

In contrast, an active lifestyle provides many advantages. Regular exercise improves health, a steady job satisfies career ambitions, and education opens doors to new knowledge. Volunteering helps others while building personal satisfaction. Even small daily tasks, like reading a book or taking a course, add up over time. As Jefferson said, the more we act, the more we accomplish.  

Of course, opinions differ. Some people enjoy a quiet life and argue that rest is necessary. Yet the evidence suggests that continuous effort, balanced with occasional rest, is the most effective way to reach one’s objectives. In the end, the world is full of diverse choices, but the consensus among many experts is that staying active leads to a richer, healthier, and more purposeful life.

Having a positive attitude matters a great deal. When people lack optimism, they tend to treat others poorly, which makes those individuals feel uneasy. I agree with this idea because a hopeful mindset often leads to employment opportunities, and keeping such an outlook is valuable both in everyday life and at home.

In my own experience, I work in a restaurant where I constantly aim to greet customers with a friendly smile. A manager I observed there habitually expressed a negative outlook, and that behaviour was clearly detrimental. I believe it is unhelpful to adopt a sour demeanour, especially at work. A constructive attitude can open doors to jobs and careers, and I think the habit of staying positive stems from the values my parents have taught me.

Secondly, some of my acquaintances seem constantly pessimistic, and that is not beneficial. There is a common misconception that negativity can be advantageous, but in reality it often leads to poor decisions and strained relationships. My mother frequently reminds me not to focus on negative thoughts, telling me that they bring no good. My grandmother repeats the same advice. Following their guidance, I try to keep a bright outlook, which helps me avoid the pitfalls that negativity creates.

Thirdly, positivity is crucial in the workplace. Consider the case of a young woman who applied for a position at our restaurant. She attended the interview, but her demeanor lacked enthusiasm and optimism. My boss decided not to hire her because she didn’t show a willing attitude. This illustrates how many employers look for employees who can interact positively with customers and colleagues. Across different occupations, a cheerful disposition is expected because it improves teamwork and customer satisfaction.

In conclusion, anyone who wants to secure a job should learn how to stay optimistic. If you notice you are slipping into a negative mindset, it is wise to change it. Negative attitudes are not helpful in professional or personal settings. By cultivating a positive attitude, we not only boost our own chances but also make those around us feel more comfortable. Ultimately, keeping a constructive outlook is a skill that benefits everyone.

The proposal to shift from a traditional five‑day school schedule to a four‑day model has been gaining attention as a way to balance academic demands with the many responsibilities students face outside the classroom. By shortening the weekly school routine, we can keep the same total instructional time while offering a free day that students can use for personal needs, work, or enrichment.

One practical way to make this change is to reduce the number of instructional days by one and lengthen each remaining school day by about two hours. This approach keeps the curriculum on track while allowing teachers to devote more uninterrupted attention to each lesson. With longer periods, students have a better chance to finish assignments, work on group projects, and seek clarification from peers or instructors. A single extra hour could be reserved for tutoring or a brief after‑school club session, which would help those who are struggling in a particular subject.

The fourth day can be freed up entirely for optional activities. Some learners would appreciate more time in the library, where they can study, borrow books, or use computers. Others might prefer a sports session or an arts club, which often compete with regular class periods for after‑school slots. Offering a day without scheduled lessons gives students the flexibility to pursue hobbies or to receive one‑on‑one help that is otherwise hard to fit into a packed timetable.

For many families, the new schedule creates a valuable window for health appointments and other personal obligations. In a typical five‑day week, parents sometimes have to miss school for a doctor visit or a family emergency, which leads to lost instructional time and extra paperwork. With a free day, such appointments can be arranged without disrupting the school day, and students can return without falling behind.

Teachers, who often juggle their own family duties, would also benefit. An extra day off each week would give them more time for personal errands, parenting responsibilities, and relaxation. This, in turn, could translate into higher morale and more energy when they are in the classroom.

Older students, especially seniors preparing for university applications or part‑time work, need dedicated time to explore career options, write essays, and attend college fairs. A free day can be set aside for these tasks, ensuring that they do not have to sacrifice study time for real‑world preparation. Freshmen, who are adjusting from middle school routines, could use the same day for orientation, mentorship sessions, or low‑key activities that help them feel comfortable in a new environment.

Community involvement is another positive side of the model. Schools could partner with local businesses to organise volunteer programmes on the free day, allowing students to help clean streets, assist at animal shelters, or support neighbourhood events. Supervised service‑learning projects would give learners a sense of purpose while building strong links between the school and the community.

Although the change may pose challenges for students who hold part‑time jobs, the schedule can be adapted. By extending the school day, the overall working week can stay the same length, leaving the extra day open for employment. Those who need more daytime hours can simply use the remaining free day to fit in shifts, keeping both work and study in balance.

Finally, it is worth noting that students can still meet the usual workload because longer class periods give them more depth of study. The combination of a longer school day and a true free day prevents the need for rushed work and reduces stress.

In conclusion, the advantages of a four‑day school week clearly outweigh the drawbacks. The additional free day offers time for health appointments, family activities, extracurricular interests, and community service, while longer daily lessons support academic progress. With proper planning and occasional adjustments, this model can serve the majority of learners and create a healthier, more productive school experience. Everyone deserves a few days each week away from school, and a four‑day schedule makes that possible.

Many teachers and parents think that schools ought to make a set of elective courses mandatory for every pupil. The belief is that when teenagers try a variety of creative or hands‑on subjects, they can uncover interests that they never considered before and recognize talents they might have hidden. This discovery, in turn, can guide them toward personal growth and open doors to future careers, which is why the debate over electives is still relevant in modern education.

If a student is obliged to attend classes that do not match his or her interests, the chances of losing motivation rise sharply. A bored learner may feel indifferent, miss several sessions, and ultimately achieve lower scores. Poor grades can trigger frustration and a sense of failure, which often leads to disengagement and even dropping out of a course. Without the necessary credits, the student risks not meeting graduation requirements, limiting the possibility of enrolling in college or securing a decent job. In the long run, a lack of qualifications can make it harder to find stable employment, and this chain of disadvantages may contribute to serious social problems such as homelessness.

Electives, however, can also be a powerful tool for identifying and honing individual strengths. When a pupil chooses a subject that aligns with his or her abilities, the classroom becomes a place of genuine enthusiasm rather than drudgery. Positive involvement tends to raise the level of effort, improve performance, and generate a desire to learn more. As a result, the student earns the credit that is needed for graduation and builds a portfolio that future employers will appreciate. For instance, a student who discovers a talent for drama may be invited to act in local productions, gain experience on stage, and even attract the attention of casting agents. That skill set can lead to a professional career, visibility, and a higher income, showing how electives can translate into real‑world opportunities.

The idea that each person has a particular set of skills does not imply that those skills are limited to a single domain. Exploring a range of electives can reveal multiple areas in which a student feels comfortable and proficient. Combining several competencies—whether they are artistic, technical, or academic—creates a broader appeal for employers who value diverse abilities. Moreover, the experience gained from taking different courses helps students build confidence, increase their social network, and prepare for the challenges of adult life.

Looking ahead, the benefits of elective subjects become even more apparent after high school. A well‑rounded set of interests makes the transition to college smoother and enriches a student’s resume, which can be crucial when applying for scholarships or specialized programs. In adulthood, those same interests often serve as a foundation for personal projects, hobbies, or even entrepreneurial ventures. While it is true that some critics argue that teenagers may not be motivated enough to take electives seriously, the evidence suggests that when the choice is guided by genuine curiosity, the impact on academic success and future prospects is considerable.

Therefore, despite occasional concerns about low enthusiasm, making electives an essential part of school curricula seems wise. By giving pupils the chance to experiment, discover, and develop unique talents, schools help them avoid the negative cycle of disinterest, poor grades, and missed career chances. In the end, a student who knows his or her strengths is far more likely to graduate on time, pursue higher education, and secure a stable, fulfilling job.

Author Ralph Waldo Emerson wrote, "To be yourself in a world that constantly tries to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment." Currently, your accomplishments, acts, and attitude speak of you and how great you are. Around the world, many people think doing something else is a humble act—for example, in your career, area of work, or school, doing something that is not your responsibility, or showing that you have a big heart and how important it is to show to the world that you try to become different. I agree because when you are yourself, people see something special in you and try to be the person you are—a person who likes to learn new things, perhaps imperfect at first but never giving up to be different among many people. Three reasons why being yourself is important are: first, other people will come to like you; second, you will become an inspiration for everyone; third, your accomplishments can change the mentality of many people around you.

First, being yourself is important because other people will come to like you. It is a situation where you always go the extra mile—for example, in school, explaining to a friend how to solve any math equation, even though it is not your job in class. You are only a student, and it is the teacher's responsibility to explain to the friend. The accomplishment is that many people will come to like you.

Second, being yourself is important because you will become an inspiration for everyone. This applies in many areas, such as at home, in the neighborhood, at school, college, and even at church. For example, if your neighbor sees you cleaning your yard or house or helping other neighbors—like cutting grass and helping each other—you can become a motivation for other people. That is how you complete your accomplishment of being an inspiration for others.

Last, being yourself is important because your accomplishment can change the mentality of others. People see your progress in life and may ask themselves, "How did they do it?" You can leave a message and tell them how you did it, and if they try it, they can do it too. For example, in families we always see different types: one that has jobs with lower salaries, and another that owns its own company. If we are the type of person who likes to help our own family, we will transmit that as good vibes, hope, etc.

In conclusion, as the author said, we constantly try to do extra things to achieve great results and accomplishments in life. More than 50 percent of the world does this because most people see the benefits of helping others. Most importantly, the world sees a positive side of this message: the author says we should always do something else, and our greatest accomplishment can serve as an example for another person around us because, beyond example, we can be an inspiration for many people in the world.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once observed, “To be yourself in a world that constantly tries to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment.” I share his view because living authentically reveals a special quality that people notice and often wish to copy. Around us many individuals treat stepping outside their prescribed roles as a humble gesture—whether in their work, school, or community—yet the deeper impact is that they display a genuine commitment to helping others. My agreement rests on three points that illustrate why staying true to oneself matters.

First, when you act in a way that goes beyond what is expected, others tend to emulate that behavior. Imagine a student who, despite not being the teacher’s assistant, takes the time to explain a difficult math problem to a classmate. This extra effort shows responsibility and generosity, encouraging fellow students to offer assistance in similar situations. Over time, more people adopt this habit of going the extra mile, creating a ripple effect of mutual support.

Second, being yourself can serve as an inspiration for those around you. Whether at home, in the neighborhood, school, or even in places of worship, small actions convey strong messages. A neighbor who regularly tidies their yard, mows lawns for others, and offers a helping hand subtly demonstrates that community care is possible. Residents may start to mirror these practices, recognizing that personal kindness can make the entire area more pleasant and cooperative.

Finally, your personal achievements have the power to change the mental outlook of many people. By sharing the steps you took to reach a goal, you provide a practical roadmap that others can follow. For example, if a family member runs a small business instead of accepting a low‑salary job, the story behind that decision spreads positive energy, hope, and optimism. Relatives and friends see the possibility of a different, more rewarding path and begin to consider similar choices for themselves.

In short, Emerson’s insight holds true today: the world is full of people who perform unexpected deeds, and these actions are often humble yet profoundly influential. By staying true to ourselves, we become role models, sources of motivation, and catalysts for change. The majority of society benefits from such authenticity, and our greatest accomplishment is the example we set for others to follow.

Many schools and companies are beginning to use a shorter, four‑day schedule in order to reduce the consumption of natural resources and save energy. Some people argue that my school should not follow this model, claiming that we do not waste water, electricity or paper and that extending the day by two hours would not help. I believe the opposite: adopting a four‑day week and lengthening each school day slightly would actually be good for our school and our community.

Critics say that our campus uses its supplies and power responsibly, because they are necessary for learning and for providing modern facilities. They also maintain that shortening the week would not bring any noticeable benefit. Indeed, our classrooms, laboratories and computer labs need the electricity we draw, and we recycle paper whenever possible. However, these claims ignore the sheer scale of our operation. The school occupies a large building, runs dozens of air‑conditioned rooms, and serves one of the highest student populations in the county. Even responsible use adds up when multiplied by so many users, and the cumulative impact can be significant.

One strong reason to support the change is the environmental advantage it would bring. Recent data from my county shows that the amount of resources used by our institution has risen by seventy percent over the past few years. At the same time, the demand for timber in the region has grown as a result of increased paper consumption, harming local forests and the overall ecosystem. By cutting back on the number of school days and making each day more efficient, we could reduce paper waste, lower the need for extra heating or cooling, and lessen the pressure on surrounding natural areas. This would give the school a cleaner image and help protect the environment for future generations.

A second benefit lies in better control of energy use. Our classrooms are equipped with many devices—computers, smartboards, projectors—that draw a considerable portion of the school’s electricity. Studies from energy‑saving websites indicate that about eighty percent of a school’s power consumption comes from these technical tools. Because we have the largest enrollment in the county, the total load on our electrical system is especially high. If we trim the week to four days while adding a couple of hours each day, the devices would be on for a shorter total period. This reduction would translate into lower electricity bills and a smaller carbon footprint, making the campus a more sustainable learning environment.

Some might argue that we already use resources wisely, so there is no need for a change. Yet, even efficient use can become wasteful when the numbers are large. Moreover, the practical difficulties of operating a large school for five days—more buses running, more lights staying on—contribute to unnecessary consumption. A four‑day schedule would streamline daily activities, encourage staff to plan lessons more tightly, and give students a clearer sense of purpose during the shorter week.

In short, shifting to a four‑day school week and extending each day slightly would help us conserve resources and manage energy more responsibly. It would protect the environment, cut electricity costs and demonstrate that our school is committed to sustainable practice. Would you not agree? Think about what you would do at home—would you try to limit the electricity you use to lower your bills? The same logic applies here. The change is a simple, effective step toward a greener, more efficient school community.

Many schools ask pupils to finish a piece of work during the summer holidays so that learning does not stop. The question often raised is whether the task should be selected by the teacher or by the student. From my point of view, the most effective approach is for students to decide the topic and the form of their own project.

When a student creates the project himself or herself, it becomes much easier to stay motivated. A learner already knows which subject or skill feels tricky, and by choosing a project that directly addresses that difficulty the work feels relevant and manageable. For instance, an ESL learner might decide to write short essays in English each week, focusing on vocabulary that was confusing during the school year. Because the topic is chosen by the student, the assignment is more comfortable, and the learner can adjust the difficulty level as needed. This personal control also reduces anxiety; the student is confident that he or she understands the material and can complete the task without constant help.

Carrying out a self‑chosen project throughout the break helps retain the knowledge gained earlier. If students stop working altogether, they are likely to forget important concepts and fall into the habit of procrastination. Continuing their own work provides regular practice that reinforces memory. Take, for example, a student who builds a digital poster about a geography unit; the act of collecting information, organising it, and presenting it keeps the ideas fresh. By the time the new term starts, the pupil is already comfortable with the material and can participate actively in lessons. Moreover, independent projects teach organization, time management, and problem‑solving, skills that are valuable both in school and beyond.

Of course, teachers should still provide clear expectations and a framework. Setting simple criteria such as topic selection, required resources, and a final presentation ensures that the work meets academic standards while still allowing creative freedom. This balance lets students enjoy autonomy and still receive constructive feedback when they submit their project.

In conclusion, giving pupils the chance to design their own summer projects is a sensible way to keep learning alive, to address personal challenges, and to strengthen abilities that will help them succeed in the upcoming school year. When students own the process, they stay engaged, retain what they have learned, and develop valuable competencies without relying heavily on teacher direction.

Working in a team versus working alone: which approach is more useful? The evidence suggests that teamwork produces better results. When people collaborate they can share knowledge, divide tasks, and support one another. This sharing often leads to faster completion of projects and higher‑quality outcomes.  

First, group work makes it easier to obtain help when a problem arises. In many school assignments or workplace projects a single individual might become stuck on a difficult part and lose valuable time. If two or more people are present, the person who is stuck can ask a teammate for an explanation, a hint, or a suggestion. This immediate assistance reduces the risk of errors and speeds up progress. Moreover, people can exchange ideas they would not have considered on their own. One student may suggest a method for solving a math problem that another refines and applies, producing a solution that is both creative and efficient. Collective brainstorming can generate ideas that enhance the final product, making teamwork a powerful engine for success. Even so, a few individuals maintain that working by themselves is preferable, claiming that it offers uninterrupted concentration. However, they overlook the fact that solitary effort often lacks fresh perspectives and may result in repeated mistakes.  

Second, collaboration distributes the workload. A single person trying to finish a large project, such as a research report or a software development task, often has to do everything by himself, which can become overwhelming. By splitting the work among several members, each person can focus on a part that matches his strengths. For instance, one student might be good at gathering data, another at creating charts, while a third writes the conclusion. This division allows each member to contribute more effectively, which in turn raises the chances of meeting deadlines and achieving high standards.  

Third, teamwork provides a built‑in system of quality control. When people work together, they can review each other’s drafts or designs, catching mistakes before they become final. A teammate might spot a typo, a logical flaw, or a missing citation that the original author overlooked. This peer‑review process not only improves the final result but also helps the individual learn from his own errors. In contrast, when someone works alone, he lacks an external perspective and may miss these issues entirely.  

Some argue that working alone is preferable because it offers uninterrupted concentration and personal freedom. They claim that solitary work lets them plan their time without interference, avoid being dragged into someone else’s mistakes, and maintain ownership of their ideas. While these points have merit in certain contexts, they do not outweigh the benefits of collaboration in most situations. Planning a project alone may indeed be simpler in the short term, but it limits the breadth of ideas and reduces the chance of finding a better solution. Likewise, being the sole owner of ideas does not guarantee success if those ideas are never challenged, refined, or expanded upon. In fact, a solitary worker can become stuck, repeat the same errors, or waste time on a path that could have been avoided with a different viewpoint.  

Another criticism of group work is that some members might rely too much on others or produce subpar contributions. It is true that freeloading can happen, but effective teams usually have clear roles and expectations. When tasks are assigned and each member knows what is expected, the likelihood of poor effort drops. Moreover, team members can encourage one another to stay on track, provide feedback, and remind each other of deadlines. This social pressure often leads to higher overall performance than a single person working in isolation.  

The experience of a typical school project illustrates the advantage of teamwork. Suppose a group of five students must prepare a presentation on climate change. One member handles research, another gathers multimedia resources, a third designs slides, a fourth writes the script, and the fifth rehearses delivery. Each step benefits from the expertise of the others, and at the end the presentation is richer, more polished, and more accurate than if one student tried to do everything alone. The same principle applies in the workplace: a software team that combines programmers, designers, and testers can develop a product that meets user needs more reliably than a lone developer working through trial and error.  

In conclusion, although working alone can offer focus and independence, the evidence and practical examples show that cooperation leads to more success in the majority of cases. The ability to ask for help, share ideas, divide responsibilities, and receive feedback are all powerful advantages that a group provides. Therefore, for most academic assignments, professional tasks, and everyday challenges, working with others is the more effective strategy.

Creating a homework club is one practical way to raise student achievement. In my view, such a club can make a real difference because it gives pupils the chance to work together, reduces stress, and leaves evenings open for personal life. The first advantage is academic: with teachers and peers available after class, learners can solve problems that otherwise keep them stuck. A child who is confused about a particular assignment can stay a little longer, ask questions, and receive guidance from someone who has just explained the concept. This immediate support often leads to higher scores and a stronger grasp of the material, and it also stops the fear of failing tests that many students feel.

Second, a homework club frees up time at home. Instead of trying to finish all the work alone late into the night, students can complete most of it in a supportive setting, leaving the rest for family, friends, or leisure activities. For many, the club feels like a place they would happily join, because it lets them relax after school, watch a film, or hang out without worrying that a pile of unfinished assignments will haunt them later.

Third, the club helps reduce fatigue. Knowing that help is nearby lowers anxiety about grades, allowing students to sleep longer and feel more refreshed for the next day. In a world where school demands a lot, the chance to recover mentally and physically is valuable.

Finally, the club fosters a sense of gratitude and confidence. When students realize they are not alone in their struggles, they develop perseverance and feel appreciated for the effort they make. Solving problems together often brings new techniques or insights that can be used in future tasks.

In conclusion, a homework club can improve grades, give students more leisure time, ease the mental load, and boost morale. These outcomes support the idea that schools should establish such clubs to help learners succeed both academically and personally.

I consider myself good at drawing, especially when I depict natural scenes such as the night sky dotted with stars, the calm moon, dense woodlands, and rolling oceans. Drawing, in my view, is a way to show how many different styles of art can be combined. There are countless kinds of artistic expression, and among them I most enjoy the ones that involve creating images on paper. While drawing, I can decide what to include and what to leave out. If something does not turn out the way I intended, I have the chance to erase or redraw it. Painting is another medium that I like because it lets me translate emotions directly onto the canvas – a splash of colour can reflect sadness, happiness, anger or frustration, depending on what I am feeling at that moment.

Art is one of the talents that brings me the most pleasure. I can turn a blank sheet into anything I imagine, and I have noticed that many collectors are willing to spend a great deal of money for original drawings or paintings. Some buyers do not care whether a piece costs a few hundred dollars or several million; they pay simply because they find the work beautiful. Although many people possess artistic abilities, some feel that their creations are not good enough and discard them. Yet they often overlook the fact that there will be individuals who appreciate the unique vision behind the work and are ready to pay for it. For others, the cost of materials is high, so they keep a piece for personal reasons or to show it to family members. They might sell it to a relative, but usually not for a huge sum, preferring the sentimental value over financial gain. Occasionally, when an artist makes a mistake and chooses not to fix it, the piece remains unchanged because they hope a wealthy collector might find it attractive later.

I believe it is worth trying to sell art because the potential income can be substantial. Creating works of art is not an easy job – patience is essential, especially when a slip-up forces you to start over. However, the same slip‑up can become a source of inspiration, allowing you to transform an error into a new, pleasing element. Moreover, art often involves turning something that looks unattractive into something attractive; what may seem ugly at first glance can be corrected and improved with skill.

Some people think that art is boring, but that is not true for someone who truly enjoys it. When I am passionate about painting, I forget about perfection and let my hand follow my impulse. I do not worry about whether the result looks messy because the act of creating makes me feel happy. At times, I lose control momentarily and simply let the brush move across the paper, and that spontaneity can produce a sense of satisfaction that outweighs any concern about the final appearance. I have experienced the same feeling when I allowed my body to work without overthinking; the outcome was surprisingly pleasing and added to my happiness.

Other creators become stressed when their finished piece does not match the image they had in mind. I have felt that stress too, worrying that my sketch does not look as good as I imagined. Nevertheless, patience is a crucial habit in this field. Art is challenging, but it becomes less intimidating the more you practice. At the moment I am proficient, yet I am still learning. Even when a piece proves difficult, maintaining patience and continuing to practice gradually makes the process easier and improves my abilities. Consistent work leads to better results and a greater appreciation of my craft.

In summary, art offers both personal satisfaction and commercial opportunity. By trying to sell their creations, artists can earn money and possibly turn a hobby into a viable career. The rewards are worth the effort, and the experience of creating something from an idea, correcting mistakes, and expressing emotions remains one of the most rewarding activities I know. Therefore, I encourage others who enjoy drawing and painting to consider sharing their work with the public, because the potential benefits outweigh the occasional frustration.

Why do people need to follow their own instincts and ideas?

In my view, individuals should rely on their own gut feelings and personal ideas when making choices. Trusting oneself forms the basis of any sound decision; without that confidence, neither others nor the person can stand behind the choice. When we believe in our own judgment, we are less likely to doubt the outcome.

Firstly, basing decisions on one’s own instincts encourages independence. Ideas that arise from inside are usually more authentic than those borrowed from others. Instead of waiting for someone else to suggest a solution or searching online for ready‑made answers, a person can tap into their own thoughts. This approach not only speeds up the thinking process but also protects against copying or plagiarism, making work feel original and personal.

Secondly, listening to inner cues helps solve problems quickly. If an unexpected situation occurs, waiting for external advice can waste time. By trusting one’s own instinct, a person can act immediately, which demonstrates self‑assurance. Such confidence reduces the need to constantly seek guidance from teachers, peers, or experts.

Moreover, self‑belief influences how others perceive us. For instance, imagine a student preparing to give a presentation. If the student doubts their ability, the teacher may also feel uncertain, which can affect the grade. When confidence is lacking, the learner may keep asking for reassurance, distracting from the task and harming performance. By contrast, a confident presenter tends to earn respect and higher marks.

In conclusion, making one’s own decisions starts with trusting oneself. Before seeking external help, people should first check their inner conviction. Without personal faith, no one else will be able to support the choice, and the value of the individual’s work diminishes. Therefore, cultivating self‑confidence is essential for both effective problem‑solving and gaining the trust of others.

I believe that many ideas we have about students’ attitudes toward work and future success are not always accurate. The students I have met tend to think that the most reliable source of truth is personal confidence combined with real achievement. In other words, they hold the view that feeling sure about one’s abilities and having concrete results in life are the keys to what really matters. I agree with this position to a large extent, especially when we think about the long‑term picture.

First, confidence is essential for learners. It is both the feeling that you are capable of doing something and the trust you place in yourself. When students are confident, they are more likely to take on challenges and keep trying after setbacks. This kind of self‑trust is not the same as arrogance; it is a realistic belief that one can improve with effort and practice. Confidence gives them the courage to ask questions, to practice speaking or writing, and to tackle new subjects. I have seen many students who, despite occasional doubts, maintain a steady belief in their own potential and therefore make steady progress.

Second, achievement should not be the only measure of a student’s worth. Many students view success as something that must be earned through hard work or special skill, and they often think that any accomplishment is automatically valuable. While achievements are certainly important, they are only one piece of a larger puzzle. Life also includes moments of rest, family time, and simple enjoyment. The true value of work, I think, lies in being able to pursue a better life while still finding pleasure in everyday activities. Working hard is necessary, but it must be balanced with the ability to pause, spend time with loved ones, and appreciate each hour and year.

When we talk about the future, we usually mean a period farther ahead in time or a greater extent of something. For students, planning ahead means considering the possibilities for a stable and satisfying career. A career is more than a single job; it is a series of related positions that often bring increasing responsibility. It usually requires specialized training and, in many cases, a higher level of education. A profession, on the other hand, is a particular field of work such as medicine or law, which demands specific knowledge and ethical standards. A trade is a hands‑on occupation that also needs special training, but may not require as much formal schooling as a profession. Understanding these differences helps students see that they have many options after school, not just a single path.

Another important factor is experience. Some people argue that students lack real work experience and therefore cannot be trusted with important tasks. Experience, however, is simply the knowledge or skill that comes from having been through a particular situation. It is not only about external exposure; it also involves a willingness to learn and adapt. I have met a friend who built a distinguished career in medicine. Her path illustrates how a clear professional identity can coexist with continuous personal growth. The students I know often bring a sincere, honest perspective to their learning. Sincerity means truly believing what you say and acting accordingly, which can be more valuable than a polished presentation.

In addition, praise and precaution play roles in the classroom. Giving genuine admiration for a student’s effort encourages them to keep trying. Precaution, such as careful planning or taking steps to avoid mistakes, helps reduce risks later on. For example, keeping important documents safe or double‑checking calculations are simple precautions that can prevent larger problems. Both praise and precaution are tools that help students develop a responsible attitude toward their work.

The importance of tolerance and compassion cannot be overlooked either. Tolerance means allowing others’ opinions or behaviors, even when they differ from our own. Compassion is the willingness to understand and help people who may be struggling. Students who work together with tolerance and show compassion create a healthier learning environment. These qualities also make the student’s perspective more respected; they are not dismissed simply because they lack professional experience. Rather, their sincerity earns them credibility.

Finally, respect is crucial. When people respect those who are still developing skills, they are less likely to become angry or dismissive. Respect acknowledges the effort and the intent behind actions, even when the results are not perfect. It also reminds us that security and confidence are personal traits; a student who feels secure in their abilities does not need to hide behind insecurity.

In conclusion, I think students should continue to build confidence and strive for achievements, but they must also keep the future in mind. Hard work should be balanced with moments of joy, family, and thoughtful planning. Knowing the difference between a job, a profession, a career, and a trade helps them see multiple possible paths. Experience, sincerity, praise, precaution, tolerance, compassion, and respect are all part of a well‑rounded approach to learning and future employment. By integrating these ideas, students can develop a solid foundation for a fulfilling life that goes beyond immediate tasks.

In recent years many schools have introduced the possibility of studying from home, letting students join lessons through a computer instead of being physically present in the classroom. Does this really help learners? My own experience suggests that it often does not. I know a person who participated in virtual classes and, rather than concentrating on her work, she used the flexibility to avoid her assignments. She would delay submissions, claim the material was too confusing, and spend hours on unrelated activities. In her case, remote attendance did not lead to any improvement in grades or understanding. Moreover, staying at home can weaken a student’s sense of belonging to a school community, which further reduces motivation to keep up with the curriculum.

First of all, studying from home makes it simple for students to put academic duties on the back burner. The environment lacks the usual classroom constraints, so a learner can finish a deadline later, pull up a game, or chat with friends without anyone noticing. Although some pupils manage their time responsibly, many exploit the freedom to postpone work that is due for weeks. For instance, I have observed classmates who submitted assignments weeks after the deadline, using the excuse that the material was too confusing. The ease of making up reasons for missed work encourages a habit of procrastination, and the homework pile grows larger. In addition, the online setting often prevents learners from raising doubts during the lesson because there is no immediate opportunity to ask a question on screen. This lack of real‑time clarification can make students feel even less accountable for completing the work on time.

Second, the absence of a teacher’s direct supervision reduces motivation to stay on task. When lessons are delivered through a screen, there is less immediate pressure to work, because the instructor cannot see the student’s workspace. This can make many learners feel that they can skip or delay a task without any penalty. For example, a student might claim they “didn’t understand the instructions” even though they actually watched the lecture. Without a physical presence reminding them of deadlines, they tend to spend the time they should be studying on social media, video games, or chatting with friends. In addition, the recorded format often leads pupils to watch the material only partially, thinking they can catch up later, but they never do. Consequently, the amount of genuine effort spent on coursework drops sharply.

Third, many students who join classes from home seem to learn very little. They often treat the online session as a break rather than a learning opportunity. While some might claim they are taking a rest, in practice they spend most of the time talking, playing games, or scrolling through social media. When assignments appear, they either copy from a classmate’s work or search for answers online. This behaviour means they are not internalising the subject matter; they are merely completing forms to avoid penalties. Some learners say they will study later, but they usually postpone everything until the deadline approaches, at which point they resort to shortcuts. As a result, even if they manage to pass an exam, the underlying knowledge remains shallow, leading to difficulties in later courses.

In conclusion, allowing students to attend school from home does not bring any clear advantage. The flexibility that online classes provide is often used to skip responsibilities, make excuses, and engage in activities unrelated to study. The lack of face‑to‑face oversight reduces the incentive to work hard, and many learners simply copy or search for answers instead of understanding the material. Overall, the pattern of procrastination, minimal effort, and social distraction makes remote attendance more harmful than helpful. For these reasons, I maintain that remote schooling offers no genuine benefit to the majority of students.

Some people claim that learning from home would not help students because it stops them from working together with classmates. They cite studies that suggest online‑only courses often lead to weaker projects, arguing that without in‑person discussions students miss out on the richer ideas a group can generate. For instance, a number of reports note that when students cannot hear diverse viewpoints, their final work tends to be less creative and impactful.

Nevertheless, remote schooling can provide advantages that are hard to ignore, especially comfort and security. Many pupils find it easier to focus when they can choose a personal workspace that suits their habits, rather than being forced to sit at a rigid classroom desk. A recent school survey showed that a sizable portion of students prefer virtual lessons simply because they feel more relaxed and can arrange themselves in the way that best supports their learning. This flexibility can reduce stress and improve concentration, leading to better overall performance.

Safety is another important factor. Over the past few years, more than a hundred school shootings have occurred across the country, showing how dangerous campuses can become. Additionally, gangs often infiltrate school grounds, offering children negative influences that can harm both their education and personal development. By attending classes from home, students are shielded from these physical threats and from environments where harmful peer pressure may be present.

Finally, parents benefit from the shift. When children study remotely, families no longer have to worry about their daily commute or the chance of encountering violence on the way to or from school. This reduces anxiety and allows parents to focus on supporting their children’s learning at home.

In short, while the lack of face‑to‑face teamwork is a drawback, the gains in personal comfort, protection from violence, and parental peace of mind support the view that allowing students to attend classes from home can be a beneficial option.

I do not agree with the suggestion that school hours be lengthened in order to save energy. In my view, such a policy would add considerable pressure to already busy students and would affect a large number of them.  

Many learners already hold part‑time jobs after classes, sometimes working as much as ten hours a week. If the school day were to start later, these students would have to spend even more time on campus, leaving them less room for paid work. A reduction in working hours would mean a drop in earnings, which is crucial for families that rely on the teenager’s contribution to buy groceries or pay for basic needs.  

Beyond earning money, students also shoulder important domestic duties. They often look after younger siblings, help tidy the house, wash dishes, prepare meals, and even give their parents a short break. These tasks make the balance between school and home life manageable. Cutting into that limited after‑school time would disrupt both the household routine and the student’s ability to support their family.  

For many young people, the few hours left after school are a chance to unwind and develop personal interests. Some play sports such as soccer, basketball, or tennis, while others prefer quiet activities like reading or taking a walk alone. These moments are essential for mental health and happiness. If teachers forced the school to end later, the extra two hours each day would be taken from these leisure pursuits, leaving students with a more rigid, exhausting schedule.  

Think of the mothers who, years ago, worked after school to put food on the table. Their effort is heroic, and their hard work has already enabled their children to attend school today. Extending the school day would interfere with the current situation where students can focus on studying because their parents have made such sacrifices.  

In short, while saving energy is important, the costs of longer school hours appear to outweigh the benefits. Keeping the present timetable respects the students’ need for rest, income, family support and personal time. Alternative energy‑saving measures should be explored instead of imposing extra hours on learners.

Many schools have begun to set up mentorship programmes that bring older pupils together with younger ones. The purpose is to give both groups a chance to support each other and to prepare for the responsibilities they will face as they grow older. I agree that these schemes are worthwhile because they create real opportunities for learning and collaboration.  

First, the older students benefit from the experience of guiding younger classmates. By being asked to explain rules, show how to solve a problem, or talk about personal mistakes, they reinforce their own understanding and develop a sense of duty. When a senior tells a junior how he avoided a similar error, both can reflect on what went wrong and how to improve next time. Moreover, senior learners sometimes encounter topics they are not confident about, such as new technology or slang, and younger students can offer fresh perspectives or help with language. In this way the relationship is two‑way: the older student practices responsibility and patience, while the younger gains confidence and a clearer view of future challenges.  

Second, the younger students receive valuable support. They have someone who has already walked the same path and can give practical advice about what to expect in school and later in life. A senior can answer questions about subjects they have mastered, explain why certain behaviours are risky, and assist when a junior struggles with a concept. Especially for pupils still acquiring English, an older peer can offer simpler explanations or demonstrate correct usage. When a younger learner faces a problem, a brief chat with a senior mentor can turn confusion into clarity, and the junior learns that asking for help is a normal part of learning.  

However, these programmes are not always smooth. Sometimes seniors are reluctant to spend time with juniors, and juniors may ignore the advice they receive. The result is a missed opportunity for both sides to grow. In my view, the problem lies in expecting older students to automatically act like adults. Just as children need guidance from adults, younger pupils need peers who listen and respect them. When senior mentors see their role as dictating rather than discussing, the junior can become defensive and tune out. Conversely, if younger students think the advice is boring or irrelevant, they may simply ignore it. Effective programmes should therefore focus on building mutual respect and making the exchange enjoyable.  

Mutual respect can be encouraged by letting senior mentors take part in short, interactive activities rather than long lectures. For example, a senior could spend a few minutes helping a junior practice English conversation, or join a group game where both share ideas. When the older student sees that the younger learner is genuinely interested, he is more likely to keep offering assistance. In turn, the junior learns that asking questions is a healthy habit and that older peers are willing to help.  

In conclusion, pairing older and younger students in school programmes offers benefits that go far beyond simple tutoring. It gives seniors a chance to practice responsibility, share their own mistakes, and reinforce their learning, while giving juniors the support and insight they need to avoid similar pitfalls. Even though occasional misunderstandings can arise, designing the activities with a clear focus on respectful collaboration can make the system work smoothly. In my opinion, schools should keep developing these schemes because they help both age groups understand each other better and prepare them for the responsibilities of adult life.

Online classes can be helpful for students who have many other commitments. How Technology Affects Everyday Life and Human Interaction  
I agree with the view that technology, although useful, can also harm people’s lives and their ability to interact with one another. Many critics say devices pull families apart or replace real conversations, and these concerns arise from observations of how technology changes daily habits.  

One major issue is becoming too attached to smartphones or video games. When people spend hours scrolling through apps or immersed in virtual worlds, they often value screen time over actual needs. In such moments, someone who could offer assistance might ignore a neighbour or a child because the phone feels more urgent. This behavior occurs across age groups and can diminish empathy and kindness in everyday encounters.  

Another problem is online shopping. Buying clothes or groceries from a screen provides convenience and a sense of independence, yet for some it turns into a compulsive habit. While a few enjoy the freedom of choosing items from home, others purchase far more than they need, wasting money and time. Relying on virtual transactions limits chances for social engagement that would normally happen in a physical store.  

Lastly, those who rarely communicate with others miss out on sources of motivation and inspiration. If a person avoids conversation, clubs, or collaborative activities, they may feel stuck and lack direction for personal growth. Over time this isolation can affect mental health and hinder future ambitions.  

In conclusion, it is important to strike a balance in how we use technology. Excessive reliance on devices harms both current well‑being and future prospects, and the evidence suggests that technology is not always the most beneficial creation for humanity.

Is it really true that the path to achievement is a sequence of setbacks? Winston Churchill, a wartime leader of Britain, once said that “true success is moving from one failure to another while still feeling enthusiastic.” I would argue that this view gives failure too much weight and underplays other important factors such as hard work, learning from mistakes, and the drive to stay motivated. While many of us certainly experience defeats along the way, I do not believe that success should be measured only by how often we encounter them.

First of all, almost every person will face at least one failure in life. In everyday life we hear stories of students who receive disappointing exam results, job‑seekers who miss several interviews, and relatives who let down family members through broken promises. These examples show that the experience of failing is ordinary rather than exceptional. Of course, there are rare cases where someone seems to glide through life without a major setback. My cousin, for instance, never let her parents down; she earned excellent grades, earned a scholarship, and now studies engineering at Virginia Tech. While she may be the exception rather than the rule, her story highlights that it is not impossible to achieve a goal without a long history of repeated defeats. In most situations, however, failure is a natural part of the learning process, and the key is how we react to it.

Next, reaching a dream usually requires effort that is repeated and never stops at a single try. If we allow a single setback to defeat us, we risk missing the opportunities that life keeps offering. When I first moved to the United States, I struggled to learn English and felt frustrated by my low scores in class. Instead of giving up, I created a schedule of extra study sessions, joined conversation clubs, and asked teachers for additional help. Over time, my language skills improved, and I eventually succeeded in university courses that once seemed impossible. This experience taught me that failure is not the end; it can be a sign that a different approach is needed. By staying open to new strategies and by seeing each missed opportunity as a chance to try again, we keep moving forward.

A third element that many overlook is enthusiasm. Without a genuine interest or excitement in the goal we pursue, motivation quickly fades, and we may settle for mediocre results or abandon our ambitions altogether. Enthusiasm fuels the willingness to get up after a fall, to persist through obstacles, and to look for alternative routes when one plan stalls. Those who lack this inner spark often accept whatever they receive without questioning whether they could have done better. In contrast, I have observed classmates who started as indifferent students but later discovered a passion for a subject, which transformed their performance. Their enthusiasm made it possible to turn a seemingly modest score into a top‑class achievement. Keeping the flame alive—whether through self‑praise, visualizing the end result, or reminding ourselves why we began in the first place—helps sustain effort across long periods of hardship.

Finally, personal history illustrates how enthusiasm and perseverance shape outcomes. When I was younger, I was praised for being the top student in my hometown school, earning high marks and the respect of teachers. The move to the United States changed that narrative; the language barrier forced me to start over, and I no longer held the same academic confidence. My drive to catch up in English became a source of renewed enthusiasm, not just a reaction to failure. I realized that even when external circumstances appear to set us back, an inner enthusiasm for improvement can turn those challenges into stepping stones. This inner energy, combined with the willingness to experiment with new study methods, ultimately allowed me to succeed in a different, perhaps more demanding, educational environment.

To sum up, I disagree with Churchill’s claim that success is defined merely by a string of failures and a constant spark of enthusiasm. While failures are a common feature of many journeys, they do not have to dominate the story. Success can also arise when a person confronts a setback, learns from it, and applies a new effort. Moreover, enthusiasm, though essential, is not the sole factor that determines victory; it must be paired with practical actions and a realistic mindset. My own experience moving to a new country, the example of a cousin who never disappointed her family, and countless observations of classmates who transformed ordinary grades into excellence all support the view that perseverance, adaptability, and a positive attitude together guide us toward our goals. Life is rarely easy, but by refusing to settle for defeat and by maintaining the motivation that keeps us looking forward, we can achieve the dreams we set for ourselves.

The skill I most rely on when dealing with texts is reading aloud. This habit has proved helpful in a number of ways. First, I find that hearing the words while I say them makes the material clearer and easier to grasp. It is as if the words settle into my mind more firmly, allowing me to recall them later. In addition, speaking the sentences lets me notice whether I pause too often or rush through difficult words. When I spot a stumbling point, I can repeat the line or look up the meaning, which improves my overall fluency.

Reading aloud also assists me in making sense of the narrative. By vocalising the events, I can picture what happens and organise the information in a sequence that is easier to remember. The combination of visual and auditory processing means I retain more details from the story. This is particularly noticeable when I try to explain the plot to someone else; I can give a clearer description because I have heard the words myself. By contrast, silent reading often leads me to forget parts of the text or lose track of the order of events.

Another advantage of reading aloud is its impact on my written work. When I have to compose an essay based on a book, I start by speaking the key ideas out loud. This externalises my thoughts and makes it simpler to decide what to include in the paper. I feel less anxious about the task because I already have a mental picture of the material, and I can check that my sentences follow the direction the author gave. Moreover, I can spot awkward phrasing or unclear transitions as I say them, which lets me edit before I write.

In short, I read out loud because it supports comprehension, helps me monitor my reading, reinforces memory of the content, and makes essay planning smoother. By hearing my own voice, I stay focused on the text, understand it better, and produce more accurate and organised writing.

Thinking before acting can make life more enjoyable and less stressful. Pausing to imagine possible outcomes helps us feel satisfied and avoid unnecessary problems. Preparing for each step of a task rather than rushing adds interest and reduces mistakes.  

Many people waste time on activities that do not help their future, such as skipping school lessons. If I miss a class, the teacher calls my parents and I face punishment. Missing lessons also harms my academic record, which later limits job opportunities. Employers may offer lower pay or fewer benefits to someone who never finished school.  

Acting impulsively often leads to bad results. For example, in my country I once skipped a lesson with a friend to play soccer, failed the test, my grades dropped, and my parents were warned. This showed that acting without reflection creates serious problems.  

My brother learned the same lesson. In ninth grade he ignored the SOL test because he preferred hanging out with friends. When he reached twelfth grade, he realized he needed to pass that exam to graduate and asked me not to repeat his mistake.  

Taking a moment to think before deciding is crucial. Ignoring this step can damage our goals and future prospects. By reflecting carefully, we increase our chances of success and can positively influence the world.

From my perspective, it is highly unlikely that a first impression can be erased completely. This is because humans tend to anchor their opinions on the initial view they receive, and that anchor persists even when new information follows.

I remember the first time I tried playing soccer. I was a complete beginner, stepping onto a pitch full of strangers from different places. The game went on, and my teammates began to comment on how naturally I moved the ball and how much they enjoyed watching me. Soon enough, every time people saw me, they would remark, “You play really well.” The praise stuck, and even after more than a year without meeting those players, the comment still surfaces in casual conversations.

Some argue that an impression—whether positive or negative—can be changed if one works hard enough. In principle, yes, but the effort needed is huge, and it takes a long time to overwrite the original memory. My experience shows that the first impression acts like a mental fingerprint that stays visible unless deliberately overwritten by consistent actions over many months or years. Therefore, I agree that while transformation is possible, it is not easy to achieve quickly.

Working together in class is clearly a worthwhile practice for students. There are several strong reasons why group work is better than studying alone. First, when several people contribute, the pool of ideas becomes richer and more varied. Every member can add something new, which often leads to a higher‑quality final product. In addition, students who feel unsure about a task can receive immediate help from peers. A teammate who already understands the material can explain it in simpler terms, allowing the struggling learner to catch up faster and gain confidence.

Second, group activities develop essential communication skills that are useful both inside and outside school. By talking, listening, and negotiating, students learn how to express their thoughts clearly and how to respond constructively to others. This practice improves written work as well, because feedback from group members helps spot mistakes and strengthens arguments. Good communication also builds a sense of belonging, creating friendships that might not otherwise form. When a teacher assigns a project and puts students into mixed groups, the chance to meet classmates they never talk to becomes a pleasant surprise, enriching the overall classroom atmosphere.

Third, working in teams gives a taste of real‑world collaboration, which is valuable for future jobs and personal relationships. In most workplaces, success depends on the ability to share responsibilities, support colleagues, and solve problems together. The same holds true for families, where cooperation and mutual assistance are daily necessities. Therefore, the habit of helping others and accepting help prepares students for life’s later challenges. Some students do worry about being distracted or copying answers, and teachers sometimes prefer solitary work to avoid cheating. Yet these concerns can be managed with clear guidelines and the use of individual contributions, while the long‑term advantages of teamwork remain far greater.

In sum, encouraging students to complete assignments in groups is a smart teaching choice. It fosters more creative ideas, speeds up learning, strengthens communication, and nurtures relationships that last beyond the classroom. By allowing classmates to support one another, teachers not only improve academic results but also equip learners with the cooperative skills they will need in future careers and family life. The occasional downside of distraction or copying is minor compared with the benefits of shared effort and mutual growth. I believe schools should continue to promote group work, because it genuinely helps students succeed now and prepares them for a successful life ahead.

Scientist Albert Einstein once wrote that “imagination outweighs knowledge.” I completely agree with his view. In my opinion, imagination brings happiness, assists other people, and can lead to a satisfying career. Let me explain why.

First, imagination contributes to personal happiness. When you imagine pleasant scenes, your mind fills with positive emotions. By creating these mental pictures, you boost your mood without needing any physical activity.

Second, imagination can be a useful tool in helping others. Picture a child crying in a shopping centre because her unusual outfit draws attention. Instead of ignoring her, you might ask her to think differently: “Imagine everyone looking at you because they admire the style you chose, as if you are walking through a grand palace.” By reshaping the situation in her mind, you help her feel accepted and less upset. Such brief mental reframes often ease anxiety and encourage a calmer response.

Finally, imagination plays a role in finding a good job. Parents sometimes warn that fantasies won’t pay the bills, but I believe that creative thinking is essential for career success. Consider someone who wants to become a home designer. Without imagination, the designs they produce could be dull or impractical, resulting in a dismissal from the firm. In contrast, a writer who can dream up countless scenes is more likely to produce many books and earn a substantial income. Thus, a vivid imagination can open doors to rewarding employment that may even surpass traditional professions.

In summary, I agree with Einstein’s statement. Imagination makes us happier, supports others, and helps us secure suitable work. I think it is one of the most valuable assets we possess.
