Generic_Name wants to own a car that represents his future, but he faces obstacles because his mindset is mostly negative. Many people never reach their targets for the same reason – a lack of optimism can shut down any effort before it even begins.  

A positive outlook is the cornerstone of achievement for three reasons. First, it fuels confidence. When someone thinks optimistically, he or she feels ready to take on any difficulty. For instance, Generic_Name usually looks for the good in everyday situations – at school, at work and in his personal projects. That confidence keeps him from being scared of upcoming tasks, and it helps him keep moving forward. A second example shows a friend who also embraces positivity, conquering each new challenge with the belief that effort will pay off, and she works steadily toward her own goals.

Second, a constructive attitude changes how we view obstacles. Instead of seeing problems as roadblocks, a positive thinker treats them as opportunities to grow. Generic_Name often tells himself that life includes challenges that must be faced if he wants to succeed, and he never quits when things get tough. Another illustration is his teammate at the office, who prepares for any possible hurdle and meets each one with a hopeful mindset. Because he anticipates difficulties, he is never caught off guard, and his readiness makes the process smoother.

Third, optimism builds self‑trust. When people feel secure about who they are and what they can do, they stay motivated and resist discouragement. Generic_Name, for example, already enjoys a solid job and a strong academic record because he believes in his own abilities. Another example is a classmate who, thanks to her confidence, has completed all her personal aims, built a family and secured a great career. Some might argue that positivity alone isn’t enough to guarantee success, but that view ignores the fact that confidence and perseverance are natural outcomes of a hopeful attitude. In other words, a positive mind inevitably produces a secure self and a refusal to give up.

In short, people need optimism, the ability to treat difficulties as challenges, and a sense of self‑security if they want to succeed. By cultivating these traits, they can overcome setbacks and reach their goals. If you want to achieve your own aspirations, start by reshaping your attitude. Adopt a hopeful perspective, face every problem as a chance to improve, and trust in your own strengths. That simple change can turn a dream into reality.

Do you think students would benefit from being able to attend class from home? I think that a few learners could gain from online schooling, but I still disagree that it would be the best solution for most. Going to school in person offers advantages that are hard to replace, such as sports practice, a lively classroom environment, and access to a variety of elective programmes.

One key advantage is the chance to engage in sport. Many pupils are passionate about activities like football, basketball, or athletics, and schools provide the facilities and time for them to train regularly. Playing sport keeps students active, reduces the risk of boredom, and offers a positive outlet that can steer them away from harmful behaviours. When I feel down, joining a team practice lifts my mood and lets me share my enthusiasm with classmates. In this way, physical education not only builds fitness but also creates a supportive community.

Another reason is the way school helps prevent monotony. When students sit in front of a screen all day, they can quickly become restless and disengaged. In a real classroom, teachers can use interactive techniques, lively discussions, and hands‑on activities that keep learners motivated. Moreover, being with peers allows students to ask questions, work together on assignments, and form friendships that help them both academically and socially. I recall how a classmate helped me when I struggled with a homework problem, something that would be harder to achieve over a video call alone. Physical attendance also opens doors to field trips, museum visits, and university tours, which broaden horizons and deepen knowledge of history and culture.

School also lets pupils choose electives and specialised courses that match their interests. Institutions across the country offer subjects ranging from cooking and music to health‑assistant training, electrician work, or police studies. These programmes give students a taste of possible future careers and teach practical skills such as budgeting, applying for scholarships, or understanding university requirements. At my school, we received guidance on selecting courses, building credit for university, and deciding which college to aim for, all within the school schedule.

That said, not every student can attend in person. Some must work after school, live far from the campus, or care for family members, leaving remote learning as the only feasible option. For these learners, online or video‑conferencing classes are essential to earn credits and stay on track toward graduation. While distance learning cannot replace the social and physical benefits of a campus, it does serve as a necessary safety net for those facing unavoidable obstacles.

In conclusion, although remote schooling can help particular students who lack transport, family responsibilities, or work commitments, the majority of learners profit more from being physically present at school. Sports, a dynamic learning atmosphere, and diverse elective offerings give students experiences that boost health, motivation, and future planning, making in‑person attendance the preferable choice for most.

I do not agree with the claim that imagination is more valuable than knowledge. In my opinion, knowledge turns ideas into real achievements. Imagination can be compared to dreaming; it allows us to see possibilities, but it does not automatically produce results. When a person has real knowledge, he or she can take concrete actions toward future goals. For instance, someone who studies business can launch a company, hire staff, and organise deliveries that satisfy real customers. All of these activities occur in the outside world, not merely in the mind.

Realising these goals usually means finishing school, attending college, and earning a degree, which takes time and dedication. The student must adopt a focused mindset and keep encouraging himself or herself to do better. Moreover, knowledgeable people can help friends or classmates. They can explain how to find a job, how to set up an own venture, and inspire others to pursue their own paths. The assistance they provide often triggers a chain reaction: the person helped may later help others, and the process continues.

In contrast, imagination is essentially a mental activity, useful when we are asleep or day‑dreaming, but it cannot replace the information required to meet everyday challenges. Thus, while imagination may spark ideas, knowledge is indispensable for turning those ideas into reality.

Many people argue that teenagers should not decide on a future job too soon because they are still young and have limited experience. However, I believe it is a good idea for students to start thinking about a career early. When a student knows what they want to do at a young age, they can use high school as a chance to explore that field in depth. Instead of trying several unrelated subjects and wasting time, they can concentrate on the subjects and activities that match their goal. This focused approach usually results in a richer knowledge base by the time they graduate. It also helps them avoid the confusion that many young adults feel when they have to choose a career after finishing school. Students who decide early are often more motivated and can set realistic short‑term targets, such as choosing the right electives or internships, which builds confidence and practical skills. Moreover, the experience they gain while still in school can be turned into a clearer plan for university or vocational training. Critics might say that an early decision limits flexibility, but if a student remains open to learning new information and adjusting their goals as needed, early commitment does not become a restriction. Ultimately, starting a career plan early gives students a head start and makes the transition to adulthood smoother.

I agree with the statement that a first impression cannot be fully altered, even when we deliberately try to change it. The instant we encounter someone, a quick mental picture of our demeanor, attitude and general behavior forms, and it tends to remain fixed.

A first impression includes many aspects—how we sit, the tone of our voice, the gestures we make while speaking, the way we eat, and the emotions we seem to convey. Because these details are absorbed so rapidly, they are hard to erase later. For instance, a person who has been adored since childhood will not suddenly become a completely different individual when he meets a new lover; the earlier image continues to dominate. Likewise, a newcomer who appears out of nowhere in a group cannot erase the picture that others already have of him; the original view stays strong.

Even if we assume that others will attempt to copy or adapt that image, the effort is usually unsuccessful. Picture someone trying to reproduce a dish that a friend once prepared. He may follow the same steps, but without knowing the exact ingredients or the secret seasoning the original chef used, the finished meal will never taste exactly the same. In the realm of personal impressions, the same logic applies: a second attempt lacks the precise cues that made the first impression unique, so it cannot replicate the original effect.

First impressions resemble a feeling or a mental photograph; they are stored in a part of memory that highlights vivid details and tends to overlook later corrections. They may be based on truth or on a fabricated story, yet once set they resist change. A student who pretended to have a perfect family to earn the respect of classmates succeeded in creating a positive initial view, but any later attempt to rewrite that impression would have little impact because the original belief is already lodged in people’s minds.

Consequently, it is sensible to accept that first impressions are nearly immutable. Instead of trying to remodel our own image or to mimic someone else’s, we should focus on being authentic and presenting qualities we can genuinely uphold. Attempts to alter or copy will often end in disappointment and wasted effort, because the reconstructed version can never match the original. Recognizing this reality encourages us to treat our first impressions with care and to avoid unnecessary frustration.

It is often claimed that first impressions are virtually impossible to alter. I agree with this view because they are formed almost instantly and tend to stick in our minds as a lasting feeling or image.

The speed at which a first impression appears makes it difficult to control. When someone behaves in an unexpected way, we instantly label that moment with an emotion—shame, confusion, or embarrassment—before we have time to think or adjust our response. In most cases the impression that is created during that brief encounter stays with us. Yet, there are times when a subsequent situation can soften that impression. It depends on how often the behavior occurs and whether we have had prior experience that changes our emotional reaction.

One common illustration is a student in a classroom who suddenly makes a loud sound. The noise draws everyone’s attention, and the student feels a strong sense of shame. He cannot quickly pretend everything is normal because the reaction was so obvious. The blush on his face and the uncomfortable feeling are immediate, and they are hard to erase. Even if the student later tries to laugh it off, the initial impression remains part of the memory.

If such an embarrassing event happens regularly, the feeling attached to it can shift. Frequent exposure to awkward moments can make us familiar with the sensation, and over time we learn to respond without panic. For example, when my family asks me embarrassing questions—about whether I have a girlfriend or what I did last weekend—I have grown accustomed to these queries. Instead of feeling mortified, I smile and give a straightforward answer because the situation feels normal to me. Likewise, in school, when a friend teases me about a crush, I reply calmly, knowing that these are everyday interactions. My past experiences have turned what once felt like a painful moment into a routine one.

The pattern holds true for many everyday embarrassments. When the event is a one‑off, the shame and confusion are intense and linger. When it repeats, our emotional reaction becomes less charged, allowing us to act naturally. This habituation reduces the impact of future awkward moments and helps prevent them from ruining the whole experience.

In the future, I hope that when I face a sudden embarrassing situation, my accumulated experience will kick in automatically. I want the initial shame to be brief and then fade, so that I can stay composed and avoid letting the moment become the worst one of my day. By treating occasional embarrassments as part of life rather than rare catastrophes, I believe I can lessen their effect and keep my focus on the present.

I agree with the school board’s decision to lengthen the school day by one and a half hours because the extra time would make a noticeable difference for both pupils and instructors. With a longer period in each class, students would have more room to complete activities that often run short of time, such as worksheets, note‑taking, or group projects. When a lesson ends before a task is finished, the remaining work can be rushed or left for homework, which sometimes leads to confusion or incomplete practice. Giving an additional hour and a half means that every class can finish its planned work without feeling rushed, so students can absorb the material more thoroughly.

Teachers would also gain from the extended schedule. They would have a larger window to explain new concepts, answer questions, and conduct demonstrations without worrying that they have to cram everything into a tight period. This extra time would reduce the pressure of constantly covering the syllabus at the last minute, allowing teachers to focus on clear explanations rather than hurried summaries. Moreover, it would give them a chance to plan and organize materials ahead of time, because they could finish preparation after a class instead of squeezing it into short breaks.

Having more minutes in a lesson also supports deeper learning, especially for subjects that students find difficult. When there is extra time, a teacher can revisit a topic, go through step‑by‑step examples, and give individual help to pupils who are struggling. This repetition and tailored assistance can boost confidence and lead to better results on tests and assignments. As a consequence, grades are likely to improve because students will have mastered the content rather than having to guess or rely on incomplete notes.

If the school day were not lengthened, teachers would face the same challenge of trying to fit a full lesson into a short period, and pupils would have to seek help later or fall behind. Students might need to ask the next class for clarification, or they could leave the work undone until after school, which can cause fatigue and lower motivation. The extra hour and a half would prevent these problems by providing sufficient space for every activity and ensuring that no one is forced to catch up after hours.

In sum, adding one and a half hours to the school day offers a clear advantage for learners, who can finish their work and receive more support, and for teachers, who can teach more effectively and have time to prepare. This change would benefit everyone involved and help the whole school community perform better academically.

Dear Principal,

As a student, I believe the school lunch program should offer both nutritious options and foods that students enjoy. A completely healthy menu is desirable, but it must also consider the tastes of the pupils; a middle ground would satisfy both health goals and student preferences.

First, many of us do not pay much attention to what we eat. We often pick fast‑food items or snacks that are convenient but not good for our bodies. In my own class, pizza is the most popular choice, and when it appears on the lunch tray it usually leads to stomachaches and a feeling of sluggishness. Aside from milk, there is little on the menu that provides the vitamins and minerals we need. With such a limited selection, it is difficult to encourage proper eating habits.

Second, healthier lunches can improve how we feel during the school day. When the meals contain fruits, vegetables, and protein, students tend to be more alert and less stressed. Good nutrition supports growth and can reduce the risk of illnesses later in life. Providing regular balanced meals also helps us develop habits that will benefit our bodies as we get older.

Third, taking favourite foods away completely can backfire. When the cafeteria stopped serving fried chicken on Fridays, many classmates simply skipped lunch because they missed the food they liked. This shows that a total ban on beloved items may cause lower participation and even wasted meals. In short, I suggest rotating the menu so that some days focus on wholesome meals and other days include the foods students prefer. A balanced approach would make students happier, more likely to eat, and their bodies would receive the nutrients they need.

I hope the administration will consider this plan to promote both satisfaction and health among the school community.

John Lubbock once said, “Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it.” This idea suggests that each person decides how they become, but the statement also raises concerns about how children can drift away from a confident self‑image when they feel uncertain. Their underlying traits can dominate their behavior, and I’m not convinced that this always means they gain control beyond anyone’s reach.

First, much of our self‑image is shaped by external forces. As a teenager, I found myself altering my habits simply because I wasn’t pleased with the way I was seen by peers. The opinions of others can trigger insecurity, prompting us to adopt new habits or interests in an attempt to feel better. These changes often come from sources that are not entirely ours to govern: the internet, social media, rap lyrics, and countless other cultural currents constantly whisper new standards of what is cool or acceptable. Because these influences are so pervasive, they can guide our choices in ways we barely notice, making it seem as if we are being steered without consent.

Second, this points to a broader reality: society provides a huge menu of ideas, and each person picks a few to follow. For example, when I moved to Virginia, I felt the pressure to conform to the local “normal” way of behaving. People in California, artists, musicians, and even popular YouTubers all wield influence over audiences worldwide, earning money by directing attention to particular lifestyles. Kids, like adults, are exposed to these voices, and sometimes they end up mimicking what they hear, whether it’s a catchy rap line or a trending fashion trend. The result is a mix of personal agency and external pressure.

Nevertheless, we still have the power to decide which influences we accept. Not every online trend or celebrity narrative will align with our values, and we can actively reject or reshape them. By consciously choosing positive role models and limiting exposure to harmful content, we can keep the dominant forces from dictating our character entirely. In this sense, Lubbock’s claim remains valid: we are the ones who ultimately give shape to ourselves, even though many surrounding forces attempt to pull us in different directions.

Finally, acknowledging the reality of outside pressures does not diminish our ability to act. The world presents new challenges every year—political upheavals, environmental concerns, and health threats—that can cause fear and anxiety. Yet by staying aware of the ideas that inspire us, we can turn uncertainty into motivation rather than paralysis. When we take control of the influences that surround us, we move forward rather than getting stuck.

Do you think students would benefit from learning at home through an internet connection? Many argue that online classes give pupils more time for assignments and make studying easier. Others say that staying away from the school building makes it simpler to focus. However, I maintain that such a setup is actually harder for most learners because there is no teacher nearby to clarify confusing points. Without face‑to‑face guidance, students often end up missing key ideas and not really learning anything. For me, attending school is the better choice because it offers direct help from instructors, a chance to meet classmates, and the safety of a familiar environment.

Some learners prefer to work on their own, while many still need the assistance of teachers. My sister, for instance, stays after school to ask teachers for clarification whenever she is stuck. She tells me that they explain topics step‑by‑step and give her the confidence to tackle assignments. Moreover, she values the personal relationship she builds with her teachers; they motivate her and point out where she can improve. When she fails a test, she revisits the material with the teacher, which leads to a clearer understanding and better scores. These after‑school meetings show that teachers are willing to go beyond the regular timetable to help their students succeed.

Beyond academic support, school provides social experiences that are hard to replicate at home. Some of my peers, like my brother, enjoy playing sports during breaks because it allows them to chat with friends and feel part of a community. He finds school lively and secure; the campus becomes a place where he can meet new people and share interests. That sense of belonging is important for mental well‑being and for developing confidence. In addition, schools host clubs, music sessions and other activities that keep learners engaged and prevent boredom. Such non‑academic pursuits can actually reinforce the material taught in class, because students see how knowledge connects to real life.

Critics claim that online learning is suitable for those who like working alone and do not need a lively atmosphere. They argue that the house environment eliminates distractions and lets students concentrate. While quiet surroundings can be helpful for some tasks, many students also need occasional social interaction and motivation from peers. Moreover, teachers are often eager to organize study groups or extra sessions that create a supportive network, something that virtual platforms cannot always provide. Therefore, the benefits of having a structured school setting outweigh the convenience of staying at home.

In conclusion, attending school offers direct teacher guidance, opportunities to form friendships, and a variety of activities that enrich learning. Online classes may appear flexible, but they remove the personal touch that many learners depend on. The presence of caring teachers who review material after class, the chance to play sports or join clubs, and the general sense of safety all contribute to a more effective education. For these reasons, I believe students should keep coming to school rather than rely solely on remote instruction. A solid academic foundation, built at school, paves the way for future success in college and work.

People often face situations that have serious consequences for themselves and for others. When they rely only on personal instinct or vague ideas, they may miss key information that experts and authorities can provide. This is why consulting knowledgeable figures is usually the safest way to deal with matters that affect health, safety, and the community.

Legal rules illustrate how external guidance protects everyone. For example, the use of illegal drugs is prohibited in most regions, and obtaining a drug requires a special permit and meeting an age requirement. Alcohol, while legal, can only be bought after a person reaches a certain age, typically 21. Carrying a firearm follows a similar pattern: a licence must be issued and the buyer must be older than a minimum age. Driving is another area where regulation matters. To operate a vehicle, a licence is required, and applicants must pass a test at around 16. Even after getting a licence, new drivers are usually not allowed to drive alone; a more experienced adult must sit beside them to ensure they gain proper experience.

Work also shows why external rules are useful. Most jobs come with a set timetable that tells employees when to arrive and when to leave. Following this schedule helps keep the workplace running smoothly. If an accountant decided to ignore the morning shift and appeared only in the afternoon, the company could suffer because financial records would be delayed or inaccurate. In addition, each position has defined duties that match an employee’s abilities. Deviating from those responsibilities can lead to dismissal, as employers expect people to complete tasks within agreed limits.

Society places limits on what individuals can do in public spaces. Even if someone feels a strong urge to destroy a library or shout at strangers, such actions are not permitted because they could cause harm or loss. Trespassing on private property to take a flower is another example; the owner’s rights must be respected. These restrictions remind us that personal freedom does not mean the right to act without regard for laws or social norms.

In short, leaving people to decide everything on their own can be risky. It is not that individuals should have no choices; rather, they need proper direction from experts and governing bodies, especially when they are young and still forming their sense of right and wrong. Guidance helps balance personal liberty with the broader needs of health, safety, and order.

Most schools now provide a remote‑learning option, letting pupils join classes from their own homes through the internet or video‑conferencing tools. In my view, this flexibility can make a real difference for a number of students, because it gives them a chance to balance schoolwork with other responsibilities that might otherwise conflict with a fixed timetable.

Take, for instance, a student who works after school. Many high‑schoolers hold part‑time jobs that run from early evening to late night. With school starting at 7:30 am, these young workers often have to rise before sunrise and head straight to class while still exhausted. I have seen a friend whose job keeps him busy until 11 pm; after that he must be up by 5 am the next morning to attend the first lesson. The combination of long shifts and too little sleep leaves him struggling to stay awake during the early period, which in turn hurts his concentration and his homework completion. Because they lack time to rest and study, his grades suffer. If he could attend some lessons online, he could keep his job schedule, get more sleep, and still finish the coursework he needs, which would likely improve his overall performance.

A second group that would benefit is teenage mothers. Pregnancy often forces young girls to confront strong social pressure and personal doubts about returning to school. Some feel judged for having a baby at such a young age and worry that teachers or classmates will look down on them. In addition, after the baby is born they need to devote a lot of time to feeding, changing and comforting, leaving little room for regular classes. When they try to stay in the ordinary school system they frequently drop out, believing there is no practical way to manage both motherhood and studies. A distance‑learning program would let these students study from home, avoiding the need to sit in crowded hallways and giving them the ability to take care of their child while still keeping up with lessons. This can help them finish the required credits and graduate, opening the door to future opportunities they otherwise might miss.

In short, allowing students to join classes online or by video call is a sensible move. It helps those who must work night shifts to keep both employment and education, improves their chances of getting enough rest and doing well academically, and provides a lifeline for pregnant teens who face stigma and heavy caregiving duties. By offering this option, schools can support a wider range of students, enabling them to complete high‑school studies even when their lives are unusually busy. The flexibility of remote learning, therefore, is a valuable addition that can boost graduation rates and give many pupils a fairer shot at a better future.

I believe the headteacher should allow students to bring their mobile phones to school, but only during break periods and other times when classes are not in session. Phones can stay turned off during lessons, and if a student needs to make a call for an emergency or to inform a parent that school has ended at 3:50 p.m., they will be able to do so. Moreover, many youngsters today feel it is important to have a phone with them, not only for fun but also to stay in touch with family. Some students do use the devices to chat with friends during lessons, which can distract them and cause teachers to give detention. However, if the rule is clear – phones must be silent and off while a teacher is teaching – most pupils are likely to follow it. The risk of misuse can be reduced by reminding students of the consequences, and a few warnings will usually be enough to keep them on track. In my opinion, giving students the opportunity to carry their phones for emergencies and after school helps both families and pupils, while a strict “no‑phone” rule during class time protects the learning environment. Therefore, I support the principal’s proposal to let students bring phones to school, provided they are used only when it is appropriate.

I agree that staying true to yourself can be difficult at times, yet it also brings important benefits. In today’s society many people avoid being alone, but some still cherish the chance to be themselves. When you allow yourself to follow your own path, you often find more energy to work because there is nothing pulling you in different directions. It is easy to become bored and waste time, so instead of letting that happen, I push myself to study and tackle tasks with effort. At the same time, life cannot be a constant grind; we need moments of fun. Going out with friends gives a break from work, preventing burnout and keeping experiences balanced. Trying to be yourself does not guarantee that you will accomplish great things, but it does give you a chance to do activities that make you happy for the rest of your life. Feeling odd about who you are is normal at first, but becoming stronger helps you handle those moments.

First, I have found that allowing myself to be independent encourages me to generate my own ideas and helps me judge what is good or bad for me. By relying on my own thoughts rather than simply copying others, I become more resilient. When I first moved to America alone, I felt very lonely and missed my family’s presence. The language barrier made everything confusing, and I initially thought I would never enjoy being on my own again. However, that experience showed me how valuable it can be to push through the discomfort, and later I realized that the struggle was part of the growth.

After a couple of years I decided to take control of my choices without constantly looking at what others were doing. I stopped comparing myself to friends or family, which lifted a heavy burden off my shoulders. The feeling of being left out faded, and I learned to stay calm by taking deep breaths. Now I no longer worry about whether I fit in because I have become accustomed to my own way of living; in fact, this habit has made me a bit more self‑reliant.

Finally, I now manage most responsibilities on my own, and that independence has set me apart from many of my peers. During the last year, my family urged me to learn how to handle things without their help before turning eighteen. I was nervous because I felt incapable of doing anything without them, but I chose to practice being self‑sufficient. By caring for my daily tasks, planning my future career, and solving problems by myself, I have turned what once seemed impossible into a source of confidence. I used to think I could never do anything on my own, but after learning to stay true to myself I have become truly independent.

Ralph Emerson’s famous line, “To be yourself in a world that constantly tries to make you something else is the greatest accomplishment,” overlooks the real challenge most people face. Simply staying true to one’s own identity is not enough; true success comes from actively shaping the environment around us rather than allowing society to dictate our choices.

First, being independent means refusing to surrender decision‑making power to outside forces. When we let others decide what we should study, what career we should pursue, or how we should spend our free time, we quickly lose a sense of direction. Without personal choices, it is easy to feel adrift, to grow tired of routines that do not reflect our genuine interests, and to end up living a life that feels imposed rather than chosen. Making our own decisions helps us define what matters to us, giving us a clear path forward and protecting us from the fatigue that results when we passively accept the expectations of the outside world.

Second, accomplishing great things requires doing what we love. If we follow a path dictated by others, even a promising career can become a burden once the initial excitement fades. By contrast, when we align our daily work with our passions—whether it is a sport, a creative activity, or a professional field that excites us—we stay motivated for the long haul. Passion turns effort into enjoyment; we are less likely to quit or feel burned out because the task feels like a responsibility rather than a chore. This internal drive fuels sustained progress and makes the journey toward our goals feel rewarding rather than obligatory.

Third, only we can accurately gauge our own strengths, values, and desires. While friends, family, and cultural norms provide valuable perspectives, they cannot fully understand the nuances of our personalities and ambitions. Allowing them to steer our life choices risks overlooking crucial information about ourselves, leading to misguided career decisions and unfulfilled aspirations. Taking control of our own direction ensures that we pursue the right opportunities, set realistic objectives, and make adjustments as we learn more about who we are.

In conclusion, letting the world decide our fate brings dissatisfaction and regret. The path to genuine accomplishment lies in asserting personal agency, shaping the conditions in which we operate, and following our passions. By continuously making our own choices and staying true to what we enjoy, we create a life that is both purposeful and enjoyable, rather than a passive existence shaped by external pressures. Embracing this active stance is the real key to achieving the greatest triumphs in life.

A positive attitude is essential for success in life. While it is clear that individuals who approach each day with optimism tend to make valuable contributions to society, the reality is that most people still fall short of this ideal. They often display a negative outlook, which hampers their personal growth and the welfare of those around them. Changing such attitudes is necessary because a constructive mindset improves family life, enhances workplace performance, and helps lift the circumstances of others.  

When people keep a hopeful attitude, their relationships at home become stronger. They listen more patiently to children, cooperate with partners, and handle household challenges without unnecessary friction. This sense of calm spreads to the wider community, fostering cooperation and reducing tension. For instance, many families experience stress when members lack patience with one another. If everyone cultivated a more tolerant attitude, everyday disputes would decrease and the overall quality of life in society would rise. Moreover, even when individuals realize that their current behavior is damaging, they often choose to adapt because they understand that a better outlook leads to healthier personal and social outcomes.  

In the workplace, a good attitude proves equally important. Employees who greet coworkers with courtesy, address customers politely, and tackle problems with a smile tend to collaborate more smoothly. They build trust and encourage teamwork, which makes projects run more efficiently. By contrast, workers who respond irritably to queries can quickly turn a routine interaction into a conflict. A single negative remark may cause the customer to feel disrespected, and that negativity can ripple back to the employee, creating a hostile work environment. Employers therefore benefit when staff maintain patience not only with clients but also with each other; it shows respect for every person involved and sustains a productive atmosphere. Even when faced with a customer who is rude, a calm and courteous response can prevent the situation from deteriorating, illustrating how a controlled demeanor serves the entire organization.  

A positive attitude also has a ripple effect beyond the immediate environment. Someone who thinks optimistically can influence friends, classmates, and coworkers to reconsider their own choices. In schools, teachers who model respectful and encouraging behavior help students develop healthier attitudes. When pupils feel supported, they are more likely to treat their peers and teachers in the same way. This shift prepares them for adult life, where a balanced mindset can lead to sound decisions in work, personal finances, and community involvement. As graduates enter the workforce, those who keep a constructive outlook often secure better positions, serve customers with confidence, and provide reliable support to their families. Over time, such individuals contribute to a society that values cooperation and well‑being.  

In summary, adopting a positive attitude can dramatically improve relationships with family, increase effectiveness at work, and uplift the lives of others. People who practice respect, patience, and encouragement tend to enjoy stable employment and harmonious interactions. By choosing to change from a negative stance to a hopeful one, individuals not only enrich their own futures but also help create a healthier, more supportive community. The habit of maintaining optimism therefore remains a fundamental key to personal and collective success.

Modern technology has reshaped the way we handle everyday tasks. It is now possible to buy groceries, download e‑books, and play video games without ever speaking to another person. While these conveniences save time, they also shrink the opportunities for direct human contact, and that reduction carries a range of negative consequences for both personal wellbeing and social cohesion.

One clear impact is felt in schools. Teachers increasingly deliver lessons through screens, but the digital medium often fails to create the personal bond that a classroom setting can foster. A student may watch a recorded lecture or attend a virtual class without receiving the immediate clarification that a live teacher can offer. I recall growing up in a country where there was little digital infrastructure. My teachers would write assignments on the board, explain each step, and repeat explanations whenever a pupil seemed confused. That process built a solid connection between learner and educator. Today, many students sit in cafeterias while their classmates stare at smartphones, exchanging fewer words about their day. The loss of those brief, face‑to‑face conversations mirrors the broader decline of human interaction that technology encourages.

Technology also encourages people to stay indoors and disengage from the world outside. When a high‑definition TV or a game console can keep us entertained, the motivation to go outside diminishes. Some individuals even ignore real‑life crises happening beyond their windows, treating headlines of suffering as distant background noise. This indifference is partly because constant digital stimulation dulls our emotional responsiveness. The fear of missing an update, a favorite sports match, or a social media notification can make us numb to the suffering of others. As a result, empathy can weaken and personal resilience may erode.

Another drawback is the way technology fuels laziness. In the past, if I needed a reference book, I would walk to the library, browse the shelves, and physically engage with the material. Now, a few clicks on a laptop can deliver the same content, allowing me to lounge on the couch. The same pattern appears when eating: previously, a family or group would venture to a restaurant, share plates, and talk about their experiences. Today, many people simply order meals through an app, eat alone, and scroll through their phones. The act of gathering around a table, hearing each other’s voices, and building memories has been replaced by silent individual consumption.

At the workplace, technology’s benefits are undeniable, yet its distractions can be costly. Employees are bombarded with notifications, and if a favorite football team is playing, the temptation to check the score can be overwhelming. In such moments, people pull out their phones, watch highlights, and lose focus on their responsibilities. The resulting loss of concentration can lead to missed deadlines, poor performance, and, in extreme cases, job loss. Without these digital interruptions, many of those professional setbacks might have been avoided.

Moreover, reliance on devices while driving increases safety risks. Texting, scrolling through social feeds, or taking video calls behind the wheel diverts attention from the road. A single missed turn can cause a collision, and the driver becomes responsible for the injury or death of others. These accidents not only destroy lives but also generate legal and financial burdens for the involved parties. The speed and ease with which information travels can never compensate for the loss of human life.

Finally, technology has contributed to broader geopolitical threats. The same tools that bring convenience also enable the development and deployment of powerful weapons, including nuclear arsenals. As nations invest in advanced military systems, the probability of large‑scale conflicts rises, endangering global stability. The disconnect created by overreliance on screens can blind us to the moral responsibilities that underlie such investments.

In sum, technology, despite its many conveniences, has produced several harmful side effects. It weakens face‑to‑face communication, diminishes emotional engagement, encourages sedentary habits, creates workplace distractions, raises safety hazards, and fuels dangerous military developments. Without technology, we would be forced to rely on more primitive methods, but the cost of those methods—caving into our own isolation—would be a stronger, more socially connected humanity. The evidence suggests that over dependence on digital devices makes us less human, more passive, and ultimately less capable of thriving in the real world.

I agree with Albert Einstein that imagination outweighs knowledge. While knowledge supplies facts, imagination opens the mind to possibilities that facts alone cannot reveal. It acts as a bridge that transports us from the familiar realm of information to new, uncharted ideas. However, the mental pictures we create sometimes stretch beyond what our brain can actually manage, leaving us confused or unsettled.

There are moments when knowledge proves more useful. When a problem appears difficult, a mature mind tends to draw on past experience. For instance, a student stuck on a tough math question often recalls similar exercises and applies tried‑and‑tested strategies. Likewise, reading a book can improve vocabulary and comprehension directly, giving the reader concrete tools that imagination cannot replace on its own.

Nevertheless, imagination and knowledge frequently work together. Think about building a new piece of furniture. At first, the mind wanders, generating several design concepts. Then existing knowledge about materials, measurements, and tools decides which idea can actually be realized. The two complement each other: imagination supplies the vision, and knowledge supplies the practical blueprint.

Both qualities can also bring drawbacks. An overly vivid imagination may cause a person to feel helpless, especially when one imagines that happiness is out of reach. An unrestrained imagination can lead to unfair play among friends, as a child might devise a game that treats peers unequally and consequently lose companions. Knowledge, meanwhile, can fuel bragging, creating social distance; a top‑scoring student who flaunts a friend’s low grade may find that friendship damaged.

Consider a sixteen‑year‑old seeking a job. He is not the most academically gifted and carries a few poor grades. His chance of landing a decent position largely depends on how much he knows about the labor market and interview techniques. If he does not study hard, students with stronger knowledge will out‑compete him, and he may remain unemployed. In a desperate situation he could ask friends for food, only to discover later that repaying those debts could push him toward homelessness.

Children illustrate imagination at its peak. At night they often see monsters hiding in closets, demanding a parent’s check. Adults reassure them that there are no monsters, but the child still hears odd noises and calls out for help. Eventually the child leaves the room and realizes the sound was simply a parent moving furniture. The episode shows how imagination can turn ordinary sounds into frightening tales, while knowledge—understanding that parents are still awake—helps calm the fear.

In short, imagination fuels creativity and pushes us beyond the limits of what we already know, but knowledge provides the necessary grounding that makes ideas feasible. Both are essential, and a balanced use of each leads to richer learning experiences and more harmonious social interactions.

Getting things done is the key to moving ahead in life. When we finish the work that is given to us, we clear the path for the next challenge. Without completing each assignment, progress stalls and future opportunities become harder to reach.

Consider people who hold jobs. Whether they work night shifts or daytime schedules, their main purpose is to finish the tasks assigned to them. They achieve this by breaking the work into clear steps and following a logical order. If a worker jumps straight into a project without planning, confusion quickly arises. For instance, imagine someone named Sam who has a large design project. He begins by outlining a sequence of actions, listing the supplies he will need and deciding which parts to finish first. As he proceeds, he discovers minor missing items, gathers them, and then keeps working according to his plan. By consistently applying this systematic approach, Sam can see his project through to completion.

We all face moments when something must be finished before we can move on. Skipping the work or failing to organize it leads to a buildup of undone tasks, which can turn into a heavy burden later. This is why setting a clear plan is essential. When we know exactly what we need to do, the process becomes manageable and we avoid last‑minute scrambling.

Students illustrate the same principle. A typical student strives to complete classwork promptly so that evenings can be free for leisure or study. By paying close attention during lessons, verifying the answers on the spot, and submitting assignments correctly, they avoid the need to redo work at home. This habit not only protects their free time but also boosts grades, showing that early completion pays off.

In many industries, the rhythm of production depends on a steady flow of completed work. Think of an automobile assembly line. Each worker is responsible for a specific operation—welding a panel, installing a dashboard, wiring an engine. If any step is delayed, the whole line slows down and the finished cars may miss their delivery dates. The line only keeps moving when every employee finishes his or her part on schedule. This illustrates how deadlines and careful execution keep the larger system running smoothly.

Leaders also rely on a disciplined approach to achieve success. CEOs, for example, spend considerable time mapping out goals and allocating resources. They decide what products a store will stock, which marketing campaigns will launch, and how to inspire their teams. By laying out a clear roadmap, they ensure that the organization moves toward its objectives without unnecessary detours. When leaders and their teams follow a well‑thought‑out plan, the business often reaches its targets more efficiently.

The underlying lesson is simple: consistent effort and thoughtful planning unlock better results. Whether it’s a manual job, academic work, or a corporate strategy, the pattern remains the same. If we neglect the current assignment, it will interfere with the tasks we intend to tackle next. Conversely, when we devote attention and energy to each step, we build momentum that carries us forward.

In short, dedicating ourselves to the work we receive today paves the way for future achievements. By treating each task with purpose, mapping out the required actions, and persisting until completion, we set ourselves up for success across all areas of life. The habit of finishing what we start is a reliable pathway to unlocking more opportunities and reaching our goals.

Prime Minister Winston Churchill said, “Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm.” This is a great idea. Although some people might argue that if you keep going from failure to failure it means you cannot do it because you are not a genius, I disagree. In my opinion, if you don’t lose your enthusiasm, you will be successful.

The best example is AiDiSheng’s development of the light blob. He faced thousands of failures but never gave up; he never lost enthusiasm. After many more failures, he finally created the first light blob in human life. It shows that if you don’t lose enthusiasm for something you focus on, you will do it perfectly, as you wished.

My other reason is to be audacious and keep trying. When you are experiencing failure after failure, your friends might say to stop because they think you will not succeed. They are just giving you a suggestion.

If you stop, you will lose enthusiasm for something that attracts you simply because they said you will not succeed. Trust yourself, keep trying, and don’t lose your enthusiasm.

In my opinion, enthusiasm is not easy to have. The only way to have it is through someone or something that attracts me. I would like to focus on having enthusiasm like when I play video games for a whole day. I cannot study for a whole day because it is tough. What if I had enthusiasm for studying? Then I would be successful too.

Fail is not dreadful; the awful thing is losing enthusiasm, which can become incurable. Believing yourself, even with many failures, and continuing to try will lead to success.

Winston Churchill famously said that “success is moving from one failure to another without losing enthusiasm,” and I think his view captures a key truth. Some critics argue that repeatedly failing shows a lack of talent or that you are simply not cut out for a certain task. I disagree. I believe that if you keep your excitement alive, even while you stumble, you are more likely to reach the outcome you desire.

A clear illustration of this idea comes from the story of AiDiSheng, who worked for years to create the first “light blob” in human history. He faced countless setbacks, adjusting his designs and trying new approaches each time. Instead of giving up, he stayed driven, never allowing his passion to wane. Eventually his persistence paid off and he achieved a breakthrough that had once seemed impossible. This tells me that when you stay enthusiastic about a goal and keep working on it, you will gradually improve and eventually master it.

Another reason for staying motivated is to be courageous. As you encounter failure after failure, friends or acquaintances might suggest that you stop, warning you that the project is hopeless. If you heed their advice and quit, you lose the very drive that keeps you interested. It is vital to believe in yourself, to keep pushing forward despite the doubts. Trusting your own judgment prevents enthusiasm from fading away.

I also recognize that enthusiasm does not appear automatically. It usually needs a spark—something that captures your attention. For example, playing video games can keep me absorbed for an entire day, while studying often feels exhausting. If I could generate the same excitement for my schoolwork that I feel for games, I would probably succeed more quickly. The lesson is clear: once you find a source of genuine interest, you can harness it to overcome obstacles.

Finally, it is important to remember that failure itself is not terrible; it is the loss of enthusiasm that truly hinders progress. Even after many mistakes, believing in your ability and continuing to try usually leads to success. By holding onto enthusiasm, you turn setbacks into stepping stones on the path to achievement.

Distance learning is becoming a popular alternative in many schools, allowing students to attend lessons from their own homes through online platforms or video‑conferencing. In my view, this approach does not benefit learners, and I will explain why.

First, the home environment is often filled with distractions that make it hard for students to stay focused. Without a teacher physically in the room, learners can easily drift off into unrelated activities—checking phones, browsing the internet, or even doing chores. This lack of supervision means they may not engage fully with the material, and as a result they absorb far less information than they would in a classroom setting where the teacher can prompt them back on track.

Second, online settings increase the temptation to cheat. When no one is watching, students might copy answers from classmates, look up solutions on the web, or even ask a family member to complete assignments for them. They may think that a quick internet search can replace true understanding, and this habit often leads to superficial learning. Moreover, the feedback loop is slower: if a pupil does not grasp a concept, they cannot ask the teacher right away for clarification, and misunderstandings can pile up until exam time, causing poor performance despite passing the course.

Third, mental‑health and social support are weaker in remote education. A bad day can cloud a student’s attention, and in school a teacher, coach, or counselor can step in and offer encouragement or advice. At home, such support is usually limited to family members who may not have the time or expertise to address school‑related issues. Students dealing with personal or family problems may feel more isolated, which can worsen their mood and reduce their willingness to participate. Over time this isolation can damage self‑esteem and limit their ability to form meaningful relationships.

Fourth, live video‑conferencing can be less effective than face‑to‑face teaching. Technical problems, spotty internet connections, or a simple lack of enthusiasm can make the lecture hard to follow. Even when a lesson is broadcast, students often feel reluctant to replay it because they do not see the value in doing so. In contrast, a classroom teacher can answer questions instantly, provide extra examples, and ensure that every learner comprehends the topic before moving on.

Fifth, extracurricular activities suffer. High‑school athletes, musicians, or artists need regular practice, team meetings, and competition to develop skills and build a resume. If classes are held online, they miss out on those routine interactions and may fail to qualify for scholarships or future opportunities. The absence of these real‑world experiences narrows their options and prevents them from discovering interests that could shape their career choices.

Lastly, career counseling becomes scarce. Many students rely on personal conversations with school counselors to explore possible professions, plan university applications, or set long‑term goals. Online learning often leaves these meetings as brief virtual chats that lack the depth needed for thorough guidance. Without regular face‑to‑face contact, students might not receive the individualized support that helps them make informed decisions about their future.

Overall, remote learning deprives students of crucial elements that foster academic success: direct supervision, quick help, peer interaction, emotional support, and opportunities to develop talents outside the core curriculum. While flexibility is attractive, the drawbacks outweigh the advantages. I therefore argue that schools should limit or avoid distance‑learning options and keep traditional classroom attendance for most subjects, especially during the high‑school years when these formative experiences are most vital.

Many people lack experience with basketball, but there are a few practical suggestions that can help anyone get started or improve their performance. The first consideration is the playing environment. While some games are held indoors and others take place outside, I tend to favor outdoor courts, especially during the warm months of spring and summer. The temperature should be mild—neither uncomfortably hot nor excessively cold—so that players can concentrate without worrying about health risks. It is also wise to avoid days with extreme weather, such as very high heat or strong cold, and to stay away from days when the wind is gusty. Wind can make the ball difficult to control and affect the overall flow of the game. Good times to play are daylight hours because visibility is high and players can see the ball, the hoop, and the court markings clearly. Nighttime, by contrast, can make it hard to spot the lines and the rim, increasing the chance of errors. Therefore, schedule sessions for daytime and choose days with stable, pleasant weather.

Next comes the equipment, which is crucial for a smooth game. A well‑inflated basketball with a good grip is the basic requirement; a flat, even court surface ensures the ball does not roll away unexpectedly. The playing area should be large enough to accommodate the full action of the sport, giving players enough room to dribble and move. The hoop must be mounted on a sturdy pole that reaches the correct height for the players, allowing the ball to travel easily into the basket. The rim should be wide enough to catch the ball comfortably, and the net should be of appropriate length so that rebounds are predictable. Finally, the court markings— including the three‑point line, the free‑throw line, and the boundary line— must be clearly visible and accurately placed. These lines guide players when positioning shots and help enforce the rules correctly.

The third pillar is the skill set and preparation of the players. Physical fitness is essential because basketball demands endurance, quickness, and agility. A strong cardiovascular base keeps stamina high throughout the match, reducing fatigue. Teamwork can change the course of a game; coordinated passing and mutual trust turn a losing side into a winning one. Regular practice sharpens shooting accuracy and creates new scoring possibilities. Focusing on making openings in the defense and rehearsing those moves in training sessions can give players an edge. Strategic thinking is equally important; consider how to exploit the opponent’s weaknesses and develop adaptable plans for different game situations. Planning ahead provides backup tactics in case the primary approach fails. In short, anyone who wants to excel in basketball must combine consistent training, attention to fitness, and a willingness to work together, all while paying close attention to the details of the environment and equipment.

If we get a good career, we can earn good money and enjoy life because we are doing what we like, not just a simple job.

Another example: Once we decide what our goal is, we keep our mind occupied by it and work hard to reach it or to accomplish what we truly desire. No matter how difficult it is, we can succeed because it is what we want to be, what we like, and what leads to a good future and a good life. For instance, if we get a good job we can earn good money and we don’t have to worry about that; we can simply enjoy life and strive to work hard every day.

Another reason is that we have to keep ourselves busy doing something we like. If we don’t, we may encounter trouble that prevents us from accomplishing what we want. For example, we might do drugs, drink alcohol, and similar things, which I think is bad because it interrupts our way, distracts us, and makes us lose our path and faith for ourselves. One mistake could cost us everything we have worked for. So we must stay focused if we truly want to become a professional or someone we aspire to be.

On the other hand, some people think that inactivity also serves a purpose. They claim we can live our lives regardless of whether we work hard for our goals—some say it’s fine not to strive. They argue that what happens in our life is for a reason or like destiny. However, I think they are wrong because we can decide what we will become. That’s why God gave us free will, so we can choose what we will fight for and make decisions that help us accomplish whatever we want in this life.

In conclusion, I believe we can accomplish many awesome and great things if we work hard for our goals and keep our mind occupied with good, loving activities such as in our jobs, school, or career. By staying productive, we gain benefits that help our life. Also, we must be careful not to get distracted by harmful things like drugs or alcohol.

I think we have to take care of our life like a treasure because this life is what God give us. We must be careful with the decisions we make; if we make mistakes, we can learn from them. I find it wonderful how much we can accomplish when we do something we love.

In my view, people should keep working toward the objectives they value and keep their attention fixed on what they truly want in life. When we stay busy with purposeful activities, we give our minds a direction that helps us reach higher. If we constantly think about our aims, we use our time more wisely and often achieve more. For instance, in school, a student who puts effort into studying and concentrates on finishing assignments, earning good grades and graduating, is more likely to secure a satisfying career and earn enough money to enjoy life. The work feels rewarding because it matches personal interests rather than being just a routine task.

Another example can be found in any personal ambition. Once the goal is clear, the mind stays focused on reaching it, working hard even when obstacles appear. The reason we keep going is that the goal represents what we enjoy, what we want for our future, and what we consider a good life. A well‑paid position, for example, reduces stress about finances, allowing us to relax while still pushing forward day after day.

Some may argue that doing nothing can also be useful, claiming that everything happens for a reason or that destiny decides our lot. However, I think this view ignores the freedom we have to shape our lives. By using the free will that God gave us, we can choose the path we fight for and make decisions that help us reach our wishes. If we simply sit idle, we lose the chance to steer our own future.

Moreover, staying inactive may tempt us toward harmful habits such as drug use or excessive drinking, which pull us away from our purpose. These distractions can derail our progress, make us lose confidence, and turn away from the life we want. Therefore, it is wise to keep ourselves engaged in activities we like, which protects us from such temptations.

In summary, working persistently toward our goals and maintaining a productive mindset bring many positive results in education, work, and personal life. At the same time we must guard against distractions that can ruin our plans. Treating life as something valuable and learning from any mistakes we make shows that the world can offer great achievements when we pursue what we love.

Most students look forward to summer vacation because it feels like the most enjoyable part of the school year. They use the time to be with their families and friends, but some teachers argue that the break is too long and that pupils forget what they have learned by the fall. I believe that the summer period is special and beneficial, mainly because it gives us the chance to spend more time with the people we value most.

During the school months, many parents work ten‑ to twelve‑hour shifts, sometimes on Sundays as well, which makes it difficult for them to be present in daily family life. Summer holidays therefore become a window when we can share meals, travel, and talk without the constant rush of school deadlines. For me, the warm weather brings many positive memories: I went on trips with my mother, visited relatives, and took part in religious activities. These moments helped me feel supported and gave me practical advice about studying, behavior, and career choices. My mother, in particular, is always there during both good and tough times, encouraging me to make wise decisions and avoid mistakes that she herself learned to avoid when she was young.

The bond with family and faith matters because they form the foundation of who we become. While school teaches facts about history, science, and math, the lessons learned at home—such as patience, responsibility, and compassion—are just as essential. My own schedule reflects this balance: I focus on homework and projects on weekdays, and then spend Saturdays and Sundays with my family and at church. When I look back, the summer vacations I have enjoyed helped me develop both academically and personally.

Some educators worry that a two‑month break leads to memory loss. In reality, we still keep the key ideas and skills we practiced during the school term. When we return, a short review session is often enough to refresh our minds, because the knowledge stays stored in our brain even if it is not actively used for a while. This suggests that a longer summer does not undermine learning; instead, it gives us a mental reset that can improve performance later on.

I also disagree with proposals for a year‑round school calendar that would replace summer with only three‑to‑four short breaks. If the school year were continuous, families would have fewer opportunities to travel together or to spend quality time with relatives who live far away. My own experience shows how easily a heavy workload can crowd out personal moments: one summer, I told my uncle I could not join a family trip because I had a pile of presentations due the next week. He reminded me that these trips are once‑in‑a‑lifetime chances to bond, and later I realized I missed a valuable time with my parents.

Having a clear agenda helps us make the most of every period. When it is “school time,” we concentrate on learning; when it is “family time,” we relax and enjoy each other’s company. This division reduces stress and allows us to appreciate both aspects of life. Summer holidays give us the freedom to implement such a schedule without the pressure of daily assignments.

Finally, the importance of family cannot be overstated. Some students live far from their parents, and the only times they can meet are during holidays. For families who are together every day, the summer provides a chance to deepen relationships, create memories, and support each other emotionally. Teachers, too, benefit from a similar break, as they need time to recharge before the next term.

In conclusion, a two‑month summer vacation is not excessive; it respects the need for both education and personal growth. It lets students retain what they have learned while also enjoying meaningful moments with family and faith. By keeping weekdays for studies and weekends for loved ones, we can maintain a healthy balance that prepares us for future challenges. Therefore, I support keeping summer breaks long enough to allow everyone to relax, reconnect, and return to school refreshed.

Influence is a word that covers many meanings and can be described in many ways. I believe the term is mostly negative because it tends to push people toward actions they would not choose on their own. It is the kind of language that convinces others to do something that may be harmful.

A typical example is when a friend offers you alcohol, wine, or drugs. This is a clear form of negative influence, encouraging you to try substances that can damage your health. Likewise, a buddy might say, “Let’s go and take that bicycle,” or another peer might suggest you join in a theft. These suggestions are not just playful ideas; they are attempts to steer someone toward illegal or unethical behavior. Some people also imitate the lifestyle of others who look glamorous or successful but whose habits are unhealthy or unrealistic. Copying a trendy diet, buying the latest gadgets without thinking, or constantly buying fast‑food meals such as McDonald’s, sugary drinks like Red Bull, and salty snacks are everyday ways influence works against our well‑being.

When children hear these kinds of influence, they are especially vulnerable. Friends or older peers can persuade them to skip school, try drugs, or eat junk food, shaping habits that stay with them for years. Even adults can feel pressure to buy things they don’t need simply because advertisements or social pressure make it seem normal. In these cases, influence acts like a subtle force that makes the wrong choice feel attractive or necessary.

That said, the word influence can also point to positive effects. For instance, a good teacher or mentor can guide us toward better habits, helping us improve at work or develop healthier attitudes. When used this way, influence describes something helpful and constructive. However, the everyday usage of the term most often highlights the harmful side, because it is frequently associated with persuasion that leads to bad decisions.

In conclusion, while influence can describe beneficial guidance, its common meaning is harmful. It tends to force many people—especially young ones—into wrong or unhealthy actions, convincing them to follow paths they might otherwise avoid. Recognizing the power of influence helps us stay aware of when it is pushing us toward good choices and when it is pulling us toward negative ones.

Technology has largely improved people’s daily experiences despite worries that it reduces face‑to‑face interaction. While some fear that screens replace real contact, the practical benefits of digital tools outweigh the drawbacks.

For personal communication, the internet lets us stay in touch with friends and relatives who live far away. Video calls, messaging apps, and social media make it possible to talk instantly with loved ones overseas, to arrange meet‑ups, and even to make new acquaintances. These platforms break down geographic barriers and often increase social activity rather than diminish it.

In the workplace, digital tools are essential. Companies store customer details, order histories, and internal documents in searchable databases, keeping vital information organized and secure. Email, instant messaging, and video conferences speed up internal coordination, so employees learn about their tasks promptly. This rapid exchange reduces delays and helps teams stay aligned, boosting overall efficiency.

Education has also benefited. Many schools now allow students to bring laptops, which replace the need to carry heavy textbooks every day. All course materials, notes, and reference books are available online, and assignments can be submitted with a single click. Teachers can supplement lectures with videos and interactive resources, making explanations clearer and more engaging. This digital shift saves time and supports a more flexible learning environment.

Some people argue that technology harms human relationships, especially older adults who find the new tools unfamiliar. However, the evidence shows that the positive changes—greater connectivity, more productive work, and richer learning experiences—are far more significant. In most cases, technology complements rather than replaces personal contact, and its advantages are evident across a wide range of activities.

It is usually wiser to turn to several people when you need help with a problem or a question. When you ask a group, the answers tend to vary; some may echo each other, while others offer completely different ideas. This diversity is valuable because it broadens your perspective and helps you see the issue from angles you might have missed on your own. By contrast, relying on a single source can be risky. That person might be unfamiliar with the subject, could misunderstand what you mean, or simply give you incorrect information. For example, if you ask only a parent, you might get advice that works for one situation but not for yours. Even trusted friends may not always hit the nail on the head, especially if they are shy about sharing their opinions or suspect you might reject their input.

Asking a variety of individuals also reduces the chance that you trust the wrong person. Some people hesitate to speak up because they fear being judged, or they think the listener won’t grasp the difficulty. I recall a friend once who faced a tricky math problem. He asked the teacher, who tried to interpret his query, but the explanation did not match the question he had posed. Turning to a classmate sitting beside him solved the mystery, because that peer understood the exact wording and could give a suitable solution. This shows how different viewpoints can fill the gaps that a solitary opinion leaves.

In short, seeking advice from multiple people gives you a richer set of responses and a higher likelihood of finding a reliable answer. It balances the risk of a single mistake with the benefit of shared knowledge, allowing you to make a more informed decision.

This program benefits both younger and older students in several important ways. By encouraging older learners to share their knowledge, it opens up new possibilities for the younger participants and helps them mature into confident, capable individuals. At the same time, the older students gain valuable experience in teaching, planning and organizing, which sharpens their own abilities and prepares them for future responsibilities.

One of the strongest advantages is that younger students acquire fresh ideas and useful information through direct interaction with older peers. When older learners explain concepts, demonstrate techniques, or share personal anecdotes, the younger participants receive more than just textbook content—they get insights that make learning feel relevant and meaningful. This exposure helps them think about potential career paths and decide what subjects they truly enjoy. Moreover, because the older students often volunteer their time, the younger ones feel supported and are motivated to reciprocate by teaching what they have learned to classmates or friends. For example, a teenager who learns basic budgeting from an older mentor may later explain those skills to a younger sibling, reinforcing both sets of learning and strengthening a sense of community.

Older students also gain significant growth from the act of teaching. Organizing a lesson forces them to think critically about how to present information in a clear and engaging manner. They must consider what the younger audience already knows, identify gaps in understanding, and choose the most effective strategies to bridge those gaps. This process cultivates focus, patience, and a deeper grasp of the subject matter. As they plan schedules, set goals, and anticipate questions, they naturally become more disciplined and better able to manage their own academic tasks. The experience of being trusted with responsibility often leads them to reflect on their own abilities and to ask self‑directed questions such as “What would I need to know to teach this topic well?” and “How can I adjust my approach if something isn’t working?” Those reflections accelerate personal development and give a sense of maturity that textbooks alone cannot provide.

Another key benefit is the boost in communication confidence that younger learners receive. Regularly speaking with people of different ages encourages them to step out of their comfort zone and practice articulating ideas clearly. As they encounter new faces and varied viewpoints, they become less shy and more comfortable expressing opinions in front of a group. Over time, this translates into better performance in school presentations, group projects and everyday interactions. The supportive environment created by the program means that mistakes are seen as learning opportunities rather than failures, which helps sustain motivation and reduces anxiety about public speaking.

Finally, the program fosters mutual skill improvement. Younger participants often introduce simple, innovative methods that can simplify a topic, while older students bring more structured approaches and deeper expertise. This exchange allows each side to discover new ways of studying—whether that involves creating flashcards, revisiting material repeatedly, or watching short instructional videos. By tailoring learning techniques to individual needs, students can progress faster and retain information more effectively. When everyone works together, the collective result is a richer, more diverse learning experience that benefits each person’s future academic and professional life.

In summary, the program creates a dynamic environment where knowledge, confidence and organization are enhanced for both younger and older students. It prepares younger learners for future challenges, cultivates mature teaching abilities in older participants, improves communication skills, and encourages the sharing of diverse learning strategies. These combined effects make it a valuable resource that supports personal growth and prepares students for success beyond the classroom.
