If we never act, what should we do?  
Thomas Jefferson once reminded us, “Never be idle; a great deal can be accomplished when we keep moving.” Staying busy gives us the chance to chase the dreams and targets that define our lives.

Some people argue that doing nothing can also be useful. They say a higher power has a plan for each person, that a vision needs time to mature, or that we should pause and think before we act. These views suggest there are legitimate reasons to step back.

Nevertheless, there are clear reasons why regular action matters.  

First, the people around us often back us up. Family, friends, and coworkers want us to thrive because they care about our wellbeing and wish to spare us hardship. Their support shows that we are capable and loved, which boosts our motivation.  

Second, taking chances and doing something helps us grow. When we try new things, we learn about our strengths, limits, and preferences. Each trial builds confidence and teaches us how to manage future risks more effectively.  

Third, staying true to ourselves is essential. Following our genuine hopes lets us picture the future we desire. This inner assurance, strengthened by the encouragement of loved ones, gives us the drive to keep going even when obstacles appear.  

All together, if we recognize that we can succeed, lean on the help of those who believe in us, keep ourselves motivated, and confront risks head‑on, we are far more likely to reach our goals. In contrast, neglecting to act greatly reduces the chance of achieving anything meaningful. Therefore, the wisest path is to stay active, take calculated risks, and stay authentic.

In my view, it would be helpful to change the school cafeteria menu. At the moment the meals are sometimes acceptable, but for the most part they are unappealing and repetitive. Many students complain that the same dishes appear week after week, which makes the lunchroom unattractive and even leads some people to skip meals.

Adjusting the price is another good step. Some pupils cannot afford to buy lunch, especially when the cost is relatively high. A modest reduction in prices would make meals affordable for students who have limited money.

Letting everyone know what the daily menu looks like would also be useful. Posting a schedule on the front door or sending a notice would let students see which foods will be available and choose dishes they enjoy.

The length of the lunch break is worth revisiting as well. An hour is typical, but many students want extra time to talk with friends, finish homework, or discuss class topics with teachers. A slight extension or more flexible timing would allow them to eat comfortably and still have time for social or academic activities.

Overall, improving menu variety, lowering prices, announcing meals in advance, and adjusting lunch‑time length would make the cafeteria experience more positive for most students.

When I think of wisdom, I imagine my grandfather’s life. He grew up in poverty, often without enough food, but he always valued education. The nearest school was about three miles away, and he walked there every day while his neighbours barely attended any classes.

His family consisted of a mother, a father who worked in construction, and one brother. My grandfather helped his mother cook and get the children ready for school. He found learning enjoyable, though few in his village could afford it.

A terrible loss came early. When he was five, his father was killed on a worksite. A gang ambushed him, and three gunshots left him bleeding on the ground before anyone could reach him. The memory stayed with him for years.

Later, his brother fell seriously ill for about two months. In 1976 medical treatment was scarce and expensive, so the family prayed each night. Despite their efforts, the brother died in his sleep. A simple burial took place; his mother cried for weeks before accepting the loss.

As an adult, my grandfather married my grandmother and they had two sons and two daughters. They applied for a U.S. visa. The immigration test required memorising a handbook with up to two hundred possible questions, only fifty of which would be asked. He passed, travelled to Virginia, and started working at a restaurant because his English was limited. He took a second part‑time job, saved money for eight months, and finally brought his wife and children to America. I was born soon after we settled in Generic City, and today he teaches at a local school, feeling satisfied with his present circumstances.

In short, perseverance, schooling, and faith enabled my grandfather to move from extreme hardship to a stable life abroad.

I recently met the manager of the Amazon office in Generic_City to discuss possible employment. While there I saw how large‑scale production works and realized that a career at this firm would give me the kind of fast‑paced environment I thrive in. One of the main reasons I target Amazon is that several people I know—my friends and my older sister—are already working there. Their stories have highlighted the company’s focus on training and rewarding its staff, which motivates me to join the same team. Although many describe Amazon as demanding, I see that intensity as a challenge I am ready to take. A rigorous work setting can help me develop discipline and become more productive.

The position I am most interested in is box packing inside the fulfillment centre. Packing requires speed, accuracy, and consistent quality, and I feel drawn to this hands‑on role. I have some informal experience handling small shipments at my father’s small store in Generic_City, and that has given me a basic sense of the workflow. I understand that new hires often start without pay while they complete orientation, and that arrangement does not deter me; a week of unpaid training is acceptable because it will give me the practical knowledge needed for the job.

After I finish high school I plan to study at a university in the afternoons. Working mornings at Amazon would let me keep a regular schedule, earn a steady salary, and still dedicate time to my studies. Many students successfully balance school and part‑time work, and I hope to follow that model. The money I earn would directly support my parents who are covering my tuition, textbooks, and everyday expenses such as clothing, shoes, and supplies. A reliable paycheck would also relieve some of the financial pressure on them, especially as university costs rise. In addition, I would like to save enough to purchase my own car. Currently my parents are the only ones who transport me, and owning a vehicle would give me independence and reduce the strain on them.

Before deciding on Amazon I spent a few months in a beauty salon called Generic_Name. I performed haircuts and handled appointments, but the owner repeatedly ignored my contributions. Over a weekend I earned only about $150, which was insufficient to cover rent and basic needs. That experience made clear how important a supportive workplace is, and I want a job where my efforts are recognized. My limited packaging experience from assisting my father in the Bodega has taught me the importance of organization, attention to detail, and the satisfaction of completing orders correctly. While the setting was modest, it gave me an early taste of the skills Amazon expects from packers.

My brother passed away last year, leaving me as the only child supporting my parents. Since then they have sometimes struggled to meet my needs, and I feel a stronger responsibility to provide financial assistance. This loss has intensified my desire for a stable job that can bring security to the household. My father constantly reminds me that I am his only remaining child and urges me to become a strong, productive member of society. His advice has shaped my belief that success is not only personal but also a duty to the family that raised me.

Amazon is a brand many students admire, and shoppers worldwide rely on it for everyday purchases. When my peers say they dream of working for Amazon I think about the constant flow of orders, the technology used in its fulfillment process, and the reputation of a company I already trust for most of my clothing and footwear. That familiarity makes the prospect of contributing to Amazon feel natural and inspiring. The company’s flexible overtime policy would allow me to work extra hours on weekends, which would increase my earnings and help me pay tuition faster. I am prepared to put in those additional hours because the extra income is crucial for both my education and my family’s wellbeing.

My immediate goal is a permanent packing position. In that role I will learn to scan items, secure them in the right boxes, and prepare them for shipment. I promise to give my full effort, ask questions whenever needed, and keep improving with each shift. Even though new employees must absorb a lot of information in the first weeks, I am confident that a brief unpaid training period will give me the foundation needed to become an efficient packer. Once I settle into the role, I intend to maintain high‑quality work, attend any further training, and look for ways to add value—such as assisting with quality‑control checks or suggesting process improvements.

With a steady job at Amazon I would achieve the independence I have long wanted: financial freedom to buy a car, reliable resources for university expenses, and peace of mind knowing my family will not have to bear all my costs. I would be grateful if you could consider my application for a position in your fulfillment centre. I am ready to start as soon as possible, willing to spend the first week learning, and committed to becoming a dependable employee who adds value to the team.

Thank you for reviewing my letter. I look forward to hearing from you and, hopefully, to joining Amazon’s dedicated workforce.

I disagree that failure is a useful part of life. Success matters a great deal because it gives people the opportunity to try many things and maintain a comfortable, stable position. When someone fails repeatedly, the desire to keep going often disappears, making it difficult to contribute or reach earlier goals. Moreover, continual failure can drain the energy needed for later effort, especially if a person relies heavily on past achievements.

Staying on the same course for too long raises the risk of failure. Doing exactly the same tasks day after day can create complacency; without noticing early warning signs, skills weaken and career prospects decline. To avoid this, it is wise to check progress regularly, look for new challenges, and change the approach before the situation worsens.

However, an early setback can also serve as a motivation. Failing at the start often forces people to find extra courage and work harder, which may later bring them to a higher level of competence. Many great innovators first experienced failure before they succeeded, and their perseverance turned those defeats into eventual breakthroughs. In short, while failure is undesirable, it can become a stepping stone toward success when it sparks renewed effort and determination.

Removing the foods that students like best should not be done, because many children would stay away from school if lunch is not appealing. Even if the cafeteria introduces new dishes, losing familiar favorites could make lunch a source of dislike for pupils. It is therefore unwise for the principal to suggest such a plan.

Another concern is that the food may already be off‑putting. If meals are not cooked properly, or if hair from staff falls into the food, students will avoid them. For this reason lunch workers must wear hairnets while preparing meals in the morning and after noon.

The same rule should apply to produce such as bananas. Any fruit that looks damaged or overripe should be discarded, as should other items that have passed their freshness date. In general, children care only about taste; they are indifferent to nutrition unless the food tastes good.

Snacks, particularly chips, should also remain on the menu. Most pupils prefer snacks to the main dishes, so taking them away would cause resentment. The sensible approach is simply to leave the current food selection unchanged, let the staff continue serving good‑quality meals, and allow students to enjoy their lunches without extra restrictions.

Being constantly busy helps us achieve more, and I agree with that. When people keep themselves occupied, they gradually build productive habits that boost their performance. An active approach not only leads to success but also ensures that the path to it is free from the marks of laziness.

If we stay focused and take action on a regular basis, we can develop reliable routines. With these routines in place, studying, learning, and completing tasks feel more natural and comfortable. Everything becomes smoother and faster. Moreover, our peers start to see us in a more positive light, showing respect and trust. Good habits also shape a sound workflow, making it easier to tackle future challenges.

The process of success relies on continuous effort. A restaurant cannot serve tasty food without careful preparation, just as we cannot become a skilled doctor, architect, or any other professional without diligent work and sustained concentration. Therefore, working hard and staying engaged are essential keys that open the door to achievement.

The road to success will never include footprints left by idle people. When we allow ourselves to become lazy or inactive, we end up with poor results. Employers and coworkers are unwilling to collaborate with someone who lacks motivation because they cannot depend on such a person to deliver. It’s easy to think, “I have done enough,” but that mindset quickly turns into complacency. Instead, we should strive to give our best at every moment and remember that inactivity rarely serves any purpose.

By committing ourselves to hard work, we set in motion a positive cycle. The good habits we form create productive routines, and those routines generate success. Thomas Jefferson once wrote, “Determine never to be idle… It is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.” In my view, his words still ring true today—consistent activity is the foundation of lasting accomplishment.

It’s hard to deny that truthfulness plays a crucial role in our everyday lives. Most people agree that honesty is essential because it shapes the way we connect with those around us. When we know someone well and trust that they value us, we expect them to share information openly rather than hide something that could hurt us. If we choose to conceal facts, we risk damaging that very relationship, which is why many of us argue that honesty should be our guiding principle.

When we consider the people closest to us, such as family members and friends, honesty becomes even more important. These individuals often rely on our word to support them emotionally or make decisions together. If we keep silent about a mistake or a feeling, the person we care about may feel betrayed, especially when they discover the truth later. Moreover, deliberately lying to loved ones creates a lingering sadness; the deeper the connection, the more painful it feels when that bond is broken by deceit. In short, a simple lie can erode the foundation of the strongest relationships.

A pattern of dishonesty quickly turns others against us. Imagine a classmate who constantly fibs to escape blame; eventually classmates stop asking for their help because they know the person is unreliable. In personal crises, the same tendency appears: people who have been lied to often withdraw support, leaving the liar isolated when they need assistance most. The fact that lies rarely stay hidden makes it inevitable that others will find out; when they do, the revelation usually results in broken trust, which can be difficult to rebuild.

Therefore, earning trust requires a clean slate from the start. If you present yourself as trustworthy, others are more likely to believe you and cooperate. This means being open about your actions and decisions, even when it feels uncomfortable. By refusing to hide information, you show respect for others’ right to know and reduce the chance that someone will accuse you of keeping secrets. Consistency in truthful behavior helps you avoid the reputation of being untrustworthy, which is far more valuable than any short‑term advantage a lie might offer.

Beyond personal relationships, honesty brings practical benefits. Parents, for example, are more willing to give their children freedom if they know they will not misuse it. In the workplace, an honest employee is usually trusted with important tasks and may be offered promotions or better positions. Moreover, living truthfully encourages responsibility; you become accustomed to thinking carefully before speaking, and that habit spreads to other areas of life. Over time, these advantages add up to a sense of security and opportunity that dishonesty rarely provides.

It is true that speaking the truth can sometimes sting. Confronting someone with a harsh fact may cause temporary discomfort, and some people react badly to honest criticism. However, handling those moments teaches resilience. Rather than avoiding the conversation, you can acknowledge the hurt while standing firm in your commitment to honesty. If someone chooses to ignore you, you have the right to distance yourself, but you should also remain open to anyone who later shows genuine willingness to improve. By refusing to accept falsehoods about yourself from others, you also protect your own integrity.

In conclusion, being honest is not just a moral choice; it is a practical strategy for building reliable connections and securing personal success. The risks of lying outweigh any short‑term gain, because lies quickly erode trust, lead to isolation, and prevent you from reaching your full potential. While honesty may demand courage and occasionally cause pain, the resulting strength and credibility make it worthwhile. If we all aim to keep our word and tell the truth, we create a world where support, cooperation, and genuine friendship flourish.

Summer is meant to be a regular part of life for students and anyone else who needs a break. It is the time when families and friends can spend days together without the pressure of school or work schedules. The warm sunshine invites us to enjoy simple pleasures: shopping trips, swimming at the beach, or taking a short vacation. Although summer does not last forever—winter eventually returns—it still gives us a valuable window to reconnect with people we care about.

One of the biggest reasons people love summer is the pleasant climate. Temperatures rise enough to feel comfortable, but they rarely become unbearable, making outdoor activities possible. The coast offers swimming, sand‑castle building, and beach games, while lakes and rivers provide fishing or a dip after a hike. Campgrounds become lively places for weekend trips, and parks turn into spots for picnics and nature walks. For children, this means fewer school obligations and more freedom to play video games or meet friends at the park. Adults also benefit because summer vacations can be used to visit relatives, attend a county fair, or travel to places such as California, Generic City, or Florida.

Of course, summer has its challenges. The heat can climb to 100 °F or higher on some days, making it difficult to stay outdoors for long periods. Even when the temperature is moderate, heavy rain can occur, which may cancel beach plans. Nonetheless, these drawbacks do not outweigh the overall advantages. Schools close for a break, teachers enjoy a pause from their duties, and communities organize pool parties, outdoor concerts, or barbecues. The season is consistent each year, offering a reliable chance to do what we want—whether that’s diving, fishing, camping, or simply relaxing at home.

In short, summer should remain a normal and welcome time for everyone. It supplies warm weather, plenty of recreational options, and a chance to strengthen relationships with family and friends. While occasional extreme heat or rain may arise, the season’s overall benefits—free time, travel possibilities, and enjoyable activities—make it the highlight of the calendar year.

I agree with Ralph Waldo Emerson’s claim that individuality is crucial. The moment you live according to your own inner compass, some people around you will feel at ease, while others may find the behavior unsettling. Nonetheless, staying true to oneself outweighs any temporary discomfort because it unlocks abilities and possibilities that might otherwise remain hidden. Society constantly pushes us toward conformity, presenting pressures and expectations that can lead us to compromise our values or make choices we later regret.

People will often try to shape our decisions, especially close family members and friends. When they suggest a particular career or lifestyle that does not match my passions, I still have the right to refuse and pursue what feels right for me. If I listen only to external voices, I risk surrendering control over my own destiny. While criticism may increase when I achieve something meaningful, it does not have to dictate the direction of my life. Choosing my own path requires confidence and the willingness to disregard discouraging opinions.

My family background has reinforced this belief. My father left early on, leaving my mother to shoulder the financial burden while working tirelessly to keep a roof over our heads. Seeing her dedication and sacrifice motivated me to work hard every single day. The effort she put into creating opportunities for us shaped my determination to succeed, not because she demanded it, but because I felt a personal responsibility to honor her work.

Growing up in a neighborhood where gangs were prevalent added another layer of difficulty. Violence and intimidation were common, and many peers chose to join the groups out of fear or necessity. I chose a different route, focusing on education and personal development. I never pretended to be someone I was not, even when the pressure to conform was strong. This decision kept me safe from the dangers that surrounded us and allowed me to build a future based on learning rather than conflict.

Emerson once said, “To be yourself in a world that is constantly trying to make you something else is an accomplishment.” This sentence reflects my own experience precisely. By resisting the urge to fit into the expectations of others, I have been able to accomplish more than I imagined possible. Trusting both myself and a higher power has given me the inner strength needed to navigate obstacles.

In the end, the voices that oppose our choices are usually those who wish to see us stay stuck or feel threatened by our progress. Ignoring them does not mean being disrespectful; it means prioritizing personal growth. By maintaining authenticity, believing in my own judgment, and staying connected to my faith, I have found that the hardships of life become manageable and the rewards worth the effort.

Therefore, I remain convinced that Emerson was right: individuality is not only a right but also a necessary means of achieving genuine fulfillment. Staying true to oneself, even when the world seems hostile, is the most reliable path toward success and happiness.

When they understand the direction they are heading, they are less likely to spend time on material that feels irrelevant. This focus can lead to faster mastery of key concepts and, ultimately, a quicker graduation. They also avoid the extra burden of making a sudden decision later on, which can sometimes delay the end of high school.

Second, committing to a career early provides an opportunity to tailor their coursework and extracurricular activities to their future needs. High school can offer specialized classes, internships, or projects that match a student’s interests. This practical experience strengthens the knowledge that colleges expect and makes the transition to post‑secondary education smoother. When students know what they want to study, they can spend their school hours building the exact skills that will support them later.

Third, early preparation reduces the amount of time and effort needed in college or university. Many programs require students to choose a major only after several years of exploration. Those who have already explored their field in high school can begin advanced work sooner, graduate faster, and enter the workforce earlier. Even for careers that demand long periods of practice, starting to develop those skills while still in school saves years of learning later on.

In conclusion, expecting students to set a career direction before entering high school aligns with effective use of time and better educational outcomes. It helps them graduate on schedule, focus on relevant study, and prepare for further training without unnecessary delays. For these reasons, such an expectation seems both reasonable and beneficial.

The power of first impressions

When we meet a new person or encounter an unfamiliar object, our mind forms a quick judgment. This initial view is what we call the first impression, and it often guides our early actions. However, such judgments are not permanent; they can shift dramatically as we learn more. The article explores why first impressions evolve, how they can influence us either positively or negatively, and why we should be cautious before labeling something as good or bad.

A first impression is the snapshot our brain creates the moment we see, hear, or touch something new. It may be accurate, but more often it is based on limited information, which means it can be misleading. Until we gather additional details, this snapshot remains only a guess. As experience accumulates, the picture can change entirely, revealing qualities we had never noticed before.

Several factors drive this change. False assumptions, disappointment, anger, and self‑correction all play a role. For example, if we assume someone is unfriendly because they look serious, we might later discover they are simply shy. When we feel disappointed, we tend to see the whole situation in a darker light, overlooking any positive aspects. Anger can cloud our perception, making even neutral events appear hostile. Finally, our desire to be right can lead us to revise a judgment once contrary evidence appears.

Real‑life situations illustrate both the positive and negative side of first‑impression changes. Imagine buying a car that looks flawless from the outside. After a routine inspection, hidden engine problems become apparent, turning a seemingly excellent purchase into a costly mistake. On the other hand, if a friend warns you that a colleague is unreliable, you might find out the warning is based on hearsay, and the colleague proves to be trustworthy and helpful. Both cases show how early opinions can be overturned, sometimes to our benefit, sometimes to our detriment.

In my view, first impressions are valuable as a starting point, but they should not dictate final decisions. They can be helpful for forming immediate safety assessments, yet they are easily distorted by emotions and incomplete facts. Waiting a little longer before drawing conclusions allows us to gather more evidence and avoid unnecessary errors. Therefore, while the first impression is important, its influence can change over time, often leading to a more accurate understanding of people and things.

Thomas Jefferson once argued that we should never be idle, and that view still makes sense today. Most people would accept his idea, because staying active benefits individuals and society.

Youngsters often display idle behavior and show disrespect toward older people. In school, teachers may try to cover personal or sensitive topics, yet many pupils tune out, treating the subject as boring and losing valuable learning time.

Jefferson believed that any spare time should be used to help innocent or vulnerable individuals. He turned idle moments into opportunities for service, showing that free time can create positive change.

When we cooperate, idle behavior drops. Helping a classmate understand a tough idea or assisting someone in need keeps people engaged and builds a supportive atmosphere.

Sometimes idleness arises from jealousy. Some individuals feel threatened by others’ progress and try to hinder them, ignoring effort or creating obstacles, which is unfair.

In my view, we must act as a group to stop those who deliberately stay idle or sabotage others. If idle people remain unchecked, the problem repeats and harms everyone. Supporting those who are stuck can break the cycle.

Finally, many people simply dislike helping others, which worsens the issue. As a community, we can promote cooperation and remind each other that assistance is essential. This reflects Jefferson’s belief that idle time should create positive impact, leading to a more productive society.

Ralph Waldo Emerson famously said that staying true to yourself while the world pushes you to become someone else is one of life’s greatest achievements. I agree with this view because learning to follow one’s own path in a society that constantly tries to shape us can be especially challenging, yet it brings a deep sense of fulfillment that few other goals can match.

When people try to conform to external expectations, the pressure to change can feel overwhelming. Without a solid group of supportive friends or mentors, staying authentic seems almost impossible. However, even in difficult times, many individuals manage to hold onto their core values and, in doing so, demonstrate remarkable resilience. Having people around who encourage honesty makes the task easier, but the real accomplishment lies in the personal decision to resist the urge to surrender one’s identity.

Being genuine is especially tough when the surrounding community is negative or dismissive. Critics often attempt to undermine confidence by pointing out flaws or imposing alternative roles. Despite this, maintaining self‑integrity remains the most powerful response. It shows that one’s sense of self is strong enough to survive criticism and still produce meaningful results. If you stay true to yourself, the very act of persisting becomes a quiet triumph over external influence.

When others appreciate you simply for who you are, it reinforces the idea that authenticity leads to personal success. By refusing to let society dictate your behavior, you open the door to new opportunities and make decisions that feel right rather than forced. This clarity often simplifies choices, allowing you to act with confidence and achieve goals that would otherwise seem out of reach.

In a world that constantly tries to reshape us, the act of being yourself is indeed a major accomplishment. It requires perseverance, courage, and a willingness to stand apart from the crowd, and the rewards of living honestly are worth every effort.

I think adding more school time would be a bad idea. Many of us, our parents, and teachers need that extra period after classes to take care of important tasks. Students have to pick up younger siblings, go to sports practices, or see a doctor, while parents have to drive to work, run errands, or attend meetings. Teachers also live far from the school, sometimes commuting from towns like Generic_City, and the after‑school window is often the only time they can handle family duties or personal errands.

If the day were extended, everyone would find themselves scrambling to finish these obligations. A student who has to wait until 7 p.m. for the bus will still have homework to do before bedtime. That means a rushed evening of study, a late bedtime, and less chance for any fun or rest. Teachers who live far away would face the same problem. A longer school day pushes rush‑hour traffic even higher, so they would get home late, still have grading work to complete, and might need to stay up until midnight. Repeating this every day would be exhausting for anyone, even for those of us who don’t work a full‑time job yet.

Moreover, some of my classmates live in distant places. For them, a normal school day already means long trips to and from the campus. After an extra half‑hour, they would return home between 7 and 8 p.m., leaving little time for dinner, homework, or relaxation. That makes it very hard to keep up with all assignments on time. The extra time would also lead to more homework. If teachers start assigning three extra hours of work because school is longer, we would feel pressured to stay up late just to finish it, and that stress would affect our grades and well‑being.

Another point is the impact on the lunch schedule for eighth‑graders. Right now we eat around 1:40 p.m., and an extra half‑hour pushes lunch to about 2:10. That means many of us would go to class on an empty stomach, feeling irritable and unable to concentrate. Hunger would make it even harder to finish the afternoon’s work, and the school bus would have to stay later to pick us up, taking away the drivers’ own time with their families.

If the goal is to give us more learning time, I suggest changing the start time instead of extending the end. Starting school a little later, perhaps at 8:00 a.m., would let everyone wake up later, have a more relaxed morning, and leave earlier. That way we would have more daylight for after‑school activities, families could spend more quality time together, and teachers would avoid the heavy traffic during rush hour. In short, adding more minutes to the school day creates more problems than it solves, and a later start would be a far better solution.

It is a sensible plan for students to start thinking about the career they would like to pursue before they finish high school. Having several years to reflect on interests allows us to make informed decisions about what to study afterward. For example, someone who dreams of becoming a pilot could select a high‑school program that offers aviation‑related courses, giving them a chance to learn the basics of aircraft operation and understand the path toward certification.

However, not every school provides such specialized tracks, and some students simply cannot attend these institutions. Distance, lack of transportation, or the need for another person to drive them each day can make it hard to reach a chosen program. Even when a ride is available, it is not a permanent solution, so students must arrange reliable ways to get to school and back.

Still, committing to a career goal early has advantages. It can shorten the overall school timeline, allowing students to graduate sooner and move on to further studies or work without extra delays. Choosing a high‑school that matches the desired field means gaining deeper knowledge, more relevant skills, and a clearer picture of university majors. In many cases these schools demand good academic performance, which motivates students to work harder and maintain a high standard.

In short, knowing what you want to study early helps shape a focused high‑school experience. When students prepare consistently, they improve their chances of entering the best universities and turning their ambitions into reality. The main challenge is access and grades, but with effort and support, early career planning can be both realistic and rewarding.

Dear Mr. Smith,

I am writing to express my view that schools should prohibit students from bringing cell phones on campus. Allowing these devices creates a range of problems that outweigh any potential benefits.

First, phones often divert attention from the lesson. Even when a phone is silenced, the temptation to glance at a screen can break concentration. Many pupils end up scrolling through messages or social media, which means they miss key points the teacher explains. As a result, they are unable to answer questions correctly because they did not hear the instructions clearly. This loss of focus undermines the purpose of attending class.

Second, the presence of phones leads to frequent interruptions. Occasionally a device will vibrate or emit a notification, causing the student to take a break from listening. The teacher must then pause to remind the student to turn the phone off or hand it over. Each interruption eats away valuable teaching time, slowing the pace of the lesson and affecting the whole class’s progress.

Third, there is a safety risk. Some students chat with strangers through messaging apps, sharing personal details or school information without knowing who the other person truly is. This exposure could result in uncomfortable situations or even harassment, putting both the student and the school at risk.

Lastly, the temptation to use phones for cheating or to check social media while doing work encourages dishonest behaviour and creates an unfair environment for those who try to stay focused.

For these reasons, I believe a complete ban on cell phones at school would help students stay engaged, protect them from potential dangers, and allow teachers to deliver their lessons uninterrupted. I hope you will consider this policy change.

Sincerely,

John Lee

I think a four‑day work week with ten‑hour shifts has both upsides and downsides. People earn less than they would with a regular five‑day schedule, so paying bills or going on a holiday can be tougher. On the positive side, having a whole day off gives families more time to relax, watch TV together, or simply spend quality moments at home. This extra downtime can strengthen relationships because many workers rarely get together with relatives or friends.

At school, extending the day by two hours could work similarly. Students would have more classroom time to finish lessons and get extra help, while the following three days could be used for homework, projects or a part‑time job. This balance reduces constant study pressure, and the chance to work after school can teach responsibility and add income.

I believe this approach has few serious drawbacks. It offers every student more opportunities, encourages deeper engagement, and provides a safety net against burnout. Overall, the benefits outweigh the possible inconveniences.

In conclusion, the proposal presents a valuable chance to improve job prospects and academic results. Yet any plan has advantages and disadvantages for different people, so careful evaluation is needed before implementation.

Whatever we set out to achieve, most of us will keep working on it until we overcome the obstacle and reach a point where we feel successful in life. No obstacle in our personal journey can permanently stop us from pursuing what we desire in the future. If someone tells you that a goal is impossible, do not let their opinion define your limits; believe that you are capable of doing anything you decide to aim for. It would be ideal if many people could focus on a single task because a large team could finish it faster and allow others to start working quickly, but that is rarely realistic. Every project, whether it is developing new cars or constructing new houses, requires each participant to play their own part. When people imagine they can accomplish anything, they tend to jump straight in, finish the task, and finally see their dream realized.

One way to move toward this kind of success is to find a job that matches your interests or to create a venture of your own. Working for yourself means you decide what to do without waiting for instructions, but you also need to manage your workforce, keep track of how people perform, and pay those who work hard and arrive on time. For those who run their own businesses, this responsibility is essential. Most of us, however, start by working for other companies—perhaps at a shop, a fast‑food restaurant, or any other service industry. In those early jobs we earn our first paychecks, cover basic expenses, and learn how to enjoy the freedom that comes with earning our own money.

When people begin with simple tasks, they gradually look for bigger opportunities and aim to turn their ambitions into reality. To achieve a dream, you usually try it out, see if it works, and if it shows promise you continue moving forward. Helping the world with your ideas benefits both you and others, as people can adopt parts of your vision to improve their own lives. The common desire is to own a spacious house, drive a nice car, and have a large pool in the backyard. Yet, once the dream is reached, it is easy to fall into the temptation of celebration. The real lesson is that success is not only about spending money on parties; it is about using resources wisely to support those who need them most. Anyone can achieve what they want if they dedicate themselves fully, because nobody will stop a person who commits their mind to a goal. With that personal drive, you will be able to accomplish great things in the years ahead, and the future will welcome the next wave of ambitious individuals who will surpass today’s standards.

People often look for advice when they feel stuck and unsure about what to do next. Usually they don’t have a clear sense of the right path and need someone else’s perspective to help them decide.

If someone makes a poor choice, the consequences can ripple through their life and affect the people they love. A decision that leads to trouble—like ending up in prison—can change the whole family dynamic. Children may grow up seeing their parent behind bars, which can shape their view of the world and even encourage risky behaviour later on. Being separated from a spouse or children for a long stretch can cause deep sadness and emotional strain for everyone involved.

On the other hand, when a person chooses wisely and seeks reliable guidance, they avoid legal problems and keep their family relationships intact. Good advice can steer them toward actions that benefit their children’s future, giving them a stronger footing in society. Speaking with someone who has a sound moral compass and understands the situation can lead to a decision that protects the family’s dignity, so relatives don’t have to watch each other through a small prison window.

I’ve learned the hard way that listening to the wrong person can be dangerous. It can set a negative example for the whole household, making it painful to see kids and a partner through bars. Even if a mistake is later corrected, the aftermath—fines, tickets, or a small court record—still leaves a scar. The safest route is to pick the advice that feels right for you and your family, and concentrate on what will help them the most, rather than worrying about external opinions.

Moreover, the wrong choices can invite theft, betrayal, and financial ruin. Friends who turn out to be unreliable may empty your wallet, and you might hear “a friend is money in the pocket,” only to discover the pocket is a hole. My mother often repeats that warning. The best approach is to follow your gut feeling, because people who don’t understand your circumstances can lead you into serious trouble.

When you make the right decision, the doors to education and a stable career open. You can enroll in college, study a subject you enjoy, and earn a degree that leads to a decent job. With that job comes the chance to secure a nice home, a reliable vehicle, and a small reserve for emergencies. You will also be able to support your parents and avoid placing them in an assisted‑living facility. The extra income lets you buy the things your children need whenever they ask, removing the stress of figuring out how to put food on the table every day. In short, choosing wisely protects your family and gives you the chance to build a comfortable life, rather than one marked by regret and hardship.

you ever consider trying skydiving? For me it sounds like a thrilling experience that would be worth a go. First, the feeling of being above the ground while watching the world stretch out below is something most people never experience. You can see the treetops, farms, and distant towns as if you were a bird, which is exciting. Also, falling from a plane gives you a sense of control and freedom, almost like flying without a plane.  

A common worry is fear of heights. If that’s something you struggle with, doing the jump together with a friend or family member can make the situation less frightening. Knowing someone else is there for support can turn the anxiety into confidence. Moreover, once you have completed the drop you often notice that your fear of high places begins to shrink. Later, you might even feel comfortable riding a roller coaster or taking a flight, because you have already faced the height you once dreaded.  

Another attraction of skydiving is the chance to spot things you rarely get to see. While in the air you could catch a glimpse of wildlife that is hard to view on the ground, such as birds gliding at a distance or animals moving in fields. You might also spot unusual structures, like tiny houses perched on hills, or a dog and a cat playing on a lawn. The view can sometimes include unexpected details that make the jump memorable.  

Beyond the view, skydiving opens the door to places that are hard to reach by car. Imagine landing in a tropical island such as Bora Bora, where the nearest road is a boat ride away. The activity lets you travel to remote destinations without the need for long drives or heavy traffic, which can be a big plus for adventure‑loving people.  

However, the sport is not without risks. If a jumper doesn’t know how to open the parachute or how to steer during descent, they could land badly and hurt themselves. Proper training is essential, otherwise the excitement can turn into a dangerous accident. This is why many beginners start in an indoor facility where they can practice the body position and get used to the sensation without wind or altitude.  

For that reason, I would suggest trying indoor skydiving first. It provides a safe environment to learn the basic techniques, and when you feel comfortable you can graduate to an outdoor jump. On the real jump, a qualified instructor handles the equipment, so you mainly focus on enjoying the scenery and the thrill of the freefall.  

In conclusion, skydiving is fun, offers amazing sights, and can help you overcome a fear of height. It may even inspire you to travel to far‑off places you otherwise couldn’t visit. The only catch is that safety matters, and indoor practice can make the outdoor experience smoother. If you ever get the chance, I think you should take it – the view and the feeling of freedom are worth the effort.

Imagine a classroom where the teacher tells you to stay after the final bell to finish your tasks. You may wonder why this is necessary, but I think adding after‑school clubs or programs is a good idea for most schools. They can help students finish their work more quickly and understand it better, especially when homework feels dull at home.

First, sitting still while doing assignments can become boring, and many pupils lose interest. When they take part in an activity instead, the time feels more purposeful. For example, if a child loves playing soccer, they might complete their math worksheet quickly so they can join the team. Activities such as math games, card challenges, or science experiments turn routine tasks into something enjoyable. This enjoyment keeps students focused, which in turn speeds up their work and often leads to a deeper grasp of the concepts.

Second, teachers can use these activities to explain ideas in a more engaging way. Instead of lecturing in a quiet room, they can demonstrate a principle through a hands‑on project, a quick game, or a group discussion. When students see the relevance of what they are learning in a fun context, they are more likely to remember it and apply it later. This makes the material clearer and encourages them to take the assignment seriously.

Third, the presence of an adult who checks on progress helps maintain motivation. Some children struggle to start their work because they do not see its importance. Consistent encouragement shows them that completing homework can have a real impact on grades and future opportunities. Because many students give up when the work feels too heavy, the structure of a club can act as a safety net, preventing them from falling behind and building confidence over time.

Finally, effort and persistence are key. Even when the task looks tough, students who keep pushing themselves usually succeed. After‑school programs remind learners that the effort they put in now pays off later, not just in school but in life as well.

In conclusion, after‑school activities provide a useful platform for completing homework, clarifying concepts, and keeping motivation alive. By reducing boredom, offering alternative learning methods, and giving steady support, these programs can help students achieve better grades and develop habits that will serve them beyond the classroom.

Many people consult more than one person for advice. About two‑thirds of respondents say they do. The main reasons are varied viewpoints, personal experience, and a confidence check on their own judgment. First, each advisor sees the problem from a personal angle. Background and knowledge affect how they interpret it. Some may be sure, others may lack information or suggest risky steps. Hearing several perspectives prevents a single, possibly biased, view from dominating. Second, those who have already dealt with a similar issue can offer practical knowledge. Their experience tells what may happen and which steps often go unnoticed. This helps the seeker anticipate real‑world difficulties that a purely theoretical discussion might miss. Finally, asking several people serves as a confidence test. By comparing advice with personal thoughts, the decision‑maker can see if they match common sense. This reassurance lowers doubt and makes the chosen option feel more justified. Overall, consulting multiple sources broadens perspective, incorporates lived experience, and validates personal judgment. Together, these steps lead to a more thoughtful and dependable decision.

High school students should be allowed to finish their education in three years rather than the usual four. With a more intensive schedule, learners can take extra classes during the summer and at night, which lets them leave school sooner. Graduating earlier then opens two valuable possibilities: entering college a year ahead of the standard timeline or starting work immediately. An accelerated program would give young people a head start in both academic and professional life, helping them reach personal goals faster and with more financial freedom.

A shortened timetable gives pupils a chance to complete their required courses without postponing graduation. Some students already balance coursework with part‑time jobs, and they can accelerate that process by enrolling in summer classes or attending evening sessions. Adding a few additional subjects each semester can shave a full year off the typical path. Even when a student drops an elective to make room for core classes, the trade‑off is still a quick exit from high school. Once they have earned their diploma, they can move on to the next stage of their lives instead of waiting an extra twelve months.

Early graduation also creates space for earning money before college. With another year in the workforce, students can save up for tuition, living expenses, or other costs related to higher education. This financial buffer reduces the need for loans and lessens the stress that comes from worrying about paying for college while studying. Those who take jobs in fields related to their intended majors also gain practical experience that can be useful when they finally enrol in university. In short, an extra year of work can smooth the transition to college life and improve academic performance.

Beyond simply saving money, finishing school sooner allows learners to pursue long‑term ambitions more quickly. For many, the ultimate goal is to start a career that offers stability and growth. If they can graduate in three years, they can apply for internships or apprenticeships earlier, or even launch a small business while still young. Early career entry builds a stronger professional network and may lead to promotions faster than peers who follow the traditional four‑year route. Moreover, achieving a key milestone ahead of schedule often motivates students to set additional targets—such as further certifications or graduate studies—creating a positive cycle of continuous progress.

Critics sometimes warn that a compressed schedule would cut out electives, limiting exposure to arts, sports, or technology subjects. While it is true that some electives might be deferred, students can later pick them up in college or through online platforms. The core benefit of finishing school early still outweighs this minor inconvenience, because the extra time gained can be used for personal development, volunteer work, or extra academic pursuits that might not fit into a four‑year plan.

In summary, letting high‑school students graduate in three years offers several clear advantages. It lets them complete their required curriculum sooner, gives them a head start in the job market, and speeds up the achievement of personal and professional goals. A combination of summer and evening classes makes this schedule feasible without dramatically increasing stress. Even if it means sacrificing a few electives, the ability to work a year earlier and to enter college with less debt is a strong incentive. Schools should therefore consider revising their calendar to support an accelerated pathway, helping young people become more independent and better prepared for the future.

A few years ago, before my uncle entered his career as a doctor, I watched him wrestle with panic attacks caused by long hours of study at medical school. He realized that constantly studying was taking a toll on his mental health and decided to try other activities that would give him a brief distraction while also easing the pressure. In my view, encouraging every student to take part in at least one extracurricular activity is a sensible idea because it offers a range of ways to unwind—through sports, book clubs, or community‑service projects—and brings about significant improvements in well‑being.

Participating in sport, for instance, can be a powerful aid to physical health. Most school days involve sitting at desks for many hours, and evenings are often spent on the sofa. The human body, however, needs regular movement to stay fit. Even a modest routine of twenty minutes of exercise a day can stimulate circulation, strengthen muscles, and keep metabolism active, which is especially useful for adolescents whose bodies are still developing. The simple act of getting up and playing a game or jogging helps break the cycle of inactivity and contributes to a healthier lifestyle.

Book clubs provide another appealing option for students seeking a mental break. When the mind feels overloaded, picking up a novel can transport you to distant lands, real or imaginary, without leaving your room. Reading exposes you to new perspectives, emotions, and situations—whether adventure, romance, or drama—that are unlike anything you encounter in everyday life. These stories not only distract you from the pressures of coursework but also inspire fresh ideas. Meeting with fellow readers to discuss a book allows you to share impressions, compare interpretations, and sometimes discover someone who feels exactly the same way, reinforcing a sense of connection.

Engaging in community service benefits both recipients and volunteers. By helping local organizations or assisting neighbours, students learn the importance of teamwork and empathy. The act of giving can generate personal satisfaction and a feeling of responsibility. Moreover, many schools award credits or scholarship points for volunteer hours, which can ease the path to higher education. For students who have never tried volunteering, this can be an eye‑opening experience that adds purpose to their time outside the classroom.

Overall, every learner should pursue at least one after‑school activity. Whether it is sport, literature, or service work, these pursuits offer a productive pause for the body and mind, allowing students to recharge and return to their studies with renewed focus. Choosing an activity that genuinely interests you makes it easier to commit and enjoy, and making the most of the free time after school can turn ordinary evenings into meaningful, balanced experiences.

Many teachers and other adults expect teenagers to have a clear idea of what job they want once they reach high school. In my view, this expectation is misplaced because most young people simply are not ready to make such a big decision on their own. First, a considerable number of students already manage adult responsibilities outside school. They work part‑time, pay for rent, utilities, and phone bills, and often have to balance a heavy workload with their studies. Juggling a demanding job and school assignments leaves little room for thoughtful career planning. At the same time, they still need to meet school deadlines, study for exams, and keep up with homework, which can be overwhelming for anyone who is also trying to earn a living.

Second, many students receive very little assistance in figuring out which career path suits them. Some instructors assume that teenagers lack the maturity needed for such a choice and, as a result, refuse to discuss future options. This lack of guidance can be especially problematic for those who cannot afford the books, software, or tutoring that might help them explore different fields. Even when a helpful mentor or community program is available, a large portion of the student body cannot access it because of time constraints or financial limitations. In these cases, the students are left on their own, without a chance to demonstrate that they are capable of handling the responsibility.

In addition, many high‑schoolers already feel stretched thin by their existing commitments. They may be dealing with family problems, caring for younger siblings, or managing their own health issues, which adds another layer of stress. The combination of these challenges and the pressure to decide on a career can lead to burnout. Some students begin to neglect their studies, focusing instead on fitting in socially or projecting a certain image. When they devote energy to “being the coolest” or building a large network of friends, academic performance often suffers. Without proper support, they struggle to keep up with normal classes and extra courses, let alone commit to a career plan.

Adults frequently overlook these realities, believing that making a career choice early will motivate students and give them direction. However, the added pressure usually makes the situation more difficult rather than easier. The teenage years are still a period of learning and growth; many are still figuring out basic life skills and coping mechanisms. Expecting them to sort through long‑term professional options while managing school, work, and personal life is simply too much to ask. The result can be anxiety, confusion, and a feeling that they are being pushed into a decision they are not equipped to handle.

Therefore, I do not think that schools should force young people to pick a career path right away. Instead, they should give students the time and resources to explore interests gradually, while maintaining strong academic support. When students feel supported, they are more likely to make thoughtful, realistic choices later on, after they have built the necessary skills and confidence. Pushing a premature decision only adds stress and can undermine their motivation to succeed in school and beyond.

Albert Schweitzer famously stated, “Example is not the main thing in influencing others; it is the only thing.” His words capture the idea that what we do, rather than what we say, is the most effective way to affect those around us. In everyday life, people notice and remember the choices we make, and these choices become the template they use when they decide how to act themselves. When we walk the path we talk about, we give a clear signal of what matters to us, and that signal is more convincing than any lecture or argument could ever be.

I agree with Schweitzer because leading by example is the most honest method of persuasion. It is not necessary to have a perfect moral stance or flawless reasoning; the simple fact that someone can see our actions and relate them to our personality is enough to make them listen. Children, coworkers, and peers all absorb cues from those they admire, whether the behavior is praiseworthy or problematic. We have always been shaped by the examples set by our families, teachers, peers, and now by countless online personalities.

Some may argue that individuals have the freedom to become who they truly want regardless of outside models, or that reactions to specific situations are driven solely by momentary feelings. While personal agency is certainly important, the reality is that our environment constantly sends us subtle messages. Even when we think we are making a private decision, someone nearby may observe and later imitate our response. In that sense, influence often operates without us being aware of it, and our everyday conduct becomes the only practical source of guidance.

The phrase “actions speak louder than words” is a familiar reminder of this principle. If we want to guide another person’s life, the most dependable tool is our own behavior. Each person has unique preferences, habits, and values, and these details can subtly steer others toward similar choices. For instance, a child who repeatedly sees a parent reading at night may be encouraged to develop a love for books without any explicit advice. The impact of such habits demonstrates how powerful example can be.

In my view, behavior holds great weight in shaping attitudes and actions of those who look up to us. Whether at school, at work, or on social platforms, people tend to model what they see rather than what they hear. Even small gestures—holding a door open, responding kindly in conflict, or staying committed to a hobby—can leave a lasting impression. As Schweitzer suggested, the only true way to influence others is by allowing our own conduct to become the reference point they follow.

This is why, throughout our lives, we have asked and been asked, “What do you want to be when you grow up?” The answer we give often reflects the examples we have observed and absorbed. Whether we intend to inspire or not, the choices we make create a ripple effect, showing that living out what we believe is the most reliable way to affect the world around us.

One of Thomas Jefferson’s most memorable statements reads, “Determine never to be idle… it is wonderful how much may be done if we are always doing.” The idea that idle moments rarely produce progress has shaped my view on how success is earned. I largely agree with Jefferson’s observation because it reflects the reality that most of what we obtain in life requires effort. Although occasional breakthroughs appear to happen without much work, the majority of accomplishments are built through persistent action.

The first reason I support this quote is that whatever we receive must be earned through labor. If we sit back and wait for opportunities to land in our lap, they often remain out of reach. Jefferson emphasizes that doing something constantly creates room for achievement; it is through continual work that tasks get finished and goals become attainable. The more we engage, the quicker results follow, and the easier it becomes to handle the many responsibilities that life throws at us. This active approach not only speeds up the completion of daily chores but also fosters confidence and momentum.

A second point concerns the importance of staying busy regardless of the task at hand. No matter whether we are pursuing a career, managing personal matters, or simply improving our skills, we must always find something to do. Ignoring this principle can lead to complacency and a habit of taking things for granted. By keeping ourselves engaged, we develop a sense of responsibility and avoid the pitfalls of laziness. Moreover, consistent effort often simplifies later challenges, making the path to success smoother and less stressful over time. The quote functions as a reminder that effort today prevents problems tomorrow.

Finally, Jefferson’s words underline the fact that life does not hand out rewards without cost. Accomplishments come with effort, and the benefits we enjoy are usually proportional to the sacrifices we make. Recognizing this encourages gratitude and motivates us to make the most of what we have. It also reminds us that ignoring duties can produce undesirable consequences, while fulfilling them yields positive outcomes. This perspective helps people stay focused on realistic goals and maintain a steady pace rather than relying on luck or chance.

In conclusion, Jefferson’s quote offers valuable encouragement for anyone seeking direction. It highlights that progress is possible when we stay active, that effort pays off more quickly than inactivity, and that a purposeful mindset leads to greater satisfaction. By adopting the principle of “always doing something,” we can better understand how to live responsibly, achieve our aims, and become wiser over time. This is why I believe the quotation remains a useful guide for navigating the complexities of everyday life.

From the moment we are born, each person carries several internal personalities that can clash and confuse. It is often difficult to interpret why others act the way they do toward us, and many of us tend to convince ourselves that we have full control over our lives, even though we cannot fully govern our own traits. When a baby arrives, neither the mother nor the father knows what kind of adult the child will become. There are generally two kinds of character patterns: one where individuals mask their true selves, pretending to be someone they are not, and another where people remain faithful to who they genuinely are.

At some stage in life, a number of people drift toward groups that make poor choices and repeat bad decisions. By aligning with such companions, they gradually adopt the same attitudes, becoming part of the crowd rather than standing apart. This shift happens slowly, often unnoticed, until the follower is indistinguishable from the original. Nevertheless, we always retain the power to decide differently—to accept ourselves, embrace our inner values, and stop worrying about what the outside world thinks. In this way, we can let love for who we are drive our behavior, and that love can inspire others to do the same.

The idea that a higher power already knew what traits each of us would possess before we entered this world reinforces the notion that authenticity is part of our design. When we practice self‑acceptance, we set a model for those around us, creating a ripple effect that can improve the attitudes of many.

In the end, we are not meant to live as copy‑cats. Our purpose is to carve out a distinct place for ourselves, letting our choices reflect our true nature. Whatever action we take, it will inevitably involve certain conditions, but those conditions do not have to dictate who we are. We can choose to stand out, stay true, and shape the world by being ourselves.

I agree with the adoption of the midnight weekend rule. However, this does not mean that I agree with the 10 p.m. weekday curfew.

Although many teenagers are constantly restricted, teenagers younger than 18 have their own responsibilities and obligations to themselves and their families. Teenagers need education, a home, and money.

Teenagers need education, which begins at elementary and continues through high school. In 5 or 10 years, they will support the economy, the country, and the next generation.

A home is a place where teenagers can call "home." It is not only a place to relax, but also where they feel tranquil and safe from the outside world. In this place, someone awaits them with a smile and food. They may be reprimanded, but they know this is for their well-being and future.

Logically, money is the most important fact in a teenager’s life. To earn it, a teenager must get a part‑time job or work on weekends. This is where the problem arises: teenagers aged 16 to 18 must use their valuable time after school to work. Part‑time jobs are approximately 6 hours long. If a student works from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m., there is no problem. However, if a student works between the curfew hours of 5 p.m. to 10 p.m., the big problem is that teenagers will be accused of breaking the law, even though this is unfair interference by the city.

In summary, the children of today will become the teenagers of tomorrow and the adults of the new generation.

A home is the best place for a teenager to feel comfortable, safe, and tranquil. Money is the most important thing for a teenager in the present and for their future, and time is a necessary value for obtaining it.

I agree that the weekend midnight rule is a positive step but I do not support the weekday curfew set at 10 p.m. Teenagers under 18 already shoulder considerable duties toward themselves and their families. They must pursue schooling—from elementary to high school—and prepare for the future, which will shape the economy, the nation, and the next cohort. A home is essential as a sanctuary where they can unwind, find peace, and know that someone awaits them with care, even if occasional discipline is involved. It is fundamentally about their well‑being and prospects.

Money is also crucial for adolescents today and tomorrow. To earn it, many take part‑time jobs, especially on weekends, often working about six hours after school. A schedule from 4 p.m. to 9 p.m. is reasonable, yet if the city imposes a curfew, a teen working from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. is unfairly labeled as breaking the law. This creates unnecessary tension between youth employment and municipal policies.

In short, today’s children will become tomorrow’s teenagers and adults. A stable home provides comfort and security, while earning money—through the careful use of time—prepares them for future independence. Balancing these needs with realistic work hours is vital for their growth and societal contribution.

Schools sometimes organize mentorship programs pairing younger and older students, which can benefit both groups by fostering mutual growth and understanding.

Over time, this might lead to strong, lasting relationships where former mentors and mentees recognize each other and appreciate the support received.

Finally, the program could help students overcome hesitation in expressing opinions. In a classroom setting, many feel shy about speaking up, but one-on-one interactions remove some of this pressure. Students would have more freedom to voice their thoughts on topics or subjects, which might otherwise remain unspoken. This would encourage clearer communication and self-advocacy skills for both parties.

Overall, I believe this initiative would boost confidence in interpersonal communication and make learning more enjoyable. It provided targeted help in subjects where I struggled and built a positive, motivating environment. Similar programs could address a variety of challenges students face by fostering encouragement and curiosity.

Technology significantly alters many aspects of daily life, offering conveniences such as online classes, shopping, and communication. Despite these benefits, I contend that technology predominantly has negative impacts on human interaction and habits. The overreliance on digital tools reduces face-to-face connections and reshapes lifestyles, often to the detriment of social and cultural richness.

Firstly, the rise of online shopping has harmed physical retail spaces. Many brick-and-mortar stores struggle to survive as consumers increasingly prefer e-commerce platforms like Amazon, which dominate global sales. For instance, two local shops I recently learned about—STORE_NAME and STORE_NAME—face imminent closure because customers favor the convenience of staying home and purchasing online. This shift has led to declining foot traffic, prompting these establishments to cut operating hours or offer drastic discounts to avoid bankruptcy. Employees are also at risk of losing their jobs as demand for traditional retail dwindles.

Secondly, communal areas such as parks, lakesides, and malls have become less frequented. People often opt to stay indoors, immersed in video games or online transactions. While some view digital platforms as creative outlets—like art, music, or dance—there’s a lack of physical engagement. For example, my dance instructor highlighted how reliance on cellphones can hinder genuine participation. Although technology aids in bridging communication gaps, such as using translation apps, it also creates distractions. During lessons, students sometimes struggle to answer questions because they depend on devices instead of cultivating independent thought.

Critics might argue that technology improves connectivity, enabling families to stay in touch across distances. However, this constant digital interaction often replaces meaningful in-person communication. Additionally, it erodes cultural practices as younger generations avoid outdoor play or reading, instead gaming or scrolling on screens. My cousin’s experience illustrates this: consumed by Fortnite, he neglects schoolwork, outdoor activities, and reading, leading to poor sleep and academic performance. The allure of endless digital stimulation undermines curiosity and personal growth.

Ultimately, technology’s unchecked expansion risks degrading cultural vitality and interpersonal skills. If trends continue, people may disengage from the world entirely, favoring virtual experiences over real ones. This erosion stifles innovation, knowledge acquisition, and joy. In my view, while technology is useful, its pervasive influence stifles development and happiness, altering our world in ways that are often harmful rather than helpful.

We frequently hear the quote by John Lubbock, a British naturalist and politician, who said, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." This raises an important question: do our character traits develop naturally, or do we actively shape them? I believe that we have the ability to influence our character traits such as how sociable we are, how reserved we become, or how confident we appear. This belief is the basis for my stance that we do possess a degree of control over our personality.

Take, for instance, someone who tends to be quiet. Quietness is neither inherently good nor bad—it simply means holding back thoughts for periods of time. Over time, the individual learns to balance solitude with conversation to avoid feeling isolated. Reflecting on my own middle school years (grades 6 to 7), I was largely introverted, speaking with few classmates and feeling disconnected. However, I gradually began engaging with others, eventually building a close circle of friends. This transition illustrates how deliberate effort can shift one’s personality tendencies, reinforcing the idea that traits like quietness are malleable.

Another example is sociability, a trait that often aids in forming friendships and gaining insights through interaction. While being talkative can help in connecting with others and discovering new perspectives, it may also overwhelm people if not moderated. I experienced this firsthand during grades 7 to 8. My enthusiastic conversations sometimes annoyed others, but they also taught me how to approach different individuals respectfully and observe how personalities evolve. Some peers became more agreeable after time, while others remained consistent. Recognizing this variability made me realize that I could steer my own social habits, choosing moments to engage and moments to reflect. Sociability, therefore, is not fixed but can be shaped through conscious practice.

The third trait, self-assurance, further supports this viewpoint. Confidence can be empowering, allowing us to lead or express ourselves, but overconfidence may lead to arrogance and alienate others. In competitive situations like sports, I often found myself boasting after a win, which some viewed as immature. However, I later adjusted by celebrating successes more modestly. Although emotional outbursts might seem involuntary, they are rooted in habits formed over time, indicating that even strong reactions can be redirected. This adaptability suggests that traits like confidence are choices we can refine.

In conclusion, Lubbock’s assertion emphasizes personal agency in shaping character. While external factors play a role, we ultimately decide how traits like quietness, sociability, or confidence manifest through our actions and reflections. By recognizing that character is not entirely predetermined, we empower ourselves to grow and adapt our personalities intentionally.

People often debate whether a positive attitude is essential for success in life. While some might argue it isn’t, maintaining optimism can significantly influence how we experience life. For instance, a positive mindset often fosters deeper connections with others, making us more approachable and memorable in social settings.

When we approach situations with optimism, we’re more likely to engage with others, which encourages reciprocated interactions. This mutual exchange builds rapport and creates a friendly environment that feels rewarding. Strong relationships reduce feelings of isolation and keep us occupied with meaningful interactions, leaving little room for stress to take root.

First impressions play a crucial role in social or professional settings. Positivity helps us leave a favorable impression, making us appear enthusiastic and approachable. Whether in school or the workplace, this demeanor attracts others and strengthens our ability to communicate effectively.

Research consistently highlights the negative effects of stress on physical and mental health. By cultivating optimism, we naturally lower stress levels, as positive thinking helps us reframe challenges more constructively. When we adopt this mindset, relationships improve—both with neighbors and broader networks—and we gain more opportunities to share concerns, ultimately supporting healthier habits.

In conclusion, while success depends on many factors, a positive attitude serves as a foundation that amplifies other advantages. It enriches social connections, preserves well-being, and creates opportunities for fulfillment, all of which align with living a successful and balanced life.
