Graduating in three years instead of four by taking summer courses has several drawbacks. First, students may face increased credit requirements, which could force them to overload their schedules. If they enroll in extra classes while still needing additional credits, the workload might become too heavy. Four years in high school allows students to balance regular coursework, extracurriculars, and personal interests without becoming overwhelmed. In contrast, squeezing everything into three years could lead to burnout and reduce opportunities to build a well-rounded profile for college applications.

Second, many students work during summer to earn money for future goals, such as a car or college expenses. Juggling a job with summer classes leaves little time for rest or other activities. The summer break is a rare chance to focus solely on employment, and combining it with academics would drain their energy. This could negatively impact both their mental health and job performance.

Lastly, some students prefer to take a gap year after high school to explore career options or save funds. Summer classes would disrupt this plan, forcing them to delay financial goals or personal reflection. Success in life often requires careful planning, and rushing through education might create unnecessary stress. Allowing students to spread their studies over four years helps them avoid fatigue and make more thoughtful decisions about their future.

In short, the three-year graduation path isn’t ideal. Extra summer courses could overwhelm students academically, interfere with summer jobs, and prevent those who need a break from taking it. Four years provide a healthier balance, letting students grow without constant pressure.

John Lubbock wrote, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." Everyone has complete control over themselves, no matter how bad the circumstances may be or how tough a problem is. Everyone will always be allowed to choose whether to smile or cry, to be positive or negative. For example:

My grandma is a 78-year-old lady who has worked her entire life. She is a very independent woman who always says, "If I don't do it, no one can make it as good as I can." She always maintains a positive attitude, never sitting down because she says that sitting down is a waste of time. She has always been so energetic until one day that sadly she had a really strong stroke in the middle of her brain that made her lose movement on half of her body and her voice. Her doctor told us that she would stay in a wheelchair for the rest of her life. It was hard to see someone so positive and with so much energy in a wheelchair for the rest of her life. Everyone was really shocked and depressed about it, including my mom. But even though my grandma knew what was going on, her positive attitude never changed. She took over the circumstances and never gave up on herself. She decided to remain "positive," even though it was a rough time in life. This example helped me see that everyone has their own control or can choose who they want to be in the hard or easy times.

Everyone can have the freedom to choose the environment around them, how they want to live, and with whom they want to associate. People have the ability to understand when there are toxic people around them, to comprehend how much an environment can change the way they act, to realize they can change the negative environment into a positive one. Everything in your character depends on your own person, though the environment around you can affect a lot of your character. It affects what you do on a daily basis. At the end of the day, it always depends on you who you want to be, who the people around you should make you feel, and how positive or negative it should be.

Having reactions with other people around you can show them what your character is. It can reveal your weakest parts and show how dangerous or calm you can be. Reactions are a really big part of our characters, whether we have control of them or not. How we react and respond depends on us. For many people, having their own character is really hard due to their negative or positive mood. Sometimes we want to be or act like other people we see at school, but that's like stealing their characters. At least, everyone has the freedom to choose what their character traits are or can be.

In conclusion, everyone is free to choose what their character should be, no matter if they are going through a rough time or have the whole world against them. They will always have the chance to try to be someone else's character or to build their own. It will always be what they choose their character traits to be.

Do We Shape Our Character Traits?

The British naturalist and politician John Lubbock once declared, "Your character will be what you yourself choose to make it." I fully believe that individuals possess the capacity to shape their own character traits because they retain sufficient autonomy to manage their responses and decisions. For instance, even when confronted with challenges, people can select whether to adopt a hopeful or resigned outlook, depending on how they interpret events.

My grandmother, a 78-year-old woman who worked diligently throughout her life, exemplifies this independence. She often remarked, "If I don't do it, no one can match my effort." Her relentless optimism and refusal to idle—she deemed inactivity wasteful—sustained her vitality until a severe stroke suddenly limited her mobility and speech. While the prognosis was grim, her core positivity remained unchanged. She consciously embraced her new reality, refusing to surrender to despair. This resilience demonstrated that individuals can maintain agency over their character despite physical constraints, using adversity as a catalyst rather than an obstacle.

People also have the freedom to curate their surroundings, which profoundly influences their identity. Recognizing toxic influences and actively seeking supportive environments allows individuals to foster constructive traits. Although external factors—such as daily interactions or social circles—shape behavior, the ultimate responsibility lies with the person themselves. They decide whether to internalize negativity or reject it, ultimately defining their character through consistent choices.

Additionally, our interactions with others reveal much about our character. How we react to others' words or actions exposes our strengths and vulnerabilities, showcasing whether we remain composed or react impulsively. While emotions sometimes dictate responses, deliberate effort can redirect these tendencies. Observing peers may inspire temporary imitation, yet authentic character development requires personal commitment rather than adopting others' traits.

Ultimately, regardless of circumstances, individuals retain the power to sculpt their character. Whether navigating hardship or surrounded by encouragement, everyone can strive to become the person they envision. Character, therefore, is not fixed but a dynamic reflection of conscious decisions and steadfast choices.

Failure is a widely feared element in daily life, often something people strive to evade. Many individuals avoid situations where they might fail, while fewer choose to confront such moments. However, those who do view failure as part of the learning process often achieve remarkable outcomes.

Fear shapes our decisions, influencing whether we pursue certain actions. We worry about the possibility of failure due to uncertainty about success or positive results. This mindset divides people into two groups: cautious individuals and daring risk-takers. Both approaches have strengths and weaknesses.

Cautious individuals rely heavily on past experiences to minimize risks. The term "shy" may not accurately describe them when facing new challenges, but their hesitation stems from past mistakes. Situations like answering questions in class, trying a new sport, or adopting unfamiliar clothing styles can trigger this hesitation. Fear becomes the barrier between action and inaction. If they avoid taking risks, they never discover potential results. While they might not suffer losses, they also miss opportunities for significant achievements. Such people often repeat the same errors due to prior negative experiences, like making embarrassing remarks or feeling inadequate during workouts.

In contrast, those who embrace new experiences frequently create lasting achievements. Winston Churchill exemplifies this approach. His path to becoming Prime Minister was marked by repeated setbacks, yet his persistence led to eventual success. Figures like Churchill treat failures as lessons, refining ideas, actions, and decisions through trial and error. They are proud not of their mistakes, but of the lessons learned and the growth from each failure. While they might occasionally repeat errors, they ultimately emerge victorious by applying new insights.

Enthusiasm drives people toward their goals, whether it’s protecting a nation during wartime, mastering a musical instrument, or nurturing a family. The level of enthusiasm depends on the individual, not the goal’s size. A person determined to become president must possess similar commitment as someone striving to exercise regularly. Short-term or long-term objectives alike require sustained motivation, which can either weaken after failure or grow stronger from it.

Consider my experience learning to dual-wield nunchakus. As a right-handed person, mastering the left-handed movements was painful. My forearms turned red from constant practice, and many questioned my persistence. I persevered because of my strong enthusiasm for mastering the skill. After months of training, I succeeded, though I’m still not an expert. Now I can avoid hitting myself, which proves the value of consistent effort.

Those who repeatedly face failure sometimes reach dangerous limits, even risking death. While most failures don’t have fatal consequences, they can still limit one’s abilities. Conversely, tragedies sometimes strengthen resilience. One boy, passionate about cycling, lost his leg in a severe accident. Despite months in a wheelchair, he refused to give up after rehabilitation. He returned to riding, reclaiming his passion and proving that determination can overcome even the toughest setbacks.

In conclusion, I agree with Churchill’s perspective: failure is essential for growth, and enthusiasm fuels progress. We must persist—not just until we succeed, but until failure becomes impossible. Whether we choose comfort or challenge, the key lies in maintaining unwavering passion for our goals.

Many students will gain advantages from learning at home because they may face situations that make attending school difficult. Some individuals prefer the comfort of their own environment, especially if they feel uncomfortable in a crowded or social setting. While I personally would choose to attend school to meet new people and build connections, I recognize that remote learning can be a beneficial option for others.

The first point is that students might choose home-based classes due to personal concerns about interacting with others. They could believe that classmates behave poorly or disrespectfully, leading to anxiety. Parents might also worry about negative peer influences or fear their child will be treated unfairly. Additionally, students with health issues may avoid public stigma and feel safer learning privately.

The second reason relates to the desire to avoid daily school routines. Some learners feel self-conscious or fear judgment from others, which can discourage attendance. When students face embarrassment or past negative experiences at school, staying home allows them to study without external pressure.

Finally, if forced to decide between these options, I would still support attending school. Direct interaction helps students understand the value of learning together and receiving guidance from teachers. It also enables them to address bullying and reassure peers that seeking help is normal rather than shameful.

In conclusion, offering online classes gives students flexibility in managing their education. Though outcomes depend on individual circumstances, autonomy in choosing a learning style can reduce external stress. It is important, however, not to let others’ opinions limit personal growth.

There is a great deal of responsibility in our world that requires individuals to face numerous obstacles. The city council is currently considering implementing a weekday curfew at 10 p.m. and a midnight curfew for teenagers. I acknowledge your concern, but I strongly oppose this proposal for several reasons.

Firstly, many teens have commitments after school, such as part-time employment or extracurricular activities, which often extend into the evening hours. Others may simply face heavy traffic that delays their return home. While I recognize that driving late at night is risky due to fatigue and reduced alertness, it is unfair to assume that teens lack the ability to handle these challenges. In fact, teenagers frequently stay awake for longer periods, not out of boredom, but because they need to manage work, sports, or other essential tasks. We are capable of maintaining focus and can operate responsibly on the road, even after late hours.

In addition, imposing an early curfew overlooks the fact that many teens are aware of the dangers of nighttime driving. The real threats come from intoxicated drivers and unpredictable wildlife, such as deer, that are more active after midnight. There is also the risk of encountering unsafe individuals on the road. As experienced drivers, we understand these hazards and take steps to stay safe, including remaining cautious and limiting exposure to hazardous situations.

I believe that enforcing a curfew before 12 a.m. would unnecessarily restrict teen mobility, particularly when they are engaged in legitimate activities. Our decision to stay up late is driven by necessity, not neglect, and we exercise caution to mitigate the risks associated with night-time travel. I hope the council will consider these points and recognize the importance of allowing teens to manage their responsibilities without undue restriction.

In this paper, I will argue why people should believe failing in life is so important. Because if you fail at least one thing, it helps you become more confident and prepares you for the real world. It also helps you realize that if you want something, you have to fight for it.

However, that year was different—the teacher told my mom how amazing I was in math and other subjects. I’m happy I failed first grade because it showed me that failing once doesn’t mean I have to give up. I had to fight back, which I did.

I always tell myself, "You have to fight back. Never give up on your dreams, no matter how difficult they are." When I was a kid, my dream was to become a lawyer. One time in school, we had to say what we wanted to be when we grow up, and I said I wanted to be a lawyer. One student told me, "How could you be a lawyer? You’ll never complete that career." I told him, "You never know." I know I’ll be a lawyer because if you don’t fight back for your dreams, you are a failure. I’m not a failure person. I don’t allow others to tell me that I’ll never make it.

If you fail one time or more, it doesn’t mean you’ll never succeed. It’s the opposite. At 18 years old, I’ve failed many times, but I always kept this in mind: I learn a new lesson each time. Every failure I’ve had I took as a lesson to help prepare for the real world and how it works.

Some people may think I’m wrong to think like this, but they’re the wrong ones because no one is perfect in life. Everyone makes mistakes or fails at something.

To be a successful person in life, you have to take steps one at a time. No matter how many times you fail, keep going. You’re going to make it, don’t let others tell you exactly what to do.

In the future, I hope people never give up on their dreams just because they failed once or more. I also want to show people who say, "You’ll never make it," that you can do it all by yourself.

When considering whether failure is essential for life success, I firmly believe that experiencing setbacks is crucial. Many people doubt this, but I will explain why embracing failure builds confidence, prepares individuals for real-world challenges, and motivates them to fight for their goals.

My mother often told me, “Stay confident; I believe in you.” In first grade, a teacher informed her I was struggling in math and might fail the class. I did, but my mother reassured me, explaining that failure doesn’t reflect intelligence—it highlights difficulty. She emphasized I could overcome it, and I proved her right the following year. Though I retook first grade, the teacher praised my progress, demonstrating that initial failure wasn’t final. This taught me resilience: one setback doesn’t define your future, but how you respond does.

As a child, my dream was to become a lawyer. When classmates doubted me, I refused to accept their negativity. I told myself, “You must fight back,” believing quitting would label me a failure. Their skepticism mattered less than my determination. I understood that giving up erases possibility, while persistence keeps dreams alive.

In my 18 years, I’ve faced numerous failures, but each taught me valuable lessons. Mistakes became stepping stones, sharpening my readiness for adulthood’s realities. Some might dismiss this view, insisting failure signals inadequacy, but perfection doesn’t exist. Everyone stumbles; the key is learning and moving forward.

True success requires incremental progress and relentless effort, regardless of how many times you fall. Let others doubt—your journey belongs to you. Future generations should remember that one failure isn’t defeat but a chance to rebuild stronger. Prove critics wrong by chasing goals despite obstacles. Failure, when embraced, fuels growth far more than fear ever could.

Mastering a specific domain is undeniably impressive, as it reflects deep experience and confidence in one's actions. While expertise carries both benefits and drawbacks, I maintain a perspective that differs from Emerson's assertion that mastery entails stagnation. 

Contrary to Emerson's view, I believe that even when someone achieves mastery, personal and professional growth remains continuous. Daily life offers new insights, especially through recognizing mistakes and learning from broader life lessons, which often enhance skills across all areas. However, this stance is likely to face opposition, as some individuals may hold rigid beliefs about expertise or prioritize alternative philosophies.

Commitment to a goal demands ongoing development because it shapes long-term aspirations and potential fulfillment. Poorly chosen pursuits can lead to future regret or frustration, wasting significant time and effort. Thus, careful consideration of one’s objectives is essential before dedicating oneself fully.

The advantages of mastery are significant: expertise grants autonomy, as others rarely need to direct your work. Tasks become more efficient and effortless, fostering a sense of accomplishment and excitement. Opportunities for high-value roles, financial rewards, and entrepreneurial independence are more accessible. Nevertheless, challenges exist—intense competition requires continuous effort to outperform rivals and maintain standards. Errors in business ventures, for instance, must be addressed swiftly to preserve reputation and competence.

In conclusion, mastery does not preclude growth. Mistakes, rather than hindering progress, can fuel new achievements. Stagnation in personal and skill development is avoidable through persistent self-improvement and adaptation. Remaining in a current role does not preclude striving for greater proficiency each day.

I am convinced that technology should be restricted in numerous settings. Firstly, devices often contribute to mental health problems and widespread addiction. Smartphones, in particular, can harm users in severe ways. For instance, staring at screens excessively damages vision over time, and over-reliance on digital tools may impair people’s judgment.

In residential environments, technology frequently causes domestic tension. Children’s excessive screen time fuels family conflicts, and devices are commonly misused to harass others or share unsuitable content such as invasive photos. Additionally, prolonged use of gadgets leads to anxiety and sleep disturbances.

Educational institutions require limits as well. Allowing unrestricted access to technology enables cheating, reduces students’ ability to write manually, and increases opportunities for bullying. Moreover, the constant presence of devices divides attention during lessons, hindering academic progress.

Public spaces also suffer from tech-related dangers. Drivers distracted by phones cause accidents, while financial fraud through hacking or phishing targets personal accounts. Data breaches further endanger privacy, as hackers exploit personal information for harmful purposes.

In summary, technology’s rapid advancement exacerbates addiction and risks. Overuse damages health, strains relationships, and fosters unethical behavior, necessitating stronger controls to protect well-being.

Honestly, honesty isn’t always easy or always difficult—it depends on the situation. When we make a mistake, we often feel guilty, and admitting it helps lift that weight off our minds. Express your words with genuine respect and love; this shows you value their feelings and your relationship. Over time, this habit fosters deeper trust and connection.

I believe implementing a curfew for teenagers could be beneficial, and here’s why. Firstly, during the week, young people attend school most days unless it’s a holiday or they’re unwell. Having them return home early reduces the likelihood of them wandering the streets late at night, which is unnecessary in the first place. Secondly, being indoors by 10 p.m. on weekdays helps keep individuals out of dangerous situations. Fewer young people would be exposed to nighttime criminal activity, lowering the risk of harm from offenders. Late hours are often associated with heightened crime rates, so earlier curfews could decrease such incidents. Thirdly, drug availability is a major concern. If teens must be home by a certain time, their opportunities to encounter dealers and experiment with substances would diminish significantly.

If such a law were introduced, the schedule could be reasonable: weekdays from 10 p.m. and weekends until midnight. Beyond these hours, anyone out should have a compelling reason, such as an emergency. This framework would likely steer teens away from unnecessary trouble. The curfew isn’t unreasonable—it’s a fair window that balances safety with freedom. No one is barred from going out entirely, just from staying out excessively. I’d support extending this to adults over 18 too, since many in that age group enjoy nightlife. However, the primary focus should be those under 18, as they’re still learning responsibility and need more guidance on what’s permissible.

This policy isn’t meant to punish but to enhance community safety. If teens are breaking rules, curfews alone won’t fix their behavior, but they might prevent harm. After-school activities remain unaffected, giving youths opportunities to engage safely. Exceptions exist—like attending a party—yet limits must apply to avoid misuse. Penalties should start with warnings and escalate if rules are ignored repeatedly.

My stance acknowledges that some oppose curfews, arguing teens know right from wrong. While I understand their concerns, I also recognize the reality that many still make poor choices. The law doesn’t stop socializing; it simply reduces exposure to street risks. It’s a tool to protect vulnerable individuals without stifling freedom entirely. Teens might lose sleepovers or face strict deadlines at parties, but the trade-off is safety. Being caught staying out past curfew could lead to legal consequences, such as records affecting college applications. A poor academic record paired with legal issues might deter universities, even for high-achieving students. This weighty downside must be weighed against potential risks.

Current restrictions include driving curfews, which limit late-night road use for minors. While there are pros and cons to expanding curfews, the advantages outweigh the drawbacks. The only downside I foresee is legal repercussions for those caught breaking the rule. Overall, extending curfews nationwide could save lives, deter crimes like abduction or assault, and keep teens from unnecessary danger. It’s a measure worth serious consideration for broader implementation.

Changing school lunches to healthier options won’t have a meaningful impact. Despite long-standing efforts, many schools still serve unbalanced meals, and students’ attempts to influence the menu often fail. For instance, a cafeteria might offer pizza alongside rice and grilled chicken, yet most students still gravitate toward pizza.  

While it’s important for schools to promote better eating habits, it’s equally crucial to recognize that many students skip meals entirely, neglecting nutrition throughout the day. A realistic improvement would involve eliminating less nutritious items like pizza, hot dogs, and chicken nuggets. These could be replaced with options such as baked potatoes, vegetable pasta salads, or plant-based alternatives for vegans, like veggie burgers. However, schools should prioritize cost-effective changes—spending resources on upgrading facilities like floors seems impractical when funds could instead enhance meal quality.  

Complaints about poor-quality lunches are common, but students rarely act on them by bringing homemade food. This suggests a resigned acceptance of the status quo. Though occasional healthy dishes appear, they are not transformative solutions. To address this, students would be better off preparing meals at home, avoiding reliance on inconsistent school menus. Reforming lunch programs requires strategic planning, not superficial changes, and students’ autonomy in their food choices remains the simplest solution.

Manners play an important role in everyday interactions. When people respond politely with phrases like "thank you" or "you're welcome," it creates a positive cycle of respect. Being courteous and expressing gratitude encourages others to mirror those behaviors. Small gestures, such as acknowledging someone's help or offering a friendly smile, can lift their mood and strengthen relationships.

If you approach others with kindness and use polite language, they are more likely to respond similarly. For instance, if you greet someone with "hello" or show appreciation, they might return the gesture. Simple words like "yes, sir" or "thank you" can make a difference, especially if you hope to receive the same courtesy in return. Practicing these habits consistently builds mutual respect and trust.

Positivity also helps in making new connections. When you thank someone who assists you or share encouraging words, you not only brighten their day but also leave a lasting impression. Expressing gratitude in daily situations—whether it’s holding a door or offering help—reinforces the value of good manners. Everyone benefits when kindness becomes a shared norm.

Even in challenging moments, maintaining politeness matters. If a mistake occurs, apologizing sincerely and offering a kind remark can restore harmony. Demonstrating respect in conversations or transactions ensures others feel valued. For example, asking a cashier how their day is going or thanking them for their service creates a supportive atmosphere. These actions reflect your character and encourage reciprocity.

Acts of kindness extend beyond verbal cues. Offering assistance, such as picking up an item someone dropped, or leaving a generous tip at a restaurant, shows appreciation for their efforts. Similarly, if a coworker seems stressed, asking if they'd like a break or sharing a small treat can make a meaningful difference. These gestures reinforce the importance of treating others well.

In summary, manners and kindness create a ripple effect. They foster goodwill, improve interactions, and make communities more pleasant. By consistently practicing courtesy and empathy, we encourage others to adopt the same values. Remember, showing respect doesn’t just benefit the recipient—it enriches your own relationships and contributes to a more compassionate world.

Self-confidence and achievements often seem tied together, but the question remains: which comes first? While some argue that praise and success build confidence, my belief is that confidence must precede achievement. Without it, even well-meaning efforts fall short. Let’s explore this idea through daily experiences and broader life lessons.

Firstly, confidence drives consistent effort and learning. Consider a doctor who continually updates their knowledge to tackle emerging diseases. Their self-assurance allows them to embrace challenges without hesitation. Similarly, someone learning a second language, like Spanish for an English speaker, faces hurdles such as nuanced vocabulary differences. Fluency takes years of practice, yet confidence sustains the journey. A native speaker might never master their own language entirely, but knowing progress is possible keeps motivation alive. Without that initial belief in oneself, even routine tasks feel insurmountable.

Secondly, positive self-regard is crucial for completing goals. Think of exam periods: procrastination and anxiety can derail even the most prepared student. Yet, those who attend classes daily, despite feeling unprepared, often find clarity under pressure. Their confidence prevents panic from clouding judgment, turning anxiety into productive focus. Conversely, hesitation breeds procrastination, while self-trust transforms uncertainty into actionable steps.

Thirdly, confidence helps manage fears of the unknown. Job interviews, for instance, require boldness when facing unfamiliar environments. Self-doubt can paralyze, but believing in one’s abilities overrides uncertainty. Employers seek candidates who project certainty—not perfection—because they understand adaptability is key. Without confidence, opportunities shrink, as fear overshadows potential.

Others claim achievement breeds confidence, suggesting success naturally uplifts self-esteem. For example, passing a standardized test after months of study can feel validating. Yet, failure in repeated attempts does not negate confidence entirely. Even when setbacks occur, resilience rooted in self-belief can lead to eventual triumph. Moreover, confidence gained from prior accomplishments fuels new challenges, creating a cycle of growth.

Ultimately, confidence is the spark that ignites action. It enables people to pursue goals despite obstacles and reinterpret failures as lessons. Praise or accolades may follow achievement, but the courage to start—to face uncertainty—comes from within. Cultivating self-trust, not waiting for external validation, is the surest path to lasting success. My advice? Embrace confidence as your foundation; let it guide you beyond fear into possibility.

It’s widely accepted that limiting teenagers’ exposure to late-night environments can benefit them in several key areas. Introducing curfew rules that require young people to remain indoors after 10 p.m. could positively affect their school performance, social interactions, health, and financial stability.

First, such curfews would support academic success. When teens aren’t roaming outside at night, they can secure more restful sleep, leading to better concentration during lessons. Without late-night outings, they also have additional time to study at home, which often results in improved homework completion and higher test scores. Over time, this structured evening routine fosters stronger learning habits and overall academic achievement.

Second, these rules would enhance social well-being. Many residents view night-time activity in public spaces as risky, assuming teens might associate with delinquent groups. By staying home during evening hours, teenagers avoid negative stereotypes and are more likely to build trusting relationships. Their efforts to engage in positive home-based activities—such as studying or hobbies—make them appear reliable and approachable, fostering smoother interactions with neighbors and peers.

Third, medical benefits arise from reduced exposure to hazardous situations. Nighttime streets often pose dangers, including potential conflicts with others who might misinterpret a teen’s presence as threatening. By being indoors, young people minimize the risk of physical altercations and injuries that could require urgent medical care, ensuring safer, healthier lives.

Finally, economic advantages emerge from redirecting energy toward productive pursuits. For instance, a teen who avoids late-night wandering might seek after-hours employment, earning money while staying away from unsupervised street activity. This combination of work and curfew compliance helps build financial independence, allowing savings for future needs and reducing reliance on risky, unproductive behaviors that waste time and resources.

In summary, enforcing curfews after 10 p.m. supports teenagers’ development across academic, social, health, and economic dimensions. Such regulations encourage disciplined lifestyles, protect against street-related dangers, and create pathways for growth without introducing harmful risks.

Failure is an essential part of learning, as Winston Churchill emphasized when he stated that success comes from moving through setbacks with persistent energy. Personal experience shows that repeated attempts build the resilience needed to reach goals. Everyone encounters obstacles, and without them, achievement feels hollow. A single setback does not ruin a person’s chances; instead, it offers a chance to rethink strategies and keep striving.

The first lesson came after I scored poorly on a world history test. The initial reaction was frustration, wondering if I could ever improve. Looking at the graded paper later helped identify the problem: I had misread some questions. From that moment, I made it a habit to read each question carefully before responding. Even when time felt tight, pausing to review the prompt made a difference. Guessing without understanding the context often led to mistakes, so I committed to reviewing material each night. This change turned future results around, eventually earning the top score in the class.

Another valuable insight was that effort matters in every subject, no matter how challenging. My mother saw my first exam result and urged me to keep working harder. Although I doubted myself, her belief encouraged me to attend extra help sessions and focus during lessons. This approach helped me grasp both exam content and everyday assignments. By staying attentive, I not only passed the final test but also developed a deeper grasp of the material.

Finally, repeated attempts teach that initial results are not permanent. Crying after another low score, I learned that failure is not a sign of low ability but a signal to adjust methods. My mother shared her own history of early academic struggles, explaining how perseverance eventually led to success. She reminded me that progress builds over time, even if results seem slow. After months of dedicated study and practice, I retook the same test and passed, proving that effort can overcome setbacks.

Some argue that success can happen without failure, suggesting shortcuts or effortless achievement. Yet this view ignores how much growth depends on confronting mistakes. Without challenges, opportunities to refine skills disappear. Each failure strengthens the drive to keep going. When you stumble, it does not mean defeat—instead, it calls for renewed focus. Over time, these efforts accumulate into meaningful progress, showing that setbacks are stepping stones, not roadblocks, to lasting accomplishment.

A career decision at a young age

Many societies expect students to choose a career path early, often before they enter high school. The question is whether forcing young students to commit to a specific career is beneficial. I believe that identifying a career early can be advantageous, especially for those pursuing long-term professions such as medicine, law, education, or social work.

Early specialization allows students to build foundational skills and knowledge. For example, future doctors who begin studying biology in middle school are better prepared for medical school later. Similarly, aspiring teachers who explore education early develop a stronger teaching philosophy. Starting young also increases the chances of accessing scholarships, internships, and advanced programs that enhance career readiness. A young engineer who begins robotics clubs at school gains hands-on experience that older peers might miss. These opportunities create a competitive edge and strengthen the nation’s workforce.

However, there are drawbacks. Young students may lack the maturity to evaluate their interests fully, leading to regret if their passion changes later. They might also become overwhelmed by academic demands, losing motivation over time. For instance, a high school student who chooses business but later discovers a love for music may struggle to pivot without additional effort. Early burnout is a risk, as excessive focus on one subject can reduce overall curiosity.

In conclusion, early career decisions are worthwhile if supported properly. Schools and counselors should guide students through assessments and exploratory programs to ensure choices align with their strengths. Encouraging flexibility, mentorship, and access to diverse experiences helps young individuals make informed decisions. When backed by careful guidance, committing to a career path early can lead to both personal fulfillment and societal benefit.

Schools Should Not Dictate Students’ After‑School Activities

Extracurricular involvement is a point of debate in many schools. Some argue that institutions should supervise what students do outside the classroom, claiming it promotes better learning. I, however, believe students should choose how they spend their free time after lessons.

The first reason is that some learners need to work to support their families. Many families depend on their children’s earnings to cover basic needs. Working students often lack energy for studying, finding it hard to focus on homework or exam preparation. A dedicated study session might assist with assignments, but jobs still eat into precious after‑school hours, limiting chances for clubs or sports. Nonetheless, part‑time jobs teach responsibility and financial planning, skills that help in college planning. Because of this, pupils must sometimes skip hobbies they enjoy to meet their obligations.

Another group must return home early to care for younger siblings while parents are busy. Without affordable childcare, these students handle cooking, cleaning, and basic supervision. They could join a club on days when a parent is home, yet juggling chores and schoolwork leaves little room for such pursuits. Homework and household tasks can overwhelm them, and the pressure to manage both equally can affect their academic performance.

Finally, there are students who simply wish to pursue interests such as sport or the arts. Many attend basketball, baseball, gymnastics, painting, or language clubs regularly. These activities are enjoyable and can develop talent. When learners choose their own clubs, they feel more motivated and in control of their personal growth. Schools guiding them toward specific tasks could discourage genuine enthusiasm.

In summary, forcing school control over after‑school life disregards individual needs. Recognizing each student’s circumstances encourages mutual understanding. When society acknowledges the diverse challenges faced by learners, we become more compassionate and better equipped to support one another’s goals.

Mixed-age programs in schools often pair older and younger students to share support. I will explain three ways this setup benefits both groups.  

Firstly, younger learners gain valuable assistance from older peers who possess more knowledge. As the initiative grows, it encourages students to join in, creating study groups where individuals focus on specific tasks. This collaboration fosters engagement and mutual respect as participants explore new ways to learn together.  

Secondly, the program helps struggling students by supplying academic resources. Older participants may donate materials like binders, books, or writing tools, while younger ones can organize fundraisers—selling food or homemade items—to fund supplies. This shared effort teaches responsibility and shows how teamwork solves practical problems.  

Finally, the program strengthens the school community. By working side by side, students build relationships that extend beyond classrooms, creating a supportive network for learning and growth. These connections benefit both teenagers and adults, proving that the initiative is a meaningful tool for student development and community building.  

In summary, intergenerational student partnerships improve academic support, resource sharing, and community ties. This system not only aids younger learners but also reinforces older students' skills, making it an essential part of education.

Ralph Waldo Emerson once claimed that "to be yourself in a world constantly trying to make you something else you’re not" represents the highest achievement. I disagree with this view because today many young people, including children and teenagers, gravitate toward friends who behave, speak, and act exactly alike. It’s unsettling, yet this reflects our society, where fitting in provides a sense of security and approval even when it isn’t necessary.  

Another reason for my disagreement is that the younger generation increasingly relies on technology rather than genuine human interaction. This dependency makes it harder for them to pursue individuality, as they often mimic trends instead of expressing personal desires. It’s astonishing how some feel compelled to conform just to appear smart, despite real intelligence being more than what a test score can measure. In my own case, I’m a student mimicking peers simply to earn a diploma—even though such a credential offers limited real-world value but is still viewed as impressive on resumes.  

Ultimately, I’m caught in this cycle to satisfy family expectations, who prioritize the diploma itself over my personal well-being. This highlights a broader issue: seeking external validation often overshadows the courage to be authentic, making Emerson’s ideal seem unrealistic in today’s culture.

Is it arduous to remain true to yourself in a world that urges you to become someone else?, ponder this?, we inhabit a sphere where conformity dominates, overshadowing authentic self-expression and joy. Moving forward, I aspire for systemic transformation, believing agency persists. May emerging generations possess the audacity to reshape the world into a compassionate, harmonious realm.

It’s hard to be yourself in a world that tries to make you something else.  
Think about it: we live on this world, trying to be like everyone else, instead of just being ourselves and living happily.  

In this paper, I will argue about how the world is trying to change us day by day, how we get influenced by it, and end up changing, and how every year that goes by our generation gets worse and worse.  

The world tries to find a way to make us change every day.  
We as humans have stopped and thought about what we want for our future.  
Why would I want to be like everyone else?  
Do I want to be a wealthy person in this society?  
Do I want to accomplish all my goals?  

Those are the types of questions that we should ask ourselves and think deeply about.  
Where will we end up in the future by following the steps of the rest of the world?  

Because in this world, if you want success, you have to be yourself.  
The world is not going to do it for you.  

We get very influenced by the world on our activities, the way we talk, the way we dress, the clothes we use, our religion, and a lot of stuff.  
If we don’t like or don’t do these things, we are not cool for the world.  

A good example is the clothes we wear.  
If we don’t use clothes and shoes that are trending or popular right now, we are not cool for society.  

Maybe the reason we don’t use them is because we don’t have money, time, or access to buy them.  
Or maybe we simply don’t like them.  

For the world, this means we are not cool or cute.  
Because we don’t wear certain clothes.  

It shouldn’t be like that, though.  
Some people get bullied by this, and some even end up depressed because they can’t afford them.  
It’s very sad to know that this world is like this.  

Sadly, every year that goes by, our generation gets worse and worse.  
The reason is the world influencing us in such a bad way.  

All the new drugs that are killing people, the wars between countries, and the new artists who sing about drugs, killing people, and sex are bad influences on our generation.  

If we don’t start being our own selves and doing the right things, eventually we are going to end up really bad.  

Some people say that this world is bad and only gives us bad influence, but they’re not right.  
It’s not necessarily the world’s fault—it could be us letting ourselves get involved or influenced by bad stuff, then saying it’s the world’s fault when it’s really our fault for getting involved in bad stuff overall.  

In the future, I hope this world changes because we still have time to do it, and it’s not impossible.  
I just hope that the coming-up generation has the courage to change the world and make it a good, friendly world.

Being your own authentic self in a world that pushes you toward conformity can feel challenging. This essay will examine how societal pressures shape our identities, why this influence matters, and how each passing year seems to intensify these struggles for my generation.

Every day, society attempts to mold individuals into its idea of perfection. We often pause to question: what do we truly desire for our future? Would we rather follow the crowd and accumulate wealth, or embrace individuality? Asking ourselves these questions helps clarify our paths. In reality, success rarely follows a cookie‑cutter model—true fulfillment usually comes from defining personal goals rather than mimicking others. The danger lies in passively adopting others' ambitions, which can lead us far from our genuine aspirations.

We absorb countless external cues—from popular trends to media portrayals. These influences affect our speech, appearance, beliefs, and even financial decisions. For instance, fashion trends dominate social approval: if your wardrobe doesn't align with the latest styles, you may feel judged. Reasons for this exclusion vary—limited funds, time constraints, or personal taste. Yet society often equates not following trends with being unattractive or unsuccessful, fueling exclusion and bullying. Such pressure can push vulnerable individuals toward depression, illustrating a harsh reality: self‑worth should never hinge on external validation.

Over time, the stakes appear to grow. Societal norms increasingly tolerate harmful behaviors—whether through drug abuse, violent conflicts, or artists glorifying destructive lifestyles. These influences can corrupt impressionable minds, steering them toward risky choices. Without asserting personal agency, this path risks escalating into serious consequences, both personally and collectively.

Some blame society entirely, overlooking personal responsibility. While external forces play a role, it's our willingness to engage with them that determines the outcome. Proactively avoiding harmful influences is crucial to safeguarding well‑being.

In conclusion, I hope future generations will reclaim autonomy. While change may seem daunting, collective courage could reshape this world into one that celebrates individuality. The key lies in choosing authenticity now, before the cycle of external pressure becomes irreversible.

Would you rather ask one person or multiple for advice  

I believe that consulting multiple individuals for guidance yields more substantial benefits. At one point, I encountered a quote by LeBron James asserting that, if you need counsel, always seek more than one perspective—because while one may be correct, another might not. Thus, there is no justification for avoiding additional sources; indeed, approaching someone you admire for advice can prove highly advantageous.  

If you are reluctant to engage with others, you may choose to solicit input from a single confidant or explore alternative methods altogether. Should you prefer a singular source, select someone whose reliability ensures they can offer constructive feedback and valuable insights. In my own experience, I would turn to a deeply wise figure who consistently makes prudent decisions, thereby enabling me to emulate their thoughtfulness and avoid imprudent judgments. Ensuring you approach a reputable advisor is crucial, as unfavorable guidance can precipitate poor choices.  

Obtaining counsel from a single individual can also be advantageous—particularly when sharing confidential details. A lone confidant may preserve privacy, whereas divulging personal matters to several parties risks unintended exposure, potentially leading to rumors and eroded trust. Consequently, for sensitive information, confiding in one person might be essential. If you distrust others, you might opt for your counselor, whose confidentiality ensures she will neither disseminate your disclosures nor critically misunderstand your circumstances. Reflecting on her own past experiences, she may demonstrate unparalleled empathy.  

Remember, seeking advice—whether from one or many—can prove invaluable. Nevertheless, if you consult someone whose decisions are unethical, their counsel could encourage harmful behavior, steering you toward regrettable outcomes. Good advice possesses the power to transform lives profoundly.

It is a common belief that changing one's mindset is nearly impossible. While some argue that altering deep-seated beliefs is too difficult, I disagree. A fixed mindset can evolve through intentional effort, leading to greater success and personal growth.

Humans constantly face life changes, which offer chances to refine objectives and pursue better futures. Those who resist change often cite obstacles, yet no change is ever completely blocked. Even when transformations appear challenging, they open doors to fresh possibilities. Avoiding starting points due to fear of failure is counterproductive; instead, viewing transitions as opportunities to enhance skills and pursue dreams is more effective. Personally, shifting to a growth-oriented mindset has helped me set new ambitions, boost self-confidence, and develop resilience. This approach has broadened my horizons and renewed my determination to achieve goals.

The chance for transformation extends throughout life, offering pathways to expand knowledge and apply skills. For instance, embracing technological advancements in various fields can reshape careers, encourage creativity, and foster innovation. Each day brings new ways to learn and build projects that benefit society. This continuous learning process builds expertise and adaptability in any profession.

Focusing on future aspirations requires refining strategies and refining existing plans. By addressing shortcomings and applying lessons from past errors, individuals can strengthen their self-development. Many neglect their goals due to repeated mistakes, but understanding and correcting these flaws is key. Regularly reflecting on personal growth and adjusting methods ensures steady progress toward ambitions.

Creating actionable plans enhances the ability to turn ideas into reality. Mapping out achievable steps, acquiring relevant skills, and executing projects systematically turns abstract goals into tangible outcomes. This structured approach also supports financial stability and professional growth, allowing individuals to contribute meaningfully to their communities and families. Over time, consistent improvement builds credibility and opens doors to new opportunities.

In summary, changing perspectives is achievable through persistent effort and adaptability. Though challenging, shifting mindsets unlocks potential for success, creativity, and lasting fulfillment. Embracing transformation is essential for realizing personal aspirations and enriching future prospects.

This trial-and-error process cultivates resilience, unlike those who abandon challenges at the first setback. Society rewards persistence; skipping effort limits potential.

Additionally, pursuing new goals unlocks more opportunities. In today’s world, our achievements influence our opportunities and privileges. Suppose my objective is to become a police officer. Once I reach that milestone, aiming higher—like advancing to a leadership role—would boost my skills and status economically, physically, and mentally. Mastery of new goals fuels simultaneous growth.

"The more we learn, the more we know,  
and the more we know, the more we grow."  
It’s never too late to keep evolving.

It stands for Junior Reserve Officers’ Training Corps and offers practical insights into the armed forces, including physical training, public speaking, and basic command structures.

Another class that aligns with my future ambitions is Economics. While it’s a standard high school requirement, I appreciate how it teaches financial literacy, budgeting, and market principles—knowledge that will be useful throughout military service and beyond. 

Without early career planning, many individuals risk struggling to find meaningful work after graduation. For instance, my mother wanted to become an artist but dropped out of her art program due to financial pressures and the lack of arts education at her former school. Since everyone must eventually work, it makes sense to begin exploring career options in high school. By taking JROTC and Economics, I am laying a foundation for my future as a Marine. These courses not only fulfill graduation requirements but also equip me with the tools needed to succeed in my chosen field.

When I worked at Mango Paradise, my supervisor was an exceptionally bitter individual who constantly directed anger toward staff. Despite his demeanor, I cared little about his negativity and always greeted colleagues with a cheerful smile, perhaps softening how he interacted with us. One day, he experienced heightened distress when a family member required hospitalization; his demeanor shifted, becoming visibly sorrowful, deeply shaken, and overwhelmed due to his wife’s cancer diagnosis. I approached him during that period, requesting to converse; he consented. I intended to express empathy and assure him of our unwavering support through every need. Unfortunately, his wife passed away, and as I had assured him, we remained by his side, reinforcing positivity by reminding him his wife would find peace, free from suffering. He deeply appreciated our compassion during that crisis, subsequently proposing a salary increase; although many accepted, several declined. He fundamentally transformed thereafter—many of us continued working there and began earning beyond our regular salaries.

Every human life encounters challenges that prompt surrender, yet individuals with a positive outlook spur perseverance and life continuity. In my family, financial hardship arose when my father was terminated from his position, threatening eviction due to unpaid rent over nearly four months. He felt profound despair, frantically seeking employment for approximately three months without success, fearing loss of our home. My mother, like most devoted partners, comforted him, saying, “Don’t worry, sweetheart; we’ll resolve this as we always have. I’m here to support you.” Instantly, his demeanor brightened, he thanked her for unwavering trust, retrieved car keys, and embarked on job searches. He secured new employment yielding slightly higher income, resolving our monetary crisis.

During tenth grade, my algebra instructor repeatedly urged us to trust in ourselves. Initially, confusion often led us to neglect her guidance, disappointing ourselves for failing to attempt problems. In the first quarter, many students in our class scored poorly. We assumed our grades would remain stagnant. Following her interventions, some pupils altered their mindsets—though not voluntarily—her dialogues instilled belief that we could accomplish any goal. Later, as our attitudes shifted, she too evolved. By the second quarter, students celebrated improved scores ranging from 50 to 90, attributable to varying changes in perspective. We focused more attentively, embraced tasks beyond our initial knowledge, and credited her influence. Even when we sometimes angered her by doubting ourselves, her persistent encouragement guided our growth. She became, in my view, the most exemplary teacher and confidante—always supportive and instructive. Consequently, she remains a favorite among my peers and myself, demonstrating how positivity profoundly impacts life.

Schools now offer programs that allow students to attend classes online, and these can bring both benefits and drawbacks. The approach varies across schools—one may provide digital lessons while another prefers traditional face-to-face instruction, and not all students react the same way. Some learners appreciate the flexibility of online study, while others find it harder to stay motivated without direct supervision.  

Online classes let students progress at their own speed without waiting for peers to finish assignments. However, technical issues like weak internet connections can interrupt lessons, making it difficult to complete tasks on time. The lack of a shared classroom environment also means fewer opportunities to interact with classmates who are the same age, which can reduce motivation. Without physical group settings or immediate access to classmates, students might fall behind on assigned work.  

When studying remotely, figuring out complex topics alone can be stressful. Online resources sometimes provide inaccurate information, leading to mistakes on projects. While instructional videos are helpful, they may not cover every subject thoroughly. In contrast, asking a teacher in person during a lesson offers clearer explanations, increasing comprehension. The absence of a teacher during urgent questions can leave students struggling to meet deadlines. Procrastination is another risk: if students postpone assignments, believing they will finish them later, they often fail to submit work on time.  

Interaction with peers of similar age plays a key role in learning. Studying with friends fosters shared study habits and collaborative problem-solving. Online programs often limit such exchanges, as classmates may be enrolled in different courses or separated geographically. Socializing becomes harder when focused solely on coursework and a computer screen, reducing chances to build connections.  

A heavy workload in a single day can overwhelm students, especially if they don’t understand the material. Completing assignments on time is vital, but copying online sources instead of learning the content can harm progress. Procrastination or distractions might lead to rushed submissions, resulting in poor grades or incomplete courses.  

Schools aim to offer flexible attendance options, balancing convenience with structured learning. While online programs may free up time, some students misuse them by neglecting coursework. Unexpected personal challenges can also hinder online study if students lack guidance. Ultimately, online attendance suits some learners better than others—it depends on individual discipline and need for peer support. However, without proper motivation, technical access, or age-matched peers, achieving success online remains uncertain.

Homework clubs after school could greatly benefit students who find their assignments confusing or unclear. While some might argue homework is unimportant, it actually influences grades significantly, contributing up to 10% of a student’s overall score. A single missed assignment might seem small, but it can prevent students from mastering essential material needed for tests or quizzes. If a student fails to complete even one piece of work, it could have consequences, such as struggling on upcoming assessments.

Middle school students face heavy workloads, managing homework across seven or more subjects. With many teachers assigning two or three tasks per class, staying organized becomes challenging. Without extra support, it’s easy to fall behind. Homework clubs would give struggling learners a chance to clarify doubts with teachers, who can explain lessons in more detail. For those with busy schedules, staying after school one day a week could provide dedicated time to tackle all pending work.  

These clubs wouldn’t simply provide answers; they would teach problem-solving skills so students truly understand the content. Over time, this approach could boost grades, helping students move from B to A levels. Schools would also benefit, as completed homework improves academic performance and reflects positively on the institution. Teachers could see genuine effort rather than rushed submissions, while students who struggle with deadlines would gain consistency.

In conclusion, homework clubs address a widespread problem by reducing stress and enhancing comprehension. Students often neglect assignments, believing they don’t matter, but timely completion is crucial for success. After-school support would free up afternoon time for other activities, fostering both academic and personal growth. Implementing this system would make homework less daunting and encourage better habits across the school.

Achieving success often involves setbacks, and these moments should not be seen as reasons to doubt oneself. Winston Churchill famously remarked that "Success consists of going from failure to failure without loss of enthusiasm." I agree with this perspective because persistence is essential when pursuing goals. While immediate success is rare, continued effort despite challenges typically leads to eventual achievement.

Some might argue that success does not require constant failure—that failure itself is unnecessary for growth. However, real-world experience shows that even the most prepared individuals encounter obstacles, and each obstacle provides valuable lessons. Setbacks are natural parts of growth; they teach us what doesn't work and sharpen our resolve for the next attempt.

Maintaining enthusiasm is crucial, as losing interest midway through the process can halt progress entirely. Enthusiasm fuels patience and resilience, qualities that help individuals stay focused even when results are delayed. Failing repeatedly may initially feel discouraging, but adapting after each setback builds the determination needed to overcome future challenges.

Conversely, success often comes from those who actively pursue it rather than passively waiting for opportunities. Research indicates that many people avoid taking initiative, preferring comfort over effort, which limits their potential. Those who adopt a proactive mindset and treat failure as a learning tool, rather than a reflection of their abilities, are better positioned to succeed. A steadfast commitment to goals, paired with adaptability, creates a powerful foundation for achievement.

In summary, Churchill's view aligns with the reality that success frequently involves navigating multiple failures while preserving motivation. While failure alone does not guarantee success, the willingness to persist without losing drive is a defining characteristic of those who ultimately succeed.

For example, legal proceedings, occupational contexts, educational settings, or non-majority age thresholds may impose limitations on unilateral choices. These domains reflect constraints where decisions transcend individual purview.  

I contend that humanity ought to retain the privilege of self-directed choices, provided adherence to societal norms enables genuine lifeownership and accountability.  

Indeed, exercising free will to select courses of action—and owning their consequences—is vital. A flawed choice holds significance only insofar as it offers learning opportunities; occasional error is tolerable, and correct outcomes are gratifying. The crux lies in possessing the liberty to craft one's existence, embrace mistakes, and evolve.

If people worked 4 days a week with 10-hour shifts, it would be bad for their health and personal life. First, working 10 hours a day and 4 days a week leaves insufficient time to rest. Consequently, you would be tired, exhausted, and have a bad mood from lack of sleep. Second, personal life suffers because there would be no family time or opportunities to socialize with friends. Thus, I conclude that a 10-hour daily shift is not the best way to live.  

In terms of education, specifically schools, as a student, I would not be excited about attending class for 10 hours a day. The reason is that I have responsibilities outside, such as working, studying for school, and attending soccer training on weekends. Also, I would not be able to get a job by the time school ends during weekdays. I'm sure there are students like me who have obligations beyond school.  

Now, if I had to attend school 10 hours a day and 4 days a week, my learning would definitely suffer instead of improving. I would not be able to memorize everything because there would be too many topics to cover. As a human being, my brain and body need rest to retain information. In conclusion, whether at school or work, 10-hour days are not beneficial for professional and personal life. They can harm health and emotions, causing stress or bad moods. Moreover, they could disrupt personal life by preventing time to fulfill responsibilities outside work.

Conserving energy is essential, and one of the most effective ways to achieve this is by maintaining regular work hours. While working fewer days might seem appealing, increasing daily shifts to ten hours often does more harm than good. I disagree with this approach because it compromises health, personal well-being, and productivity.

Most traditional workplaces—such as offices, supermarkets, or service centers—operate on an eight-hour schedule. This structure allows employees to manage their workload while leaving adequate time for rest and personal activities. In contrast, a four-day workweek with ten-hour days would disrupt this balance. The extended daily hours leave little room for recovery, which can lead to fatigue, irritability, and long-term physical strain.

Beyond the workplace, this model would also negatively impact personal life. With limited free time, relationships and social commitments suffer. For students like myself, the situation becomes even more challenging. If classes or training sessions were stretched to ten hours over four days, balancing part-time jobs, sports, and academic responsibilities would become nearly impossible. Extended learning sessions reduce focus and retention, as the brain needs downtime to process information.

In summary, longer daily shifts do not foster efficiency or well-being. They increase stress and diminish quality of life, making them a poor substitute for healthier, sustainable routines. Maintaining standard hours supports both professional and personal growth better than extreme schedules.

Have you ever been pressured to pick a career path before finishing high school? I certainly have, and I believe young adults should take a gradual approach instead of making such a crucial life choice too early. Choosing a career isn't merely about the person or the timing—it's deeply personal. While deciding whether to pursue a career is optional for each student, rushing this decision often leads to regrets.

Firstly, I disagree with the notion that students should follow adults' career advice blindly. Many young people simply accept suggestions from teachers or family, only to end up in fields they neither enjoy nor excel in. This mismatch can destroy their confidence, drain their time, and even jeopardize their financial stability. For instance, a child pressured to become a doctor might lose interest in science over time, while one encouraged to become an architect could discover hidden talents in design. Positive role models—like supportive parents or mentors—can help teenagers explore options, but without guidance, many dismiss career possibilities altogether.

Secondly, expanding practical knowledge about workplaces is essential. Teenagers need exposure to real-world experiences: watching professionals share their daily routines or hearing stories from people who succeeded and others who struggled. Consider two scenarios: one person who completed a career-oriented program and earns a stable income, versus another who dropped out and faces hardship. Both examples show the importance of preparation. Jobs aren't always glamorous—whether it's construction in extreme weather or office work, challenges exist regardless of the profession. Understanding these realities helps young people make informed choices aligned with their passions.

Finally, high school is the ideal time to explore interests. If someone loves drawing, architecture might suit them. Conversely, someone fascinated by engineering or biology could aim for tech or medical fields. Inspiration plays a key role—people like the famous architect of Dubai’s marvels demonstrate how creativity can shape extraordinary projects. However, many lack direction due to financial constraints or unstable family situations. Without opportunities to study or train, some opt to leave school early to work. This highlights the need for mentorship programs, apprenticeships, or career fairs that teach the value of education and alternative pathways. 

Ultimately, rushing career decisions harms more than it helps. Young adults should have the freedom to learn, fail, and rediscover themselves before committing to a lifelong path. Balancing exploration with practical support ensures they build futures they truly want.

Many believe that failing in life is harmful. This essay argues that failure, despite its challenges, can lead to success. Three common reactions people have to failure—sadness, maintaining enthusiasm, and self‑criticism—support this idea.

First, people often feel sad when they fail. They have tried their hardest, expecting to succeed, and may never have imagined such a result. Some even cry when they face disappointment.

Second, others stay motivated after their first setback. They see a positive outcome and believe they can avoid failure next time. This persistence helps them keep moving forward rather than giving up.

Third, some individuals become angry with themselves for small mistakes. Although this frustration seems negative, it actually drives learning. Reflecting on errors improves future performance.

Some argue that failure undermines success. However, those who do not lose enthusiasm after falling can achieve great results. They continue striving until they succeed, turning each failure into a lesson.

In conclusion, while failure can feel painful, it often opens the door to real progress. Those who manage their emotions wisely can use setbacks as stepping stones to success.

It is essential that they are allowed to select their own career paths rather than being pressured by family expectations. Many young people lack alternatives and are directed toward fields chosen by their parents, despite increasing recognition of teenagers' right to make their own educational decisions in recent decades. Guidance that encourages pursuing subjects they enjoy from an early age fosters continuous growth in their thinking abilities. This disparity motivates many to migrate to countries like the U.S., where education is seen as a pathway to stability and success. For example, twelve-year-olds from these nations arrive with ambitious aspirations, aiming to support their families and achieve professional prominence. However, rising populations in these countries make employment difficult regardless of qualifications, and some parents discourage schooling by asserting it won’t lead to meaningful outcomes. This erosion of youth ambition can contribute to social unrest, as seen in heightened tensions in multiple nations. Parents must recognize the value of education and support their children’s career goals rather than dismissing them.

Understanding future opportunities early has become critical in today’s world. While some adolescents globally neglect education, U.S. students benefit from robust systems that enhance their employability and overall well-being. Post-high school, their career trajectories are often already mapped out. They serve as role models for peers, securing stable jobs and demonstrating the benefits of proactive planning. Encouraging students to clarify their career interests before high school empowers them to maximize their learning during college and inspires others to value education. By prioritizing early career awareness, teenagers can achieve personal success while reinforcing the broader significance of skilled preparation and lifelong dedication.

Online education can offer advantages for students who face challenges with academic performance and tardiness caused by oversleeping or transportation issues. Traditional school attendance consumes significant time that could otherwise be dedicated to extracurricular interests such as sports or leisure activities at home.

I support the shift to online learning over physical attendance because many students find it easier to engage academically from the comfort of their homes. Those who struggle with irregular sleep patterns often miss early morning classes due to oversleeping, which can make school commutes difficult. Virtual classrooms typically allow flexible entry times, reducing stress and enabling students to log in when they're fully alert. This consistency helps maintain energy levels, improving concentration and participation during lessons. Similarly, illness-related absences are less disruptive online, as students can keep up with coursework without falling behind, thereby minimizing grade-related anxiety.

Another benefit is maintaining progress during travel or other commitments. With a laptop, learners can attend sessions remotely, ensuring fewer missed assignments compared to in-person classes where physical presence is mandatory.

Critics might highlight concerns about prolonged screen exposure and potential dishonesty during assessments. Extended focus on digital displays could cause eye fatigue, and monitoring online tests poses challenges. Nevertheless, these drawbacks don't outweigh the convenience and accessibility benefits that online education provides for students in specific circumstances.

Starting sooner would give them more time to pursue advanced degrees or gain work experience.

I believe this because life often presents challenges where perseverance is essential. Continuing to strive even after repeated disappointments usually leads to eventual achievement. Trusting in one's ability and working diligently increases the likelihood of reaching goals.

Others argue that success involves progressing through failures while experiencing discouragement. Some people claim that repeatedly attempting the same task, even without improvement, helps build expertise over time. While this mindset may encourage repeated efforts regardless of immediate results, it might lead to stagnation if progress feels unattainable.

A recurring debate exists between viewing success as moving from failure to failure with or without enthusiasm. Those preferring the latter avoid relentless repetition and seek reassurance, whereas others persist in repetitive attempts, convinced they will eventually succeed. Personal choice dictates which approach aligns with individual resilience and mindset.

In summary, both perspectives highlight valuable truths. Maintaining enthusiasm during repeated setbacks can drive growth, while accepting occasional discouragement may suit different personalities. Whether one remains passionate or adapts their approach, the key lies in how one navigates failures on the path to achievement.

While implementation requires careful planning, the potential to enhance retention and reduce repetitive instruction makes it a promising alternative.

Summer provides a lengthy hiatus for students, with a two‑month vacation that allows them to step away from classroom duties. Some educators argue that this break is too long and propose adopting a year‑round calendar, which would shorten the summer period and extend the winter recess. However, I maintain that keeping the traditional summer vacation is preferable because the season’s extreme heat makes learning uncomfortable, and students often use this time for family trips and personal pursuits.

First, the weather in summer is often unbearable. Temperatures frequently reach well above 35 °C, which can cause students to feel overheated, experience headaches, and become irritable. Such conditions diminish concentration and can lead to lower academic performance or conflicts in class. Moreover, students who work outdoors—such as those in agricultural or construction jobs—find it especially difficult to perform tasks effectively in the intense heat compared to milder climates. The discomfort hinders focus on studies and even on simple daily activities.

Second, the extended break is valuable for social and personal development. Families frequently plan trips to beaches, parks, or foreign destinations during these months, allowing students to spend quality time with loved ones. The freedom from school obligations also enables part‑time employment, providing an opportunity to earn money while gaining real‑world experience. These activities are best scheduled when academic demands are absent, as they require uninterrupted time and focus.

In conclusion, although summer’s heat poses challenges for learning, the season remains essential for relaxation, travel, and employment. Altering the schedule to shorten this break would deprive students of these benefits. Given that summer offers a unique, once‑a‑year chance to recharge, it deserves to stay intact as a well‑earned respite from the rigors of the school year.

Churchill, the former British prime minister, remarked that true success means moving through repeated setbacks without losing drive. This insight resonates with individuals pursuing aspirations.

If failure is viewed as a stepping stone toward achievement, it can inspire determination, foster reflection, and provide practical knowledge.
